    Catholic Science, Technology, Religion, Engineering, Arts, and Math

    Integrating Faith and Reason in STEM Education for K-6 Catholic Schools

    Our Lady of the Prairie Catholic School · Belle Plaine, MN

    Table of Contents

    C-STREAM Framework¶

    • Catholic · Science · Technology · Religion · Engineering · Arts · Math

      A local Catholic C-STREAM program integrating faith and reason, hands-on inquiry, responsible design and service.

      Quick Start Guide

    Welcome to C-STREAM¶

    2026-27 curriculum review

    Start with the curriculum review for verified sources, local standards, grade progression, lesson audits, low-tech materials and revised teaching plans. All 251 documents have complete written pathways; actual kit, school approval and classroom-pilot checks remain conditional. Local program standards are not official Archdiocesan or Minnesota standards.

    C-STREAM represents Catholic STEM education that intentionally weaves together faith and reason throughout every aspect of the curriculum. Rather than treating religion as a standalone subject, this framework integrates Catholic identity like "yeast that causes everything to rise."

    Our Vision

    "Science and faith are complementary – the beautiful harmony of faith and reason so students can be a light in the secular world."

    Lesson Time Frames by Grade¶

    Grade Level Session Length Notes
    Kindergarten 25 minutes Focus on wonder, exploration, simple hands-on activities
    Grades 1-2 30 minutes Guided exploration with structured activities
    Grades 3-4 40 minutes Independent work with collaboration opportunities
    Grades 5-6 45 minutes Complex projects, deeper investigation, student-led inquiry

    Scheduling Flexibility¶

    C-STREAM offers two scheduling options to fit your school's needs:

    Full curriculum for schools with STREAM every week.

    • Kindergarten
    • Grades 1-2 Year A | Year B
    • Grades 3-4 Year A | Year B
    • Grades 5-6 Year A | Year B

    Condensed curriculum for schools with STREAM every other week.

    • Kindergarten
    • Grades 1-2 Year A | Year B
    • Grades 3-4 Year A | Year B
    • Grades 5-6 Year A | Year B

    Two-Year Rotation (Grades 1-6)¶

    For combined-grade classrooms, we offer Year A and Year B versions:

    • Year A & Year B cover the same core skills with different projects, saints, and contexts

    • Core skills recur with increasing independence; project contexts vary. Check the grade review for overlaps and prerequisites rather than assuming no repetition.

    • Kindergarten has a single track (students only experience it once)

    What Makes C-STREAM Special¶

    The "A" in C-STREAM encompasses Arts (both visual and musical), with hands-on creation first:

    • Visual Art: Observational drawing, pattern, purposeful model design, composition and visual communication

    • Music: Rhythm, sound investigation, composition and attentive listening

    Digital art, animation and music tools are optional extensions when they materially improve the learning objective, not prerequisites for arts learning.

    The 12 Success Factors¶

    These twelve design principles guide the local program. Consult the source register before making an official standards or accreditation claim.

    1. Faith-Reason Integration

    Present faith and reason as complementary, while distinguishing scientific evidence, theological teaching and a classroom metaphor.

    2. NCEA's 10 Characteristics

    Use a local STREAM reflection checklist. Exact NCEA publication alignment and accreditation status are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

    3. Hands-On, Project-Based Learning

    Students apply leading-edge technology to "hands-on, minds-on projects" that build critical thinking and collaboration.

    4. Service-Oriented STEM Applications

    Connect STEM skills to Catholic social teaching through "Hands and Feet of Christ" projects.

    5. Cross-Curricular Integration

    Intentionally connect disciplines – math, science, art, music, religion, and language arts.

    6. Balance with Traditional Subjects

    STEM receives emphasis but not at the expense of other subjects; maintain the whole-child approach.

    7. Start Early

    Begin high-quality STEM education as soon as children enter elementary school.

    8. Teacher Professional Development

    Investment in educator training on bringing faith and reason together in the classroom.

    9. 21st Century Skills Focus

    Emphasize problem-solving, communication, collaboration, and critical thinking.

    10. Catholic Heritage in Science

    Leverage the Church's rich scientific legacy (Mendel, Copernicus, Pasteur, Lemaître, and more).

    11. Community and Industry Partnerships

    External connections with parishes, universities, and industry partners enhance programs.

    12. Wonder and Curiosity as Foundation

    Approach education from the perspective of wonder, exploration, and faith.

    Year at a Glance¶

    Term Weeks Focus
    Fall 1-12 Exploration, wonder, establishing routines
    Winter 13-22 Deeper investigation, long-arc projects
    Spring 23-34 Application, service projects, celebration

    Choose one sequence, not an additive menu:

    • Bi-weekly: 17 meetings in one grade-band rotation.

    • Weekly: A 34-slot planning calendar; holiday and multi-week document counts require the grade-band pacing check.

    • Extensions: Use additional meetings for retesting, data, artistic revision and communication; do not add every optional project to the year.

    See the scope and sequence for learning priorities and the lesson map for document-level counts.

    Curriculum Review

    2026-27 curriculum review¶

    Reviewed beginning October 4, 2026. This is a local curriculum-development review, not an Archdiocesan approval or certification of official standards coverage.

    Current generated program totals are regenerated with the lesson/material maps rather than inferred from filenames or old report snapshots. They describe documents and planned evidence/use—not observed student outcomes or physical school holdings.

    Start with the executive review, then choose the relevant grade review and read the actual lesson before teaching. The audits distinguish baseline concerns from revised lessons; complete written instructions do not replace a counted kit, local safety/access checks or an actual classroom trial.

    Completed reference library: all 251 K-6 documents now have complete conditional written pathways. See the K closeout and source-verified external candidates. The other three band reviews likewise document closure of their written package queues. Remaining physical/source/pilot gates are explicit in the school release checklist.

    Before scheduling¶

    1. Choose one schedule and one rotation, not all available tracks.
    2. Check revision, technology, materials and open concerns in the lesson audit.
    3. Use the local progression to select the younger/older grade expectation.
    4. Prepare the actual kit and verify accommodations and school safety procedures.
    5. Collect one individual piece of evidence, even when students work in teams.
    6. Record what students demonstrated; do not infer mastery from participation.

    Hold any unresolved P0 activity. Substitute a documented safe lesson that meets a stated objective rather than improvising with unknown materials, unavailable equipment or unsuitable weather.

    Executive curriculum review¶

    School: Our Lady of the Prairie, Belle Plaine, Minnesota; Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis. Planning year: 2026-27. Review/completion work: October 4, 2026.

    Overall judgment¶

    The baseline was a substantial useful activity bank, not a uniformly usable, verified academic program. The completed repository now provides 251 complete conditional lesson references, intentional local K-6 progression, individual planned evidence, scalable materials, realistic periods, source boundaries, teacher/family systems and automated consistency checks.

    This is document completion, not an Archdiocesan approval, full state-subject coverage certification, physical-kit inspection or classroom-outcome study. The school release checklist identifies the checks a repository review cannot perform.

    Preserved structure and completed lessons¶

    Band Weekly files Bi-weekly files Complete references
    K 20 17 37
    1-2 40 34 74
    3-4 37 34 71
    5-6 35 34 69
    Total 132 119 251

    All original lesson URLs, baseline dispositions/priorities and meeting allocations are preserved. The final state is 251 rebuilt packages, 0 improved-only, 0 unchanged outlines. Audit history is not erased or downgraded to imply formal safety closure.

    Across all alternatives the library represents 345 teaching meetings. That is not one pupil's year. Choose one weekly/bi-weekly track and rotation; compare actual meetings with school holidays. Native periods remain 25/30/40/45 minutes.

    The current generated summary gives map/resource totals. The validation record and band reviews document content, timing, quantity and evidence checks rather than inferring readiness from a filename.

    Strengths preserved and weaknesses corrected¶

    Area Baseline strength/concern Completion response
    Academic learning Authentic inquiry, design and computing contexts; targets/evidence often vague Specific objectives, actual fair retests, worked/labeled model data and individual evidence thresholds
    Catholic identity Wonder, faith and service; some forced analogies or unsupported biographies/quotes Truth, dignity, stewardship and user needs shape decisions; sourced heritage and clear belief/evidence boundaries
    Substitute usability Useful activities but hidden setup, unspecified handouts and missing cleanup Complete written packages, exact kits/roles, background, troubleshooting and native timed sequences
    Developmental fit Band organization but insufficient distinct expectations Grade-specific support/challenge, K/Grade 1 nonreader responses and scaffolded age-appropriate mathematics
    Technology Genuine creation possible but equipment/apps often assumed Hands-on primary paths where appropriate; actual execution/operation remains Required when its objective needs it
    Arts/mathematics Design/measurement contexts but decoration and advanced calculation could substitute for learning Purposeful artistic choices/feedback and justified quantities/data; no artistic-polish or handwriting mastery proxy
    Minnesota seasons Valuable nature/weather themes but unreliable outside conditions Indoor pathways, explicit dated observations, actual/model-data labels and school-managed plant care
    Materials/safety Reusable common materials but vague special items/conditions Normalized identities, teacher tools, safe stop rules, capacity/turn plans and separated component/access/stock records
    Families/assessment Journals/newsletters available but participation/home support could obscure mastery Individual objective-linked evidence; plain-language family copy; no routine homework/purchase/donation prerequisite
    Progression/scope Rotation options but overfilled calendar quotas and inconsistent prerequisites Checked meeting counts, one selected sequence, local progression and repeated skills with increasing independence/evidence

    Standards environment and traceability¶

    For 2026-27, verified Minnesota implementation editions are science 2019, arts 2018, ELA 2020 and social studies 2021. Mathematics 2022 begins full implementation in 2027-28; retain the 2007 planning baseline unless the school intentionally transitions early. CSTA 2026 was published in July 2026 and uses different elementary organization from 2017.

    The 18 CST competencies are locally created, not fabricated Archdiocesan benchmarks. They survive lesson changes and support 126 grade targets/stages. The local map contains 929 planned evidence links.

    The external matrix provides 29 narrow, source-verified candidates using sixteen identifiers across twenty-six lessons. A separate register records twenty-four inspected arts/CSTA identifiers. State-agency arts copies retain MDE-copy/school review; CSTA is national, not automatically adopted Minnesota guidance.

    Final MDE tables inaccessible through normal retrieval are not replaced with guessed science/math/ELA/social-studies numbers. The program complements primary subjects; a topic resemblance, device or local code cannot certify official coverage. Obtain school-issued OMCE guidance before claiming institutional alignment.

    Classroom practicality¶

    Every reference supplies native-period directions, exact class-size quantities, individual evidence, safety/access, troubleshooting, cleanup and family copy. No package requires hidden institutional knowledge as its written minimum; actual kits, software, room, contacts and approvals still need local confirmation.

    The eight reported individual OHM-135 Snap Circuits kits are preserved as reported—not inspected—stock. Four selected Grades 3-6 routes use matching manual/project checks and bounded hardware waves. Snap is not automatically equivalent to protected-AA or modular electronics; K remains optional adult demonstration only.

    The original conditional first-year budgets remain $229.52 / $476.04 / $854.32 / $2,367.84. They fund a modest core on stated cohort/stock assumptions, not every optional item in every alternative track. Prices/specifications and actual replenishment require local checks. Do not purchase every catalog row.

    Technology labels describe the selected primary pathway, not every extension. Paper reasoning can preserve computational concepts but cannot establish actual software, sensor, robot or electrical operation. Declare what was deferred.

    What to do next at school¶

    1. Select the actual schedule/rotation and next reference, not the entire bank.
    2. Complete the counted-kit, safety/access and pretest release checks.
    3. Pilot younger/older references; measure real preparation/cleanup and supply use.
    4. Gather individual evidence, with two dated observations at local mastery checkpoints.
    5. Finish authorized official-source/institutional review before restoring stronger claims.

    There is no remaining written-package queue to disguise as "future improvements." Remaining release work is real school/source/pilot evidence, explicitly separated from the repository checks and recorded in the implementation plan.

    K-6 Catholic C-STREAM philosophy¶

    Local program philosophy. Planning date: 2026-10-04. School year: 2026-27. Not an MDE- or Archdiocese-approved curriculum.

    Purpose¶

    C-STREAM joins Catholic identity and faith with science, technology, engineering, art and mathematics. Students study creation carefully, ask honest questions, make and improve things, reason with quantities, communicate creatively and consider the dignity of people affected by their choices. Their growing skills can serve God, neighbor and the common good in everyday life and many vocations, not only future technical careers.

    Catholic identity is more than an opening prayer. It shapes truthful reporting, stewardship, respectful collaboration, ethical technology use, purposeful work and service. Faith and reason strengthen inquiry rather than competing with it. Use an authentic connection when it deepens learning; do not attach a forced theological metaphor to every fact. Distinguish Church teaching, devotional tradition, an educator's analogy and scientific evidence. See the verified teaching and guidance in Standards Sources.

    Classroom commitments¶

    • Hands-on first; technology for a reason. Begin with observation, objects, sketches, paper algorithms, cardboard models, rulers and reusable materials. Use devices when they materially enable programming, research, measurement, accessibility or another objective. Device consumption is not computer science. State None / Optional / Recommended / Required, explain Required, and provide a valid low-tech fallback where possible. Never claim the fallback proves a digital operation it does not perform.
    • Real disciplinary learning. Science asks for evidence; engineering tests solutions against needs and limits; mathematics supports reasoning; art involves intentional observation, form, meaning, critique and revision, not just decorating a finished product. Lessons need not give equal time to every domain, but the year should intentionally revisit all six local domains.
    • Failure is information. A weak prototype or unexpected result is a reason to investigate, not a judgment on the student. Reward evidence-based revision, intellectual honesty and thoughtful choices rather than winning or polish.
    • Safe and inclusive by design. Use school-approved materials and age-appropriate tools; make adult-only actions explicit. Avoid unknown substances, unsafe projectiles, mains electricity, loose button batteries and strong small magnets. Address allergies, choking hazards, water, sharp/hot tools and outdoor exposure. Use fictional or anonymous data rather than sensitive student/family information. Do not use classmates as experimental subjects for risky activities.
    • Every child can show learning. Model short oral/picture directions for K-1. Offer pointing, building, acting, drawing, oral explanation, scribing and assistive tools. Preserve the target while reducing irrelevant reading, writing, sensory or motor demands. Rotate roles; do not let a confident partner supply all the reasoning. Challenge adds depth, not compulsory expense.
    • Practical, reusable and weather-resilient. Prefer low-cost multipurpose kits and light preparation. Plan for 10, 15, 20 or 25 students with explicit quantities, team roles and cleanup. Outdoor learning has an indoor alternative; January cold, limited daylight or a cancelled outing must not erase an essential target.
    • No routine homework. Teach and assess core learning at school. Family conversations or observations are optional, ungraded invitations with an in-class equivalent. Participation never depends on home devices, purchases, donations, transport or an adult teaching the lesson.

    Fit the school's periods¶

    These are example single-period budgets, including safety, setup and cleanup. Adjust for the actual activity; do not squeeze a full investigation into a shorter period by removing evidence or safety. Use a second meeting when needed.

    Period Hook, objective, safety and demonstration Explore/build/test, including setup Individual check and explanation Cleanup
    25 minutes 4 13 4 4
    30 minutes 5 16 5 4
    40 minutes 6 23 6 5
    45 minutes 7 26 7 5

    In short periods, use one meaningful test or design choice. In longer periods, add repeated testing or revision, not filler. Some processes need several meetings; store labelled work and resume rather than assigning completion at home.

    Evidence, continuity and honest claims¶

    The eighteen local standards and seven-grade progression survive lesson changes. Combined-grade classes share a context but use separate grade-level success criteria. Weekly/bi-weekly schedules and A/B rotations need their own checked opportunities to learn and demonstrate those targets.

    Keep assessment light but real: observation, an individual explanation, a sketch, a tested model or a data record. Participation and attractive group products are not mastery. Apply the individual evidence rule at planned checkpoints, and record what still needs teaching or assessment. Evaluate understanding of taught Catholic ideas and ethical choices, never private belief, perceived holiness or family religious practice.

    External standards claims require a verified edition, grade/benchmark, matching lesson task and individual assessment. These local competencies do not certify full science, mathematics, arts, ELA, social studies, CS or religion coverage. The program complements primary subjects and OMCE guidance; local school/diocesan review remains necessary.

    Teacher design test: Can a capable teacher or substitute explain the purpose, prepare the kit, teach safely, include every learner, finish cleanup and identify each child's learning within the available period? If not, simplify the activity, improve its supports or allow another meeting without weakening the target.

    Standards sources and implementation status¶

    Planning date and source access date: 2026-10-04. Target school year: 2026-27. All source entries record research on that date; the register distinguishes directly inspected text, indexed document references and failed retrievals. These are concise paraphrases, not reproductions of standards. Source years are edition labels; they are not necessarily adoption or implementation years.

    Classification and claim limits¶

    • Official standard: Minnesota's adopted subject standards. Their public-school implementation dates are a reference for this Catholic school's planning, not a finding that every public-school accountability requirement applies here.
    • Official guidance/teaching: MDE implementation guidance; Archdiocesan guidance or policy; Vatican/USCCB teaching. These are not interchangeable with numbered academic benchmarks.
    • National standard/framework: CSTA, NGSS, National Core Arts Standards and ISTE. Use selectively; no Minnesota or Archdiocesan adoption is inferred.
    • Local program standard: The eighteen CST-* competencies in Local Standards. Not MDE-approved, not Archdiocese-approved, and not a complete subject curriculum.

    Source verification does not establish lesson alignment. No external benchmark number is assigned to a lesson by this research. A claim requires the exact edition, applicable grade, verified benchmark, matching student task and assessment evidence. A topic resemblance or a local code is insufficient. All generated external-alignment fields remain VERIFICATION REQUIRED until that benchmark + lesson + individual assessment/evidence mapping is reviewed. A verified source, implementation date or local-code entry does not remove this hold.

    Minnesota: the 2026-27 baseline¶

    The directly inspected MDE newsletters and enacted rules establish these dates. Older projected transition timelines must not override the later confirmations. Assessment rollout dates are not substitutes for instruction implementation dates. In particular, the October 2023 newsletter called the social studies and math dates anticipated; the enacted rules and April 2026 confirmation, not that earlier forecast alone, establish the transition years used below.

    Area Use for 2026-27 Verified implementation status Grade scope and limits Evidence
    Science 2019 Minnesota Academic Standards in Science Full implementation occurred in 2024-25; already implemented in 2026-27. Official rule applies K-12. Use the actual benchmark for each K-6 grade, not a generic elementary topic. Direct inspection of the final grade/benchmark tables remains VERIFICATION REQUIRED. MN-01, MN-02
    Mathematics 2007 Minnesota K-12 Academic Standards in Mathematics as the existing-edition planning baseline 2022 standards are adopted, but implementation begins 2027-28, not 2026-27. Clearly label any early use as transition/enrichment. Official new rule applies K-12. The MDE existing-edition PDF is identified below, but was not directly readable; confirm the school's 2007 benchmark selections and transition decision: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. MN-01, MN-03, MN-08
    Arts 2018 Minnesota Academic Standards in Arts Education Full implementation 2023-24; ongoing in 2026-27. MDE's April 2026 notice says the next review is 2027-28, with a later implementation year to be set in rulemaking. A review is not a replacement standard. State-agency workbook directly shows individual grades K, 1-8, plus HS; K is encoded as grade 0. Do not reuse the older 2008 K-¾-5 band labels as the 2018 structure. Five arts areas; local visual design does not cover all five. MN-01, MN-04, MN-05
    English language arts 2020 Minnesota K-12 Academic Standards in ELA Full implementation 2025-26; already implemented in 2026-27. Official rule applies K-12. Reading, writing, and listening/speaking/viewing/exchanging ideas support explanations and communication. Exact grade-table organization and K-6 benchmark selection remain VERIFICATION REQUIRED. MN-01, MN-06
    Social studies 2021 Minnesota K-12 Academic Standards in Social Studies Effective at the beginning of 2026-27; this is its implementation year, not a future transition. Official rule applies K-12. Community needs, resources and technology impacts are possible connections, not proof of coverage. Final grade/benchmark selections remain VERIFICATION REQUIRED. MN-01, MN-07
    Computer science integration Verify CS-bearing benchmarks within the applicable subject edition MDE confirms CS-integrated benchmarks in 2019 science; their subject implementation is 2024-25. The 2018 arts workbook identifies CS-related benchmarks. There is no separate CS implementation deadline verified by this research. Do not give every K-6 grade the same benchmark or treat device operation as CS. The full integrated K-12 collection, subject-specific grade rows and any additional current legal/framework deadlines are VERIFICATION REQUIRED. MN-01, MN-05, MN-09

    Catholic teaching: verified paragraph references¶

    All paragraphs below were seen on the official Vatican site, including page HTML where the simplified reader omitted body text. Classroom applications are local interpretations of teaching, not official academic standards.

    ID / classification Official URL and exact references, accessed 2026-10-04 Paraphrase / classroom application
    FAITH-01 / official Church teaching CCC: characteristics of faith, 159 Faith and reason are not rival sources of truth; legitimate scientific investigation need not contradict faith. Keep observations and explanations honest; do not use theology as an experimental result.
    FAITH-02 / official Church teaching CCC: the human person as God's image, 1702, 1704 Every person bears God's image; reason participates in understanding creation and seeking the good. Design for people's dignity and access, not their productivity or presumed ability.
    FAITH-03 / official Church teaching CCC: respect for personal dignity, 2293-2295 Science and technology serve human flourishing and are not morally neutral merely because they are efficient. Human experimentation has moral and consent limits. Classroom implication: safe models, privacy, no harmful experiments on classmates.
    FAITH-04 / official Church teaching CCC: persons and goods, 2415-2418 Respect creation and its resources, consider future generations, and avoid needless animal suffering. Reuse materials, minimize waste and observe living things responsibly.
    FAITH-05 / official Church teaching CCC: work and social justice, 2427-2428 Work proceeds from persons and can develop their gifts; people are not instruments of production. Value careful making, every honest vocation and service rather than speed or prestige.
    FAITH-06 / official Church teaching CCC: living in truth, 2468-2469 Truthfulness in actions and words sustains trust. Record actual results, acknowledge uncertainty and credit another person's idea.

    USCCB inspection limit: The seven themes of Catholic social teaching and care for creation were attempted on 2026-10-04 but reliable text retrieval was blocked or incomplete. Their detailed wording and any proposed USCCB-specific citation are VERIFICATION REQUIRED. The applications above rest on the directly inspected Vatican paragraphs, not on unverified USCCB text.

    Legacy public-page claims: verification and safe wording¶

    This ledger supports qualification of shared home/README pages and related resources. It does not approve their legacy attributions or change external lesson-alignment fields. The local eighteen-code framework and twelve design principles are not an NCEA standards set, an empirically validated intervention or a Cognia certification.

    ID / classification Claim and primary-source status, researched 2026-10-04 Verification requirement and usable qualification
    LEGACY-01 / national Catholic education guidance; exact attribution unverified NCEA's ten characteristics of STREAM schools and claims of meeting "NCEA standards." The directly inspected NCEA Talk, STREAM in Action: Easy to Find is a contributed practitioner article about faith, service and STREAM, not the exact ten-item publication or a review of this curriculum. VERIFICATION REQUIRED for the original NCEA title, author, edition/date, exact list and any claimed correspondence. Do not use secondary lists as proof of NCEA's precise wording or numbering. Safe wording: local STREAM reflection checklist. Neither the article nor a checklist establishes NCEA approval, accreditation or program-wide alignment.
    LEGACY-02 / local design principles; research-validation claim unverified "Research-backed"/"research-based" twelve success factors, effectiveness claims and claims of demonstrated student outcomes. No baseline study set, claim-by-claim evidence synthesis or evaluation of this curriculum was supplied or verified. NAT-03 verifies science/engineering framework guidance, not the effectiveness of all twelve local principles or these lessons. VERIFICATION REQUIRED for each empirical claim: identifiable original research, applicable age/context, supported finding and limits, plus evidence for any claimed local outcome. Safe wording: local design principles informed by selected guidance. Do not call the program research-validated, proven effective or certified because a source describes its own framework as research-based.
    LEGACY-03 / national organizational certification guidance; local award/status unverified Cognia STEM certification/accreditation or conformity claims. The directly inspected current Cognia STEM certification page describes third-party evaluation and distinguishes institutional accreditation from STEM certification. Its FAQ says accreditation is not required to pursue STEM certification and describes certification as a six-year term. These are Cognia's current process descriptions, not findings about this school or repository. VERIFICATION REQUIRED for the named institution/program's award, issuer, scope and current term; obtain Cognia-issued evidence or a verified official status record. Separate accreditation from STEM certification. Exact standards-edition conformity also needs a reviewed crosswalk and evidence. Safe wording: Cognia offers a separate STEM certification process; this curriculum makes no certification or accreditation claim. A school's accreditation does not by itself establish STEM certification, and curriculum guidance is not an award.
    LEGACY-04 / training/material attribution unverified Steno training materials, attributed inspirational quotations and other unattributed source wording in legacy public pages. No exact original publication, author/date or training document was inspected for these claims. VERIFICATION REQUIRED before attributing exact wording, describing the materials as research evidence or implying provider endorsement. Use clearly identified local paraphrases/design commitments until the original source and appropriate attribution are established.

    The NCEA article and Cognia process page are primary evidence only for what those pages actually describe. They do not establish that a historical ten-characteristic list matches the local checklist, that a provider's research validates this curriculum, or that the school has earned any credential. Unverified claims should be qualified or omitted, not converted into assertions that the publication, research or credential does not exist.

    Local K-6 C-STREAM standards¶

    Local program framework. Planning date: 2026-10-04. School year: 2026-27. These are original school-program competencies, not official MDE or Archdiocesan standards and not approved by either body. They integrate Catholic identity with science, technology, engineering, art and mathematics without replacing the school's religion or primary subject curricula.

    The fixed contract is 18 codes: three per domain. Keep codes and meanings stable when projects, materials, schedules or rotations change. Religion/faith is integrated in the Catholic domain and across practice; there is no additional CST-R* domain. Grade-specific performance targets are in Learning Progression, not new standard codes.

    Competency catalog¶

    Evidence examples are possible individual checks, not mandatory projects or claims that existing lessons already assess these skills.

    Code Competency and observable intent Examples of individual evidence
    CST-C1 Faith/reason and honest evidence. Use reason to study creation; distinguish an observation, prediction, explanation and taught faith connection; report results truthfully, including uncertainty. K-1: tell what was actually seen rather than hoped for. 2-3: revise a prediction using a recorded observation. 4-6: defend a claim, identify a limit, and explain why honest inquiry is compatible with the taught Catholic view.
    CST-C2 Dignity/service/inclusive ethical design. Respect every person's worth; identify a real need, include others, and consider who benefits or might be excluded or harmed. K-1: offer an accessible role or adapt a shared tool. 2-3: explain how a design helps its user. 4-6: evaluate an access/privacy concern and justify a safer, more inclusive design.
    CST-C3 Stewardship/resources/work. Care for creation and shared resources; use materials responsibly; value careful work and gifts used in service. K-1: sort reusable scraps and explain their care. 2-3: choose less wasteful materials without losing function. 4-6: compare resource use, durability and effects on people; explain a work/service connection.
    CST-S1 Observations/questions/evidence. Ask investigable questions; observe, record and use evidence to explain a phenomenon without overstating a conclusion. K-1: point out an observed change. 2-3: explain a pattern with recorded observations. 4-6: support a claim with data, uncertainty and a useful follow-up question.
    CST-S2 Investigations/testing/variables. Predict, plan and conduct safe tests; increasingly identify what changes, what is measured and what stays consistent; repeat and compare results. K-1: show a prediction and follow a teacher-set test. 2-3: identify the one changed feature. 4-6: present a repeatable investigation, controlled variables and a limitation.
    CST-S3 Physical/life/Earth systems/models. Observe and model age-appropriate physical, living and Earth/space systems; use models to explain relationships and identify their limits. K-1: depict an observed object, living thing or weather change. 2-3: label interacting parts. 4-6: use a model to explain a change and describe what it omits. Collect physical, life and Earth/space examples across the year.
    CST-T1 Tools/input-output/troubleshooting. Select and use appropriate tools safely; describe a system's input and output; diagnose problems using evidence rather than random changes. K-1: select a ruler or safe tool and describe its job. 2-3: trace an input/action/output. 4-6: explain a systematic troubleshooting sequence. A non-digital tool can support local evidence but not an external device-use claim.
    CST-T2 Algorithms/loops/conditions/debugging. Create, follow, represent and improve instructions; progress from sequence to repetition and conditions; locate and correct errors. K-1: give and fix movement-card instructions. 2-3: trace a loop and an if/then choice. 4-6: test an algorithm on contrasting inputs and explain a correction. Devices are optional for this local competency unless the chosen objective requires execution on one.
    CST-T3 Data/digital citizenship/technology impacts. Represent and question data; protect privacy, credit ideas and communicate responsibly; evaluate technology's benefits, limitations and effects on people. K-1: sort anonymous objects and recognize private information in a scenario. 2-3: explain a data display and a safe sharing choice. 4-6: evaluate data quality, access, privacy and a technology tradeoff.
    CST-E1 Problems/criteria/constraints. Define a user-centered problem, observable success criteria and real limits before choosing a solution. K-1: name what a model must do and one limit. 2-3: distinguish a success requirement from a material limit. 4-6: write and justify measurable criteria and constraints for a user.
    CST-E2 Build/test/redesign. Make a prototype, test against criteria, record what happened, and improve deliberately using evidence. K-1: identify a weak part and make a change. 2-3: compare before/after tests. 4-6: document iterations and distinguish measured improvement from an attractive but untested change.
    CST-E3 Tradeoffs/communicate solutions. Compare alternatives, explain design choices and limitations, and communicate an evidence-supported recommendation to an audience. K-1: show a choice and give a reason. 2-3: compare two options against a criterion. 4-6: defend a recommendation using performance, cost/resources, access and tradeoffs.
    CST-A1 Observational sketches/models. Observe closely and represent form, parts, relationships and details in drawings or made models that help understanding. K-1: show a noticed detail. 2-3: label a drawing/model so someone else can interpret it. 4-6: use multiple views, relative sizes or annotations for an accurate visual explanation. Artistic polish is not the criterion.
    CST-A2 Purposeful pattern/form/design. Use pattern, shape, form, composition, color or texture intentionally for an aesthetic or functional purpose; explain choices. K-1: create and describe a repeat or form. 2-3: choose visual features to direct attention or support function. 4-6: compare alternatives and justify choices for purpose and audience. Decoration alone is not evidence.
    CST-A3 Artistic communication/critique/revision. Convey ideas visually or artistically; discuss meaning and intent, give respectful specific feedback, and revise while preserving or clarifying purpose. K-1: explain an idea and respond to a helpful comment. 2-3: describe how a visual choice communicates meaning. 4-6: give criterion-based critique and show a reasoned revision.
    CST-M1 Count/compare/measure. Count or compare relevant quantities; estimate and measure with appropriate tools and units; consider precision and repeated measurements as appropriate. K-1: count materials and compare lengths. 2-3: record a measurement with units. 4-6: choose a tool/unit, repeat a measurement and explain precision appropriate to the task.
    CST-M2 Data/pattern representation. Organize quantities and patterns in objects, drawings, tables or suitable graphs; interpret a representation without distorting its message. K-1: make a tally or object graph. 2-3: label a table/bar display and explain a pattern. 4-6: choose a defensible representation, identify an unusual value and avoid unsupported conclusions.
    CST-M3 Grade-appropriate quantities/operations/reasoning. Use quantities, operations and relationships already taught or explicitly scaffolded in classroom mathematics; explain strategies, units and reasonableness in practical problems. K-1: show a quantity or joining/separating strategy. 2-3: justify a count, equal-group or measurement calculation. 4-6: solve and check an appropriate multi-step problem; use fractions, decimals or ratios only when their prerequisites are taught.

    What counts as demonstrated learning?¶

    Use a short observation, explanation, drawing, model, data record or performance. Offer oral, pointing, tactile, large-format, scribed or assistive responses where they preserve the skill being assessed. Reading stamina, handwriting, speech fluency, fine-motor speed and expensive supplies are not proxies for competence.

    Local assessment level Decision rule
    Beginning Student attempts the task but cannot yet demonstrate the stated grade target, even with the offered support. Record the next support.
    Developing Student demonstrates part of the target, or needs a conceptual prompt/model to complete it.
    Meets expectation Student demonstrates the full stated grade target and explains/shows the relevant reasoning, using permitted access supports but without an adult or peer supplying the answer.
    Extends learning Student meets the target and transfers, critiques or improves it in a new appropriate situation. More complicated or prettier work alone is not extension.

    Mastery rule: A group product, exposure, attendance, participation, or a single lucky result cannot establish individual mastery. At an expected-mastery checkpoint, collect at least two dated observations on separate occasions, including an individually attributable demonstration and a changed context or follow-up explanation. Both must meet the grade target. This is a local assessment policy, not an external agency requirement. If evidence is missing, record not yet assessed; if it is partial, record developing and reteach.

    Assess Catholic competencies through understanding of taught ideas and observable truthful, respectful, responsible choices. Do not grade prayer intensity, private belief, a child's perceived holiness, family religious practice, or willingness to disclose personal circumstances. Distinguish a student's design critique from the worth of the student.

    Traceability contract for integration¶

    A future lesson/assessment record should identify:

    1. Local code and grade target from this catalog/progression.
    2. Grade, schedule and rotation, unit and lesson; combined grades retain separate success criteria.
    3. Student action and evidence: what each learner will do, how the teacher will check it, and what meets expectation.
    4. Instructional stage: introduced, developing, reinforced or expected-mastery checkpoint, separate from the student's assessed result.
    5. External mapping, if claimed: source/edition, exact verified number and grade/band, paraphrased requirement, matching task, individual assessment and evidence location. Label unresolved rows VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

    Until lesson tasks and assessments are inspected, a source connection is only a candidate, not a verified alignment. Do not infer official science alignment from CST-S*, CSTA alignment from CST-T*, or OMCE approval from CST-C*. See Standards Sources.

    Scope limits¶

    • Eighteen competencies are a durable integrated-skills framework, not all religion, science, CS, engineering, arts, mathematics, ELA or social studies standards. They do not certify complete subject coverage.
    • CST-S3 requires physical, life and Earth/space contexts over time; one bridge or robotics unit cannot stand for the entire science program.
    • Local art emphasizes observation, visual design and communication; it does not represent full dance, music, theater or media arts provision.
    • Unplugged computing can assess algorithms. It cannot by itself prove actual device operation, executable programming, online research or digital-tool use when an external benchmark specifically requires those actions.
    • Mathematical sophistication follows the primary math curriculum. Extension for an older student must not become an unsupported prerequisite for a younger student in a combined-grade class.
    • The planned progression is a design target, not a finding that every existing lesson or rotation already supplies it.

    K-6 C-STREAM learning progression¶

    Local planning framework, dated 2026-10-04 for 2026-27. Not MDE/Archdiocese-approved. Use the fixed meanings in Local Standards and external-version limits in Standards Sources.

    These are observable end-of-grade targets, not new external benchmarks and not evidence of existing curriculum coverage. Each grade increases the student's agency, precision, explanation and ability to consider others. Earlier skills remain in use. I/D targets guide formative assessment; M checkpoints require the individual evidence described below. Access supports are always allowed.

    For K-1, demonstrate and give short oral/picture instructions; accept pointing, acting, construction and dictated explanations. For 2-3, add labels, repeated tests and simple comparisons. For 4-6, add independent plans, evidence, limitations and justified tradeoffs, not merely larger projects.

    Catholic integration: reason, dignity and stewardship¶

    End of grade CST-C1: faith/reason and honest evidence CST-C2: dignity/service/inclusive ethical design CST-C3: stewardship/resources/work
    K Tell or show one thing actually observed; connect careful noticing with the taught idea of wonder at creation. Offer a classmate a usable turn/role and identify someone a simple design could help. Return a shared tool, sort a reusable piece and tell why materials need care.
    1 Distinguish an observation from a guess in a demonstration; report an unexpected result honestly. Describe a user's need and make one change that helps the user participate. Choose a reusable material and describe careful work as a way to care for gifts and people.
    2 Compare a prediction with a recorded result and explain why truthful results matter, even when disappointing. Explain how a design helps a person and identify a feature that might make it hard for another person to use. Compare two material choices for waste and function; carry out and explain a less-wasteful choice.
    3 Use recorded evidence to revise an explanation; explain in simple terms that study of creation and taught faith need not compete. Ask a user-centered question, adapt a feature and explain the adaptation without stereotyping the user. Keep a simple resource record and explain a reuse decision that protects function and respects others' work.
    4 Separate an evidence-based claim from a taught faith/ethical reflection; acknowledge a limitation and credit an idea. Compare solutions for access, safety and service; justify an inclusive choice using a realistic user scenario. Compare waste, durability and repair possibilities; defend a responsible choice under a material limit.
    5 Explain how a claim is supported or challenged by evidence; distinguish scientific explanation, uncertainty and Catholic ethical judgment. Identify a possible unintended harm or exclusion and propose an appropriate safeguard before testing. Evaluate material use and possible effects on people/creation; explain why skilled work and service matter beyond winning.
    6 Defend an honest, limited conclusion, correct an error and explain the taught compatibility of faith/reason without treating faith as test data. Defend a service-oriented design using evidence about user needs, accessibility and privacy/safety; identify a remaining ethical tradeoff. Recommend a resource/work plan considering durability, waste, repair and effects on people/creation; acknowledge a tradeoff.

    Evidence examples: Individual oral observation versus prediction (K-1); explanation of one inclusive/resource choice (2-3); annotated ethical design decision with evidence and a limit (4-6). Assess understanding and actions, not private belief or spiritual maturity.

    Science: inquiry, investigations and systems¶

    End of grade CST-S1: observations/questions/evidence CST-S2: investigations/testing/variables CST-S3: physical/life/Earth systems/models
    K Show a detail or change using senses safely; ask a question about what was noticed. Make a pictured/oral prediction, follow a teacher-set safe test and show the result. Make or describe a simple representation of an observed physical object, living thing or weather feature.
    1 Record two observations with pictures/marks and use them to answer a simple question. Compare two teacher-set conditions and identify what was different and what was observed. Identify important parts of a physical, living or Earth/space example and show a relationship using a model.
    2 Ask a testable question, record observations and explain an answer using at least one recorded result. With a scaffold, change one feature, keep another consistent and repeat a test to compare results. Use a labelled model to explain a simple change in a physical, life or Earth/space system.
    3 Use repeated observations or simple data to describe a pattern and explain how it answers the question. Identify the changed feature, measured outcome and a feature kept consistent; carry out repeated safe trials. Describe interacting parts and cause/effect in models across physical, life and Earth/space contexts.
    4 Support a claim with recorded results and distinguish the result from an explanation or new question. Plan a fair comparison, record repeated measurements and explain why a controlled feature matters. Use a model to predict a system change and compare that prediction with observation in each science context.
    5 Compare evidence from more than one trial/source, notice disagreement and propose a useful follow-up question. Identify changed, measured and controlled variables; describe a repeatable method and one source of uncertainty. Explain a physical, life or Earth/space interaction with a model and identify an important feature the model omits.
    6 Defend a claim with relevant data, address conflicting evidence and state what the investigation cannot establish. Conduct and explain a safe, repeatable controlled investigation; discuss variation and a justified improvement to the method. Use and revise models in physical, life and Earth/space contexts to explain/predict change, identify a limit and compare with evidence.

    Evidence examples: Observation sketch and explanation (K-1); individual description of changed/consistent features and trial record (2-3); investigation plan, evidence-supported claim and model limitation (4-6). Across the year, collect physical, life and Earth/space examples for CST-S3; one context is insufficient. A craft labelled "science" is not a scientific explanation.

    Technology and computing: tools, algorithms and impacts¶

    End of grade CST-T1: tools/input-output/troubleshooting CST-T2: algorithms/loops/conditions/debugging CST-T3: data/digital citizenship/technology impacts
    K Select and safely demonstrate a tool for a task; show what action causes an observable result. Put at least three pictured actions in order, follow them and locate one misplaced action with support. Sort objects by an observable feature and identify, in a scenario, information to keep private and an adult to ask for help.
    1 Explain a tool's job and describe an action/input and result/output; check an obvious problem safely. Give a precise sequence, identify a repeated action and correct a step that produces the wrong result. Record a simple sort/count and explain a safe, kind choice in a teacher-provided technology scenario.
    2 Trace input, action and output in a simple system; describe a problem and test one likely cause. Represent a sequence and repeated group of steps; follow a simple if/then choice and correct an error. Explain a simple data display, distinguish private from shareable information and acknowledge another person's idea.
    3 Compare tools for a purpose and trace a system's input/output; document a check rather than changing parts at random. Write/arrange instructions with a loop and condition, trace two possible cases and explain a correction. Collect anonymous task data, explain what it shows and choose responsible sharing/credit in a realistic scenario.
    4 Break a system problem into parts and test causes in order; explain how each check narrows the problem. Decompose a task, represent loops and conditions, and use a trace to locate and repair an error. Identify missing/misleading data and explain a technology benefit, possible harm and protective action.
    5 Choose a tool/system for function and access; document input/output checks and a justified troubleshooting sequence. Compare algorithms for the same task, test contrasting inputs and revise for correctness and clarity. Evaluate data relevance and collection limits; explain privacy, credit and access decisions in a technology use case.
    6 Defend a safe tool/system choice and use documented checks to distinguish likely causes from unsupported guesses. Design and explain a decomposed algorithm with repetition and conditions; test usual and boundary cases and justify debugging revisions. Evaluate a data-informed technology proposal for accuracy, privacy, accessibility and social effects; justify safeguards and a tradeoff.

    Evidence examples: Individual tool explanation and movement-card trace (K-1); loop/choice demonstration and privacy scenario (2-3); algorithm trace, troubleshooting log or technology-impact recommendation (4-6). Local algorithms can be unplugged. Claim actual device programming only after individually checking executable work on a device; cards alone do not establish it.

    Engineering: requirements, iteration and decisions¶

    End of grade CST-E1: problems/criteria/constraints CST-E2: build/test/redesign CST-E3: tradeoffs/communicate solutions
    K Name a problem and show what a solution should do using a teacher-given material limit. Build a simple model, try it and identify/change a part that did not work. Show a design choice and give a reason using words, pointing or a demonstration.
    1 Identify a user, one success criterion and one material/time limit before building. Test a prototype against a stated criterion, change a feature and try again. Compare two choices for the task and explain a preferred choice with a demonstrated result.
    2 Distinguish what a solution must accomplish from a limit on making it; sketch a possible solution. Record before/after results and explain how a change addressed a weak part. Compare two options against a criterion and explain what is gained or given up.
    3 State a user's problem, an observable criterion and a constraint; explain why a proposed design addresses them. Run the same success test on two versions and explain an improvement using recorded results. Present a solution with a labelled model/sketch, results and one remaining weakness.
    4 Write measurable criteria and constraints with a scaffold; use them to compare possible designs before construction. Use repeated measurements to revise a prototype; explain whether the change improved the stated criterion. Compare alternatives using performance evidence and a material/cost limit; explain a tradeoff to an audience.
    5 Prioritize a user's criteria within time, materials and safety limits; justify a plan before building. Document multiple versions and comparable tests; justify a revision and distinguish improvement from an untested change. Recommend a design using more than one criterion, evidence and an acknowledged resource/access tradeoff.
    6 Define and justify a user-centered problem, measurable success criteria and resource, safety and access constraints. Conduct and document evidence-driven iterations under constraints; explain unresolved failure and a justified next test. Defend a solution using performance, cost/resources, ethics/access and tradeoffs; answer a critical question with evidence.

    Evidence examples: Individual demonstration of a changed part (K-1); before/after record and reason (2-3); criteria sheet, test record and defended recommendation (4-6). A failed prototype can provide strong learning evidence. Failure during engineering is information, not failure of the student.

    Art: observation, purposeful design and communication¶

    End of grade CST-A1: observational sketches/models CST-A2: purposeful pattern/form/design CST-A3: artistic communication/critique/revision
    K Draw or construct a representation with a noticed detail and identify what it shows. Create a repeated pattern or selected shape/form and describe one choice. Explain what an artwork/model communicates and respond to one respectful suggestion.
    1 Represent important parts observed in an object and explain their placement. Choose pattern, color or form for a stated purpose rather than adding it without a reason. Describe an intended idea and make a change after a specific helpful comment.
    2 Make a labelled sketch/model that another person can use to identify parts or relationships. Use shape, pattern or composition to guide attention or support a function; explain the choice. Explain how a visual feature communicates an idea; give specific kind feedback and show a revision.
    3 Use observed detail and relative sizes in a drawing/model to clarify a relationship. Compare two arrangements/forms and choose one for meaning, appearance or function with a reason. Present an intended message, identify a feature that supports it and revise using audience feedback.
    4 Use labelled views or an annotated model to explain observed structure while distinguishing imagined features. Select visual features for purpose/audience, test alternatives and explain how the choice affects meaning or use. Give criterion-based feedback and revise a work to clarify meaning while explaining the decision.
    5 Represent an observed system with purposeful views, relative scale and annotations; identify a representation limit. Compare form, pattern or composition alternatives for function and aesthetic intent; justify a purposeful choice. Compare interpretations, critique specific choices respectfully and document a revision consistent with intent.
    6 Produce an accurate observational representation suited to an audience; distinguish measured, estimated and symbolic features. Defend pattern/form/design choices considering aesthetic intent, function, audience and constraints. Communicate a complex idea artistically, use respectful evidence-based critique and explain how revision strengthened or changed intent.

    Evidence examples: Observed-detail explanation (K-1); annotated sketch and reason for composition (2-3); alternative designs, critique and explained revision (4-6). Do not grade realism or neatness unless explicitly taught and relevant. This visual/design strand does not certify complete arts coverage.

    Mathematics: quantities, representation and reasoning¶

    Targets use the mathematics already taught in the primary classroom. Numbers, units and operations are chosen accordingly; advanced content must not become a hidden prerequisite. A scaffold is instruction, not proof of mastery of an untaught operation.

    End of grade CST-M1: count/compare/measure CST-M2: data/pattern representation CST-M3: grade-appropriate quantities/operations/reasoning
    K Count a small set with one-to-one matching and compare length, amount or number directly. Sort objects, show a simple repeating pattern or object graph, and describe a visible comparison. Model joining/separating small quantities or compare shapes/amounts; show how the answer fits the task.
    1 Count needed materials, compare quantities and measure a length with equal nonstandard units without gaps. Make a tally/picture display or represent a repeat and explain what a symbol/unit stands for. Use taught addition/subtraction with objects or drawings to solve a material/count problem and explain the strategy.
    2 Estimate and measure a task quantity with a taught standard unit/tool; record the unit. Create a labelled table/picture/bar display of simple data and describe a comparison or pattern. Use taught quantities/operations in a practical problem; explain the strategy and check with a model or estimate.
    3 Choose an appropriate taught unit, measure consistently and compare repeated measurements. Organize repeated-test data in a labelled table/graph and describe how a result changes. Use taught equal-group/measurement reasoning to solve and check a project problem, stating what quantities mean.
    4 Measure with appropriate precision, record units and explain why a tool/unit suits the question. Choose a suitable display, label its scale/units and use it to support a comparison without distorting the data. Apply taught whole-number or fraction/measurement reasoning to a project problem and explain why the result is reasonable.
    5 Estimate, repeat measurements and explain variation/rounding appropriate to the task and tool. Represent data clearly, identify an unusual value and distinguish a pattern from a claim the data cannot support. Use taught fraction/decimal or multi-step reasoning for materials, measurement or cost; check the answer and units.
    6 Choose units/tools and a justified measurement method; explain precision, repeated results and limits. Choose and defend a data/pattern representation, interpret variation and identify a limitation or misleading presentation. Solve and defend a taught multi-step quantities problem, using ratio/rate reasoning only after prerequisites; check units and reasonableness.

    Evidence examples: Count/compare demonstration (K-1); measurement record and explained representation (2-3); checked practical calculation and interpretation of data (4-6). A graph in a group poster is not proof that every student can interpret it.

    Separate planned instructional-stage matrix¶

    This matrix is a local intended progression, not an audited lesson-coverage map or a student-results record. Every code recurs every year.

    • I - Introduced: model and encounter the foundation; collect a formative check.
    • D - Developing: guided practice with increasing independence.
    • R - Reinforced: revisit and transfer prior learning at the new grade target; continue formative checks. It does not mean the skill is finished.
    • M - Expected mastery checkpoint: plan individual assessment of that grade's target. M never means a student has mastered it merely by exposure.

    CST-C1 I D R M R R M
    CST-C2 I D M R R R M
    CST-C3 I D R M R R M
    CST-S1 I D M R R R M
    CST-S2 I D D R M R M
    CST-S3 I D R M R R M
    CST-T1 I D M R R R M
    CST-T2 I D D R M R M
    CST-T3 I D D R R M M
    CST-E1 I D M R R R M
    CST-E2 I D R M R R M
    CST-E3 I D D R R M M
    CST-A1 I D M R R R M
    CST-A2 I D R M R R M
    CST-A3 I D D R M R M
    CST-M1 I M R R R R M
    CST-M2 I D M R R R M
    CST-M3 I D R M R R M

    The checkpoints are local instructional choices, not state/diocesan deadlines. All Grade 6 M entries refer to the local Grade 6 target, not mastery of a whole national 6-8 band or the entirety of a subject.

    Turning a plan into verified learning¶

    1. Select a small number of primary codes for each lesson; do not claim all eighteen because students built something.
    2. Give each participating grade its own target and success criterion. An older student's answer or a mixed-grade team's product does not establish younger students' competence.
    3. Rotate meaningful roles and include a brief individual demonstration or explanation. Track who supplied which evidence, not just team completion.
    4. At M checkpoints, apply the individual mastery rule: two dated occasions, including an individual performance and a changed context or follow-up explanation, both meeting the grade target. Record missing evidence as not yet assessed, not mastered.
    5. Map actual lessons and evidence separately for weekly/bi-weekly schedules and A/B rotations. A second rotation may revisit a code with a harder task; it must not defer a grade's essential target until the student has left it.
    6. If time, weather, devices or materials change, preserve the target and valid assessment, not necessarily the activity. Use indoor alternatives, unplugged representations or another meeting when they retain the assessed skill. Do not relabel a materially different skill as equivalent.
    7. Flag unmet targets and uncertain external mappings for parent integration. This plan alone does not prove that any existing schedule can yet deliver and assess all targets within its available meetings.

    Two to four primary codes per lesson is a useful planning limit, not a mandated quota. Short checks can overlap when each skill is actually demonstrated. Keep evidence in the school-approved assessment system; do not collect personal or family data merely to make a project feel authentic.

    K-6 scope and sequence¶

    Choose a feasible year¶

    Retain the existing periods: K 25 minutes, Grades 1-2 30 minutes, Grades 3-4 40 minutes, Grades 5-6 45 minutes.

    • Bi-weekly: Select one existing 17-session track.
    • Weekly: Select one band/rotation. The common Year A scaffold covers 34 calendar slots, including two breaks, for 32 teaching meetings. Check Year B against its grade review; fewer documents can cover longer units and do not prove identical pacing.
    • Do not combine weekly and bi-weekly tracks or add all thematic menu entries to the selected year.
    • Core: Preserve inquiry, measurement/data, purposeful art, design/test/ redesign, unplugged computing and Catholic ethical reflection.
    • Recommended: Additional investigations or retesting that deepen an existing objective.
    • Optional/enrichment: Specialty robotics, advanced software, elaborate exhibitions, field trips and extra build variants when they add learning.

    The legacy index's single-week/multi-week/long-arc quotas double-counted meetings. The corrected planner and downloadable audits replace that arithmetic. No grade should be scheduled simply by counting filenames.

    Band 17 meetings: contact minutes 32 meetings: contact minutes
    K 425 800
    1-2 510 960
    3-4 680 1,280
    5-6 765 1,440

    These totals include distribution, transitions, assessment and cleanup. The weekly program has more practice time; equal mastery in half the time is not assumed.

    The audited weekly Year B tracks for Grades 3-4 and 5-6 represent 33 meetings, or 1,320 and 1,485 minutes, respectively. Their units include the nominal winter-break slot; reconcile this with the actual school calendar rather than treating it as an extra guaranteed teaching meeting.

    Program unit spine¶

    This is a local planning organization of recurring concepts, not a claim that every legacy lesson already has this title or alignment. The actual lesson-level unit, rotation, evidence and disposition are in the lesson map. Use the band reviews to select ready lessons and adapt themes to the real school/liturgical calendar.

    Unit and bi-weekly slots Concepts and competencies Principal local standards Main evidence/project Weekly depth
    1. Wonder, observation and tools; 1-2 Notice, ask, predict; tools carry out human purposes; truthful observation CST-C1, CST-S1, CST-T1, CST-M1 Oral/drawn observation; directional or tool demonstration Repeat observations and introduce team routines
    2. Structures and forces; 3-4 Problem, criterion, constraints, stable forms, fair comparison CST-E1, CST-E2, CST-M1, CST-A1 Bridge/tower prototype, measured test and revision Compare alternatives and retest under the same load
    3. Creation, patterns and community; 5-6 Living/physical systems as appropriate; purposeful pattern; service CST-S3, CST-C2, CST-A2, CST-M2 Model or useful design with an explanation of who benefits Observe/change one feature and collect individual explanations
    4. Light, sound and sequences; 7-8 Physical systems, input/output, algorithms and visual/audio communication CST-S3, CST-T2, CST-A3 Light/sound model or paper algorithm with a trace Safe circuit investigation or actual digital execution when justified
    5. Evidence, faith/reason and local conditions; 9-10 Honest evidence, biography/source checks, weather/measurement/data CST-C1, CST-S1, CST-S2, CST-M2 Investigation record with evidence and uncertainty Compare observations across time; revise an explanation
    6. Life, stewardship and service; 11-13 Change over time, systems, resource care, inclusive design CST-C3, CST-S3, CST-E1, CST-C2 Indoor growth/habitat model or service prototype Repeated observations, testing and feedback
    7. Systems, redesign and responsible technology; 14-16 Algorithms, mechanisms, criteria, tradeoffs and ethical impacts CST-T2, CST-T3, CST-E2, CST-E3 Debugged plan or tested mechanism with a justified improvement Evaluate alternate designs; digital/hardware extensions only when meaningful
    8. Communicate and reflect; 17 Explain learning, compare earlier/later work, revise communication CST-A3, CST-E3, CST-C3 Individual explanation plus a team display/model Practice feedback, revise display and collect final evidence

    Codes are local program competencies, not official benchmarks. Each individual lesson claims only what students actually practice and demonstrate. Not every unit needs every domain. Arts must include purposeful choices and communication; counting decoration as art or a tablet as computing is insufficient.

    Grade-specific progression and memorable experiences¶

    Grade Entry/prerequisite to establish End-of-grade performance to seek Signature experience and next step
    K Follow one modeled oral instruction; compare visible objects Observe, build, point/draw/tell one change; count/compare a small set Structures that connect/help; next explain a problem and simple instruction sequence
    1 Reestablish safe tool use, oral sequencing and counting Build for a purpose, trace a short sequence, describe a result Paper bridge; next explain choices and represent results
    2 Repeat Grade 1 demonstrations rather than assume they were taught in the other rotation Explain design choice, compare measured results and revise an algorithm/design A service structure/mechanism with a before/after explanation; next conduct fair tests
    3 Model criteria, test procedure, measurement units and a simple table Test a design under fixed conditions and use evidence to suggest a revision Measured bridge; next use repeated measures and clearer evidence
    4 Recheck fair testing, recording and distinguishing prediction from result Use measurements and evidence to improve a design or explanation Structures, indoor weather inquiry or safe circuits; next compare against multiple criteria
    5 Establish criteria/constraints, repeated observations and respectful feedback Compare designs using evidence, criteria, cost/resources and an ethical reason Service design or environmental model; next defend a tradeoff and identify limitations
    6 Reestablish data quality, computational trace and explanation of users' needs Defend design choices with evidence, tradeoffs, cost, ethics and performance Inclusive design exhibition or fictional evidence investigation; next transfer methods to independent inquiry

    These are desired local outcomes, not automatic promotions based on exposure. The learning progression gives competency-level introduced/developing/reinforced/expected indicators and individual evidence.

    Rotations and prerequisites¶

    Year A and B are alternative entry years, not beginner/advanced levels. Every rotation must reintroduce the design cycle, safe tool routines, relevant vocabulary, measurement method and computing representations. Younger students receive modeling and accessible responses; older students extend evidence, independence and justification.

    Repeat the skill intentionally, not an identical worksheet or unexamined product. Keep a small portfolio so a returning student can compare earlier and later reasoning. When a project recurs, increase only an appropriate dimension: independence, precision, data, number of criteria or ethical tradeoffs.

    Seasonal and workload controls¶

    • No required objective depends on outdoor access in a Minnesota winter. Use room-temperature materials, safe indoor observations and prepared data when appropriate; do not claim a paper model supplies real weather data.
    • Growing investigations require observations over time. Schedule follow-up checks explicitly; a single period cannot demonstrate a life cycle.
    • Start with reusable kits and common classroom materials. Specialist kit reservations and digital accounts are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    • Keep projects small enough to test and assess in the native period. If a longer project is selected, label the meetings and storage/reset steps.
    • Use the audit's prep/cleanup estimates as planning estimates, not measured teacher timings. Time a first run and record improvements.
    • No routine homework. Family questions and activities are optional and do not supply evidence required for participation or mastery.

    Grade-band evidence¶

    Read the detailed K, 1-2, 3-4 and 5-6 reviews for exact track counts, original strengths/gaps, targeted revisions, remaining developmental concerns and unit newsletter snippets.

    Grade Reviews

    Kindergarten curriculum review¶

    Current result: all 37 Kindergarten lesson documents are complete instructional references. The autonomous second pass replaced the remaining 29 outlines, without agents, and verified their directions, timings and quantity tables. Document-complete is not classroom-certified. Physical supplies, school approvals, individual accommodations and actual trials remain required.

    Download the current 37-row audit | Teacher/substitute routines | Source-verified external candidates

    1. Baseline and change record¶

    All 37 lessons and both track READMEs were inspected in the first pass. Original baseline dispositions remain 23 KEEP + IMPROVE, 13 REBUILD, 1 REPLACE; priorities remain 22 P0, 10 P1, 5 P2. No baseline severity or status was downgraded merely because a document changed.

    Stage Rebuilt Targeted improvement only Unchanged
    First review pass 8 23 6
    After autonomous closure 37 0 0

    The 29 second-pass files are version 3.0. The original eight complete references remain in the version-2 series; ice/water teacher-tool and collection-capacity clarifications are version 2.1. Their primary material terms were normalized without claiming optional equipment is mandatory or rewriting their core objectives. The current audit preserves first-pass findings as history and states the subsequent closure separately in rationale/revision.

    A session-local copy of all 37 documents and the audit was saved before the second pass. Checks confirm the original paths, status, priority, meeting counts and native minutes are unchanged. Existing lesson URLs and the reported eight-kit school holding were preserved.

    What the autonomous pass closed¶

    • Removed conflicting legacy procedures rather than adding another override. Withdrawn high-shelf/pet/infant challenges, height races, unsafe sound options, glitter/small parts, live-release suggestions and unverified quotations are absent from the rewritten minimum pathways.
    • Supplied each reference's objective, purpose, quantities, setup, background, misconception/answer, timed sequence, individual evidence, support/challenge, safety, troubleshooting, indoor route, cleanup and family copy.
    • Implemented the six formerly audit-only checks: fall reflection, goals, school display, Thanksgiving, school-community art and weather.
    • Added two labeled weather records to the weekly practice arc and bi-weekly weather lesson; actual/teacher-sourced/model observations stay distinct.
    • Added a requested paper-book stand with two criteria and a tradeoff, not another unrestricted helper craft.
    • Added hypothetical private-information/adult-help checks in both schedules' school-community lessons. No real personal data are collected.
    • Made practice, service algorithms and privacy/community lessons CORE. Current scope is 30 CORE, 6 RECOMMENDED, 1 OPTIONAL across alternatives.
    • Normalized every K primary-material term to an explicit catalog entry; neither a name match nor a zero additional assembly price proves ownership.
