    Family communication system¶

    October 2026. C-STREAM is Catholic identity + science + technology + religion/faith integration + engineering + arts (including music) + mathematics. C shapes purpose/dignity/stewardship; R is explicit faith teaching/reflection. Music belongs within A; M means mathematics. Art involves observation, composition, form, performance or communication, not decoration alone.

    One copy system, not competing guides¶

    1. At unit launch, complete the newsletter block.
    2. At completion, change planned verbs to what students actually did and include a specific result/skill. Send an additional update when objectives change.
    3. Keep the teacher-only trace: lesson path, objective, selected local code, individual prompt and evidence threshold. Verify official/Church source claims separately. VERIFICATION REQUIRED for unverified quotations, diocesan requirements or biographies.
    4. Copy through the school's actual approved newsletter/email/paper route. Provide translation/read-aloud support as locally arranged; no invented platform.
    5. Keep learning at school. No routine homework, purchases, donations, accounts, outdoor exposure, home device, photo submission or event attendance required. All home activities below are optional, ungraded and can be skipped.

    Existing entry points Weekly Parent Sheet and Parent Communication Guide use the same block. Do not send two contradictory versions. If an exceptional required home task is proposed, document why it cannot reasonably happen in class, obtain school approval and provide an equally accessible school alternative; the default remains no routine homework.

    Ready-to-adapt unit examples for every grade¶

    These are example copy, not claims that these units have already been taught or an independent scope/sequence. Adapt to the actual band lesson and assessed objective. Do not claim device programming if the class used paper.

    Kindergarten - Notice and make patterns¶

    What we explored: Repeating patterns and careful observation. What students did: Sorted large classroom objects, built a two-part pattern and drew or pointed to its next part. What they learned: To notice a repeating unit and show what comes next. Our Catholic connection: We practiced caring for shared materials and giving each classmate a turn as we explored creation with gratitude. Ask your child: "Can you show the two parts of your pattern and what comes next?" Try this at home, optional: Make a clap-pause-clap-pause pattern together for one minute; use silent hand motions if sound is uncomfortable. No supplies.

    Teacher trace: each child completes/explains a pattern orally or by pointing; adult modeling/read-aloud replaces independent reading. Select the matching arts/math code from Local Standards.

    Grade 1 - Sound and rhythmic phrases¶

    What we explored: How a pattern of sound and silence makes a rhythmic phrase. What students did: Compared gentle tapping sounds and composed a four-beat phrase using claps and pauses. What they learned: To repeat a phrase and explain one intentional sound/silence choice. Music was an artistic activity, not just background noise. Our Catholic connection: We used our gifts to listen to and include one another; a silent pattern was an equally welcome response. Ask your child: "Can you perform your four beats and show where the pause is?" Try this at home, optional: Echo one four-beat phrase with hands or silent motions for a minute. No instruments or recording required.

    Teacher trace: individual phrase/repetition, not participation or singing talent; select the taught A/math/science competency only where evidenced.

    Grade 2 - Directions and debugging¶

    What we explored: Algorithms: ordered instructions, and how to fix an error. What students did: Used large arrow cards to move a paper pointer on a desk grid, tested the route, and changed an incorrect turn. What they learned: To explain how the changed instruction affected the route. This was unplugged computing, not a claim that software was programmed. Our Catholic connection: We considered how clear, respectful directions help other people and why responsibility matters when using tools. Ask your child: "Which arrow did you change, and where did the pointer go after that?" Try this at home, optional: Give a seated partner two safe hand-motion instructions, then reverse them and compare. No blindfold, walking maze or food.

    Teacher trace: individual sequence trace and correction; actual device execution is assessed later if it is a separate objective.

    Grade 3 - Paper bridges and fair comparisons¶

    What we explored: How changing a paper structure can change its performance. What students did: Planned, built, tested and improved paper bridges under common test conditions. What they learned: To name an observed result, keep test conditions the same, and explain a change using evidence, even when a bridge collapsed. Our Catholic connection: We considered how reliable structures serve people and why using shared materials responsibly matters. Ask your child: "What stayed the same in your two tests, and what did you change?" Try this at home, optional: Look at the shape of an ordinary book spine or folded paper already nearby and talk about what a fold might change. No building, weights, purchase or homework submission required.

    Teacher trace: use the rebuilt bridge lesson and its exact individual check; this copy does not impose a different span/load.

    Grade 4 - Indoor insulation and evidence¶

    What we explored: Comparing how materials affect temperature change. What students did: Used a teacher-prepared indoor comparison, measured at the same planned times and represented results on paper. What they learned: To compare temperature changes with units and describe what was held constant. Conclusions were limited to the classroom test. Our Catholic connection: We considered responsible resource use and how good evidence can inform care for people and creation. Ask your child: "Which comparison result supported your claim, and what stayed the same?" Try this at home, optional: Discuss why a familiar blanket may help keep a person warm. No heating, outdoor experiment or materials needed.

    Teacher trace: publish this only after the planned safe indoor investigation; no claim about outdoor testing, hot liquids or guaranteed material performance.

    Grade 5 - Closed electrical paths¶

    What we explored: What happens when a protected low-voltage circuit path is closed or opened. What students did: Took supervised turns connecting a protected AA pack and current-limited light module, then opened the path and compared outputs. What they learned: To identify a complete path and explain the observed change. Drawing a circuit alone was not the practical test. Our Catholic connection: We discussed using knowledge responsibly and caring for equipment and people rather than wasting energy or taking unsafe shortcuts. Ask your child: "What changed when the path opened, and which observation showed that?" Try this at home, optional: Point to a familiar room-light switch and discuss its purpose without opening it, handling batteries or touching wiring.

    Teacher trace: each child's actual supervised circuit action and explanation; record any missing hands-on evidence as NE.

    Grade 6 - Design choices for people¶

    What we explored: How criteria, cost and user needs influence a design. What students did: Compared classroom paper/model prototypes and communicated a design choice using measured evidence and a clear visual explanation. What they learned: To defend a choice and name a tradeoff or limitation. Our models were not certified devices or real-world solutions. Our Catholic connection: Human dignity and stewardship informed whom the design included and how resources were used. Ask your child: "Which result supported your choice, and who might need a different design?" Try this at home, optional: Discuss one familiar door handle or container: who might find it easy or difficult to use? No disability simulation, purchase or alteration of household equipment.

    Teacher trace: individual evidence/tradeoff explanation; select only practiced engineering, arts, math and Catholic competencies.

    Project/events/donations and privacy¶

    The school provides required materials and class work time. An optional event celebrates the same evidence, not family-funded polish. Invitations include a non-attendance route (in-class sharing or a generic newsletter summary). Requests for clean recyclables say explicitly: "Donations are optional; every student will have school-provided supplies." Staff screen all donated items.

    Use anonymous/general class descriptions by default. Student names, images, audio, scores and identifiable work require the school's verified consent/ privacy process; no public upload or personal account is assumed.

    Parent simulation¶

    A teacher can answer "What is my child learning?" with: a specific concept, student action, individual success evidence, Catholic decision and next learning step. A bare "fun craft" or "used an iPad" is insufficient. Progression/official alignment belongs to the shared review; local codes are not state or diocesan accreditation claims.

    What a row means¶

    Each traceability row connects a local program standard -> grade band -> schedule and rotation -> unit -> lesson -> planned assessment evidence. Filter the CSV by local_standard, grade_band, rotation and schedule. For example, filter CST-E2, 3-4, A, Weekly to find build/test/redesign opportunities and the evidence a teacher should collect.

    The combined-grade row does not imply identical expectations for both grades. Use the grade-specific performance descriptions in the progression and the support/challenge guidance in the lesson. Students may enter either rotation; introduce required procedures and vocabulary before increasing independence.

    The audit's status records the baseline disposition, while revision records subsequent changes. A lesson marked REBUILD and rebuilt has been revised; a baseline concern is not erased from the change record. improved is not a substitute-readiness certification. Read the band review and the actual lesson before scheduling.

    These are editorial alignment judgments about intended student work. They are not evidence that a class has mastered a standard. A general exit check may support only part of a competency; teachers must collect the individual performance evidence specified in the local progression.

    Material queries¶

    Filter the material-usage CSV by grade_band, schedule and rotation to see what the selected lessons name. item_id connects an exact canonical/alias name to the normalized inventory. This is text matching only, not verified reference_kind separates physical inventory from executable-platform access, teacher-prepared documentation and reported holdings. RESOURCE:* and STOCK:* references have no invented purchase price or verified ownership. Local access and hardware preflight remain explicit. A manufacturer manual is not the circuit kit, and a paper portfolio is not observed student mastery. This is text matching only, not verified item specifications, quantity sufficiency, ownership or safety. Unmatched and ambiguous terms are retained visibly for reconciliation rather than assigned an invented substitute. The inventory's verified-use count remains separate from these textual occurrences.

    The reconciliation queue groups remaining occurrences by exact term, grade and source lesson, with an explicit follow-up reason. A suggested triage category is not a supplier/item equivalence: software/access, record formats, quantity phrases, ambiguous adhesives and safety-critical parts still need their actual lesson specifications. It is a work queue, not a purchase list.

    Official standards claim gate¶

    Every generated external-alignment field is VERIFICATION REQUIRED. This is intentional, not a substitute for the source research. An official claim needs all of the following:

    1. Applicable adopted/implemented version and school year.
    2. Verified exact benchmark identifier, grade and source URL/document.
    3. Student action that actually practices the benchmark.
    4. Specific assessment evidence for the relevant part of the benchmark.
    5. Reviewer/date and any scope limitations.

    A topic resemblance, Catholic quotation, tag, device, or project photograph does not establish official alignment. This enrichment program does not replace the school's science, mathematics, arts, ELA, social studies or religion curricula.

    The separate exact external matrix now contains 29 source-specific candidates using sixteen identifiers. Its verified source scope and school/MDE-copy/national-framework boundaries are explicit. The general local-map field does not silently upgrade every other standard claim to official alignment.

    Updating and validating¶

    The four band-audit CSVs are the source of the combined maps. From the repository root in PowerShell:

    .\scripts\Build-CurriculumMaps.ps1
.\scripts\Build-CurriculumMaps.ps1 -ValidateOnly
.\scripts\Test-CurriculumMaps.ps1
.\scripts\Test-LessonReferences.ps1
mkdocs build --strict

    For the current K version-3.0 reference set, update lesson metadata and the individual-evidence definitions together, then run .\scripts\Sync-KindergartenAudit.ps1 and .\scripts\Test-KindergartenReferences.ps1 before regenerating the maps. The K validator checks 29 autonomous references/37 native meetings, class-size arithmetic and complete audit evidence; it does not approve physical kits or certify learning outcomes.

    The script fails explicitly on missing or duplicate lessons, invalid schema/enums, schedule/rotation mismatches, wrong period lengths, missing evidence fields and unknown local standard codes. It also verifies that every lesson file appears exactly once and all 18 codes exist in the catalog. It checks inventory identifier uniqueness and nonnegative prices/quantities, and produces a material-term index without guessing unresolved matches. -ValidateOnly also rejects missing or stale generated maps; run generation after editing the source audits or inventory and include those maps in the change. It does not infer official alignment, substitute usability, safety, developmental appropriateness or classroom mastery from a passing schema.

    The all-grade reference validator compares frozen baseline keys, requires a complete package for every selected lesson, checks actual local-code presence, contiguous native meeting intervals, class-size coverage and relative links. The band reviews retain the separate material-arithmetic/content desk checks. Structural validation is not an observed classroom trial.

    Kindergarten external standards: source-verified candidates¶

    Checked October 4, 2026 for 2026-27. This is progress beyond topic-level alignment, not a school approval, observed mastery or complete subject crosswalk.

    Download the source-specific candidate links. The initial twelve arts links use four exact arts identifiers; the completion pass adds four national-CS links using two directly verified CSTA 2026 codes. Each record states the actual task, individual planned evidence and source/ authority boundary rather than claiming full subject coverage.

    What was actually verified¶

    The workbook was downloaded directly from Perpich, Minnesota's state arts education agency. Its key identifies grade 0 as Kindergarten and the identifier positions as arts area, grade, strand, anchor standard and benchmark. Visual arts is area 5; music is area 3. The VisualArts sheet's Kindergarten rows 7-19 and the Music sheet's Kindergarten rows were inspected directly.

    Exact identifier Worksheet / row Concise paraphrase of the inspected requirement
    5.0.2.3.1 MN2018ArtsEdStandardsVisualArts / 9 Make art that communicates an idea through artistic foundations.
    5.0.2.4.1 MN2018ArtsEdStandardsVisualArts / 11 Identify choices in one's own original artwork.
    5.0.4.8.1 MN2018ArtsEdStandardsVisualArts / 16 Describe distinctions between images and real objects.
    3.0.2.3.1 MN2018ArtsEdStandardsMusic / 8 Choose a musical sound to share.

    These identifiers and their Kindergarten placement were seen in the source, not manufactured from another grade or inferred from a topic. Use the source register for the verified 2018 edition's implementation status and source classification.

    What remains conditional¶

    The workbook itself says the MDE-hosted Excel is the official version. The directly inspected state-agency copy establishes its displayed codes and content; a final MDE-copy corroboration and school curriculum review remain required before a formal program-wide official-alignment claim.

    Each proposed link was matched to the rewritten lesson's actual directions and evidence check. It is not a claim that pupils already demonstrated the benchmark. A table row must meet its stated scope:

    • Original art requires a child-created or child-directed representation. Merely selecting a supplied picture does not prove art creation.
    • A stated choice must concern the child's own artwork. Counting points or watching a teacher is not sufficient.
    • Image/object distinctions are visual-arts evidence, not proof of full science-standard coverage.
    • The music link requires a student-directed choice and sharing of an actual musical sound. Silent gestures or only rests can satisfy the local pattern route but do not establish that external sound-sharing benchmark.

    The CSV status deliberately separates source verification from institutional review and classroom outcomes. The generated local-standard map retains its general external-alignment verification hold and links here for these narrowly checked candidates.

    National CS follow-up¶

    The current CSTA viewer directly supplied EK-ALG-IM-03 and EK-DAT-DC-08 in its PK/K placement. The first concerns the human process of naming a goal, breaking it into smaller steps and ordering them; the gratitude/service algorithm references now model and individually check that process explicitly. The second concerns collecting data to answer an age-appropriate question with two or three variables/attributes. Actual cloud-category/time records can evidence this target with teacher help; invented model records cannot. Neither code is a Minnesota adoption claim, a requirement for an iPad or evidence of executing computer code.

    Science and mathematics: no guessed identifiers¶

    Normal retrieval of the final MDE science and 2007 mathematics documents on October 4 returned browser-verification pages, not readable benchmark tables. A normal integrated-browser attempt did not provide readable PDF text; its request API was unavailable. No challenge bypass or invented code was used. The attempted Revisor 3501.0710 is marked repealed, so it was not substituted for a current Kindergarten table; the attempted science section 3501.0970 returned 404.

    Exact science/math identifiers therefore remain VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Obtain the final applicable documents through normal authorized access and match the exact task/evidence. The 2007 mathematics planning baseline and 2027-28 transition date remain as documented in the source register.

    Factual content checks beyond standards¶

    The autonomous pass also directly inspected NASA stars, USDA monarch biology and CCC 638-645. New lesson language paraphrases rather than reproduces them. Stars/models, four living biological stages and Resurrection distinctions are kept separate. Unverified inherited quotations/biographies were omitted from the 29 rewritten minimum pathways rather than left beside contradictory source gates.

    Source-verified external alignment candidates¶

    Combined candidate matrix | Verified benchmark register | Authority and implementation register

    This matrix is separate from the local standards map. It provides exact external identifiers, individual grades, lesson tasks, planned evidence and claim boundaries. It is not full subject coverage, school/diocesan approval or proof that students mastered a benchmark.

    Sources and versions¶

    Minnesota arts, 2018¶

    The state-agency Perpich workbook was directly inspected, including exact Kindergarten and Grades 1-6 rows. The workbook defines grade 0 as K and shows arts area, grade, strand, anchor standard and benchmark in each identifier. The inspected identifiers are listed individually in the register, not manufactured from a grade pattern.

    The workbook itself identifies MDE's hosted Excel as the official version. The source-verified state-agency copy therefore retains a MDE-copy corroboration and school-review hold for formal institutional claims. Its 2018 edition is the implemented arts reference for 2026-27.

    A visual-design topic is insufficient. Proposed links require actual child-created or child-directed art, appropriate artistic foundations and the specific evidence the benchmark expects. A mechanical redesign alone is not artistic revision; a picture in a lesson is not evidence of art creation.

    CSTA national computer science, 2026¶

    The publisher's current viewer and its ordinary public index/detail responses were inspected directly. The exact identifiers, grade placement and clarifications are recorded in the register. Retrieval used the same unauthenticated read operations as the public viewer, not restricted materials or a login bypass.

    Elementary grades have separate identifiers; Grade 6 uses the 6-8 band. Do not reuse the 2017 elementary bands as 2026 grade organization. This is a verified national framework, not automatically adopted Minnesota or Archdiocesan standards.

    Respect the full scope:

    • Grade 2 algorithm creation includes sequence, events and repetition.
    • Grade ¾ mappings cover sequence, events, repetition and selection across one or more algorithms, with the appropriate written/visual representation.
    • Grade 5's representation includes variables and the required structures.
    • The selected middle-school correctness benchmark needs a given algorithm, specified inputs, expected/actual outputs and verification by trace or execution.
    • Paper can evidence permitted tracing/conceptual work, but never actual software execution or robot/sensor operation.

    Partial practice is described as partial or omitted from a full benchmark claim. A named code, apparatus or teacher demonstration cannot supply missing individual evidence.

    Source-specific records¶

    • K evidence and limits
    • Grades 1-2 candidate data
    • Grades 3-4 candidate data
    • Grades 5-6 candidate data

    The matrix gives each grade's evidence rather than assigning both grades in a band the same external expectation. Access supports can preserve a target; when an alternative changes it, record the scope and deferred evidence.

    Unavailable official tables¶

    Normal retrieval of final MDE science, mathematics, ELA and social-studies tables did not provide readable source documents. Browser-verification HTML is not the underlying standard, and a repealed rule or NGSS/Common Core identifier is not a substitute. No guessed external number is published. Use the local framework for the taught enrichment outcomes and withhold unsupported official coverage claims pending authorized source access.

    The school release checklist identifies the remaining institutional/source checks without blocking documented safe local learning simply because an unsupported external claim is withheld.

    Regeneration and verification¶

    .\scripts\Build-CurriculumMaps.ps1
.\scripts\Build-ExternalAlignment.ps1
.\scripts\Build-ExternalAlignment.ps1 -ValidateOnly

    The external builder checks exact source IDs/URLs/editions, grade placement, lesson existence/band, required scope/evidence, authority boundaries, duplicate links and generated-matrix freshness against the source-verified register. Editorial task/evidence review and actual classroom assessment remain separate.

    Curriculum gap analysis¶

    A gap can be missing content, insufficient depth, missing individual evidence, an unsuitable prerequisite, or an unusable teaching procedure. The existence of a file or tag does not close it. The detailed band reviews and audit rationale fields provide the lesson-level evidence.

    Autonomous K closure: all 37 K documents are complete references, with dated weather comparison, hypothetical privacy/adult-help scenarios, requested book criteria/tradeoffs and formerly audit-only individual checks implemented. Every K primary-material term is cataloged; twelve arts candidates have exact source-verified identifiers. This closes those document-level gaps, not actual school stock, official full-subject coverage or observed mastery.

    All-grade closeout: the other 214 lesson documents are also complete conditional references. Fair retests, individual checks, grade-specific support/challenge, complete timed sequences and explicit material/pathway boundaries replace the earlier package queues. Baseline weaknesses remain historical evidence, not a claim that every old defect is still active. Full external subject coverage and actual mastery remain separate checks.

    Program-wide gaps and controls¶

    Area to investigate Baseline concern or evidence limit Improvement and closure evidence
    Official standards No structured, verified benchmark-to-task-to-assessment map in the baseline Source register and local map added; official benchmark alignment remains VERIFICATION REQUIRED until reviewed against the applicable version.
    Grade progression Combined-grade activities do not automatically define seven distinct expectations Local K-6 performance progression; collect individual evidence at the younger/older expectation rather than awarding mastery for exposure.
    Pacing Legacy planner/menu totals double-count time and extend beyond the claimed year Corrected calendar and document-level meeting records; compare the chosen track with the actual school timetable.
    Substitute usability General guide refers to quick-reference packets without proving they exist Revised reference lessons and common template; complete remaining scheduled P1 lessons and conduct actual kit walkthroughs.
    Early readers Written journals, vocabulary and independent directions can hide a reading prerequisite Model, point, draw, tell and manipulate; verify an emerging reader can meet the objective without another child doing the thinking.
    Devices and computing Equipment/app use can be mistaken for computational thinking Require an algorithm trace/debugging explanation; distinguish that from real digital execution and hardware operation.
    Indoor access Nature, weather and growth topics do not guarantee an indoor pathway Specify the indoor procedure and objective; prepared data/models must not be described as a child's firsthand measurement.
    Materials/cost Specialty kits and assumed school stocks obscure a minimum budget Normalized core inventory, budget ceilings and kits; verify local stock and distinguish optional legacy equipment from core purchases.
    Assessment Group products and participation can hide individual understanding A named oral/drawn/demonstrated evidence check and objective-linked rubric for each scheduled lesson.
    Catholic identity Prayers, metaphors, saint references and technological enthusiasm are not enough Students give an age-appropriate reason about truth, dignity, stewardship or service; verify historical/scriptural attributions.
    Arts Digital tools and decoration can replace genuine artistic learning Observational sketches, purposeful form/pattern, communication, feedback and artistic revision; assess the stated art objective, not polish.
    Homework/equity Take-home continuation can make household support a hidden prerequisite No routine homework; class evidence and optional no-purchase family questions.
    Safety "Safe materials," unspecified samples and small electrical parts are not sufficient controls Exact approved supplies, adult-only steps, stop rules and local policy checks; hold unresolved P0 activities.
    Year A/B continuity A returning student's changed project does not prove more sophisticated reasoning Reestablish prerequisites in either entry year; preserve a small portfolio and increase independence/evidence, not simply product size.

    Content questions that must not disappear¶

    The repository has named activities in physical, life and Earth science, structures, weather, light/circuits, robots/coding, art and service. This is evidence of available contexts, not complete subject coverage. Use the lesson map to locate intended evidence, then check the following across the selected schedule and both rotation entry years:

    Competency Minimum closure evidence
    Electricity before middle school A safe, age-appropriate complete/open-circuit investigation with an explanation; neither a craft light nor a robot alone proves understanding.
    Data interpretation Each student interprets a table, graph or organized comparison appropriate to the grade.
    Measurement progression Count/compare -> consistent unit -> record/compare -> repeated measurements -> justified precision and limitations.
    Engineering redesign An actual second test after a justified change, not only a drawing of an imagined improvement.
    Life science Observations or an explicitly labeled model explain living things, change or interdependence; plants need follow-up time.
    Earth/space science Evidence/modeling of weather, seasonal change or systems, with a scientifically accurate explanation.
    Physical science Students investigate an effect such as force, motion, light, sound, energy or circuits rather than only name it.
    Unplugged computing Students trace, predict, debug or revise instructions; later grades encounter loops/conditions/data as appropriate.
    Technology ethics A reasoned decision about users, accessibility, resources, privacy or impacts; not just a device rule list.
    Catholic scientific heritage A verified, relevant example with a distinction between biography, Church teaching and scientific evidence.
    Stewardship A concrete decision about reuse, waste, care or service and a student explanation.
    Hands-on mathematics Quantities/measurements/data used to reason about the activity, not decorative numbers.
    Student choice A choice within understandable criteria/constraints, followed by a reason.
    Independent and collaborative work Team activity plus an individual check; roles do not permanently assign one child all reasoning or tool use.
    Communication A drawing, model, oral explanation or display communicates evidence to an audience and receives feedback.
    Learning from failure Students describe what a test showed, change an appropriate feature and try again without blaming the student.

    Do not "fill a gap" by adding another topic title. Identify the exact grade, rotation, meeting, student action and evidence; reduce competing activities if necessary. The scope and sequence prioritizes fewer, better investigations.

    Band-level evidence and next work¶

    • Kindergarten: nonreader access, short-period routines, observation/manipulation and safe indoor options.
    • Grades 1-2: oral-to-recorded explanation, instructional sequences, measured comparison and accessible design choices.
    • Grades 3-4: fair tests, data, real redesign and grade-appropriate arithmetic.
    • Grades 5-6: systems, evidence quality, computing, inclusive design and justified tradeoffs.

    See the implementation plan for priorities and teaching-release gates. A desk review cannot certify that any of these competencies has been mastered by actual students.

    Prioritized implementation and change record¶

    The repository review implements high-value changes rather than stopping at recommendations. It does not certify every legacy activity as classroom-ready, every official benchmark as covered, or the school's actual inventory as sufficient.

    Priorities and release conditions¶

    Priority Work Owner to assign locally Release evidence
    P0 - Must fix Unsafe or unspecified materials/procedures, inaccurate attribution, unverified required official-standard claims, unusable primary instructions Principal/safety lead and teacher Read the revised activity; identify hazards, stop rules and exact supplies. Remove or correct inaccurate claims. Hold unresolved P0 activities.
    P1 - High priority Complete remaining substitute directions, individual assessment, grade-specific prerequisites, low-tech/indoor alternatives and pacing Curriculum lead and grade teachers A second adult can teach from the document/kit; native period includes evidence and cleanup; younger/older expectations are explicit.
    P2 - Improvement Refine kits, replenishment counts, arts choices, data follow-up, accessibility and family communication Teachers and materials coordinator Pilot notes show a workable setup, each student's evidence and realistic resource use.
    P3 - Enhancement Additional robotics, software, digital creation, external visits and elaborate exhibitions Program lead A documented objective makes the additional cost/time worthwhile; privacy, availability and accessibility are approved.

    The audit's P0/P1 labels record baseline priority. A revised baseline P0 lesson can be released only after reviewing the revised procedure, not merely because its CSV says improved or rebuilt.

    Final completion gate¶

    Do not label the entire program "substitute-proof" until every scheduled core lesson has passed the document/kit walkthrough and classroom pilot. The written package queues are closed; this gate refers to real local release evidence, not another unimplemented lesson-outline backlog. The seven simulations are necessary desk checks; actual student learning and classroom timings need observed evidence.

    Seven required simulations¶

    Simulation Concrete written pathway and correction Desk result and remaining local check
    1. Substitute arrives 20 minutes before Grade 3 Bridge Engineering has a 40-minute sequence, pretest, fair load method and individual evidence. Handoff uses its conservative 13-kit allocation rather than nine generic kits. Conditional pass with prepared kit; check real location, counts, room, accommodations and pretest. Use the named different fallback if unavailable and record deferred objectives.
    2. K child cannot read All K minimum pathways use oral/picture modeling, pointing/dictation and child-directed manipulation. K routines define actual pair/trio turns. Document pass; reading/handwriting not prerequisites. Actual access needs and individual evidence still require teacher observation.
    3. iPads unavailable Every lesson identifies its primary requirement and named fallback. Algorithms/models remain distinct from real execution/operation. Local low-tech learning continues; required software/robot/sensor operation is deferred, not falsely awarded from paper or watching.
    4. Minnesota January, -10 F All reference packages state indoor routes; actual/supplied/model weather observations are labeled. Growth/care and wet cleanup are explicit. Document pass for indoor learning; do not report model data as measured weather. School plant care, hygiene and room conditions still need checks.
    5. Enrollment reaches 25 Exact class-size allocations, role turns and concurrent checks replace serial queues. Generic groups use seven trios/two pairs; pair-based lessons keep their larger kit budget. Snap uses bounded station/wave plans. Arithmetic/logistics pass; real room, inspection throughput, supplies and processing needs are untested. Unobserved evidence remains unobserved.
    6. Limited funding Modest no-device core and reusable kits; purchase ceilings verified without assuming donations/loans or all specialty gear. Conditional budget pass; verify stock/prices/specifications and the chosen track's consumption. Safe procurement is not improvised to preserve a price.
    7. Parent asks what is learned Each reference has family copy, an objective/evidence threshold and grade support/challenge. Progression and maps explain increasing sophistication. Document pass; explain what actually happened and was demonstrated, not just planned targets or group participation. Home invitations remain optional.

    School release checklist¶

    Repository completion means a complete written pathway, traceable planned evidence and passing document checks. It does not establish physical kit condition, the school's permissions, individual access needs or actual learning. These are concrete checks the school can complete, not more curriculum reports to commission.

    Before the selected lesson¶

    Check Responsible role to assign Record before release
    Calendar and objective Grade teacher One schedule/rotation; actual date, native period, core objective and chosen physical/device/paper pathway.
    Counted kit Teacher/materials coordinator Actual location, issue/return quantities for the enrolled class, missing/damaged items and teacher-only tools. A catalogue name or report is not a count.
    Safe materials School safety lead/teacher Condition, allergies, ingredients, age guidance, water/hygiene, tool restrictions and activity-specific stop rules.
    Electrical pretest, if used Qualified school adult Matching model/manual/project, safe supply/covers/protection, correct approved diagram and successful inspection/test. No invented Snap component or battery allocation.
    Device/access pretest, if used School technology lead Approved actual host/app/version, privacy/account/accessibility settings, executable test and working turn plan.
    Individual access Teacher/support staff Reading, motor, sensory, language and physical accommodations preserving the target; consent for physical assistance.
    Prepared content Teacher Exact source/model-data/picture content, no unverified biography/quotation and no personal student data in fictional scenarios.
    Handoff Teacher/substitute Kit and lesson together, actual school contact, objective check, cleanup and fallback. First-use kit construction/charging/freezing happens beforehand.

    If an essential condition fails, hold that pathway. Use only the named alternative, state its changed objective and record deferred evidence. Paper reasoning cannot release actual software execution, robot operation, circuit construction, live observations or measured weather.

    Pilot evidence: collect, do not assume¶

    Pilot at least one younger-grade and one older-grade complete reference, then the next scheduled unit. Record:

    1. Actual first/repeat preparation and in-class transition/cleanup minutes.
    2. Correct material allocation and actual consumption/returns.
    3. Each child's objective-linked demonstration and support used.
    4. Whether every child received a meaningful choice/tool/test turn.
    5. Unexpected safety, accessibility, space or timing constraints.
    6. The one change needed before the next use.

    Compare the written threshold with the actual result: for example, a structure held ten seconds unaided, a two-command route was correctly predicted and debugged, or a child explained a recorded change using evidence. Do not replace a missing result with participation, photographs or a certificate. Use two dated individual observations where the local progression specifies an expected-mastery checkpoint.

    Source and institutional review¶

    • Confirm the school's 2026-27 mathematics baseline/transition decision.
    • Obtain school-issued OMCE religion/culture policies and applicable curriculum expectations through authorized school channels.
    • Obtain inaccessible final MDE benchmark tables before restoring exact science/mathematics/ELA/social-studies claims.
    • Corroborate state-agency arts copies against the MDE official edition for a formal institutional alignment claim.
    • Treat CSTA 2026 as a verified national framework, not automatically adopted Minnesota or Archdiocesan standards.
    • Use only the precise task/evidence scope of an external-candidate mapping. A source-verified identifier is not proof the pupil mastered it.

    The local C-STREAM competencies can guide teaching while these formal external claims remain withheld. They complement, not replace, primary subject curricula.

    Reported eight Snap Circuits kits¶

    The holding reports eight individual OHM-135 kits. Record actual manufacturer model, matching instructions, completeness, condition and age/power approval for each SC01-SC08. The classroom guide gives the bounded wave plan and evidence checks. An out-of-service kit is not a station; one wave cannot serve 25 pupils in eight groups of at most three. K remains optional adult-demonstration only.

    Initial evidence, not conclusions about every lesson¶

    • A Kindergarten robotics unit requires charged, paired robots and iPads. Direction, prediction and sequencing can also be taught physically; actual robot-operation objectives must remain distinct from an unplugged fallback.
    • A Grades 1-2 bridge session labels a papal bridge metaphor as Scripture. That attribution is inaccurate and needs correction, not repetition.
    • A Grades 3-4 bridge lesson includes efficiency ratios without establishing whether those calculations fit the younger grade's prerequisites.
    • A Grades 5-6 forensic session leaves sample preparation, "safe" unknown substances and fictional evidence unspecified. A substitute needs a complete, non-accusatory investigation with no unknown powders or real student profiling.
    • The general substitute guide asks for a quick-reference card without proving that such a card exists for every activity.
    • Home, planning and template pages emphasize digital art. Art also needs purposeful observational drawing, model design, pattern, composition and communication without a device.
    • Materials guidance mixes classroom basics with specialty robots, loan kits and apps. Availability, quantities, annual consumables and minimum operating cost must be separated.

    Audit method and change policy¶

    Four grade-band workstreams inspect every lesson, record baseline findings, and make targeted improvements before publishing their audit. A separate standards workstream verifies authoritative sources. Program integration uses these records rather than inferring alignment from lesson titles or tags.

    The internal mapping is grade -> rotation/schedule -> unit -> lesson -> demonstrated skills/local standards -> materials -> assessment. Evidence records distinguish original quality from the revision state.

    Audit dispositions are KEEP, KEEP + IMPROVE, REBUILD, REPLACE and REMOVE. No file is deleted merely because an alternative is preferred. Recommendations retain useful activities and identify safety, accuracy and substitute-readiness issues first.

    Quality uses four evidence levels: 0 absent/unsafe, 1 named but underspecified, 2 teachable with a specific support or remaining check, 3 explicit and independently usable. Dimensions include academic rigor, developmental fit, Catholic integration, standards evidence, hands-on engagement, instruction/substitute clarity, low-tech access, cost/preparation, assessment, inclusion, safety, scalability, family communication and progression. Scores are editorial judgments, not classroom-outcome measurements.

    Verification limits: A document review cannot certify actual school inventory, individual accommodations, equipment condition, classroom outcomes, diocesan approval or complete coverage of the primary subject curricula. Unverified official benchmarks are marked VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

    Getting Started

    C-STREAM quick start guide¶

    October 2026. C = Catholic identity; S = science; T = technology; R = religion/faith integration; E = engineering; A = arts including music; M = mathematics. Catholic purpose shapes choices, not only opening prayer. Art involves observation, composition, form, pattern or communication, not just decoration/digital tools.

    Before the first meeting¶

    1. Confirm weekly/bi-weekly schedule and A/B rotation with the school. Use the lesson index; do not assume the same Week 1 filename or commercial-kit schedule for every band.
    2. Read the actual lesson objective, background, vocabulary, safety, individual check and timed sequence. Use the common lesson format.
    3. Confirm supplies and location with inventory checklist. Default 10/15/20/25 pupils = ⅘/7/9 teams <=3. School provides required supplies.
    4. Perform the teacher pretest and count trays. Have the substitute fallback ready.
    5. Prepare family copy. No routine homework.
    Grade Native period Protect inside this time
    K 25 minutes Oral modeling, each child's action/evidence, 3-minute cleanup
    1-2 30 minutes Hands-on turns/test/redesign, individual check, 3-minute cleanup
    3-4 40 minutes Evidence-based testing/redesign, individual check, 3-minute cleanup
    5-6 45 minutes Reasoning/tradeoffs, individual check, 4-minute cleanup

    Your first two weeks¶

    Start with a completed band lesson, not a generic untimed welcome sequence. Model "notice -> try -> tell"; nonreader card. State "Today I can..." and give every child a turn to show the objective. Next meeting, use observation/design/measurement appropriate to prerequisites. Failure in engineering is information, not failure of a student.

    If a source question arises, say "We need to check that" and record VERIFICATION REQUIRED. The Catholic heritage guide is background for source checking, not a mandatory biography every lesson. No internet image search, unlicensed image or unverified quotation is needed.

    If conditions change¶

    • Time short: stop new construction; keep individual evidence and cleanup.
    • Kit absent: use the named safe fallback, recording any objective change.
    • Devices absent: unplugged concepts still work; real programming/robot execution evidence must be deferred, not claimed from drawings.
    • Unsafe materials/weather: stop and use a seated indoor task; notify the responsible school adult if safety needs escalation.

    Next links: materials plan, technology plan, assessment, FAQ, differentiation, templates.

    📚 Master Lesson Distribution¶

    Count meetings, not project labels¶

    For the weekly scaffold: 13 + 13 + 6 = 32 teaching meetings, plus two break slots. The earlier single-week/multi-week/long-arc quotas double-counted time and must not be added together.

    Choose the actual grade/rotation documents, total their planned meetings, then compare with the school's calendar. Use unexpected spare meetings for retesting, individual evidence and artistic revision. If meetings are lost, reduce project scope rather than removing assessment or cleanup.

    Conversation Starters by Unit Type¶

    For Robotics/Coding Weeks: - "Can you show me how you programmed the robot?" - "What went wrong and how did you fix it?" - "How can robots help people?"

    For Building/Engineering Weeks: - "What made your structure strong?" - "If you could rebuild it, what would you change?" - "Who might use something like what you built?"

    For Science/Exploration Weeks: - "What was the most surprising thing you learned?" - "What do you wonder about now?" - "How does this show us God's amazing creation?"

    Parent Quick Explanations¶

    What is C-STREAM?

    C-STREAM stands for Catholic Science, Technology, Religion, Engineering, Art & Music, and Mathematics. It's like STEM, but with Catholic faith woven throughout. Your child learns that faith and science work together to understand God's amazing world.

    Why Catholic STEM?

    Catholic education has always valued both faith and reason. We help students see that the same God who inspired the Psalms also created the laws of physics. Learning about creation helps us know and love the Creator.

    How can I help at home?

    Ask questions! Show curiosity about what your child is learning. Point out science and engineering in everyday life. Wonder aloud about how things work. Most importantly, help your child see God in the amazing world around them.

    ✅ Assessment & Progress¶

    Evidence of learning, not participation percentages¶

    Evidence What to assess
    Individual oral explanation, drawing or demonstration The stated science, mathematics, computing or design objective
    Test record and revision Whether the student uses evidence to explain an improvement
    Ethical or stewardship choice An age-appropriate reason about people/resources, not the child's personal piety
    Collaboration and effort Record separately from mastery; successful group work does not prove every student's understanding

    Use a simple objective-linked rubric and the local progression. Do not grade handwriting, artistic polish or reading proficiency unless it is the actual objective.

    Progress Tracking¶

    Each trimester, assess: - [ ] STEM skill development - [ ] Faith integration understanding - [ ] Collaboration growth - [ ] Wonder and curiosity cultivation

    C-STREAM FAQ and troubleshooting¶

    October 2026. Start with Quick Start and a completed lesson template. Generalist teachers can teach a clear lesson; not every legacy file is ready. Confirm rotation/calendar and the actual lesson rather than promising no repetition or universal substitute-readiness.

    Time and classroom management¶

    Running long? Stop new construction, retain the individual check and cleanup, store dry labeled work and continue next meeting. Do not delete evidence collection to add an extra activity or prayer.

    Finished early? Ask for a repeated fair test, alternative constraint or explanation of evidence. Faster pupils are not automatically unpaid helpers.

    Students excited/arguing? Give instructions before materials, use a stop signal, assign builder/tester/reporter and rotate actual turns. Ask each to show an idea and test alternatives under the same conditions. Refer persistent behavior/safety concerns through actual school procedures.

    A child needs more time? Model one step, reduce choices, pre-cut/larger materials, allow gesture/voice/scribe/quiet or seated response. Keep the concept criterion unless documenting an explicit objective change.

    Missing supplies or technology¶

    Problem Safe response Learning limit
    Building blocks absent Paper/cardstock/sticks with a stated new constraint Compare evidence; do not silently claim identical load capacity
    Robot/app/host unavailable Desk-grid arrow cards and pointer Sequence/debugging concepts only; execution/robot mastery deferred
    Internet absent Teacher-vetted read-aloud source or confirmed offline tool Actual online/source-navigation objective may change
    Some devices work Document turn/reset time, smaller test rotations or more meetings Each child needs individual real-device evidence if that is O1
    Electrical gear damaged Switch off/disconnect; OUT OF SERVICE; safe paper-path model Paper path is not practical circuit-building mastery
    No safe materials or weather Seated observation fallback Record actual observation objective, not unperformed investigation

    Do not open personal accounts, install unapproved apps, bypass safeguards or improvise power supplies. Technology Plan. Borrowing lead times/fees/stock are VERIFICATION REQUIRED, not guaranteed two-week free access. Library planning.

    Assessment¶

    How do I grade? Use the objective -> prompt -> success condition -> individual evidence chain. Project rubric. Participation, effort, handwriting, neatness and confidence are not mastery. An artistic criterion is used only for an explicit arts objective.

    What if the model fails? A child can still explain valid evidence and redesign. A successful team model does not prove each member understands. NE means not yet evidenced; unobserved/absent/device-blocked is not a zero.

    How much paperwork? Short roster evidence during work plus one exit check; review termly with Progress Tracker. Named records/photos follow verified school privacy/consent practice; do not assume a digital account or public portfolio.

    Faith, arts and grade differences¶

    Faith connection feels forced? Use a concrete Catholic decision about dignity, truth, stewardship or service. R identifies the explicit reflection. Prayer supports but does not substitute for this purpose. Verify Church quotations, biographies and standards; never make an experiment theological proof.

    Hard science/faith question? Acknowledge uncertainty, distinguish observation from belief/interpretation and consult the verified source record or appropriate school faith educator. Avoid a simplistic "science only how, faith only why" rule or "God is an engineer" analogy.

    What does A mean? Arts including music: observational drawing, composition, visual communication, form, rhythmic phrases and performance, not just digital art/decoration. M means mathematics.

    K cannot read? Use Show, Try, Tell. An attempt is welcome but does not automatically demonstrate the concept. Assess pointing/sorting/building/telling with the same explicit success condition.

    Mixed grades / older students need challenge? Same materials can support different evidence expectations; use the shared progression and actual prerequisites. Add repeat trials, constraints, measurement or tradeoffs, not untaught ratio work or leadership as a substitute for subject learning.

    Safety and families¶

    No button cells, latex balloons or projectiles in the core; no neodymium magnets in K. Stop unsafe activities, isolate hazards and contact the school's responsible adult. Possible battery/magnet ingestion needs urgent emergency escalation. Use indoor alternatives in unsafe Minnesota conditions.

    No routine homework, required donations or home purchase/device. Explain concept + action + evidence + Catholic choice using family communication.

    🔄 Curriculum Flexibility Options¶

    C-STREAM offers flexible scheduling to meet your school's needs:

    Year A / Year B Rotation (Grades 1-6)¶

    For schools with combined grade classrooms (1-2, 3-4, 5-6), we provide a two-year rotation:

    • Year A: Complete curriculum with one set of projects and contexts

    • Year B: Same skills and concepts with different projects, saints, and applications

    Core competencies intentionally recur with increasing independence. Contexts vary, but the grade reviews identify actual overlaps and prerequisites. Kindergarten does not require Year A/B since students advance to 1st grade.

    Weekly vs. Bi-Weekly Scheduling¶

    • Weekly (34 calendar slots): Check multi-week meetings and holidays against the grade review; this is not 34 lesson files.

    • Bi-Weekly (17 sessions): Condensed curriculum for schools with STREAM every other week

    🙏 Catholic Identity Integration¶

    Catholic integration is expressed through age-appropriate truth, wonder, dignity, stewardship and service. Prayer or a saint reference alone does not establish a meaningful connection. Review and verify any historical or scriptural attribution. Existing lessons may include:

    • Opening Prayer — Connected to lesson theme

    • Scripture Connection — Relevant Bible verse

    • Wonder Question — Sparking curiosity about God's creation

    • Catholic Scientist — When applicable, historical Catholic STEM contributors

    • Faith Reflection — Closing connection to Catholic teaching

    Review and readiness¶

    See the Kindergarten review and complete 37-row audit. Weekly and bi-weekly are alternative schedules, not lessons to combine into one year. Existing URLs remain unchanged.

    All 20 weekly documents are now complete instructional references after the autonomous closeout. Use the K teacher/substitute routines and the actual lesson's quantities and checks. This is document readiness, not physical-kit approval or classroom certification.

    Source/readiness gate: inherited unverified quotations/biographies were omitted from the rewritten minimum paths. Use school-approved religion sources for any optional reading. The source-verified arts candidates remain subject to MDE-copy/school review; exact science/math alignment and Archdiocesan approval are not implied. CST codes are local.

    Safety gate: use the selected reference's single minimum pathway and named alternative; no withdrawn activity list is a substitute plan. Check actual supplies, accommodations and school hygiene policy. No routine homework or family donations/purchases are required.

    Quantity convention: for 10/15/20/25 pupils, pairs with a final trio make 5/7/10/12 active teams. Supply tables budget ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve kit for odd enrollment. Kit totals are not a claim that 25 pupils form 13 pairs/trios.

    📋 Kindergarten Pacing Notes¶

    • Shorter activities with clear transitions

    • Guided exploration with teacher modeling

    • Hands-on materials whenever possible

    • Partner work rather than large groups

    • Simple vocabulary with visual supports

    • Safe movement options only when clocked; the minimum pathways are seated/accessibly directed

    📚 Materials Overview¶

    Minimum reusable classroom supplies (availability must be checked)¶

    • Paper, crayons, large picture/arrow cards and teacher-drawn grids

    • Ordinary wooden blocks or KEVA: up to 260 blocks for 25 pupils

    • Flashlights with secured battery compartments: up to 13 pair kits plus teacher light

    • Smooth cardboard, paper cups, tape, glue sticks and large paper shapes

    • Individual drawing/dictation records; enclosed adult-managed seed cups

    Optional additions; no checkout or class-set device prerequisite¶

    • One Dash/tablet or Sphero/tablet for teacher-controlled demonstrations or supervised real-hardware evidence

    • ScratchJr only when school-approved and pretested; paper algorithm pathway supplied

    • No Little Bits/circuit kit is needed for the light-transmission lesson; circuits are not assessed there

    🎯 Kindergarten Learning Goals¶

    By the end of the year, kindergarten students will be able to:

    STEM Skills¶

    • Follow a simple design process (think, plan, create, test)

    • Explain tool input/output and test picture algorithms; real robot operation/programming only when individually demonstrated

    • Make observations about the natural world

    • Build simple structures and test them

    • Recognize patterns in math and nature

    Faith Integration¶

    • Understand that learning about the world helps us know God better

    • Practice gratitude for God's creation

    • Show kindness and help others through STREAM work

    • Wonder at the beauty and order of creation

    21st Century Skills¶

    • Work cooperatively with a partner

    • Share ideas with the class

    • Try again when something doesn't work

    • Ask questions about how things work

    Week 1: Welcome to C-STREAM¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Welcome and observation / one 25-minute meeting
    Domains / big idea S, A; a detail we notice is different from a question we want to investigate
    Student objective / why "I can show a detail and ask a question." Scientists begin by noticing and wondering.
    Catholic connection Wonder at creation and respectful listening; use the source guidance in the routines below.
    Local standards CST-S1: observed detail/question; CST-A3: picture/oral communication. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 5 minutes / 4 minutes included

    Before class and exact materials¶

    Read K routines. Make 5/7/10/12 active pair/trio teams; budget ⅝/10/13 kits at 10/15/20/25 pupils. Draw one large leaf with visible branching lines on each kit's half-sheet. Alternatively use an adult-inspected clean large leaf; pictures avoid allergies.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: large leaf drawing 5 8 10 13
    Student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: timer, roster, crayon and one demonstration drawing reused from a kit. No letter cards, slideshow, purchased journal or printing required.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Observe: notice a detail. Question: something we want to find out. Represent: show an idea with a picture, gesture or words. Misconception: a guess is a detail we saw. Point to the actual drawing. If asked "Why does a leaf have lines?" Say that living leaves have veins that transport water and other materials; our drawing is a model, not a live leaf.

    Exact sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Invite wonder and a short original prayer if customary. Say C-STREAM is a time to notice, make, test and care; acronym recall is not the target.
    2. 4-8: Model "I see a line" versus "I wonder what the line does." Point to the evidence. Draw the detail, not a perfect leaf.
    3. 8-17: Partners inspect, swap pointing roles and each draw/select a detail. Ask "What can you point to?" Begin individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child points to a genuine detail and asks/selects one question. Offer "What does this part do?" or "Are all leaves alike?" Record support.
    5. 21-25: Two children share; retain dated sheets; count drawings and crayons; clear tables. Thank partners for listening.

    Success, access and SAFETY¶

    Success: each child connects a picture/gesture to an actual detail and a question. Do not score enthusiasm, letters or drawing realism. Support: offer two details; scribe an oral question. Challenge: ask how a question could be checked. Large pictures only for mouthing/allergy concerns; no taste, close smelling or collecting. Fully indoors.

    If things go wrong and family copy¶

    No leaf/drawing: draw a plain leaf with three branching lines on the board. Child only guesses: ask where the claimed feature appears; keep the question. Early finish: compare a partner's representation. Follow the routines' cleanup. Family: We noticed a detail and asked a question. Ask, "What did you actually see, and what do you still wonder?" No routine homework or supplies required.

    kindergartenroboticsalgorithms

    Weeks 2-3: Exploring Movement with Sphero¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / title K / Movement and instructions / Exploring Movement with Sphero
    Time Two meetings, each 25 minutes, including cleanup
    Meaningful domains C, T, M
    Big idea A tool responds to input; an algorithm is an ordered set of steps.
    Student objective "I can predict a two-step path, try it, and fix one step."
    Why Clear directions and checking results help us use tools responsibly.
    Catholic connection Include every partner in making decisions; tools should benefit people, not exclude them. CCC 2405, teacher paraphrase.
    Local standards CST-C2, CST-T1, CST-T2, CST-M1; local program codes, never official benchmarks. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology requirement Optional: picture-grid pathway is primary; real Sphero driving extends tool input/output.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Beginner / Light: 10 minutes for paper kits; optional robot setup 20 minutes plus charging / 3 minutes inside each meeting

    Before class¶

    1. Make 5/7/10/12 teams for 10/15/20/25 students: pairs, with a final trio for odd enrollment. Prepare ⅝/10/13 kits; the extra kit at 15/25 is a reserve. Assign chooser, mover, and checker; swap roles after each trial.
    2. Draw one 3-by-3 grid per pair, with 10 cm squares. Mark the lower-left square START and the upper-left square FINISH. Draw another target one square right of START. No printing is necessary.
    3. Make four large cards per pair: two upward arrows, one right arrow, one STOP hand. Here arrows mean one square up the page/right on the page, not a robot's facing direction.
    4. Draw a paper robot at least 8 cm wide per pair. Place kits at seated tables and write a roster with columns A (algorithm), I (input/output), H (real hardware drive), P (real programming).
    5. Optional hardware: use one school-approved, charged Sphero and one paired tablet. Before children arrive, open the installed Sphero Edu version, select the robot, enter Drive, aim/calibrate toward the far end, and test its lowest practical speed and stop control. Keep a 1 m clear demonstration lane and an adult beside it. If pairing or safe stopping fails, omit hardware. A substitute need not troubleshoot Bluetooth during class.

    Supplies and exact quantities¶

    Supply / allocation 10 15 20 25
    Per student: half-sheet observation paper; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each
    Per pair/team: grid; large paper robot 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each
    Per pair/team: four command cards 20 32 40 52
    Class: large demonstration grid and robot 1 each 1 each 1 each 1 each
    Teacher: roster, timer 1 each 1 each 1 each 1 each

    Optional class supplies, any enrollment: one robot, one tablet, one roll painter's tape. There is no class-set purchase or family donation requirement. Reuse grids/cards in meeting 2.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    • Input: what we give a tool; point to an arrow or control.
    • Output: what the tool does; move the paper robot.
    • Algorithm: steps in order; point left to right along cards.
    • Debug: find a mismatch, change a step, try again.

    A paper model follows the stated grid rule because a person moves it. In Drive mode an adult steers continuously; this is operating hardware, not writing a program. Real robots can drift, lose connection, or respond to sensors; they do not necessarily execute a command exactly.

    Misconception: "Robots know what I want." Explain that our model needs explicit steps; a machine depends on controls, software, sensors, and conditions.

    If asked, "Can robots think?" "Some machines use complicated software to choose actions. This classroom robot responds to its controls. It is not a person."

    SAFETY¶

    Keep children seated outside the optional robot lane. No chasing, racing, throwing, body maze, beanbag toss, or robot on a table edge. Stop the robot before retrieving it. Adult handles charging and battery compartments; inspect for damage. Use large paper pieces, not coins or tiny tokens. Offer seated pointing instead of body movement. Never physically guide a child's hands without permission.

    Meeting 1: input and output (25 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3 (3 min): Invite a brief prayer for including others. Show two arrow choices: "Which way will our robot move?"
    2. 3-7 (4 min): Model one arrow, one-square output, and STOP. Optional adult Drive demonstration replaces the last two minutes, not adds time. Name the difference between a card model and a real steering control.
    3. 7-16 (9 min): Pairs try UP then STOP and RIGHT then STOP from the same START. Swap roles every trial. Each child chooses and predicts one move before a partner executes it. Teacher begins individual I checks while circulating.
    4. 16-20 (4 min): Finish remaining I checks: child points to input and predicted/observed output. Accept pointing, speech, or drawing; do not repeat already documented checks.
    5. 20-22 (2 min): Ask "What did we give it? What did it do? How did we include our partner?"
    6. 22-25 (3 min): Collect cards, park paper robots, return crayons; adult stops and stores optional hardware.

    Meeting 2: sequence and debugging (25 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3 (3 min): Recall input/output; show START and FINISH two squares up.
    2. 3-6 (3 min): Model UP, RIGHT: it misses FINISH. Ask "Which step needs changing?" Change RIGHT to UP; reset and retest.
    3. 6-15 (9 min): Pairs build UP, UP, STOP. Mover follows cards only. Each child then tries the intentionally wrong UP, RIGHT path and changes one card. Third child receives a full chooser turn, not just checker duty. Teacher starts individual A/count checks now.
    4. 15-20 (5 min): Finish remaining individual checks while partners rehearse: each child orders two arrows, predicts the endpoint, and corrects one wrong card. Record A and count two moves aloud/on fingers; no 25-child serial exit line.
    5. 20-22 (2 min): Share one correction and one fair-turn action.
    6. 22-25 (3 min): Reassemble four-card kits, collect grids and individual drawings, clear tables.

    Evidence and what success looks like¶

    Record I and A separately as independent / prompted / not yet. Success is a correct prediction of two one-square moves and a correction that reaches the pictured target, plus identifying a tool input/output. Neat writing, knowing left/right on one's body, or driving speed are not assessed.

    H may be recorded only for a child who actually controls the real robot and stops it safely; an adult demonstration is observation, not child operation. P stays not assessed in this unit. No-device success demonstrates algorithms and model input/output, not operating or programming real hardware.

    Questions, support, and troubleshooting¶

    • "What happens if we change the order? Did the output match your prediction?"
    • Support: offer two pictured choices; cover unused squares; child points while adult moves the token. Avoid screen or motor demands.
    • Challenge: design a three-command route and explain one correction; no speed competition.
    • Wrong route: reset to the same START, read one card at a time, and fix only the first mismatch.
    • Confused arrows: hold the page in one fixed orientation and point to the destination square.
    • Robot drift/disconnection: adult stops, checks aim once, then returns to paper; do not report a paper success as hardware success.
    • Minnesota indoor fallback: the seated grid is the full lesson in any weather. No outdoor or internet requirement.

    Optional family snippet¶

    We predicted and corrected picture instructions and practiced fair turns. Ask: "Show me two steps and one way to fix them." Real robot driving was optional and was recorded separately from algorithm learning. No homework or device purchase.

    kindergartenobservationstewardship

    Week 4: Wonder Walk¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / title K / Observation / Wonder Walk
    Time 25 minutes, including transitions and cleanup
    Domains / big idea C, S, A / Observations tell what we notice; questions tell what we want to find out.
    Student objective / why "I can show two details I noticed and ask one question." Careful looking helps us study and care for creation.
    Catholic connection Leave living things undisturbed and reuse materials; stewardship is a responsibility, not permission to take everything. CCC 2402, paraphrase.
    Local standards CST-C3, CST-S1, CST-A1; local, not official. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty None / Beginner
    Prep / cleanup Light: 10 minutes / 3 minutes within lesson

    Before class¶

    1. Default indoor plan: seat pairs at tables. Provide one clean fallen leaf and one smooth rock at least 5 cm across per pair. Use large teacher-drawn leaf/rock pictures if allergies, mouthing, or availability make specimens unsuitable. Say that a drawing is a representation, not a specimen.
    2. Fold a half-sheet into two observation boxes for each child; put crayons within reach. Draw an eye and a question mark on the board.
    3. With 10/15/20/25 students, make 5/7/10/12 teams (pairs/final trio) and prepare ⅝/10/13 kits, including one reserve for odd enrollment. A third child receives their own paper and a turn with each object.
    4. Optional outdoor path: school policy permits it only with required adult coverage, accessible dry route, safe weather, and no icy surfaces. Choose two stops within a two-minute walk. If clothing/transit would exceed the four-minute allowance, use indoors. Check headcount at exit, each stop, and return; do not assume 25 children can be supervised outdoors by one adult.

    Materials¶

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Per student: half-sheet; crayon 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each
    Per team: large leaf/picture; large rock/picture; tray 5 each 8 each 10 each 13 each
    Optional per team: magnifier 5 8 10 13
    Teacher/class: eye/question drawings; roster; timer 1 set 1 set 1 set 1 set

    Outdoor only: one rigid paper backing per child (10/15/20/25); no collection bags or camera needed. Teacher checks specimens and supplies handwashing access.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Observe: notice with safe senses; point to eyes. Detail: a small part you notice, such as a vein or speckle. Question: something to investigate. Stewardship: careful use and care.

    A detached leaf was part of a living plant; a rock was not. Do not classify living things by movement alone or demand a living/nonliving judgment about a detached leaf. Plants are alive although they do not walk. Observation can include accessible hearing, touch of approved items, or description; sight is not the only valid pathway.

    Misconception: "My guess is something I saw." Distinguish "I see lines" from "I think water goes through them."

    If asked, "Why does a leaf have lines?" "The lines include veins that carry water and other materials. We can see a pattern; our drawing alone does not prove what is inside."

    SAFETY¶

    No tasting, unknown plants, wild mushrooms, animal remains, feathers, nest disturbance, or smelling unknown materials closely. Adults inspect/clean specimens; pictures are equivalent observation targets when needed. No looking at the Sun through eyes or magnifiers. Keep magnifiers out of direct sun; wash hands after specimens. No collection or picking. Cancel outdoor work for cold, ice, storms, unsafe heat, or insufficient staffing.

    Numbered sequence: 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-3 (3 min): Brief prayer for care of creation. Model "I notice a line" and "I wonder where it goes." Explain safe looking and gentle hands.
    2. 3-5 (2 min): Indoors: distribute trays and demonstrate passing. Outdoors: walk to first stop and count children.
    3. 5-11 (6 min): Look at first object/stop. Each child points to one detail, then draws it in box 1 or dictates while adult sketches. Ask "What do you actually notice?"
    4. 11-17 (6 min): Pass second object/observe second stop without moving away from the group. Add a second detail in box 2. Partner asks one question using "I wonder..." or chooses between teacher's two question pictures. Teacher begins recording individual detail/question evidence now.
    5. 17-19 (2 min): Indoors: return trays. Outdoors: return inside and count children. Keep drawings.
    6. 19-22 (3 min): Finish remaining individual checks during paired sharing: each child shows two details and a question. Do not repeat documented checks or require 25 serial speeches. Ask "How did we care for the things we studied?"
    7. 22-25 (3 min): Collect reusable materials, wash hands, save drawings. Teacher adds one question to the Wonder Wall later, not extra class time.

    Evidence and success¶

    On the roster record two observed details and one question for every child: independent / prompted / not yet. A child may point, dictate, sketch, or choose a picture; do not judge realistic drawing skill. Successful evidence is specific ("three lines," "bumpy edge"), not just "I liked it." One stewardship action is returning materials or leaving an organism untouched.

    Questions and contingencies¶

    • "Which detail can you show me? Which idea would we need to test?"
    • Support: use large drawings, tactile approved leaf models, oral description, two pictured choices, or a seated observation partner.
    • Challenge: compare the two objects using a visible feature and ask a testable question.
    • No specimens/magnifiers: use large teacher drawings and naked-eye observation; report observations of the drawings honestly.
    • Too many questions: collect one per child orally; the adult may jot a key word rather than a full sentence.
    • Minnesota indoor fallback: use the default table lesson unchanged at -10 F. A nearby window is optional, not a required outdoor view.

    Optional family snippet¶

    We drew or described two observed details, asked a question, and practiced leaving creation undisturbed. Ask: "What did you notice, and what do you still wonder?" A safe window observation is optional; nothing must be brought from home.

    Weeks 5-6: Building with KEVA Planks¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Plan
    Grade / unit / time K / Structures / two meetings of 25 minutes each
    Domains / big idea C, E, M; the base and arrangement affect whether a structure stays standing
    Student objective / why "I can count blocks, test a low tower, change its base and test again." Evidence helps builders improve.
    Catholic connection Care for shared tools and others' work; skilled work can serve people.
    Local standards CST-C3: resource care; CST-E2: before/after test; CST-M1: count up to ten chosen blocks. Official alignment: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology / difficulty / prep / cleanup None / beginner / 10 minutes / 4 minutes in each meeting

    Before class and exact materials¶

    Read K routines. Use 5/7/10/12 active pair/trio teams and ⅝/10/13 budgeted kits. Inspect blocks; test one low six-block model; draw a two-attempt picture record. KEVA is optional branding; ordinary large stable wooden blocks work.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Kit: 20 large blocks 100 160 200 260
    Kit: tray/mat 5 8 10 13
    Student: sheet; crayon, per meeting 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each

    Teacher: timer, roster and one shared measuring ruler. Demonstrate using a budgeted kit, then return it. Retain the first meeting's sheets at school.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Base: bottom supporting parts. Stable: stands without a hand holding it. Test: check against a criterion. Redesign: change and test again. Misconception: tallest means best. Criterion is ten seconds unaided, with the same six blocks, not maximum height. If asked why a tower falls: identify slipping, leaning or a changed support; do not promise widening always wins.

    Meeting 1: a fair starting test, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Discuss buildings serving people and caring for shared supplies.
    2. 4-8: Model six blocks on a low base. Teacher times ten seconds, hands away.
    3. 8-17: Partners build with six selected blocks, swap turns, count and test. Teacher gives a common start/stop signal; begin individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Each child counts the chosen set, points to the base and reports standing/falling. Record actual results, including falls.
    5. 21-25: Draw/retain a first-attempt picture; count blocks back; clear trays.

    Meeting 2: change and retest, 25 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Retrieve drawings, not unverifiable memories. Restate six blocks/ten seconds.
    2. 4-8: Demonstrate changing only base arrangement with the same blocks.
    3. 8-17: Each partner chooses a base change, rebuilds and observes the same timed test. Rotate the trio's builder turn; start individual checks.
    4. 17-21: Child indicates the change, counts the set and compares two outcomes. Ask "What stayed the same? Did your change help in this test?"
    5. 21-25: Save dated evidence, return all 20 kit blocks, thank partners, clear.
