The 15 replacements omit unsupported quotations and history rather than retain unsafe or unverified legacy options behind labels. Earlier reference bodies remain unchanged. Official benchmark alignment is not claimed; the parent owns that integration. Home extensions are optional, with no routine homework.

    Grade Level: Grades 1-2
    Framework: C-STREAM
    Last Updated: October 2026

    Welcome to C-STREAM¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Weekly A / Welcome
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, S, A / Careful noticing comes before explanations.
    Student objective / why "I can draw two things I notice, ask a question and choose a first learning step." Scientists and artists use attention rather than guesses.
    Catholic connection Practice truthful noticing as a way to study and care about creation; distinguish a taught belief from an observed feature. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C1: honest evidence and faith/reason; CST-S1: observations, questions and evidence; CST-A1: observational representation. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Choose three familiar dry objects per kit: a leaf picture, pencil and smooth block. Draw eye/question/footstep icons. Keep biographies and acronym memorization out of the assessment.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: noticed detail / question / next practice step. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Leaf picture / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Pencil / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Smooth wooden block / kit / items 4 5 7 9

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Observe = notice with senses; question = something to investigate; goal = an action to practice.

    A question such as "Does this roll?" can be tested; "It looks happy" is an interpretation. Briefly name C-STREAM areas, then let children investigate.

    Common misconception: A drawing or guess automatically explains why something happens.

    If asked: "Can faith and science go together?" Say that Catholic schooling values both faithful living and careful reasoning; the object test answers a testable question, not every question about meaning.

    SAFETY¶

    Only screened dry classroom objects; no tasting, sharp specimens or unknown plants. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Wonder and first goal - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Show an object and offer an original short prayer for careful learning. Name one observed detail and one guess.
    2. 3-7: Model looking, drawing two visible details and asking "What happens if I turn it?" Show a picture-step goal.
    3. 7-20: Each child chooses an object, draws two details, asks a partner a testable question and tries a safe turn/roll test on a tray. Teacher checks each child.
    4. 20-26: Children point to what they actually saw, distinguish it from their prediction and draw one practice goal; partners suggest a clearer detail.
    5. 26-30: Return the three objects to each tray; save goal pages for Week 18. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What did you notice rather than guess?
    • How could we check your question?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Point to two represented details and ask one oral question; choose one concrete first step.

    Grade 2: Distinguish observation from prediction, ask a testable question and give a reason for a useful next step.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. No scientist-name, acronym-recall or all-domain mastery is inferred.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Offer two objects and eye/question icons; teacher repeats each question orally. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Suggest what evidence would answer a second question without inventing an explanation. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No leaf picture: use a second familiar dry object. A broad question: help narrow it to turning, rolling or comparing without supplying the answer.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We practiced observation, drawing and honest questions, then chose a learning action. Ask: "What did you notice rather than guess?" Optional: describe two visible details on a familiar object. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Sources and claim boundaries¶

    These are local program competencies, not official Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmark numbers. See local standards and the source register. Catholic care, dignity and honest-inquiry applications follow that register; no unsupported scientist/saint biography, Scripture quotation or devotional history is required to execute this lesson. No external historical or official numeric claim is made.

    grades-1-2year-aroboticscoding

    Weeks 2-3: Sphero Coding Adventures¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Coding / Sphero Coding Adventures
    Time Two meetings of 30 minutes; 60 minutes total
    Domains C: responsible sharing; T: input/output and algorithms; M: comparing travel
    Big idea A stored sequence runs without continuous steering; observations help us debug.
    Student objective "I can predict a short program, run it, and change one instruction."
    Why Programmers check results rather than blaming people or guessing.
    Catholic connection Share equipment fairly and report results honestly; teacher application of stewardship, CCC 2407 and 2415.
    Local standards CST-C3: equipment care/turn record; CST-T1: connect/run/stop demonstration; CST-T2: ordered program and one debug; CST-M1: compare two travel lengths. These are local, not official benchmarks.
    Official standards VERIFICATION REQUIRED; no Minnesota/Archdiocesan/CSTA benchmark claimed.
    Technology Required primary path: one compatible charged Sphero and Sphero Edu tablet per team, to execute stored code on a physical robot. Paper fallback assesses algorithms only.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes first setup plus manufacturer charging time; 4 minutes cleanup within each meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Confirm loan/inventory, exact robot model, current app compatibility, school-approved permissions and charging instructions; do not assume a class set exists.
    2. On each device create a tested Blocks starter: roll at heading 0, low speed for 1 second; stop; delay 1 second; roll at heading 180 for 1 second; stop. Labels vary by app version: use its installed help. Do not invent a "turn right" block.
    3. Aim/calibrate heading 0 away from students. Test on the actual surface; shorten duration/speed until travel stays inside a 1 m square. Teacher records working settings on the board.
    4. Mark dry floor bays with clear walking aisles, never across an exit. Make arrow cards for forward, wait, return, stop; no printing needed.
    5. Assign teams of 2-3: programmer, observer, safety checker. Swap after each run; teams of two combine observer/checker.

    Supplies and class sizes¶

    • Per student: one half-sheet and crayon; an individual evidence box on teacher roster.
    • Per team: one robot/tablet pair, four arrow cards, one 1 m paper measuring strip with equal hand-width marks.
    • Class reusable/consumable: floor tape, timer, whiteboard; one dry bay per active robot.
    • Teacher-only: charger, model-specific help, roster. No water, paint, attached markers, or robot disassembly.
    Students Teams of at most 3 / kits for simultaneous work Paper sheets
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    With fewer kits use one supervised robot station, not nine unsupervised moving robots. In the 12-minute practice block use three 4-minute waves (three teams per wave for 25 students); other teams predict on paper. With only one kit, this is a demonstration/partial practice lesson: record children not yet assessed and schedule another opportunity. Do not certify everyone from a group run.

    Vocabulary¶

    Sequence = instructions in order; program = stored instructions; input = our code; output = observed movement; debug = change an instruction after comparing prediction and result; loop = repeat instructions.

    Teacher background¶

    Heading is a direction measured from the robot's calibrated aim; rolling at 180 reverses travel relative to 0. Actual distance depends on speed, time, surface and calibration. A joystick is remote control, not evidence of a stored program. Misconception: a failed path means the child failed. Treat it as information. If asked "Does it think like me?" This classroom robot runs human-written instructions and sensors; people remain responsible. Avoid claims about every kind of robot.

    Exact sequence: meeting 1 (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3: State objective, stop signal and sharing rule. Optional original prayer: "God, help us use tools carefully and tell the truth about our tests."
    2. 3-7: At tables move a paper token for forward-wait-return cards. Each child predicts the ending by pointing.
    3. 7-11: Teacher shows aim, stored blocks, Run and Stop. Contrast one joystick movement with a hands-off stored run.
    4. 11-23: Teams run the tested starter. Each child points to the next block before their own run; observer compares start/end. Shorten one roll duration and rerun. Teacher records each child's run/stop or "not yet observed."
    5. 23-26: Individual oral/drawn exit: show the three actions in order; identify one observed difference between two runs.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup below; partners check care and equitable turns.

    Exact sequence: meeting 2 (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Re-aim robots and retell one sequence; newcomers receive a two-card demo rather than assumed prior mastery.
    2. 4-8: Model a deliberate too-long roll. Ask which instruction should change; show one shorter duration.
    3. 8-20: Each child predicts, runs and changes one parameter. Compare travel on the same surface using the marked strip. Grade 2 may repeat a short out-and-back sequence twice in a finite repeat block; this is not a guaranteed square.
    4. 20-24: Partner demonstration: original run, change, rerun. Teacher asks each child what changed and why.
    5. 24-26: Individual exit and roster check; identify anyone still needing a device opportunity.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions and measurable evidence¶

    • What happens without touching the joystick? Which block changes the result? What stayed the same? Did every partner get a turn?
    • Grade 1: point to/orally order three action cards; personally Run and Stop under supervision; name/draw one change. Compare longer/shorter travel with a marked strip.
    • Grade 2: create a three-action stored sequence, predict ending, change one parameter and explain both observed results; count equal travel units. Finite loop is challenge, not universal mastery.
    • Use 0 not observed / 1 with prompt / 2 independently for each criterion. A successful team path or enthusiasm alone earns no individual code credit.

    If things go wrong / indoor and no-device fallback¶

    Connection failure: check charge and selected robot once; after 2 minutes use arrow cards and a tabletop token with the same timed blocks. Mis-aim: stop, re-aim, lower speed; change only one parameter. Finish early: make a second prediction, not a speed race. No devices: each child orders three cards, another follows literally, then the child repairs one deliberately wrong card. Mark CST-T2 algorithm evidence only; CST-T1 physical robot operation is not assessed. All work is indoors; no weather requirement.

    SAFETY¶

    Only low-speed floor runs inside marked bays; seated/kneeling observers outside the bay; never chase or stand in a moving path. Teacher stops any robot leaving its area. Cords remain teacher-only and off walking routes. Follow model age/use guidance, especially small Mini components. No direct-contact assistance without consent.

    Support / challenge¶

    Support: two actions first, picture cards, adult scribing, accessible table token, peer explains buttons but does not take the child's turn. Grade 1 needs no reading or writing. Challenge: Grade 2 compares two trials at one changed duration or explains a finite repeat; no variables or autonomous navigation claim.

    Cleanup¶

    Stop all programs, power down per model instructions, count kits/cards, peel only lesson tape, return devices to labeled trays; teacher handles charging. Retain each child's prediction/change sketch.

    Family snippet¶

    What we explored: instructions that control a robot. What we did/learned: predicted a stored sequence and used observations to fix it. Catholic connection: fair turns and careful use of shared tools. Ask: "What did you change after your first test?" Optional at home: give three spoken directions to move a paper token; no purchase or device needed. No routine homework.

    Sources / verification¶

    Sphero official education site is the model/app reference; exact installed block labels and compatibility require teacher preflight. CCC 2407 and 2415 ground stewardship. No attributed quotation is used.

    Week 4: Wonder Walk Scientists¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Observation / Wonder Walk Scientists
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, A
    Big idea Observation describes evidence; a question is different from an answer.
    Student objective "I can show two details, sort with a reason, and ask a question."
    Why Careful observations help us understand and care for living things.
    Catholic connection Observe without harming habitats; practical stewardship, CCC 2415-2418.
    Standards Local CST-C3: choose a protective action; CST-S1: two observations/question; CST-S3: living/formerly living/never living reasoning; CST-A1: sketch visible details. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path. A teacher camera is optional documentation, never needed to meet the objective.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes scouting/screening; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class¶

    1. Choose indoor by default if weather, air quality, clothing, mobility access or staffing is unsuitable. Never require an outdoor walk at -10 F.
    2. Outdoor route: a short accessible loop wholly on school grounds with two nearby stops; follow school supervision policy and count students at departure, each stop and return. If 25 cannot be supervised, choose indoor.
    3. Indoor route: prepare a live classroom plant, fallen dry leaf and smooth washed stone for each table, or draw clear pictures showing their origins. Screen for allergy, sharp edges, mold and unknown plants.
    4. Fold each child's paper into two observation boxes and one question box. Draw three sorting icons: living now / once part of a living thing / never living. No worksheet reading.
    5. Model a plant sketch with two specific details, not a generic green scribble.

    Supplies¶

    • Per student: one paper, pencil/crayon; clipboard only outdoors.
    • Per pair: one plastic magnifier, optional; looking closely works without it.
    • Class: timer, three sorting icons, screened specimen/picture trays; one handwashing station.
    • Teacher-only: roster, route/weather decision, specimen screening. No collection bags: leave habitats undisturbed.
    Students Pairs / optional magnifiers Table trays (up to 5/table) Papers
    10 5 2 10
    15 8 3 15
    20 10 4 20
    25 13 5 25

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Observe = notice using a safe available sense; detail = a particular feature; living = alive now; formerly living = once alive or part of something alive; evidence = what we noticed. Plants are living even when they do not move from place to place. A fallen leaf was part of a living plant; a rock was never alive. Some examples are uncertain: "need more evidence" is acceptable. Misconception: anything moving is alive. A toy car moves but is not alive. If asked about a winter tree: dormancy slows growth; a bare tree may still be living. Do not break branches to test it.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Explain safe observation and stewardship. Optional original prayer: "God, help us notice carefully and protect your creation." Show what a detail sounds like: "three pointed edges."
    2. 4-7: Model two details, one drawing and one genuine question: "Why are the edges different?" Student points to evidence rather than copying an answer.
    3. 7-17: Outdoor: travel to two nearby stops, observe, then return within this block. Indoor: examine two tray examples at tables, with the same noticing prompts. Children draw two details and tell a partner; do not require four outdoor stops.
    4. 17-22: Sort the plant/leaf/stone examples using three icons. Each child places or points to one example and gives a reason. Grade 2 discusses an uncertain example. At 25 pupils, collect the first five individual roster checks during observation/sorting, using their drawings for the two details.
    5. 22-26: Complete individual checks at tables: two drawn details, one oral question and one care action. Up to 20 remaining children receive a brief check (five per minute); peers rehearse while waiting. Earlier checks plus this block cover 25, not 25 full speeches in four minutes.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup and handwashing; headcount if outdoors.

    Questions / success¶

    What did you actually see? Is that a guess or an observation? Was this once part of a living thing? How did leaving it in place protect it? - Grade 1: draw/point to two observable features and ask one oral question; sort one clear example with oral reason and choose "leave it" rather than disturb. - Grade 2: label or dictate two features, distinguish three categories and justify an uncertain classification using what further evidence is needed. - Record not yet / with prompt / independently for details, question, reasoning and stewardship. Do not score handwriting.

    If things go wrong / fallback¶

    Rain, ice, extreme cold, allergy or staffing concern: use the prepared indoor trays/pictures without reducing the objective. No live specimens: clearly mark pictures as evidence from pictures, not a firsthand field observation. No magnifiers: use unaided eyes. Student unsure: let them say "I need to find out," then name an observation that could help.

    SAFETY¶

    No tasting, close sniffing, wildlife handling, unknown plant touching, sun viewing through magnifiers, climbing, roadside routes or collecting feathers/droppings. Outdoors keep group within boundaries and follow school weather limits; indoors use seated accessible trays. Students may observe visually without touching.

    Support / challenge¶

    Support: teacher narration, tactile safe replica by choice, picture responses and scribing; Grade 1 never reads instructions alone. Challenge: Grade 2 compare two leaf shapes or explain why movement alone is insufficient.

    Cleanup¶

    Return magnifiers; teacher collects trays; wash hands; count students and equipment; keep sketches as evidence. Store dry materials, not mold-prone specimens.

    Family snippet¶

    We observed two details and asked a scientific question, then practiced caring for habitats. Ask: "What did you notice that you had not noticed before?" Optional: observe a plant or a picture indoors and tell two details; no outdoor trip or supplies required. No routine homework.

    Sources¶

    CCC 2415-2418 addresses care for creation and animals. Romans 1:20 is an optional Scripture reference, not a quoted scientific explanation; use a school-approved Bible (translation/verse wording VERIFICATION REQUIRED). Hildegard's biography is not needed for this investigation; any added historical claim requires verification.

    KEVA Engineering Challenge¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Weekly A / Structures
    Native time / scope 2 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, E, M / Stable bases and supports can be improved using repeatable tests.
    Student objective / why "I can test a structure, count its height or span and explain a change." Builders use evidence, not a tallest-at-any-cost contest.
    Catholic connection Return and reuse planks, give each builder a turn, and explain why caring for shared materials matters. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C3: stewardship and responsible work; CST-E2: build, test and redesign; CST-M1: count, compare and measure. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Inspect equal planks for splinters. Mark a 10 cm bridge gap between two supports. Pretest a low tower and span using three broad blocks; model a 30 cm height ceiling.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: plan or prediction / actual result / reason or revision. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 40 60 80 100
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Wooden building planks / kit / items 96 120 168 216
    Metric ruler / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Stable support block / kit / items 8 10 14 18
    Broad wooden test block / kit / items 12 15 21 27

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Base = bottom support; stable = stays standing; span = gap crossed; redesign = change after a test.

    A broad base often helps stability, but overlap and alignment also matter. Equal loads and an unchanged span make comparisons interpretable.

    Common misconception: Taller always means better, or a failure means the builder failed.

    If asked: "Was Noah mocked while building?" No story detail is needed; today we study tested structures and responsible teamwork, not an unsourced Bible anecdote.

    SAFETY¶

    Tabletop builds under 30 cm; no standing on furniture, heavy loads or hands under collapsing structures. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Stable towers - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Show a stable low tower; state criterion: stand 10 seconds below 30 cm.
    2. 3-7: Model counting equal plank layers and measuring from tabletop; compare narrow and broad bases.
    3. 7-20: Teams build with 24 planks, test 10 seconds, record height and change one base feature. Every child adds or tests a part.
    4. 20-26: Retest at the same height where possible; each child points to the changed feature and compares pass/fall records.
    5. 26-30: Remove loads first, then dismantle from the top and count 24 planks and three loads. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 2: Supported crossing - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Recall the base test; show the fixed 10 cm gap.
    2. 3-7: Model overlap on both supports and adding one broad block at a time, maximum three.
    3. 7-20: Teams build a plank bridge, test three blocks for 5 seconds, change overlap/support arrangement and retest with the same blocks. Each child counts one trial.
    4. 20-26: Each child states two load results and a support change; distinguish span from tower height.
    5. 26-30: Remove loads first, then dismantle from the top and count 24 planks and three loads. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which change helped your structure in the test?
    • What did we keep the same?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show a tested feature, count layers or supported loads and identify a change.

    Grade 2: Give two comparable counts/measurements with units and explain how keeping height/span/load conditions steady supports the comparison.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Use a demonstrated low base and large blocks; partner steadies the ruler while the child directs measurement. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Try the same-height tower with fewer planks and discuss the resource tradeoff. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No branded planks: use equal screened wooden blocks and adjust the demonstrated low span before class; record the actual span. Immediate collapse: align bases and reduce height, not add heavy ballast.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We tested towers and bridges, compared counts and reused materials responsibly. Ask: "Which change helped your structure in the test?" Optional: point to a support in a picture of a building. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Sources and claim boundaries¶

    These are local program competencies, not official Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmark numbers. See local standards and the source register. Catholic care, dignity and honest-inquiry applications follow that register; no unsupported scientist/saint biography, Scripture quotation or devotional history is required to execute this lesson. No external historical or official numeric claim is made.

    Engineering for Others¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Weekly A / Service
    Native time / scope 3 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, E, M / A useful design starts with listening to a user.
    Student objective / why "I can plan, test and improve a tool for a stated tabletop need." Listening prevents us from assuming what someone needs.
    Catholic connection Ask a classroom helper what is useful, offer accessible roles and explain how the design respects that request. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C2: dignity, service and inclusion; CST-E1: needs, criteria and constraints; CST-E2: build, test and redesign; CST-M1: count, compare and measure. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Ask a teacher/classroom helper to request moving a 5 cm paper ball 20 cm across a tray without touching it directly, with no lifting above the tray. Precut cardboard and tape. Draw start/end marks.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: plan or prediction / actual result / reason or revision. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    User = person with a need; criterion = must do; constraint = limit; prototype = test model.

    A tabletop scoop/pusher is a model for this request, not an assistive device. Successful redesign may reduce spills even if it looks less attractive.

    Common misconception: We know another person needs a gadget because of an assumed disability.

    If asked: "Can we use it on a real person?" No; we test a paper ball on a tray and ask for feedback, not medical or mobility use.

    SAFETY¶

    No high shelves, grabbing bodies, sharp reaches, mouth-held tools or lifting people. Use screened cardboard; teacher precuts. Tape stays off skin. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Listen and plan - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Teacher states the helper request; children repeat who it helps and what it must do.
    2. 3-7: Model the 20 cm tabletop route and material limit. Draw a pusher and scoop as alternative ideas.
    3. 7-20: Each child sketches two options, chooses one and directs a small cardboard mock-up using one square and two sticks. Partner acts as user and checks the request.
    4. 20-26: Each child points to a criterion and a limit; revise a sketch after specific user feedback.
    5. 26-30: Remove loose tape and return sticks; store labeled prototypes between meetings and save usable cardboard. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 2: Build and first test - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Retrieve sketches and repeat the user request.
    2. 3-7: Model attaching a broad cardboard edge to sticks with two strips, hands remaining over tray.
    3. 7-20: Teams choose one plan, build using the remaining materials and run two 20 cm tests. Rotate mover, counter and observer; record success/spill for each.
    4. 20-26: Each child gives a test result and proposes one change tied to it; mark the proposed feature on a separate page.
    5. 26-30: Remove loose tape and return sticks; store labeled prototypes between meetings and save usable cardboard. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 3: Improve for the user - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Recall recorded results, including spills.
    2. 3-7: Model changing only edge height or handle placement, not the route or ball.
    3. 7-20: Teams make their selected change and repeat two trials. Each child conducts or directs a test and records the outcomes.
    4. 20-26: Compare before/after successes out of two; partner-user gives feedback. Each child explains whether the request was better met or still needs work.
    5. 26-30: Remove loose tape and return sticks; store labeled prototypes between meetings and save usable cardboard. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What did the user ask your design to do?
    • Did the same test show improvement?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Name the user need, show a safe test and identify a change.

    Grade 2: Distinguish criterion from material limit and compare successes out of two before and after a one-feature revision.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Use two pictured design choices; accept a child-directed partner action for reaching/motor needs. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Compare scoop versus pusher against the same route and explain one tradeoff. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Ball rolls away: keep the test over a wide tray and add a stop at its edge. No improvement: keep the honest result and identify the next possible change rather than declare success.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We listened to a classroom user, tested a tabletop model and revised using evidence. Ask: "What did the user ask your design to do?" Optional: ask someone which ordinary classroom task is awkward; no home device construction. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Load = supported object; equal = same size/mass for this kit; result = observed count.

    These are model bridge comparisons, not predictions of full-size safety. Load counts compare only the same kit/span.

    Common misconception: A high load count proves every bridge of that shape is strongest.

    If asked: "Can we walk on it?" No; this is a tabletop model for broad blocks only.

    SAFETY¶

    Supports stay low and stable; no coins, heavy weights, hand pressure or standing on models. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Same-span load comparison - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Recall earlier bridge supports and state the fixed-span comparison.
    2. 3-7: Model ruler endpoints and place loads singly at the center, stopping at collapse or five.
    3. 7-20: Teams build, test, record the supported count, change plank overlap/arrangement and retest the same five loads. Every child counts a trial or directs loading.
    4. 20-26: Each child draws aligned bars for both counts, identifies the change and explains a resource-care decision. No strongest-team competition.
    5. 26-30: Remove loads first, dismantle and return all 12 planks/five loads. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How do your two load bars compare?
    • Was the gap the same in both tests?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Count supported loads and represent two results with one square per load.

    Grade 2: Label both results, explain the fixed span/load condition and justify a changed arrangement using counts.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Provide five drawn boxes and a prebuilt first bridge; children still predict/count. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Repeat a result and explain any difference instead of adding unsafe loads. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Both support five: record a tie and compare overlap/material use; do not add unlisted weights. No planks: fold paper from the allocated sheets and pretest the same safe load criterion before class.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We compared bridges with the same gap and loads and represented real results. Ask: "How do your two load bars compare?" Optional: compare two counted groups of familiar objects verbally. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Sequence = ordered blocks; run = execute; debug = correct a mismatch; audience = viewer.

    A character follows stored blocks, not the coder's spoken wishes. A single scene leaves time for each child's hands-on turn.

    Common misconception: Manual dragging the character is the same as running code.

    If asked: "Must I type thank you?" No; draw a thank-you symbol and tell its meaning. No identifying text is required.

    SAFETY¶

    Tablets stay on dry tables; no photos, names or uploads. Keep volume muted. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: One-scene thank-you - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Choose a school helper and a visual thank-you idea; predict a character's motion.
    2. 3-7: Model a connected Green Flag -> Move Right 2 -> End script. Run, reset character to the same start, then change 2 to 1 and rerun.
    3. 7-20: Each team member gets a four-minute tablet turn: choose a character, connect the three blocks, predict, flag-run, reset and change one motion number. Other members draw/predict on cards.
    4. 20-26: Each child shows the executed change and explains a visual choice. Partner offers one specific comment and the author revises the message or placement. Teacher checks during turns, not only this final phase.
    5. 26-30: Return to project Home to retain local work, lock tablets, count cards and clear tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which block did you change and what happened?
    • How does your picture thank its audience?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Individually connect/run a three-block sequence, point to the changed motion and tell the visual message.

    Grade 2: Predict the direction/step-count difference, explain the rerun and revise a purposeful visual choice after feedback.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Gratitude alone is not evidence for a Catholic competency; a paper plan is not executed code.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Provide a starter script with one missing block, large picture cards and oral message choices. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Add a Wait block only after explaining the original result; test the timing change. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Missing app or incompatible tablet: use three drawn story panels and block cards; record app execution unassessed. Disconnected blocks: drag until they snap; unintended motion: reset position before rerun.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We used a short stored animation to communicate thanks and checked a changed instruction. Ask: "Which block did you change and what happened?" Optional: give two spoken directions to a paper character. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Recipient = intended user; function = job; feedback = specific helpful comment.

    A bookmark must identify a page without damaging it; flatness and visible contrast matter.

    Common misconception: More glued decorations always make a better gift.

    If asked: "Do I have to give it away?" No; a classroom reader can test it and you may keep your example.

    SAFETY¶

    Teacher precuts; no beads, glitter, staples or personal/private messages. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Functional encouragement - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: State recipient request and kindness purpose.
    2. 3-7: Demonstrate placing the strip halfway into a book, closing gently and finding the same page.
    3. 7-20: Each child plans a clear symbol/message, colors the flat strip and tests in the shared book. Partners give one comment about readability; each author revises one detail.
    4. 20-26: Each child shows the page-marking criterion and explains how a design choice fits the recipient, without ranking gifts.
    5. 26-30: Return books and unused cardstock; retain the individual drawing/check page. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How does your bookmark help its reader?
    • What did you revise after feedback?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show a successful page mark and tell one purposeful picture choice.

    Grade 2: Explain both the functional constraint and audience choice; show a revision following specific feedback.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Offer two symbol choices, a broad strip and oral dictation; use partner book handling. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Compare two contrast choices against the same readability criterion. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Strip too short for a book: use a smaller issued book rather than add craft decorations. Recipient unavailable: teacher plays a reader using the stated request.

    Lesson at a glance¶

    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: prediction / two observed positions / explanation. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Source = makes light; shadow = blocked light region; reflect = redirect light; symbol = represents meaning.

    Moving the object changes shadow size when lamp and screen remain fixed. A mirror redirects incoming light; it does not create more light.

    Common misconception: A mirror or a shadow makes its own light.

    If asked: "Is being kind measurable like brightness?" We can observe a kind action, but spiritual worth is not measured by a flashlight.

    SAFETY¶

    No flames, lasers, glass, sunlight focusing or beams aimed at eyes. Keep classroom safely lit; teacher alone handles cells. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Shadow size - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Identify flashlight as a source and cardboard as an object that blocks light.
    2. 3-7: Model fixed lamp/screen; put cardboard at near and far marked positions and trace shadow edges.
    3. 7-20: Teams test the two positions with the same source/screen. Each child predicts and traces or points to one actual outline; rotate lamp/object/recorder roles.
    4. 20-26: Each child compares near/far shadow outlines and names the kept-same positions; distinguish observation from the hope symbol.
    5. 26-30: Switch off lights, count mirrors/cardboard, store drawings and remove tape from tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 2: Reflection - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Retrieve outlines; recall source versus reflected light.
    2. 3-7: Aim light at a mirror toward a paper screen, keeping beams away from faces; tilt slightly to move the spot.
    3. 7-20: Teams compare two mirror angles with lamp fixed. Each child directs an angle and sketches arrows from source to mirror to screen.
    4. 20-26: Each child explains which part redirected light and one model limitation; name a concrete kind action without calling it a light measurement.
    5. 26-30: Switch off lights, count mirrors/cardboard, store drawings and remove tape from tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What stayed the same in your light test?
    • Does the mirror make light or redirect it?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show blocked light and identify source/mirror using observed results.

    Grade 2: Compare two shadow conditions, name a kept-same condition and trace source -> mirror -> screen without calling a symbol data.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Use large cardboard and adult-stabilized light; child directs position and points to outlines. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Repeat a position and discuss why trace outlines may differ. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Weak shadow: teacher adjusts screen position before testing and marks the new fixed setup. No mirrors: repeat shadow evidence; reflection remains unassessed, never use glass.

    We compared shadows and reflected light, separating observations from a hope symbol. Ask: "What stayed the same in your light test?" Optional: notice a shadow indoors without aiming a light into eyes. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Star = a distant light-producing object; pattern = arrangement; model = representation.

    The Sun is a star. Dots on paper do not show actual star size or distance. We do not need Magi numbers, professions, journey dates or historical navigation claims.

    Common misconception: All stars in a picture are close together or equally distant.

    If asked: "Did the Christmas star have six dots?" This classroom pattern is not a reconstruction of the biblical event.

    SAFETY¶

    No sharp puncturing, hole-punch stations, dark-room movement or Sun viewing. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Sky pattern model - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Show the MODEL label and distinguish a classroom drawing from the actual sky.
    2. 3-7: Demonstrate counting each of six dots once and copying relative positions using a starting corner.
    3. 7-20: Each child copies the pattern with six large dots, counts and checks placement against the card. Partner identifies one moved/missing dot; author revises.
    4. 20-26: Each child points to two matching position details, gives the count and says the paper does not show real distances or sizes.
    5. 26-30: Return pattern cards and save the checked model pages. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What does your star model leave out?
    • How did you check every dot once?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Count six dots and point to two position details matching the reference.

    Grade 2: Represent the arrangement accurately enough to compare and explain one real-sky/model difference.

    We counted and represented a star-pattern model and named its limits. Ask: "What does your star model leave out?" Optional: compare a drawing of an object with the real object. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    New Year Goals¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Weekly A / Reflection
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / RECOMMENDED
    Domains / big idea C, M, T / An achievable goal has a first action and an honest record.
    Student objective / why "I can put a helpful goal into ordered steps and record one practice." A small school action is more usable than three home trackers.
    Catholic connection Choose an inclusive classroom-helping action; spiritual worth and kindness are not competitions. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C2: dignity, service and inclusion; CST-M2: represent and interpret data/patterns; CST-T2: algorithms and debugging. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Retrieve Week 1 goals if available. Prepare picture choices: share a turn, put tools away, invite a partner. Draw a three-space school tracker; do not use private family/faith disclosures.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: first step / next steps / actual school attempt. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Goal = action to practice; sequence = order; tracker = record of attempts.

    A tick records that a practice occurred, not a person's goodness. An action sequence can be checked immediately.

    Common misconception: Setting a goal proves it was achieved.

    If asked: "What if I miss a day?" Record honestly and choose the next useful attempt; no punishment or public comparison.

    SAFETY¶

    Seated role-play, no physical helping/lifting; keep personal trackers private. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Plan and practice - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Recall one earlier goal or choose a school-helping picture.
    2. 3-7: Model invite -> listen -> share a turn on three cards; intentionally swap the first two and discuss the problem.
    3. 7-20: Each child draws/orders three action cards, practices with a partner, repairs a sequence mismatch and marks one actual attempt on the tracker.
    4. 20-26: Each child explains a first step and tracker mark; teacher saves tracker for a brief opening check in the next existing lesson, not a new meeting.
    5. 26-30: Store cards/trackers in private folders; return supplies. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What is the first action in your goal?
    • What does your tracker mark actually show?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Order two or three concrete actions and identify one actual practice.

    Grade 2: Repair an order problem, explain how the action includes someone and distinguish an attempt from an outcome.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Offer two pictured steps first, then add the third if ready. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Describe an if/then response if the invited partner says no; respect the answer. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Broad goal like "be good": narrow to an observable school action. Prior goals missing: start fresh without inventing progress. At next meeting ask one actual school example before the usual hook.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We planned a helpful classroom action and recorded one real practice, not a promise of achievement. Ask: "What is the first action in your goal?" Optional: talk about a small helpful action; no required home chart. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Weeks 19-22: STREAM Exploration Stations¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Evidence workshops / STREAM Exploration Stations
    Time / domains Four meetings, each exactly 30 minutes / C, E, A, M; not "all domains"
    Big idea Focused making, measuring and revision produce evidence of learning.
    Student objective "I can show my plan, test or compare it, and explain one change."
    Why Thirty minutes permits one meaningful workshop, not four six-minute stations plus transitions.
    Catholic connection Reuse materials and honor every child's contribution; teacher application of CCC 2407/2415.
    Standards Local CST-C3: material care; CST-E2: build/test/redesign (meeting 1); CST-A2: symmetry/pattern (2-3); CST-M1: same-unit measurement (¼); CST-M2: pattern/data representation (¾). Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path. Prior robot lessons remain the place for assessed code; an optional robot demo cannot replace these workshop outcomes.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low/moderate; 10-15 minutes for each reusable kit; 4 minutes cleanup each meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Choose one workshop kit per meeting; do not put water/paint/robots out simultaneously.
    2. Prepare a picture instruction card showing plan -> try -> compare -> change.
    3. Assign table teams of 2-3 but give each child a separate evidence page. Grade 1 tells/draws; Grade 2 adds units/reasons.
    4. Keep prior science sink/float and robot ideas as optional future extensions needing separate safety and assessment planning, not hidden required stations.

    Supplies / scaling¶

    • Per student per meeting: half-sheet and crayon.
    • Per team meeting 1: 20 wooden planks or cardboard blocks, ruler/equal cubes, soft eraser as optional load.
    • Per team meeting 2: folded paper and crayons (no wet paint required).
    • Per team meeting 3: 12 pattern blocks or teacher-cut colored paper shapes.
    • Per team meeting 4: ruler or equal cubes and three accessible classroom objects.
    • Class: timer, board results chart, reusable trays; tape only if using cardboard.
    • Teacher-only: roster, kit screening and storage labels.
    Students Teams / kits per workshop Planks (meeting 1) Shapes (meeting 3) Half-sheets/meeting
    10 4 80 48 10
    15 5 100 60 15
    20 7 140 84 20
    25 9 180 108 25

    At 25 everyone stays at tables. Teacher visits three tables per practice phase; independent evidence is a brief drawing/demo, not 25 long presentations.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Redesign = change after a test; stable = stays standing; symmetry = matching across a line; repeating unit = the part repeated; unit = same-size measuring amount; data = recorded results. Different hand spans are not interchangeable units. Drawings can show design decisions without writing. Misconception: finishing a passport proves learning. Only the demonstrated workshop criterion does. If asked "Why no robots today?" Tools match the question; we already have separate lessons for actual programming.

    Four exact 30-minute meetings¶

    Meeting 1: Stable structure 1. 0-4: Show challenge: tabletop structure at least five equal blocks tall, stands 10 seconds, height below 30 cm; discuss reusing planks. 2. 4-8: Model a narrow/wide base and height measurement; each child sketches a possible base. 3. 8-20: Teams build, test for 10 seconds, change one feature and retest; each child helps one test/measurement. 4. 20-24: Record two results and show changed base. 5. 24-26: Individual: explain a change using test evidence. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Meeting 2: Symmetry studio 1. 0-4: Show matching versus nonmatching designs. 2. 4-8: Fold paper; teacher marks matching points across fold. 3. 8-20: Each child makes a purposeful symmetric design; partner checks two matching features. 4. 20-24: Revise one mismatch or explain intentional asymmetry; never equate beauty with perfection. 5. 24-26: Individual points to line and two matching features. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Meeting 3: Pattern communication 1. 0-4: Recall a two-color AB example. 2. 4-8: Model repeating unit and intentional broken pattern. 3. 8-20: Children make two AB units (Grade 1) or three ABB/AAB units (Grade 2), trade predictions and repair one broken pattern. 4. 20-24: Draw pattern and explain what comes next. 5. 24-26: Individual identifies unit and predicts next two shapes. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Meeting 4: Measurement gallery 1. 0-4: Choose one object to compare; recall equal units. 2. 4-8: Teacher models no gaps/overlaps from endpoint. 3. 8-20: Children measure three objects with same units; Grade 2 nearest whole cm if ready; record/draw lengths. 4. 20-24: Compare longest/shortest and represent results as aligned strips. 5. 24-26: Individual demonstrates measuring start and justifies one comparison. 6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / success¶

    What did your test show? Which part repeats? Did units have gaps? Why did you save usable materials? Grade 1 uses oral explanations and sketches, two matching features, AB prediction, correct endpoint and longer/shorter comparisons. Grade 2 gives measured two-trial structure results, ABB/AAB rule and three labeled comparable lengths with reasoning. Teacher records not yet / prompted / independent for each meeting's stated criterion and care action; do not assign science/robot mastery from unrelated products.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    No planks: fold cardboard blocks or make a low paper structure; same standing criterion. Limited rulers: use equal paper strips. No pattern blocks: colored paper shapes. All four workshops work indoors with no devices; no hidden loan requirement. Early finishers revise/explain rather than visit unprepared stations.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    Structures below 30 cm; hands out before collapse test; no heavy top loads or furniture climbing. Screen recycled materials; no glass, exposed staples or wet materials. Keep aisles clear and tools age appropriate. Support: prebuilt base, thick blocks, picture steps, partner stabilization and adult scribing. Challenge: Grade 2 defend a design tradeoff or compare repeated measurements; maintain individual evidence.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Count and sort kit parts; return tools, recycle scraps, store each child's labeled evidence. Four-minute cleanup is already counted. Family snippet: Over four workshops we tested structures, revised symmetry and patterns, and measured with equal units. Catholic connection: responsible reuse and respect. Ask: "What did you change after checking your work?" Optional: find a pattern or compare two familiar objects orally; no purchase/device or routine homework. CCC 2407/2415. Optional 1 Corinthians 12:4,11 is a reference, not a verified quotation. Saint biographies are not required; verify any added names/details before use.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Evidence = actual observation; belief = taught faith commitment; panel = message space.

    A leaf detail is observable; "we care for creation" states a commitment. Do not use scientist origin claims to prove either.

    Common misconception: A religious symbol is scientific evidence.

    If asked: "Who discovered the universe?" That history question is not needed for today's observation; do not improvise a name or an origin story.

    SAFETY¶

    Screen objects; no food/plant tasting, unsupervised visitors or public identifying photos. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Inquiry display - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: State that careful learning and care for people both matter in our Catholic classroom.
    2. 3-7: Model two observed details in one panel and a concrete care action in the other; label which is evidence.
    3. 7-20: Each child observes, draws a two-panel display and explains it to a partner. Partner says which detail is clear and asks one question; author revises that detail.
    4. 20-26: Each child identifies an actual detail, a question still open and a commitment/action not proved by the object. Gallery remains at tables.
    5. 26-30: Return objects and save display/evidence pages. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which part of your panel is an observation?
    • What did you clarify for your audience?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show two details and distinguish a classroom action from an object observation.

    Grade 2: Explain an open question, an evidence limit and a visual revision after feedback.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Use eye/heart icons with teacher-read meanings and child dictation. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Identify one tempting but unsupported explanation and say what evidence would be needed. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No natural specimens: use familiar classroom objects. Visitor absent: a partner is a valid audience; no scheduling requirement or new history gate.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We shared clear inquiry panels showing observed evidence and a Catholic classroom care commitment. Ask: "Which part of your panel is an observation?" Optional: ask which detail was noticed and which message was a commitment. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Dash Robot Adventures¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Weekly A / Coding
    Native time / scope 2 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, T, M / A measured robot output can test a sequence and a finite repeat.
    Student objective / why "I can run a stored Dash sequence, change it and compare travel." A different robot is a transfer opportunity, not automatically a harder skill.
    Catholic connection Share scarce tools fairly, handle them carefully and explain why responsible use serves the class; robot commands are not moral or divine commands. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Charge/check three Dash kits; connect each tablet, open a new Blockly project and pretest Start -> Drive Forward at low speed for a short distance -> Stop. Mark three 1 m clear floor lanes with start/end zones. Match installed controls to picture cards; test finite Repeat 2 with the drive block before class.

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise.
