Use local classroom aliases, not names/photos/voice uploads; disable sharing and purchases. Actual school-approved access and installed controls are checked during preparation, not assumed from this document.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Program = stored instructions; input = selected instruction; output = movement; finite repeat = a fixed number of repetitions.

    Wheel travel varies by floor and settings. Prediction and comparison require the same start, heading, floor and measured unit.

    Common misconception: Manual steering or successful group travel proves every child programmed.

    If asked: "Does a robot follow God's plan?" A robot executes human instructions; our moral choices are not robot commands.

    SAFETY¶

    Three dry low-speed lanes away from exits; no riders, added markers, collisions or moving across walking routes. Adult handles charging and damaged devices. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Transfer a stored sequence - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Reintroduce Run/Stop and safe lane use; no prior hardware experience assumed.
    2. 3-7: Teacher connects two drive blocks after Start, predicts endpoint, runs, stops and resets to the same start.
    3. 7-20: Use two waves for 10/15 pupils or three for 20/25, four minutes each, three teams per wave. Each member has about 40 seconds to select/change a block, predict, Run/Stop and identify output; other teams plan on cards.
    4. 20-26: Each child records travel in equal ruler lengths/cm and explains the changed instruction. Teacher notes actual device actions during waves; pending turns are not scored independent.
    5. 26-30: Stop robots, return to local project home, park in numbered dry charging storage and remove lane tape. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 2: Finite repeat and comparison - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Recall one measured run and recheck the saved sequence.
    2. 3-7: Compare two explicit short forward blocks with Repeat 2 containing one identical forward block; Run both from same start.
    3. 7-20: Use the same four-minute waves. Each child predicts a finite repeat, runs or changes repeat count with supervision, resets and compares the endpoint. Cards keep waiting teams tracing the same program.
    4. 20-26: Each child shows the repeated action and number of repeats, compares measured output and explains a resource-care action: careful return/sharing, not fastest-run bragging.
    5. 26-30: Stop robots, return to local project home, park in numbered dry charging storage and remove lane tape. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which instruction changed the robot's output?
    • What action repeated and how many times?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Individually Run/Stop a stored sequence and identify a changed action; trace Repeat 2 with two cards.

    Grade 2: Predict and execute/modify a finite repeat, compare two measured outputs and explain why start/heading must be reset.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. No hardware/loop mastery is claimed on a card-only route.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Provide a connected starter script and large block pictures; permit partner positioning under child direction. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain why an identical repeated code may produce slightly different measured endpoints. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Only one/two kits: fewer individual device turns fit; teach token sequencing now and record remaining device checks unassessed. No Repeat control: use two explicit identical blocks; finite-loop execution is unassessed. Failure to connect: adult restarts the app/pairing; never count manual Go driving as code.

    Indoor: The marked indoor floor lanes are the primary route; use desktop cards if safe clear floor space is unavailable.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We tested stored robot instructions and finite repeats, comparing measured travel and sharing tools responsibly. Ask: "Which instruction changed the robot's output?" Optional: trace two repeated spoken actions with a paper token. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Clean corrugated cardboard / kit / 20 cm squares 16 20 28 36
    Index cards / kit / items 24 30 42 54
    Masking tape / kit / 10 cm strips 48 60 84 108

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Access = usable participation; alternative = another option; tradeoff = gain with a cost.

    Open slots may be easier to reach but less secure. A model evaluates the stated tabletop request only.

    Common misconception: A complicated design is automatically more caring.

    If asked: "Can we test it on someone's wheelchair?" No; the tabletop organizer is not an assistive product.

    SAFETY¶

    No body attachments, mobility devices, sharp cardboard, heavy loads or elevated reaches; teacher precuts. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Two alternatives - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Read the user's actual request and three criterion icons.
    2. 3-7: Model open tray versus divided upright slots using sketches, not a finished required answer.
    3. 7-20: Teams fold two different organizers using two squares each and six tape strips each. Each child sketches a criterion and predicts a benefit/limitation. Test card visibility and retrieval with six cards.
    4. 20-26: Each child identifies which criterion each design meets or misses; record user feedback and choose one feature to revise.
    5. 26-30: Return all six cards and sort usable cardboard; label prototypes between meetings. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 2: Revise and recommend - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Retrieve the two test records, not only attractive prototypes.
    2. 3-7: Model a repeat retrieval test with the same cards/placement and an untaped hand; do not pretend disability.
    3. 7-20: Teams revise one feature, run the same three criterion checks on both alternatives and exchange a partner-user check. Each child conducts/directs one check.
    4. 20-26: Each child recommends a design with two criterion results and one tradeoff; teacher captures individual explanations while tables remain seated.
    5. 26-30: Return all six cards and sort usable cardboard; label prototypes between meetings. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which design best meets the helper's request?
    • What did your choice gain and give up?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Name the user need, demonstrate one criterion check and give a reason for a choice.

    Grade 2: Compare both options against three criteria, explain a test-based revision and a specific tradeoff.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Offer two folded starting forms and picture criterion cards; child directs a retrieval test. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Defend whether less tape can preserve function, then test rather than assert. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Organizer tips: broaden its tabletop base or lay slots flat. Helper absent: partner reads the same request; no outside delivery is required.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We compared organizer alternatives for a classroom helper and defended an accessible design choice. Ask: "Which design best meets the helper's request?" Optional: notice how an ordinary organizer helps someone find things. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Week 28: Pi Day Circles¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Mathematics and design / Pi Day Circles
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, M, A
    Big idea We can compare distances around circles using the same unit.
    Student objective "I can compare two circle edges and use circles to make a repeating design."
    Why Accurate measurement and purposeful patterns matter more than memorizing digits.
    Catholic connection Honest evidence: report approximate measures without pretending they are exact; teacher application of faith/reason, CCC 159 (source below).
    Standards Local CST-C1: name measurement uncertainty; CST-M1: compare two boundaries; CST-M2: extend a repeating pattern; CST-A2: intentional form/pattern. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path: paper/string directly show the mathematics. Robot art is not required and attaching a marker to a rolling Sphero is not part of this lesson.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class / supplies¶

    1. Choose two smooth round lids about 8 cm and 12 cm across (neither wider than 15 cm), so their boundaries fit the 60 cm yarn. Remove sharp metal edges. Trace a square to compare.
    2. Cut 60 cm lengths of yarn; prepare one equal-size block chain per team. Demonstrate wrapping yarn once with no overlap or stretching.
    3. Draw AB and AAB circle patterns on the board. Do not use food rewards.
    4. Per student: one sheet and crayon.
    5. Per team of 2-3: two round lids, two yarn lengths, 20 equal blocks about 2 cm wide (or 20 equal 2 cm paper squares) and scrap paper for comparing laid-out yarn. Check that the unit chain spans the longer boundary before class.
    6. Class: tape and board, circle/square examples; reusable lids/yarn.
    7. Teacher-only: scissors for precutting yarn; optional ruler to show approximation.
    Students Teams / lid pairs Yarn lengths Paper sheets
    10 4 8 10
    15 5 10 15
    20 7 14 20
    25 9 18 25

    Vocabulary / teacher background¶

    Circle = flat round shape; circumference = distance around its boundary; diameter = distance across through the center; approximate = close, not exact; repeating unit = part that repeats. Pi is a finite number about 3.14, the ratio of circumference to diameter. Its decimal representation does not terminate or repeat. Endless digits do not mean infinite magnitude. No ratio calculation is required of Grades 1-2. Misconception: every round-looking object is a flat circle. A ball is a sphere; its flat outline may look circular. If asked "Is pi as big as God?" No. Mathematics describes a finite quantity; a devotional analogy is not a mathematical or theological measurement.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Find a circle versus square. Explain Pi Day's 3/14 date briefly without digit recitation or theology claims.
    2. 4-8: Model wrapping yarn around one lid, marking the join, laying it flat and comparing to the same equal blocks.
    3. 8-18: Team members each help measure both lids. Align yarn starts; predict then compare. Grade 2 counts equal blocks, including "a little more than" if needed; Grade 1 points to longer/shorter. Repeat once to notice small measurement differences.
    4. 18-23: Each child traces circles in an intentional AB (Grade 1) or AAB/ABB (Grade 2) pattern. Partner extends it and explains the repeating unit.
    5. 23-26: Individual exit: identify the longer boundary, explain one measurement step and point to the repeating unit; say why a measure may be approximate.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / success¶

    Which yarn is longer when starts line up? What made our two attempts differ? What part of your pattern repeats? - Grade 1: correctly compare two boundaries; demonstrate lining up endpoints; create two complete AB units and predict the next circle. - Grade 2: record two approximate counts in the same units and justify comparison; create/extend three units of AAB or ABB; identify one uncertainty. - Teacher records not yet / prompted / independent for comparison, measurement method, pattern and honest uncertainty. No coding credit from circle artwork.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    Slipping yarn: tape the starting end or teacher models a paper strip. No lids: use two teacher-drawn circles and paper strips; describe these as drawings. No equal blocks: use identical paper squares. Entire lesson works indoors without devices. Early finishers compare a third circle, not speed.

    SAFETY¶

    No food/treats, loose coins, sharp can lids, neck loops or strings tied to students. Precut yarn; teacher manages scissors. Accessible tabletop work only.

    Support / challenge / cleanup¶

    Support: pretraced circles, oral prompts and partner stabilization without taking the child's decision. Grade 1 responds by pointing/drawing. Challenge: Grade 2 compare around/across lengths informally; no required division. Cleanup: count reusable lids/blocks, coil yarn into bags, recycle scraps and retain each child's pattern.

    Family snippet / sources¶

    We compared circle boundaries with yarn and designed a repeating circle pattern. Catholic connection: honest measurement, including uncertainty. Ask: "How did you decide which circle was bigger around?" Optional: point out two circles in a room or picture; no materials/device required. No routine homework. Pi explanation gives definition and approximate value. CCC 159 concerns faith and science; the classroom honesty connection is an application, not an official benchmark. Ecclesiastes 3:11 may be read from a school-approved Bible; no unverified quotation is reproduced.

    grades-1-2year-alife-science

    Weeks 29-31: Growing Things¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Growth / Growing Things
    Time / domains Three 30-minute meetings at roughly weekly intervals / C, S, M
    Big idea Repeated observations show changes; unequal growth alone does not explain causes.
    Student objective "I can observe a seedling, measure the same way, and describe what changed."
    Why Growers use records and responsible care, not guesses or tallest-plant contests.
    Catholic connection Care for plants/resources, honestly report no growth too; CCC 2415. The Sower is a faith parable, not an experimental explanation.
    Standards Local CST-C3: care/resource choice; CST-S1: dated observation/question; CST-S3: seed/seedling model; CST-M1: height comparison; CST-M2: dated record/class display. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path. A teacher photo of changes is optional, not required.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20 minutes first setup plus 2-3 minutes school-day care check; 5 minutes cleanup each meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Check school seed/potting-mix allergy guidance. Select one untreated bean or radish variety; read packet depth/water guidance. No fertilizer, pesticides or edible harvest in class.
    2. Prestart two teacher backup pots 7-10 days earlier. Draw three dated backup observations if live growing conditions are unavailable; clearly identify teacher/picture data.
    3. Teacher makes drainage holes before class. Put pots in leakproof trays by a safe bright indoor window, not on a freezing sill/heater. No electrical grow light required.
    4. Mark a height baseline at the soil surface. Assign a named adult to check moisture on school days and before weekends; water when needed, not automatically daily. Keep care at school, including school breaks or arrange approved adult care.
    5. Make a three-column record: date / drawing / height. Leave "no shoot yet" distinct from a missing measurement.

    Supplies¶

    • Per student: one folded record sheet, pencil/crayon, individual roster check.
    • Per team of 2-3: one pot with drainage, two seeds, about 200 mL commercial potting mix, tray space, ruler or equal cubes; measuring tool reused.
    • Class: one small water jug, scoop, spill cloth, handwashing access, board display.
    • Teacher-only: seed packet, hole tool, backup pots, plant care log; optional plant pictures.
    Students Teams / pots Seeds plus 4 teacher backups Potting mix including 2 backup pots Student sheets
    10 4 12 1.2 L 10
    15 5 14 1.4 L 15
    20 7 18 1.8 L 20
    25 9 22 2.2 L 25

    At 25 keep materials on nine table trays. Teacher controls the water jug; no queue carrying wet pots. Rotate observer, measurer, recorder roles and still collect each child's record.

    Vocabulary / teacher background¶

    Seed = contains a young plant and stored food; germinate = begin growing; seedling = young plant; nutrient = substance needed for growth; data = recorded observations. Many seeds need water, oxygen and suitable temperature to germinate. Seedlings need light for making food, plus water/air/nutrients and support. Soil is a useful growing medium, not plant food or a universal requirement; plants can grow without soil under appropriate conditions. This is a longitudinal observation, not a controlled experiment proving needs. Misconception: an unsprouted seed means its caretaker was bad or lacked faith. If asked "Why did mine not grow?" Seed viability, temperature, water and other factors may matter; our records do not isolate the cause.

    Meeting 1: plant and predict (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Show seed/seedling; state objective and care boundary. Optional original prayer asks for careful stewardship.
    2. 4-8: Explain seed food versus seedling needs; demonstrate packet-based planting depth and soil-surface ruler baseline.
    3. 8-18: Teams scoop mix, plant two seeds, lightly water according to packet and label pot/date. Each child draws what is visible and predicts a future change orally.
    4. 18-22: Make a care log and place pots in trays; choose an adult checker. Explain that not every seed will sprout.
    5. 22-25: Individual evidence: point to seed/seedling, name one care action and one observation.
    6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

    Meeting 2: observe and measure (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Retrieve pots; compare to first dated drawing, not another team's tallest plant.
    2. 4-8: Teacher models height from soil surface to top of shoot, same tool each time. Grade 1 may use equal cubes; Grade 2 nearest whole cm. Do not include pot height.
    3. 8-19: Each child measures or points to the baseline and records one observation; record "no visible shoot" truthfully. Compare own two dates. Teacher checks individuals while partners work.
    4. 19-23: Inspect moisture with teacher and update care log; discuss what we know versus what we cannot yet explain.
    5. 23-25: Optional Sower paraphrase (Matthew 13:3-9) and care reflection: plant growth is not a score for anyone's faith.
    6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

    Meeting 3: communicate changes (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Recall measurement baseline and previous record.
    2. 4-13: Final measurement/drawing using same units; each student compares two dated observations.
    3. 13-19: Display one current height per team on class chart; separate "no shoot" from "not recorded." Grade 2 explains why different heights do not identify one cause.
    4. 19-23: Pairs present change/no change and a question. Keep plants at school unless a family chooses a free take-home plant; provide teacher care instead where needed.
    5. 23-25: Individual exit: show two dated observations and one responsible care decision.
    6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

    Questions / success¶

    What changed since that date? Where does the ruler start? What if a seed does not sprout? Does our evidence prove why plants differ? - Grade 1: two dated drawings, correct baseline demonstration, longer/shorter/same comparison and one care action, all oral/drawn. - Grade 2: at least two dated measures in the same units and explanation of change; distinguish observation from an untested cause. - Score not yet / prompted / independent for observation, measurement, comparison and care; never grade germination success or home participation.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    No sprouts: retain genuine record and measure backup plant; do not relabel teacher data as student's. Mold: teacher removes affected pot sealed, cleans tray per school policy, supplies pictures. No bright window/no live growing allowed: use the three dated teacher drawings and equal-length paper plant models; assess reading/comparing observations, not live plant care mastery. Indoor work remains available all Minnesota winter; no outdoor planting required.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    No tasting seeds/plants/mix, unknown soil, spraying faces, standing water near electronics, student puncturing or glass pots. Wash hands. Teacher handles spill/mold and packet safety. Support: prefilled pots, picture steps, accessible table, adult scribing, thick equal blocks; nonreaders point/draw/tell. Challenge: Grade 2 use differences between two heights or propose a future fair test without claiming this one proves it.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Return tools, wipe trays/tables, put labeled pots safely back, wash hands and store records; adult checks care outside meetings. Family snippet: We kept dated plant records and compared change honestly, including no growth. Our Catholic connection was stewardship. Ask: "What did your evidence show, and what are you still wondering?" Optional: notice a plant or picture at home; no seed purchase, watering homework or device required. CCC 2415; optional Matthew 13 and 1 Corinthians 3:6 references use school-approved Bible (wording VERIFICATION REQUIRED). Seed-specific timing/depth must be verified against the selected packet; no universal sprouting deadline is promised.

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Growth = living change; label = identifies; stable = stands; model = representation.

    A label stand is engineering; the observed plant drawing is life-science/art evidence. A picture is not evidence of new growth this week.

    Common misconception: Dormancy or spring growth means a plant died and resurrected.

    If asked: "Did our drawing grow?" No; it represents a living plant, and our stand test answers a stability question.

    SAFETY¶

    No seed tasting, pot contact, sharp plant stakes or outdoor searching. Dry stand remains beside, not inside, the pot. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Plant-detail stand - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Notice two plant features from the real specimen or labeled picture.
    2. 3-7: Model drawing those details and folding a cardstock tent with no sharp stake.
    3. 7-20: Each child draws a plant label, folds a stand, tests 10 seconds and revises fold width/tape placement if needed. Partners check that one detail remains visible.
    4. 20-26: Each child points to an accurate plant detail and compares first/revised stand results; state how the model avoids disturbing the plant.
    5. 26-30: Keep stands away from pots, collect unused tape and return plant/picture safely. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which plant detail does your model show?
    • What did the standing test tell you?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show two observed details and a standing test/change.

    Grade 2: Explain a life-model limitation and a test-based design change without claiming growth from a picture.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Use a precreased wide tent and adult placement under child direction. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Test whether a wider base obscures any picture and explain the tradeoff. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No plants or earlier record: use a clearly labeled plant picture; growth change is unassessed. Stand fails: lower and widen it, not add a sharp stake.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Curriculum Year Year B (Alternates with Year A)
    Session Length 30 minutes
    Teaching Meetings 32 in 20 files; 34 calendar labels include 2 breaks
    Sessions Per Week 1

    🔄 Year A/B Rotation¶

    This is Year B of a two-year rotation, not a curriculum requiring Year A completion. New Grade 1 students can enter either rotation; teach/recheck picture sequences, observation and safe tool use before dependent challenges. Returning Grade 2 students need increased explanation and measured revision, not the assumption that new robot hardware is inherently harder.

    See the Grades 1-2 review and downloadable audit. This collection supplies 32 x 30 = 960 minutes, not 34 teaching sessions. Calendar labels 17 and 32 have no lessons and are break slots. If 34 taught meetings are required, locally schedule two reteach/evidence checks; do not claim those files already exist. Biweekly is 17 x 30 = 510 minutes and has less practice.

    For trio-based lessons, 10/15/20/25 pupils use ⅘/7/9 groups: two trios and two pairs; five trios; six trios and one pair; seven trios and two pairs. Optional reference routines support kit checks and individual evidence but do not replace the lesson's complete sequence, supplies or safety. Pair-based lessons keep their own allocation/reserve plan. Fewer devices use the lesson's stated waves/shared tests, not groups of four or credit for watching.

    Students who had Year A may experience:

    • Same foundational skills (coding basics, engineering process, scientific inquiry)

    • Different projects and contexts (new challenges, different themes)

    • Different Catholic classroom applications (honest evidence, stewardship, service and inclusion; no unsupported biography required)

    • Rechecked foundations with grade-specific evidence (oral/drawn Grade 1; Grade 2 reasoning, measurements and revisions)

    📚 Materials Overview¶

    Technology¶

    • Dash Robots (primary coding tool in Year B)

    • ScratchJr on iPads

    • Three complete protected lamp-path kits for the second Stars & Light meeting; paper models do not demonstrate physical circuit operation

    Building Materials¶

    • KEVA planks

    • Recycled materials

    • Craft supplies

    • Natural materials

    CSCOE Library Items¶

    • Confirm loan availability, lead time, terms and app compatibility; "2 weeks" is a planning suggestion, not verified checkout policy.

    • Dash Robot charging needed

    • Engineering kits as available

    Catholic applications¶

    Year B assesses honest claims, plant/material care, inclusive participation and real classroom-user requests. No saint patronage, historical quotation or unverified discovery story is needed. The biweekly alternate supplies a short source-checked Maria Agnesi context; it identifies her as a mathematician, not a DNA discoverer.

    Readiness and technology limits¶

    All 20 files have complete teaching plans: the 16 remaining packages are rebuilt and four earlier references preserved. Individual Grade 1/Grade 2 criteria, nonreader demonstrations, supplies for 10/15/20/25, native timing, cleanup, safety and indoor/fallback paths are explicit. Invention Labs has four fully timed meetings and before/after trial evidence. No package is certified as a classroom outcome merely because its documentation is complete.

    Dash/ScratchJr execution has a Required primary path where assessed; unplugged alternatives demonstrate algorithms, not robot/app mastery. The protected-circuit light task is non-digital; paper tracing is not circuit operation. Check actual stock/model condition and school permissions. Plant care stays at school by default; no required home purchase, watering, routine homework or donation. Official benchmark mapping remains parent-owned and is not claimed by local codes.

    Curriculum Version: Complete references — Year B

    Framework: C-STREAM

    Welcome Back Scientists¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Weekly B / Observation
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, S, A / Scientists record what they notice and ask questions they can check.
    Student objective / why "I can draw two observed details and ask a testable question." This reintroduces inquiry without assuming Year A attendance.
    Catholic connection Report observations truthfully, including a surprise, as careful study of creation. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C1: honest evidence and faith/reason; CST-S1: observations, questions and evidence; CST-A1: observational representation. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Screen a detailed leaf picture and smooth block per kit. Draw eye/question/result boxes. Plan an indoor table observation, not an unbounded nature route.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: plan or prediction / actual result / reason or revision. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Leaf picture / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Smooth wooden block / kit / items 4 5 7 9

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Observe = notice; predict = say what may happen; evidence = actual result.

    An observation is different from a guess about cause; a classroom block can be turned or rolled to investigate a child's question.

    Common misconception: Being a scientist means knowing answers rather than asking and checking.

    If asked: "What if my prediction is wrong?" Keep the result; surprise can improve the next question.

    SAFETY¶

    Dry objects only, no tasting or unknown outdoor specimens. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Scientists begin again - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Show leaf and block; model a visible feature and a prediction separately.
    2. 3-7: Demonstrate drawing two details and asking whether changing the block's face changes rolling.
    3. 7-20: Each child closely observes, draws two details, asks an oral question and tries a safe tray turn/roll test. Partner checks the drawing against the object.
    4. 20-26: Each child points to an actual detail/result, states one question and revises a guessed detail that was not observed.
    5. 26-30: Return objects/pictures and save first evidence in private folders. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What did you actually notice?
    • How could you check your question?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show two observed details and ask one question.

    Grade 2: Ask a testable question and distinguish its prediction from an actual result.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Two object choices, eye/question icons and oral dictation. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain what evidence would answer a cause question. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No leaf image: use another dry classroom object. Vague question: offer turn/compare/roll choices without supplying its result.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We began Year B with detailed observation and honest inquiry. Ask: "What did you actually notice?" Optional: notice two features of a familiar indoor object. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Sources and claim boundaries¶

    These are local program competencies, not official Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmark numbers. See local standards and the source register. Catholic care, dignity and honest-inquiry applications follow that register; no unsupported scientist/saint biography, Scripture quotation or devotional history is required to execute this lesson. No external historical or official numeric claim is made.

    grades-1-2year-broboticscoding

    Weeks 2-3: Dash Robot Adventures¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Coding / Dash Robot Adventures
    Time / domains Two 30-minute meetings / C, T, M
    Big idea A program is stored instructions; driving by joystick is a different kind of input.
    Student objective "I can run a short stored program and use a test to improve it."
    Why Responsible designers predict, test and share tools fairly.
    Catholic connection Respect every partner's contribution and agency; teacher application of human dignity and solidarity, CCC 2407. People are not robots obeying a programmer.
    Standards Local CST-C2: inclusive turn-taking; CST-T1: show input/output and stop; CST-T2: order/debug code; CST-M1: compare travel to target. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Required primary path: Dash and compatible tablet with Blockly, because children execute physical robot programs. Unplugged alternative assesses sequences, not robot operation.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes first setup plus manufacturer charging time; 4 minutes cleanup/meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Confirm actual loan, model, school-approved app/permissions and charging guidance. Use Blockly's official description and the installed block guide; do not assume generic Forward/Stop labels.
    2. Test a short program on the actual floor: drive forward 20 cm at low speed; turn right 90 degrees; drive forward 20 cm. Write installed block labels/settings on board and show Run/Stop.
    3. Mark 1 m dry floor bays and a paper target 20 cm ahead, clear of exits. Keep observers outside each bay.
    4. Make three picture cards and a tabletop token. Assign teams of 2-3 with programmer, observer and safety-checker roles; swap after each run.

    Supplies / scaling¶

    • Per student: half-sheet, crayon, teacher roster evidence box.
    • Per team: one charged robot/tablet kit, three cards, token, 20 cm target strip.
    • Whole class: tape, timer, soft paper target, whiteboard; no obstacle course needed.
    • Teacher-only: chargers and installed app guide; cords stay stored during class.
    Students Teams / kits for simultaneous practice Papers
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    At 25 use one supervised station with three 4-minute waves of three teams if only three kits exist; other teams rehearse with cards. If only one kit exists, teacher demonstration plus limited turns is partial device assessment: record children awaiting a turn, not universal mastery. Reduce moving robots to what the adult can safely supervise.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Input = our instructions; output = movement/light; sequence = instructions in order; program = stored instructions; debug = find/change a mismatch; distance = how far. Blockly executes connected blocks. Manual Go control is not evidence of writing stored code. A robot may veer due to floor/charge; distinguish this from a wrong block. Misconception: coding success is driving fastest. Accuracy and explanation matter. If asked "Does God program us?" No. People make meaningful choices; this lesson's Catholic connection is responsibility and inclusion, not mechanical obedience.

    Meeting 1 (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3: State safe stop signal and sharing objective. Optional original prayer: "God, help us include every partner and learn honestly from our tests."
    2. 3-7: Predict a tabletop three-card sequence; each child moves token once.
    3. 7-11: Teacher shows stored Blockly program and contrasts with manual driving; demonstrate Run and Stop before student use.
    4. 11-23: Teams execute tested short programs. Each child predicts, runs/stops and compares ending to target; swap roles. Grade 1 may begin with forward plus light; Grade 2 adds the turn/second movement.
    5. 23-26: Individual oral/drawn exit: show input and output; order cards matching own run. Teacher records actual device participation.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Meeting 2 (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Recall the previous run; new entrants rehearse two cards rather than needing Year A.
    2. 4-8: Teacher deliberately makes the first movement too short; model prediction, observation and one distance change.
    3. 8-20: Each child changes one block/parameter, reruns and compares to target. Grade 2 describes nearer/farther before and after; no automatic maze completion or expertise claim.
    4. 20-24: Pairs show original versus changed sequence and explain output. Optional finite repeat of a light/wait sequence for ready Grade 2 children.
    5. 24-26: Individual evidence check and remaining-turn roster.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / measurable success¶

    What is stored before you press Run? How is this different from driving? Which instruction caused a change? How did your group include everyone? - Grade 1: point to/orally order two actions, personally start/stop one stored run with supervision, show a change and one equitable turn choice. - Grade 2: build/order three actions, predict the ending, change one instruction and explain observed improvement using nearer/farther or measured distance. - Record 0 not observed / 1 prompted / 2 independent for each child's sequence, device operation, debug and inclusion. No credit for a teammate's run.

    If things go wrong / no-device and indoor fallback¶

    Connection: check correct robot and charge once; switch after two minutes, explicitly noting unassessed device skills. Token fallback uses the same prediction/change sequence; assess CST-T2 only, not Dash programming/operation mastery. Veering: stop and lower speed/shorten path on a flat surface. All work is indoors; no weather dependency.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    Low-speed dry floor bays only; stop if robot crosses boundary. Never chase, race, ride or hold a running robot. Teacher handles charging/cables. Safe accessible tabletop token alternative is available without stigmatizing a child. Support: picture cards, narration, adult scribing, two actions and large buttons; nonreaders never copy typed directions. Challenge: Grade 2 explains two trials or a finite light loop, not sensors/autonomous navigation.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Stop, save only to school-controlled device as permitted, power down, count kits/cards, clear lesson tape and return to labeled trays; teacher charges. Family snippet: We predicted and debugged stored robot instructions and shared turns respectfully. Ask: "What input changed the robot's output?" Optional: move a paper token with three spoken instructions; no device or purchase. No routine homework. Blockly official app; CCC 2407. Solanus Casey biography is optional and VERIFICATION REQUIRED before use; it is not needed to assess patience.

    grades-1-2year-bsciencearts

    Week 4: Senses and Discovery¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Observation / Senses and Discovery
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, A
    Big idea Different safe tools/senses reveal different details; everyone can contribute evidence.
    Student objective "I can describe two details and compare two objects using a safe way to observe."
    Why Observations support comparisons without requiring every child to use every sense.
    Catholic connection Respect dignity and access; do not compare a child's body to another as better/worse. Teacher application of CCC 2407.
    Standards Local CST-C2: choose an inclusive observation method; CST-S1: describe two details; CST-A1: sketch observed detail; CST-M2: sort by a stated property. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path: direct observation suffices.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class¶

    1. Screen clean large textured objects: cloth, smooth plastic lid and corrugated cardboard. Remove scents, food, feathers, spices and unknown plant materials.
    2. Teacher seals two identical rice shakers permanently, checks leakage and never opens them in class. Alternative: teacher claps two gentle sound patterns; children can observe motion instead of listening.
    3. Put texture examples and two lids of visibly different sizes at each table. Draw a two-box observation sheet on the board; folding plain paper suffices.
    4. Offer look, safe optional touch, or picture/tactile replica; never surprise-touch or blindfold a child. Show quiet space and opt-out choices.

    Supplies¶

    • Per student: one folded sheet, crayon.
    • Per team of 2-3: three large clean texture examples, two smooth lids; optional plastic magnifier.
    • Whole class: two permanently sealed shakers, timer, sorting mat, handwashing.
    • Teacher-only: shaker sealing/checking, roster, object screening; no taste/smell supplies.
    Students Teams / texture sets Papers
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    At 25 use table work plus one teacher sound demo; no five-station traffic or shared mouth instruments.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Observe = notice safely; texture = surface feel or appearance; compare = describe what is alike/different; evidence = noticed detail; sort = group by a property. Sight/hearing/touch are options, not requirements. Scientists use instruments when direct senses are unavailable or unsafe. Tasting an unknown substance is never a scientific observation method for this class. Misconception: a guessing game answer matters more than evidence. "Bumpy ridges" is better evidence than "I think it is a shell." If asked "Why aren't we tasting?" Taste can expose allergens/unsafe substances; today's objectives need no food.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: State objective, access choices and safe touch rule; optional original prayer thanks God for each person's contributions.
    2. 4-8: Teacher models two details on cardboard using looking and optional touch; contrast observation with guess.
    3. 8-17: Teams examine texture examples; each child draws/points/describes two details. Partner compares two objects using rough/smooth, size or visible ridges. Teacher checks individuals.
    4. 17-21: Teacher demonstrates quiet sealed shaker sounds or gentle claps with visible movement. Children compare patterns by hearing or seeing; no requirement to hear.
    5. 21-26: Each child sorts two objects by one stated property and explains/draws evidence. Grade 2 sorts same objects a second way. Partners name a method that includes someone who chooses not to touch/hear.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup and handwashing.

    Questions / success¶

    What did you notice rather than guess? Which observation method is safe for you? Can the same objects be grouped another way? - Grade 1: oral/pointed/drawn two details, one alike/different comparison and one grouping reason; choose an accessible method. - Grade 2: two precise details, two defensible grouping rules and an explanation that a different method can still supply evidence. - Teacher marks not yet / prompted / independent for details, sorting and inclusion; never scores use of all senses.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    Leaking shaker: remove immediately and use claps/visible motion. Sensory overload: quiet visual/tactile table by choice. Missing objects: use large teacher drawings with visible texture marks; distinguish pictured observations from touch evidence. Entire lesson is indoors and no-device ready.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    No tasting, smell jars, blindfolds, reaching into unknown bags, loud shaking near ears, loose beans/rice or forced touch. Teacher seals and counts shakers. Respect sensory and physical access without implying anyone is less blessed. Support: two picture choices, sentence starter "I notice...", oral response, larger objects and adult scribing. Challenge: Grade 2 justify two classifications or ask what a magnifier might reveal.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Return/count objects, wipe washable surfaces per school practice, recycle scraps and wash hands. Family snippet: We compared details using safe accessible observation methods. Our Catholic connection was including every observer. Ask: "What detail helped you sort an object?" Optional: describe a familiar object or picture together; no tasting or purchase. No routine homework. CCC 2407; Psalm 139:14 is an optional reference in a school-approved Bible, not an unverified quotation. Isidore's specific sensory practices are not historical evidence and are omitted.

    Tower Engineering¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Weekly B / Structures
    Native time / scope 2 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, E, M / Tower stability can be compared at the same height.
    Student objective / why "I can measure two tower tests and represent their results." Year B adds repeatability and a data display, not a tallest tower contest.
    Catholic connection Use shared planks responsibly and explain why a smaller material allocation may be a wise choice. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C3: stewardship and responsible work; CST-E2: build, test and redesign; CST-M1: count, compare and measure; CST-M2: represent and interpret data/patterns. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Inspect planks. Mark a build zone and 20 cm target/30 cm ceiling on a teacher ruler. Pretest two low base arrangements; draw pass/fall and height boxes.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: height / two trial results / changed base. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 40 60 80 100
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Wooden building planks / kit / items 96 120 168 216
    Metric ruler / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Masking tape / kit / 10 cm strips 16 20 28 36

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Stability = staying standing; height = bottom-to-top length; trial = one test.

    A broader base often resists tipping, but arrangement matters. Compare bases at similar height; changing both height and base obscures the cause.

    Common misconception: An impressive height proves a good structure or humble character.

    If asked: "Did Babel fail because tall towers are bad?" No history claim is required; we study stability and respectful teamwork.

    SAFETY¶

    Under 30 cm on tables, no furniture climbing, pushing towers or heavy top loads. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Measure the first design - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: State target: approximately 20 cm tall, stands 10 seconds, maximum 24 planks.
    2. 3-7: Model measuring from table surface and starting a standing test with hands clear.
    3. 7-20: Teams build and run two 10-second trials, rebuilding the same design after a fall. Each child measures/counts/directs a trial and records the actual height.
    4. 20-26: Each child shows height with units and two pass/fall results; identify a weak part without blaming a classmate.
    5. 26-30: Dismantle top-down and count 24 planks; retain diagrams between meetings. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 2: Same-height redesign - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Retrieve the first height/results and choose a base change.
    2. 3-7: Model keeping height approximately the same while widening or overlapping the base.
    3. 7-20: Teams change the base, run two equivalent trials and record new height/results. Each child builds/directs and explains the kept-same condition.
    4. 20-26: Each child makes a two-row results display and compares success counts out of two; explain a material-care choice.
    5. 26-30: Dismantle top-down and count 24 planks; retain diagrams between meetings. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Were the two designs tested at the same height?
    • What do your two trial records show?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Measure/count height with aligned starts and show actual standing results.

    Grade 2: Record units and successes out of two for both designs; explain a kept-same condition and limit.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Provide a low base example and equal-unit strip if cm reading is not secure. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain why a single fall does not prove a shape always fails. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No planks: use equal classroom blocks and pretest the feasible height before class, labeling the changed criterion. Both pass: report a tie and compare resource use.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We measured tower height and compared repeated stability trials using honest records. Ask: "Were the two designs tested at the same height?" Optional: point to the base of a pictured structure. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Sources and claim boundaries¶

    These are local program competencies, not official Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmark numbers. See local standards and the source register. Catholic care, dignity and honest-inquiry applications follow that register; no unsupported scientist/saint biography, Scripture quotation or devotional history is required to execute this lesson. No external historical or official numeric claim is made.

    Animal Habitats¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Weekly B / Habitats
    Native time / scope 3 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, S, A, M / A habitat model explains an animal's connected needs, not just a pretty home.
    Student objective / why "I can show a squirrel's food, water, shelter and space and explain model limits." Teacher-read evidence makes life-science research accessible to nonreaders.
    Catholic connection Care for living creatures without removing them from their habitat; distinguish a model from a real care plan. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C3: stewardship and responsible work; CST-S3: physical, life or Earth systems/models; CST-A1: observational representation; CST-M2: represent and interpret data/patterns. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Draw/read the supplied reference on each card: "A tree squirrel uses seeds/nuts as food, drinks water, uses a nest/cavity for shelter, and moves through trees/ground." Label this a simplified general model, not a species care guide. Precut materials and draw a four-need checklist.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: need / reference-supported feature / visible-or-missing check. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Habitat = place meeting needs; shelter = protected place; model = representation; evidence = reference detail.

    A nest is not the whole habitat. No live animal, internet research or seed/food prop is needed; squirrels and habitats vary.

    Common misconception: Every animal lives in a house like ours, or a cardboard habitat can keep an animal alive.

    If asked: "Can we catch a squirrel?" No; we observe/model and leave wildlife alone.

    SAFETY¶

    No live animals, droppings, food, feathers or outdoor collection; dry screened card only. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Read and represent needs - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Read the reference aloud with four icons; distinguish the animal from its habitat.
    2. 3-7: Model one need-and-place connection, not a finished required model.
    3. 7-20: Each child draws four need icons from the reference and a possible layout. Partner checks that each need appears; teacher reads/scribes labels.
    4. 20-26: Each child points to a reference-supported connection and explains why shelter alone is insufficient.
    5. 26-30: Store dry models between meetings; return unused card/tape and keep individual diagrams. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 2: Build an explanatory model - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Retrieve individual plans and state the four-need criterion.
    2. 3-7: Show a flat or folded shelter model and how arrows/icons can show food/water/space without real props.
    3. 7-20: Teams build a habitat on the cardboard square using four cardstock pieces and eight tape strips. Each child creates/directs one feature and checks all four need icons.
    4. 20-26: Each child draws the model and records a four-icon checklist: visible/missing; revise one missing or misleading feature.
    5. 26-30: Store dry models between meetings; return unused card/tape and keep individual diagrams. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Meeting 3: Check and communicate - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Recall the reference and distinguish recorded model features from living-animal observations.
    2. 3-7: Model a critique: "I can see shelter; where does the animal get water?"
    3. 7-20: Teams exchange a reference/checklist critique and revise. Each child represents the completed needs and interprets the before/after checklist counts out of four.
    4. 20-26: Each child explains two need-feature links, a corrected feature and one model limit; name a wildlife-care action.
    5. 26-30: Store dry models between meetings; return unused card/tape and keep individual diagrams. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How does your model meet this animal's needs?
    • What can the cardboard model not do?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show food, water and shelter connections and count checklist features.

    Grade 2: Explain all four connections, compare before/after coverage and name a model limit without inventing species facts.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Use four large need icons, teacher narration and partner placement directed by the child. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain why another animal would require different features; do not invent a care plan. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No reference pictures: draw icons while reading the supplied general description. Short build time: use a flat diagram model; science evidence stays the same and no structural mastery is claimed.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We modeled animal habitat needs and checked explanatory features against a read-aloud reference. Ask: "How does your model meet this animal's needs?" Optional: discuss a habitat in a familiar picture without touching wildlife. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Week 10: Ramp Races¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Motion / Ramp Races: compare rather than race
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting / C, S, M
    Big idea Changing one test condition and keeping others alike helps us compare results.
    Student objective "I can release the same car without a push and compare its stopping distances."
    Why Evidence, repeated tests and honest records are useful beyond competition.
    Catholic connection Honest evidence and respect for others' results; teacher application of faith/reason, CCC 159. Physical laws are not the moral meaning of Catholic natural law.
    Standards Local CST-C1: distinguish data/guess; CST-S2: keep fair-test conditions; CST-S3: gravity/motion model; CST-M1: measure distance; CST-M2: two-condition results. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path: direct measurement; no speed sensor or video needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class / supplies¶

    1. Test a 40-50 cm rigid cardboard ramp with one and two thin books, maximum support height 10 cm. Tape securely in a shallow tray/table lane with end catch box; runout cannot enter an aisle.
    2. Mark fixed starting point and ramp-end line. Use same toy car, ramp, lane and release method for both heights. Do not change cars or landing surfaces during this test.
    3. Prepare two-column low/high recording paper; teacher makes a shared example.
    4. Per student: half-sheet, crayon, personal prediction.
    5. Per team of 2-3: one car, ramp, two books, tape, measuring strip of equal 2 cm marks or equal cubes, catch box.
    6. Class: timer, class chart; reusable kits.
    7. Teacher-only: ramp preflight, height check, roster. No small loose balls or launched loads.
    Students Teams / complete ramp kits Individual sheets
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    At 25 use nine parallel table lanes only if table area contains each run. Otherwise three supervised lanes with three 4-minute waves; off-lane teams predict and compare teacher example data. Record any student not observed releasing/measuring.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Gravity = Earth's pull on objects; distance = how far; trial = one test; condition = test setting; fair test = keep important things the same except the planned change. At these small classroom heights gravity is effectively unchanged. A higher starting position can provide more gravitational potential energy. Runout depends on ramp/surface/car; farther stopping distance does not measure speed directly, and results may differ. Misconception: gravity pulls harder from a higher ramp. It does not in this setup. If asked "Which car was faster?" We measured stopping distance, not time/speed; that needs a different test.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-3: Explain comparison objective and lane rule; each child predicts low/high/same by pointing.
    2. 3-7: Model no-push release and measuring from ramp end to car's final front position; count equal units, always same reference.
    3. 7-10: Identify what stays the same and changed book height; pairs rehearse roles: releaser, measurer, recorder.
    4. 10-22: Run three low and three high trials per team, swapping roles. Record each result, including surprises; Grade 1 uses marks/cubes, Grade 2 whole cm if ready. Do not force a predicted pattern.
    5. 22-26: Each child points to one result for each condition, compares, and names one controlled feature; ask whether the trials agree.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / measurable evidence¶

    Did you push? Where does measurement start? What changed? Does one result prove a rule for every car? - Grade 1: release without push, compare one low/high result orally or with drawn lengths, name same car/start. - Grade 2: record at least two trials per condition, compare spread/typical result informally, name one changed and two unchanged features; no required averages. - Score not yet / prompted / independent for release, measurement and evidence-based comparison. Winning a race is not assessed.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    Car leaves lane: stop, lower ramp and add catch sides. Car does not roll: inspect wheels/ramp join and retest at same low setting; document change. Inconsistent results are valid; revisit release and surface. No kits: teacher demonstrates while children compare honest shared results, noting direct manipulation not individually assessed. Indoors year-round, no devices needed.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    Ramp below 10 cm; gentle releases only; cars not projectiles. No heavy loads, standing on furniture, chasing or lanes across routes. Teacher approves stable supports. Support: prebuilt lane, two trials per condition with scaffolded comparison, tactile equal-unit strip, scribing. Challenge: Grade 2 proposes a later different-surface test while explaining why not to combine changes today.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Park/count cars, detach only lesson tape, stack books/ramps, store data. We tested ramp heights and compared measured stopping distances with honest records. Ask: "What did you keep the same?" Optional: describe a ramp seen in a picture or school; no home experiment required. No routine homework. CCC 159. Physics explanation uses standard elementary mechanics; official benchmark alignment remains VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Albert the Great biography is optional and must be verified before adding.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Character = programmed figure; script = its stored blocks; privacy = controlling personal information.

    Each character has its own script; a message cannot be checked by watching only one shared run.

    Common misconception: Everyone in a group coded because two characters moved.

    If asked: "Can we publish my photo?" No; this class uses fictional characters and local work only.

    SAFETY¶

    Dry table tablets, muted sound, no account creation, purchases, camera use or uploads. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Two-character thanks - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Choose a fictional helper and a visual thank-you message; decide which personal detail must stay private.
    2. 3-7: Model character 1: flag -> right 2 -> End; character 2: flag -> Wait -> right 1 -> End. Predict which moves first.
    3. 7-20: Each member has a four-minute tablet turn: select a character, build/run its script, change a motion/Wait order, reset and rerun. Waiting partners trace cards and plan a visual choice.
    4. 20-26: Each child explains a changed output and privacy choice; partner gives one visual-message comment and author revises. Teacher checks Run and selected-character actions during turns.
    5. 26-30: Return to Home to retain local project, lock tablets and count block cards. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which character's script did you change?
    • What information should stay private?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Select a character, Run its stored script and identify a changed action; reject sharing a name/photo.

    Grade 2: Explain the two-script order, rerun a changed block and justify a specific privacy/message revision.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Thanksgiving feelings are not scored as a Catholic standard.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Starter scripts with one missing block, large character icons and spoken messages. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Predict whether the second character's Wait changes the first character's script, then test. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No Wait block: use two different motion counts and assess character/output, not timing. No app: use two paper story panels and cards; mark app operation unassessed.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    We executed and revised two-character thank-you animations and practiced safe local sharing. Ask: "Which character's script did you change?" Optional: tell a two-character story with no personal details. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Lesson at a glance¶

    2. Prepare two fall records per child; draw observe/build/code preference columns. If records are absent, mark fresh work clearly.
