    Difficulty / entry Developing; teach events/repeat/custom input. Lists/broadcast systems are not squeezed into this two-meeting core.
    Prep / cleanup Moderate: first 30 min, repeat 15 min; IT approval/setup extra; cleanup 4 min/meeting.

    BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS¶

    Check school contact/accommodations and approved offline/school Scratch access, local save and working editor. Pretest both complete starters; Pen extension needed only for meeting 1. Team roles operator/tracer/tester rotate, each edits and runs. No personal/shared logins or public publishing.

    Item Allocation for unit 10 15 20 25
    Paper traces; pencil 2 sheets and 1 pencil/student 20;10 30;15 40;20 50;25
    Computer with approved Scratch, simultaneous route 1/team 4 5 7 9
    Computer with approved Scratch, shared route instead 3/class alternative 3 3 3 3
    Paper starter/test reference 2/team 8 10 14 18
    Ruler 1/team 4 5 7 9
    Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

    Paper consumable; devices/tools reusable; software an access resource.

    Shared-route kit and turn plan¶

    Select one computer row; no extra demo setup or purchase is assumed. For three working approved setups, teacher preloads the complete starters below (Pen added; clone slot sprite-local), making fresh turn copies. Keep ⅘/7/9 balanced teams: two trios/two pairs, five trios, six trios/one pair, seven trios/two pairs. In each meeting, teams 1-3 use 11-19, 4-6 19-27, 7-9 27-35; 10/15 use two waves and then retest. Each pupil gets up to two minutes plus two minutes/team for reset/checking: meeting 1 restore repeat 3 to 4 on a bug copy, run both square sizes and check 160/320; meeting 2 change spacing 60 to 40, run three clones and compare -80/-40/0 with -60/0/60, then restore and rerun. Every pupil edits and executes; waiting pupils annotate call/clone traces and purposeful visual feedback. Pretest the exact access/switch/turn workflow. Log observed/assisted/NE; watching a partner is not operation. One/two setups serve that many teams per window; remaining pupils keep paper evidence and book later runtime checks. Do not enlarge groups or rush motor/access support. Shared-route evidence is editing/running a provided starter, not independent from-scratch creation.

    VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Custom block: named reusable instructions. Parameter: supplied input. Clone: runtime sprite copy. Local variable: value private to that sprite/ clone; globals are shared. Common misconception: moving automatically draws. Pen down is required. If asked, "Are clones permanent?" No; this starter deletes each after its finite behavior and starts without stored personal data.

    Complete starters and keys¶

    Meeting 1, one sprite, add Pen, make block square (size):

    define square (size)
repeat (4)
  move (size) steps
  turn clockwise (90) degrees

when green flag clicked
erase all
pen up
go to x: (-100) y: (0)
point in direction (90)
pen down
square (40)
pen up
go to x: (20) y: (0)
pen down
square (80)
pen up
say [Two sizes, one definition]

    Key: each call has four moves/four turns; perimeter 160/320 steps (Scratch steps, not screen cm). Change repeat 4 to 3 in a copy -> open three sides; fix/retest. Keep "run without screen refresh" unchecked.

    Meeting 2, new one-sprite project, create variable slot for this sprite only:

    when green flag clicked
show
go to x: (0) y: (0)
set [slot] to (0)
repeat (3)
  change [slot] by (1)
  create clone of [myself]
  wait (0.2) seconds
hide

when I start as a clone
go to x: ((slot) * (60) - (120)) y: (0)
show
say (slot) for (2) seconds
delete this clone

    Key: copies inherit slots ½/3, positions -60/0/60; all delete after their two-second display; original hidden. A global slot can change while copies run, so it is not the intended per-clone record. No forever-clone loop.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    Meeting 1: function and parameter¶

    1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "Can one definition draw two sizes?" Explain user clarity.
    2. 4-11 (7 min): Model Pen setup, custom input and 4x40 perimeter.
    3. 11-24 (13 min): Teams assemble/run starter; each edits size or executes call and records path. Shared teams begin the stated waves; waiting pupils annotate calls.
    4. 24-35 (11 min): Run 40/80 tests, diagnose three-side bug, restore four; finish shared waves and choose line color/contrast purposefully without color-only instruction.
    5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual call trace, 160/320 check, bug/retest and feedback-design explanation.
    6. 41-45 (4 min): Save approved local project, close devices, collect traces.

    Meeting 2: bounded clones¶

    1. 0-4 (4 min): Retrieve call reasoning; introduce clone copies.
    2. 4-11 (7 min): Model sprite-only variable and finite starter/key.
    3. 11-24 (13 min): Assemble/run, rotate all pupils through one edit/execution; record ½/3 and positions. Shared teams begin the stated waves; waiting pupils predict inherited slots.
    4. 24-35 (11 min): Repeat run; inspect deletion/reset. Change spacing 60 to 40 deliberately -> positions -80/-40/0; finish shared waves and restore or document chosen spacing with rationale.
    5. 35-41 (6 min): Each explains clone/local versus global, one test and school-only save/privacy boundary.
    6. 41-45 (4 min): Save locally if permitted, stop scripts, close devices, keep evidence.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    "What changes at a call? How many clones? Which variable does each inherit?" Each has correct call/clone traces, observed execution turn, corrected test and purposeful visual feedback. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 predicts another size/spacing; NE if not executed.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY¶

    No line -> Pen extension/down; overlapping clones -> local variable/positions. No approved setups -> execute paper arrows/clone cards from same starters, record reasoning only and defer runtime evidence. No private input, public accounts, infinite clone creation, copied media or flashing effects. Stop/report unsafe device/data behavior.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    Grade 5/support: large block reference, one call/clone at a time, oral trace. Grade 6/challenge: predict square(60) perimeter 240 and a spacing tradeoff. Indoor seated lesson; no home coding or purchase requirement.

    CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Teacher records actual versus paper operation and missing tests; return devices. Explored: functions/clones. Did: two sizes and three finite copies. Learned: parameters/local state matter. Catholic connection: honest, useful work. Ask: "Which test found the bug?" No routine homework.

    Weeks 26-27: Snap Circuits - Accessible Indicators¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Teacher reference
    Grade / unit Grades 5-6 / Physical Computing A
    Time Two 45-minute meetings, 90 total, including 4-minute cleanup each
    Domains Catholic inclusive design, science systems, technology tools, engineering
    Big idea A complete powered path lets a switch control a light; a usable signal also needs clear communication.
    Student objective I can explain a closed path, test an ON/OFF indicator twice and justify an accessibility improvement.
    Why Safe testing and user feedback matter more than a flashy display.
    Catholic connection Respect each user's dignity and access, not just successful builders; sources.
    Local standards / evidence CST-S3: full path; CST-T1: state predictions/repair; CST-E2: before/after test; CST-C2: access decision. Local program codes only.
    Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None: no computing device or software. Approved electrical hardware is required for operation; paper shows reasoning only.
    Prerequisites Open/closed is taught here; no earlier electronics or Ohm's-law arithmetic required.
    Prep / cleanup First inspection 30 minutes; repeat prep 15 minutes; missing instructions/approval extra. Cleanup 4 minutes per meeting included.

    BEFORE CLASS¶

    Release the hardware route only after completing the OLP Snap Circuits guide. Use the actual model's documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project from the eight individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits (OHM-135). Do not assume a push button, protected holder, LED/resistor specification or battery count. The filename is retained for existing links, not LittleBits wiring.

    User brief: "A classroom model needs an ON/OFF light and a label readable from 1 m by someone who cannot rely on color alone." It is not a medical, emergency or real safety device, and it will not be distributed to patients.

    MATERIALS¶

    • Per pupil: pencil/journal, one circuit/state/design sheet for both meetings.
    • Per team: diagram sheet, cardstock label, ruler and shared marker; dry work area. Keep the circuit on its supplied grid; label stands beside it.
    • Per hardware station: approved Snap kit with selected project parts, diagram/grid and tray. Cells/reserves follow the guide's setup card.
    • Teacher/class: manufacturer instructions, setup card, board, timer, evidence roster, adult-controlled cells and dry storage. Demo uses a station kit.
    Pupils Teams / diagrams / labels / rulers Hardware kits / trays Waves Individual sheets / pencils
    10 4 4 1 10
    15 5 5 1 15
    20 7 7 1 20
    25 9 5 2 25

    No separate LED/resistor harness, mounting tape, extra base, app or new workbook purchase for the Snap route. The protected-AA alternative remains separate.

    VOCABULARY, BACKGROUND AND SAFETY¶

    Circuit: full conducting return path. Input/output: switch action/light. Load: component transferring electrical energy. Open: interrupted path. Criterion/constraint: success requirement/limit. Tradeoff: a choice with benefits and costs. Battery chemical energy becomes electrical energy and then light/thermal energy; current is not "used up" at the lamp.

    Evidence change: Snap's slide switch has two states tested twice, not the old independently controlled supply/button four-state test. Teach ON/OFF, not push/release. LED polarity/current-limiting evidence is not claimed from a lamp project. The separate protected-AA option retains its four-state key.

    Misconception: a lit lamp proves any wiring is safe. If asked: "Can I join the battery terminals?" No; that is a dangerous short. Trace a safe open path on paper instead.

    SAFETY: follow the guide's manufacturer/age/holder gates; adult isolates the source before snap changes and inspects before restoring power. No pupil cell access, loose/button cells, mains/USB substitutions, shorts, bypassed protection, extra branches, fan blades, soldering or take-home circuits. Warm/damaged/smelly/leaking -> stop/report, adult isolates, OUT OF SERVICE. Keep labels beside the grid, not over parts or contacts.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    Meeting 1: exactly 45 minutes - path and troubleshooting¶

    1. 0-4: Purpose. Read the user brief; discuss why a clear signal can support dignity and access.
    2. 4-9: Model. Trace the approved return path, demonstrate OFF/ON, source isolation and adult inspection. Explain the two-state evidence change.
    3. 9-12: Predict. Each child labels source/switch/light/conductors/return, predicts OFF/ON and identifies a drawn gap.
    4. 12-26: Wave A. Guide routine: isolated team build, adult check, each child's two OFF/ON cycles, one teacher-managed open-path repair and checked retest. Waiting teams label diagrams and draft an accessible ON/OFF label.
    5. 26-27: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers/resets station kits.
    6. 27-41: Wave B / individual evidence. Remaining teams get the same hardware routine. Finished teams record predicted/actual results and explain one repair and safe resource choice; smaller classes use the window for repeat tests and individual checks.
    7. 41-45: Cleanup. Isolate/count/store parts and cells, save data and note unfinished physical evidence.

    Meeting 2: exactly 45 minutes - accessible indicator¶

    1. 0-4: Retrieve. Revisit each child's state/path record without assuming prior mastery.
    2. 4-9: Define criteria. Two correct OFF/ON cycles; a peer reads/interprets the label from 1 m, without color-only cues. Constraints: supplied grid, unchanged approved circuit, paper label beside it.
    3. 9-12: Plan. Each child predicts an access obstacle and sketches a justified label/layout change.
    4. 12-26: Wave A. Build/check/test; peer reads label at 1 m without coaching. Record pass/not yet, revise one paper feature and repeat the same test. No electrical redesign outside the documented project.
    5. 26-27: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers station kits.
    6. 27-41: Wave B / explain. Remaining teams run the same routine. Finished teams document before/after results; each child explains path, observed change, user benefit and limitation/tradeoff. Do not claim a real alert device is safe.
    7. 41-45: Cleanup. Isolate/count/store; collect individual diagrams/state/revision records. Paper only goes home.

    SUCCESS, SUPPORT AND TROUBLE¶

    Each child contributes to the isolated build, operates the switch, labels the full path, predicts two states, records two cycles and explains test-backed repair/redesign evidence. Log observed / prompted / not yet for physical contribution/testing separately from diagram reasoning; a functioning team kit does not certify every child's operation.

    Score 1 participation only; 2 prompted path/test; 3 independent path, state and before/after explanation; 4 additionally defends an access tradeoff and the model's limitations.

    • Grade 5/support: traced diagram, large word/symbol labels, oral records, motor assistance; still collect each child's prediction and switch turn.
    • Grade 6/challenge: justify label size/layout/readability tradeoffs using feedback. Compare two drawn faults; no undocumented loads or V=IR requirement.
    • 25 pupils: nine teams, five stations, two 14-minute hardware waves. Inspection/access overruns defer evidence, never compress safety checks.
    • No light: isolate/report; adult compares approved diagram/contacts/cells, then supplies a checked reserve. Never bypass protection or improvise parts.

    ALTERNATIVES / INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    The guide retains the original separate protected-AA push-switch/LED-resistor route and its four-state evidence key; no Snap/LittleBits components are attached to that supply. Use the same waves, replacing slide-switch tests with the specified supply/button states. Record which hardware and state table were used. Without safe hardware, retain the timed paper diagram/state/design work; record reasoning/design only; electrical operation not observed and schedule supervised completion. All work is dry and indoors.

    FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Explored: switched circuits and accessible signals. Did: tested ON/OFF twice and revised a label using peer feedback. Learned: a complete path and clear communication matter. Catholic connection: dignity in design. Name the actual Snap, protected-AA or paper route; for the AA route describe its four-state test instead. Ask: "What did your test show, and how did the label change?" No homework, family purchases or take-home powered circuits.

    Week 28: Pi Day Mathematics¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Reference
    Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / A / Mathematics
    Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes
    Objective / why / big idea I can measure three circles, calculate C/D with equal units and explain measurement uncertainty. The mathematical circle ratio is constant, our measurements approximate it.
    Domains / Catholic connection M, S, C; truthful numerical reasoning; mathematical philosophy is not required Catholic doctrine.
    Local standards CST-M3: ratios; CST-S2: repeated measurement; CST-C1: numerical versus philosophical claim. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Requirement None; calculators are arithmetic tools; Monte Carlo coding not a core objective in this single meeting.
    Difficulty / entry Developing; teach diameter through center, decimal division and units.
    Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Circle Measures.

    BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS¶

    Review contact/accommodations. Seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Select three flat rigid plastic circular lids 6-12 cm diameter/team; no cans/sharp edges or food. Adult verifies string can wrap each circumference without stretching and pilots center diameter. Copy table Object / C cm / D cm / C divided by D. Pi Day calendar date is school-selected, not guaranteed by week number.

    Item Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Paper; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25
    Plastic circular lids 3/team 12 15 21 27
    Nonstretch string 0.5 m/team 2 m 2.5 m 3.5 m 4.5 m
    Ruler; calculator; table sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9
    Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

    Paper consumable; string/lids/tools reusable; adult cuts string.

    VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Circumference: distance around. Diameter: across center. Ratio: division comparison. Uncertainty: limits in measurement. Pi is irrational (decimal neither terminates nor eventually repeats); that is a mathematical fact, not evidence that a physical measurement has infinite precision. Common misconception: measure radius instead of diameter. If asked, "Did we discover exact pi?" No; our tool estimates are rounded. Worked fictional C/D: 18.9/6 = 3.15; 25.⅛ = 3.1375; 31.4/10 = 3.14. All compare to about 3.14, not expected actual values.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "Why might every circle give a similar ratio?" Discuss honest estimates.
    2. 4-11 (7 min): Demonstrate string circumference, straight centered diameter and equal-unit division.
    3. 11-25 (14 min): Rotate wrapper/measurer/recorder across three lids; each pupil measures one and records all three values/ratios.
    4. 25-35 (10 min): Repeat one C/D pair; compare original/repeat and possible string gaps/center error. Keep both, no data correction to 3.14.
    5. 35-41 (6 min): Each student independently calculates one ratio with units, explains the three-object pattern and uncertainty, and distinguishes evidence from a philosophical view of mathematics.
    6. 41-45 (4 min): Coil string, count lids/tools, save tables and tidy.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    "Did you cross the center? Would a stretched string increase C? Why not erase an unexpected ratio?" Each has three measured pairs, one checked division, repeat/uncertainty and claim distinction. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 explains error direction; NE for missing measurement.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY¶

    Ratio near 6 -> check radius/diameter. No lids -> adult-drawn circles measured as drawings, not manufactured objects. No calculator -> use worked long division scaffold. No string around bodies, tasting, sharp cans, rolling objects or device uploads. Stop/report unsafe handling.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    Grade 5/support: center-marked lid, ruler guide, calculator/scribed reasoning. Grade 6/challenge: compare absolute difference from 3.14 and explain precision; more measurements need not get closer every time. Indoor tabletop primary.

    CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Keep raw/repeated values, count kit pieces; record incomplete checks. Explored: circle ratios. Did: three measurements and a repeat. Learned: units/uncertainty. Catholic connection: honest reasoning. Ask: "Why wasn't your ratio exact?" No routine homework.

    Weeks 29-31: Environmental Science & Stewardship¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Teacher reference
    Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Environment A / Environmental Science & Stewardship
    Time Three meetings of 45 minutes; 135 total
    Domains C, S, M, A; tools support observation
    Big idea Responsible environmental decisions need comparable measurements and honest limitations.
    Student objective I can graph a weather dataset and propose a small stewardship action without claiming more than the evidence shows.
    Why Residents, farmers, and caretakers interpret weather and use resources responsibly.
    Catholic connection Care for people and our common home; paraphrase Laudato Si' and stewardship sources, not proof of a scientific prediction.
    Local standards / evidence CST-S2: individual comparison/control explanation; CST-M2: individual labeled graph and range; CST-A3: revised visual message tested by a peer; CST-C3: individual action and resource tradeoff.
    Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; these four codes are local.
    Technology None for the primary paper-data path. Non-glass thermometers optional for live indoor practice; spreadsheet optional after paper analysis.
    Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; read integer temperatures including negatives, plot points, add/subtract. Grade 6 mean is scaffolded. No prior Year B required.
    Prep / cleanup First cards 20 minutes; repeat 10 minutes; optional thermometer equilibration 10 minutes before class. Cleanup 4 minutes/meeting included.

    BEFORE CLASS¶

    1. Use teams of at most three (⅘/7/9). Copy the complete dataset below once/team; identify it as fictional Minnesota winter practice data, never as observed school weather.
    2. Draw graph axes: five dates on horizontal axis, temperature -15 to 5 degrees C vertically. Make high-contrast large copies available.
    3. If using thermometers, adult checks non-glass instruments and places two side-by-side indoors for 10 minutes before class. They measure room conditions, not outdoor weather.
    4. Read aloud: "We will not go outside, touch unknown water or trash, open an electrical meter, or infer drinking-water safety from pH."
    5. Prepare action brief: "The school wants a classroom reminder to shut exterior doors promptly without obstructing access or exits. Test clarity, not actual energy savings."

    MATERIALS¶

    Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25
    Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25
    Graph sheet; individual exit sheet 1 each/student, reused across unit 10 each 15 each 20 each 25 each
    Dataset sheet 1/team 4 5 7 9
    Ruler; marker; blunt scissors 1 each/team, reusable 4 5 7 9
    Reused paper sign, A4 or letter size 1/team 4 5 7 9
    Masking tape 0.5 m/team, classroom display only 2 m 2.5 m 3.5 m 4.5 m
    Timer; large board graph 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1
    Non-glass thermometers, optional 2/class, not per team 2 2 2 2

    SELF-CONTAINED DATA¶

    All readings in this invented example are at 12:00 noon using comparable shielded instruments at the same height; site A is a fictional paved area, B a fictional grassy area. Snow/cloud cover and location could still confound interpretation.

    Date A air temperature (degrees C) B air temperature (degrees C) Practice context
    Jan 6 -10 -11 Cloudy
    Jan 7 -8 -9 Cloudy
    Jan 8 -4 -6 Sunny
    Jan 9 -12 -12 Cloudy
    Jan 10 -6 -7 Sunny

    Teacher key: A range = 8 degrees C; B range = 6 degrees C. A mean = -8; B mean = -9. A-B differences = 1, 1, 2, 0, 1 degrees C; mean difference = 1. These five points cannot establish climate change, an urban heat island, or a causal surface effect.

    VOCABULARY¶

    Weather: conditions over a short time. Climate: long-term patterns. Variable: a factor that may change. Range: highest minus lowest value. Uncertainty: limits on what is known. Stewardship: responsible care and use of gifts/resources.

    TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Surface temperature and air temperature differ. Comparable air measurements need consistent height, shielding, time, and instrument. A small difference may be instrument uncertainty. Graphs communicate evidence; they do not create new evidence. Never erase an inconvenient value.

    Common misconception: one cold week disproves climate change. Climate requires long-term records, not five invented days.

    If asked, "Did grass make it colder?" Answer: We can describe this dataset's difference, but cannot isolate cause without more controls and repeated observations.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    Meeting 1 - measurement protocol¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce common-home stewardship and ask why accuracy is a responsibility to neighbors.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Distinguish weather/climate, air/surface; label practice data fictional.
    3. 12-20 (8 min): Each student reads two negative values, computes their difference, and identifies time/height/shield controls.
    4. 20-30 (10 min): Teams compare five A/B pairs. Optional indoor instruments: record both readings at 20 and 25 minutes without moving them; distinguish real room readings from invented outdoor data.
    5. 30-38 (8 min): Draft a repeatable outdoor protocol on paper, including adult weather permission, instrument checks, same time, and missing-data notation. Do not execute outdoors.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: state two controls and one reason the comparison cannot prove cause.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Store data and tools.

    Meeting 2 - graph and interpret¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Check controls; keep the raw data intact.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Model an axis and one plotted pair; use symbols plus labels, not color alone.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Everyone independently plots all ten points, titles graph, labels degrees C, and keys A/B.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Compare ranges and differences. Grade 5 uses a number line. Grade 6 computes means using the worked key only after trying.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Partners critique graph accuracy and clarity; each revises one label/scale or explains why no revision is needed.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual claim: cite two actual numbers and a limitation; no climate trend claims.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): File individual graphs and clean up.

    Meeting 3 - communicate a bounded action¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Read action brief. This action is a stewardship choice, not an energy saving proven by the weather data.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Set criteria: readable at 1 m; no blame; explicitly keep entrances accessible.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams make one purposeful visual sign and include a small truthful data graph/caption.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Exchange with a neighboring team. Each tester states the action without coaching; record number interpreting correctly out of testers.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Revise and retest. For nine teams use paired exchanges, not nine full-class talks.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: explain the stewardship tradeoff, one visual revision, and a proposed real measurement needed before claiming energy savings.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Classroom display only with teacher permission; clean up.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS¶

    Which values are real observations here? How would a sunlit thermometer bias a reading? What does a range tell us that a mean does not? Who might be excluded by a rushed door-closing rule? What data would test energy savings?

    WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    Each student names two controls and one uncertainty, plots at least 9 of 10 points correctly with units, gives a supported comparison, and explains an accessible action. Art evidence is a purposeful visual choice and a recorded revision, not neatness. Grade 6 additionally computes both means and identifies the limited sample.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG¶

    Thermometers disagree: report both and uncertainty; do not average away the discrepancy. No tools/printing: board-copy dataset and draw graph. Negative numbers overwhelm: provide number line and begin with differences. Sign misread: enlarge/action-label it, test again. Never invent "measured savings."

    SAFETY¶

    No outdoor requirement; no -10 F exposure, road/parking-lot sampling, unknown water, trash handling, or electrical access. Adult manages instruments and spills; no glass/mercury thermometers. A pH strip cannot determine potability. Student plans are classroom proposals only, not permission to alter doors, thermostats, wiring, or habitat.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6¶

    Grade 5: premarked axis and number line; dictate limitation. Challenge: compare ranges. Grade 6: scaffold signed sums; challenge redesign the measurement protocol to reduce one confound and explain why more data may still not establish cause. Provide seated work and large symbols.

    INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    The dataset, protocol, graphs, and sign tests are the primary complete indoor path. Live indoor readings practice tool use only; neither path proves real outdoor monitoring.

    CLEANUP¶

    Keep original datasets, collect rulers/instruments, cap markers, remove test signs from exits, recycle drafts, and retain individual graphs for the portfolio.

    FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Explored: weather data and stewardship. Did: graphed fictional practice readings and tested a clear, inclusive reminder. Learned: honest comparisons include limitations. Catholic connection: care for people and resources. Ask: "What could your five-day graph not prove?" No routine homework; optional conversation only.

    Week 33: Easter Engineering¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Reference
    Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / A / Physical Science
    Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes
    Objective / why / big idea I can describe a physical change, compare it with chemical/biological change and create an accurate before/after panel. A model communicates both change and what remains.
    Domains / Catholic connection S, A, C; Easter's Resurrection is a distinct faith claim. Melting or growth may symbolize change, never prove Resurrection.
    Local standards CST-S3: changes/model; CST-A3: visual revision; CST-C1: faith/evidence distinction. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Requirement None; no circuit or light-sequence option.
    Difficulty / entry Introductory; teach categories with complete cards.
    Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Change Panels.

    BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS¶

    Review accommodations/contact; seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Adult seals a small ice piece in clear bag/tray and seals a second bag of liquid water as endpoint reference. Pilot visibility; actual melting within the period not guaranteed. Copy cards: ice -> water (same water, physical); iron -> rust (new substances, chemical, diagram only); caterpillar -> butterfly (living development, biological, not death/resurrection). No chemical demonstration or body data.

    Item Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Paper panel/evidence sheets 2/student 20 30 40 50
    Pencil 1/student 10 15 20 25
    Marker set; ruler; card sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9
    Sealed clear bags 2/teacher 2 2 2 2
    Ice piece; water endpoint; tray; board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

    Paper/bags consumable; tools/tray reusable. Teacher controls water.

    VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Physical change: form/state changes without new substance. Chemical change: new substances form. Biological development: living organism changes through growth. Symbol: represents meaning, not mechanism. Common misconception: every change creates a new substance. If asked, "Is ice dead?" No; water is not an organism; Resurrection is not a phase change. Melting absorbs thermal energy from surroundings; no heating required. Two panels must show same substance plus changed state/shape.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    1. 0-4 (4 min): Introduce Easter/change distinction; ask "What changed, what remained?"
    2. 4-11 (7 min): Adult shows sealed bags; pupils record actual ice appearance and endpoint-reference status.
    3. 11-24 (13 min): Each sorts three cards with reasons, makes ice/water two-panel diagram with labels/arrows and caption.
    4. 24-35 (11 min): Inspect actual bag again; record observed/not yet melted. Partners ask a science question; revise caption/arrow to avoid claiming unobserved change.
    5. 35-41 (6 min): Each correctly identifies three categories, explains same-water limit and distinguishes chosen faith symbol from scientific evidence.
    6. 41-45 (4 min): Adult removes bags/wipes tray, pupils cap markers, save panels and tidy.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    "Which panel is an observation versus reference? Is a butterfly a new substance?" Each has three correct category reasons, labeled physical-change panel, reader-driven revision and faith-symbol limit. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 adds energy/model limit; NE for unobserved change.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY¶

    No melting -> record honestly; use labeled prepared endpoint, not claim live result. No ice -> dry card model, physical observation deferred. No leaks near power; adult isolates spill and reports. No tasting, steam, fire, reactions, pressure containers, circuits or forced spiritual disclosure.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    Grade 5/support: large category cards, predivided panels, oral/scribed caption. Grade 6/challenge: explain heat transfer versus chemical composition and why symbolic similarity is not scientific proof. Indoor lesson only.

    CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Save actual/reference labels and individual exits; count tools, dry surfaces. Explored: changes in matter/life. Did: observed or modeled melting and revised a panel. Learned: categories and limits. Catholic connection: Easter distinct from natural mechanisms. Ask: "What stayed the same?" No routine homework.

    Week 34: STREAM Expo and Graduation¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Reference
    Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / A / Communication
    Time 1 instructional meeting of 45 minutes; optional Expo adds 60-75 minutes, not counted as instruction
    Objective / why / big idea I can defend one tested decision, revise an evidence caption and explain responsible resource use. An exhibition communicates what was actually learned.
    Domains / Catholic connection E, A, C; gratitude and sending forth encourage gifts in service, not certified mastery or ranked worth.
    Local standards CST-E3: result/limit defense; CST-A3: caption revision; CST-C3: resource choice. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Requirement None; paper exhibits. No live powered or hazardous demonstrations.
    Difficulty / entry Developing; retrieve actual evidence, not assume attendance/achievement.
    Prep / cleanup Moderate: first 20 min, repeat 10 min; event logistics additional adult work; cleanup 4 min included.

    BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS¶

    Check school contact/accommodations; retrieve one or two individual artifacts with raw tests. Arrange paired seated exchanges, odd enrollment one trio. Copy caption frame and fictional practice record below. Extra event requires principal-approved date, room capacity/access/egress, adult hosts, visitor/media policy and invitations; none is assumed complete. School records actual stock/location; families need not attend, buy or donate.

    Item Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Portfolio/practice record; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25
    Paper display/caption sheets 2/student 20 30 40 50
    Ruler; marker 1 each/tool team of <=3 4 5 7 9
    Board; clock; roster; event checklist 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

    Same displays reused for event; tables/chairs existing stock must be confirmed. Paper consumable; tools/portfolios reusable. No food/photos/awards essential.

    VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Curate: choose evidence for purpose. Caption: explanation beside work. Tradeoff: benefit/cost. Limit: untested claim. Common misconception: celebration proves growth for every pupil. If asked, "Can I show a failed model?" Yes, with honest test and next step. Practice record, clearly invented: "Label readable in ⅓ trials, larger text in 3/3; same 1 m distance." Difference 2 successful trials, not proof of universal access. Frame: purpose / choice / result / change / limit / resource decision.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    1. 0-4 (4 min): Give thanks for opportunities; ask "What evidence can we share honestly?"
    2. 4-11 (7 min): Model practice record/caption; distinguish invented versus actual and paper versus device.
    3. 11-24 (13 min): Each curates artifact, assembles display hierarchy and caption with result/limit; use practice record if absent.
    4. 24-35 (11 min): Paired 90-second defenses plus questions; trio fits. Revise caption after one specific reader question, rehearse accessible seated explanation.
    5. 35-41 (6 min): Each submits old/new caption, supported decision and material reuse choice; future goal may be school-task only.
    6. 41-45 (4 min): Store displays, cap/count tools, save evidence and clear room.

    Optional separate Expo: executable event plan¶

    Adults release only after checklist approval; otherwise in-class rehearsal is the completed objective. Welcome/prayer 5 min; route/access orientation 5 min; two viewing rounds totaling 30-45 min (half present then swap, individual 2-minute explanations repeated to small visitors); inclusive recognition 10 min; close/pack displays 10 min. Sum 60-75 min. Maintain seated option, adult-monitored traffic and egress. Visitors do not operate experiments. No identifiable media without school consent, no compulsory family attendance. Record actual event date/attendance/checks only after it occurs.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    "What was measured? Which claim is too large? Why reuse this display?" Each has tested-result defense/limit, specific caption revision and resource reason. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 defends a tradeoff; NE if absent. Awards/event participation are not technical evidence.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY¶

    Missing work -> labeled practice record, not invented personal achievement. Missing event approval -> keep rehearsal; no unplanned visitors. Unreadable caption -> fewer words/larger title. Unsafe crowding -> adult stops rotation/reports. No live circuits, robots, clinical models on people, refreshments, sharps or private spiritual records.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    Grade 5/support: caption frame, oral/scribed defense. Grade 6/challenge: explain test precision and next validation step, no assumed two-year attendance. Indoor displays are primary; no outdoor event needed.

    CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Save individual evidence, return exhibits safely, record deferred event/checks. Explored: communicating a year of work. Did: curated, questioned and revised. Learned: evidence and limits matter. Catholic connection: gifts for service. Ask: "Which result supports your choice?" Describe Expo as held only if it occurred. Optional conversation; no routine homework.

    Grades 5-6 Year B

    Grades 5-6 Year B Lessons (Ages 10-12)¶

    Year Overview¶

    This is the Year B curriculum for Grades 5-6, alternating with Year A in either order. Contexts differ, but design, coding, service, data, and environmental topics recur. Equivalent official standards coverage and nonrepetition are not established.

    October 2026 review and teaching conditions¶

    15 lesson documents; 33 planned 45-minute meetings (1,485 minutes), not 34 files or meetings. Week 32 is unrepresented/break; the five-meeting app unit includes nominal week 17, so schedule instructional meetings around any winter break rather than assuming five uninterrupted calendar weeks. Check liturgical and school-event dates locally.

    See the Grades 5-6 review and 69-lesson audit. Biotechnology, Renewable Energy, Biomimicry, and App Development are fully rebuilt. Retained lessons have targeted fixes and individual local checks, not complete substitute readiness. Local CST codes are not official standards; official benchmarks are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

    Entry checks: measurement, compare/count, model versus evidence, sequence and if/else. Grade 5 uses reference cards and worked examples; Grade 6 adds controls, uncertainty, means, and design/ethical tradeoffs. Neither year requires prior attendance in the other. Check advanced-unit prerequisites before use.

    The complete rebuilt primary paths are indoor and device-free. Paper App Development teaches design/event reasoning, not actual programming/operation. Physical wind tests are models, not measured electrical efficiency. Real apps require approved school-managed access and a tested compatible setup. Loans, inventory, platform permissions, and any specialty equipment are unconfirmed.

    Unsourced Scripture wording, saints' sayings/biographies, historical priority claims, current institutional roles, company practices, and scientific statistics in retained content are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching. Do not repeat unchecked quotations or promise medical/social/energy impact. No routine homework, family purchase requirement, patient-use prototypes, or public student media.

    Year B Themes¶

    • Biotechnology & Life Science (Year A includes physical science and environmental investigation; no dedicated rocketry unit)

    • Renewable Energy Engineering (vs Year A's bridge engineering)

    • App Development (Year A also uses Scratch; interface/event reasoning revisits computational thinking)

    • Biomimicry Design (adds nature-inspired form/testing, not a replacement for all robotics skills)

    • Social Entrepreneurship (vs Year A's general entrepreneurship)

    Class Details¶

    • Duration: 45 minutes per session

    • Sessions: 33 planned instructional meetings; fit multi-meeting units to the school calendar

    • Technology: paper-first models; optional approved App Inventor; Google Sites/3D design are not prerequisites

    Curriculum Version: 1.0 — Year B | **

    Week 1: Welcome Innovators¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Reference
    Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / B / Foundations
    Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes
    Objective / why / big idea I can separate a source-supported fact from an overclaim and define a useful innovation criterion. Innovation improves a process for users, not just novelty.
    Domains / Catholic connection C, E; truthful learning and service are compatible with faith. Avoid heroic unsupported histories.
    Local standards CST-C1: fact/limit; CST-E1: user criterion. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Requirement None; supplied source card and paper prototype.
    Difficulty / entry Introductory; Year B can precede A; teach criteria here.
    Prep / cleanup Light: first 15 min, repeat 10 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Innovation Foundations.

    BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS¶

    Review accommodations/contact; seat ⅘/7/9 teams. Copy source and fictional school-task cards below; teacher checks a sample three-word label at 50 cm. Provide each pupil journal/record; rotate listener/designer/reader rather than assign "expert" partners permanent technical control.

    Item Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Paper goal/evidence; pencil; journal 1 each/student 10 15 20 25
    Cardstock prototype; source/task sheet; ruler; marker 1 each/team 4 5 7 9
    Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

    Paper/cardstock consumable; tools/journals reusable, no family sourcing.

    VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Innovation: changed method/product serving a purpose. Evidence: support. Criterion: checkable success. Constraint: real limit. Common misconception: a famous person's faith proves their science. If asked, "Did Mendel explain every trait?" No; this source describes particular pea experiments; inheritance can be more complex. Verified card, paraphrase of NHGRI Mendel's Peas, checked October 4, 2026: Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian monk; he studied pea inheritance, carefully pollinating plants and comparing generations. Source does not establish "all traits blend" or a private quotation/belief. Fictional user: "I need a clear shared-tool label, not my name on a public display." Criterion: read RULER / TAPE / PAPER from 50 cm; constraint one card. Worked check: three correct words out of three, not assumed every-user access.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    1. 0-4 (4 min): Welcome to B; ask "Who benefits from a new idea?" Brief service reflection.
    2. 4-11 (7 min): Read verified card; contrast supported fact with "Mendel proved every trait behaves alike."
    3. 11-24 (13 min): Each records fact/source/limit, writes school-task goal and two label sketches; teams create one prototype.
    4. 24-35 (11 min): Reader checks three words at 50 cm without hints; revise confusing label; each helps with test. Establish norms: rotate tools, preserve failed results, avoid private data.
    5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual supported versus unsupported claim, goal criterion/constraint and one listening action.
    6. 41-45 (4 min): Save goals, cap markers, count tools and reuse paper.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    "Which sentence did the source support? How would you check your goal?" Each supplies fact/source/limit and measurable user criterion/constraint. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 identifies another needed source; NE for missing evidence, not universal leadership certification.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY¶

    Vague goal -> use three-word label. No cardstock -> paper at same quantity. Source unavailable online -> supplied verified paraphrase teaches core; no unsupervised search or invented replacement biography. No private interviews, public photos, ranking faith, sharp tools or outside trip. Report unsafe condition.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    Grade 5/support: source read aloud, criterion stems and scribing. Grade 6/challenge: distinguish source-supported history from inference about belief; justify a user tradeoff. Indoor plan independent of weather/devices.

    CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Retain individual goals/source answers, count tools, record unfinished checks. Explored: useful innovation. Did: source check and label trial. Learned: purpose/evidence matter. Catholic connection: truth and service. Ask: "Who was your idea for?" Optional conversation; no routine homework.

    Weeks 2-4: Biotechnology Basics¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Teacher reference
    Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Life Science B / Biotechnology Basics
    Time Three meetings of 45 minutes; 135 total
    Domains C, S, A; technology applications are considered, not operated
    Big idea Models help us explain living systems but have limits; technology choices affect people.
    Student objective I can label cell parts, model complementary DNA bases, and explain a benefit, risk, and dignity safeguard.
    Why Science literacy helps people understand food and medicine without overstating evidence.
    Catholic connection Faith and reason, human dignity, and responsible service; verified sources. Models are not scientific proof of God or a substitute for moral reasoning.
    Local standards / evidence CST-S3: individual cell function and complementary-base explanation; CST-A1: labeled model with a stated limitation; CST-C1: distinguish evidence from a belief claim; CST-C2: benefit/risk/access analysis.
    Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; four local codes only.
    Technology None. Optional prepared-slide microscope demonstration adds instrument observation only.
    Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; letter matching and diagrams. No genetics vocabulary assumed; no previous rotation required.
    Prep / cleanup First packet 20 minutes; repeated 10 minutes; cleanup 4 minutes each meeting included.

    BEFORE CLASS¶

    1. Make teams of at most three (⅘/7/9). Copy the teacher fact cards and case cards below. Read them; no external research or missing handouts needed.
    2. Cut each team's eight base cards: A,A,T,T,C,C,G,G. Students may instead write these letters on eight paper rectangles.
    3. Put dry nonfood materials in trays. Do not prepare fruit extraction, alcohol, candy models, body samples, or cultures. The original observation/model goals remain; extraction skill is deliberately not assessed.
    4. Optional microscope: adult uses sealed, commercially prepared plant/animal slides only; no cheek cells, blood, pond water, or broken-glass handling.

    MATERIALS¶

    Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25
    Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25
    Model/exit sheets 3/student for unit 30 45 60 75
    Fact/case packet, 2 pages 1/team 8 pages 10 pages 14 pages 18 pages
    Colored paper sheet 2/team for organelles/base cards 8 10 14 18
    Marker; ruler; blunt scissors 1 each/team, reusable 4 5 7 9
    Tape 0.5 m/team/unit 2 m 2.5 m 3.5 m 4.5 m
    Timer; large teacher diagram 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

    VOCABULARY¶

    Cell: basic unit of living things. Membrane: boundary regulating entry/exit. Nucleus: DNA-containing compartment in typical plant/animal cells. Organelle: specialized cell structure. DNA: molecule carrying inherited information. Biotechnology: using living systems or their parts to make useful products/processes.

    TEACHER BACKGROUND AND FACT CARDS¶

    • Typical plant and animal cells both have membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and ribosomes. Plant cells also have a cell wall; green photosynthetic plant cells have chloroplasts.
    • Mitochondria participate in releasing usable energy from nutrients; ribosomes build proteins. The nucleus is not a literal brain.
    • Bacteria do not have a membrane-bound nucleus. Mature human red blood cells lack a nucleus; most other human cells contain nuclear DNA. Some DNA is also in mitochondria and chloroplasts.
    • In double-stranded DNA, A pairs with T and C with G. The "ladder" model omits scale, chemistry, and many cellular processes. Many traits involve several genes and environment; DNA does not determine a person's worth.
    • Biotechnology includes fermentation and producing useful substances with cells. Classroom paper models are not experiments demonstrating a treatment's effectiveness.

    Common misconception: every cell has DNA inside a nucleus. The examples above show why this absolute is false.

    If asked, "Does a DNA code prove a designer scientifically?" Answer: Catholics believe in a Creator; scientific models describe observable molecular processes. The analogy to code is useful but is not a test proving a theological claim.

    Fictional case cards - all necessary information supplied¶

    A - Food process: A fictional cooperative uses yeast to make bread rise. Its proposal reduces waste by better batch planning. Benefits: more usable food; risks: contamination and allergic ingredients; safeguards: qualified food-safety supervision and clear ingredient labels. We do not prepare/taste food.

    B - Medicine process: A fictional laboratory uses engineered microbes to produce a useful protein. Potential benefit: more treatment supply. Questions: safety testing, price, access, and waste containment. This card does not establish approval or effectiveness of any medicine.

    C - Crop proposal: A fictional drought-tolerance crop might use less irrigation. The claimed saving is a hypothesis, not measured fact. Ask for comparable field data and effects on local farmers/ecosystems. Do not infer that every genetic modification is beneficial or harmful.

    Teacher key: several reasoned decisions are defensible. Require a benefit, a risk/unknown, affected people, and a safeguard; do not grade agreement with a predetermined commercial policy. Specific Church positions on embryo, cloning, or stem-cell cases are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching; those cases are outside this bounded lesson.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    Meeting 1 - cell models¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce wonder and dignity without ranking bodies by health/ability.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Read fact cards; model membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria, and ribosomes on board.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Each student draws a plant or animal cell and labels the five shared parts; plant model adds wall and, for a green leaf cell, chloroplasts.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Teams compare models; check labels against fact cards, revise one error or document an accurate comparison.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Each explains two functions and one model limit to a partner; optional teacher prepared-slide demonstration uses this time instead, not extra time.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: explain membrane/nucleus distinction and why a nucleus is not a brain.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Clean up, retain drawings.

    Meeting 2 - DNA matching model¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Review cell exceptions and distinguish observation/model/belief.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Demonstrate A-T and C-G complementary pairing; write sequence ATCG.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams build four rungs from eight cards, label backbone rails, then twist paper model gently. Rotating student explains each pair.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Each student independently completes complements: ATCG -> TAGC; CCTA -> GGAT. Check and explain one correction.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Discuss what model omits and why genes plus environment are more complex than a one-letter personality code.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: one valid base pair, a cell exception, and a model limitation.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Store cards and models.

    Meeting 3 - biotechnology and ethical reasoning¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Explain technology decisions need both evidence and ethical consideration.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Adult models case A: benefit, risk, affected people, safeguard.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams examine B or C using only supplied facts; list unknowns, not invented medical claims.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Each student writes/dictates a four-part recommendation. Grade 5 uses sentence frames; Grade 6 explains a tradeoff or missing evidence.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Neighboring-team exchange; revise one safeguard to better respect access or dignity.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: distinguish one scientific claim from one ethical judgment and identify information needed before implementation.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Collect individual evidence and clean up.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS¶

    Which label describes a function rather than a literal city part? What breaks the "every cell has a nucleus" claim? Which facts support your recommendation? Who might be excluded if price is ignored? What still requires a qualified expert?

    WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    Each student labels five cell parts, correctly gives at least 7 of 8 complementary letters, states one model limitation, and makes a recommendation containing benefit, risk/unknown, affected people, and safeguard. Grade 6 adds a specific evidence need and tradeoff. A pretty model or group consensus alone is insufficient.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG¶

    No colored paper: pencil symbols suffice. Letters confuse: keep reference A-T/C-G visible. Model becomes literal: revisit limitations before continuing. Ethical debate becomes personal: use fictional cooperative/lab, not classmates' diagnoses or family decisions.

    SAFETY¶

    Dry paper only; no unknown chemicals, alcohol, tasting, toothpicks, tissue sampling, live cultures, or DNA collection. Adult alone handles optional sealed slides/microscope. No medical advice or questions about students' genetic/health information.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6¶

    Grade 5: five-part diagram template, paired letters, oral reasoning. Grade 5 challenge: compare plant and animal models. Grade 6: same base model with exceptions; challenge explain why a multi-factor trait cannot be inferred from our four-rung model. Use high-contrast symbols and a scribe; preserve the same conceptual evidence.

    INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    The complete primary lesson is indoors, device-free, and independent of seasons. No microscope changes the objective: modeling, not instrument observation.

    CLEANUP¶

    Count scissors, cap markers, return cards, recycle unused scraps, retain labeled models and individual ethics exits.

    FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Explored: cells, DNA models, and biotechnology choices. Did: labeled cells, paired bases, and evaluated fictional proposals. Learned: models have limits and benefits need evidence. Catholic connection: dignity and honest reasoning. Ask: "What did your DNA model leave out?" No routine homework or home extraction.

    Weeks 5-7: Renewable Energy Lab¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Teacher reference
    Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Energy B / Renewable Energy Lab
    Time Three meetings of 45 minutes; 135 total
    Domains C, S, E, M
    Big idea Renewable sources involve tradeoffs; a model's performance is not electrical efficiency.
    Student objective I can compare sources, test a rotor modification fairly, and defend a resource-aware design choice.
    Why Communities make energy choices under cost, land, reliability, and environmental constraints.
    Catholic connection Stewardship considers neighbors and future generations; Laudato Si' source. No one energy policy is inferred from a pinwheel.
    Local standards / evidence CST-S2: individual variables/control statement; CST-E2: before/after model tests; CST-M2: each student's table/graph; CST-C3: individual stewardship tradeoff.
    Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED; four local program codes.
    Technology Recommended: primary hand-fanned rotor path uses no electrical device; guarded tabletop fan optional for more repeatable tests. This models wind-to-motion, not electricity generation.
    Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; count rotations, keep time, compare repeated measurements. No circuit assembly or energy-efficiency calculations required.
    Prep / cleanup First kit 25 minutes; repeat 10 minutes; cleanup 4 minutes/meeting included.

    BEFORE CLASS¶

    1. Make ⅘/7/9 teams of at most three. Adult inspects commercial classroom pinwheels: securely enclosed axle ends, no exposed sharp pins or detachable small tips.
    2. Mark one rotor blade so a return to the same position counts one full rotation. Each team uses the same rotor before and after modification.
    3. Make one paper hand fan/team (folded cardstock). Mark 30 cm distance between fan and rotor; use seated work and a predictable fanning pace, acknowledging imperfect airflow control.
    4. Optional adult-operated guarded fan: stable stand, 75 cm rotor distance, low setting, no extension cords through walkways. Never insert materials into its guard.
    5. Copy source cards below. Prepare a fictional community brief: "Supply useful energy year-round while considering cost, neighbors, habitats, and winter conditions." No outside research/homework.

    MATERIALS¶

    Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25
    Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25
    Data/graph sheet 1/student/unit 10 15 20 25
    Safe enclosed-axle pinwheel 1/team, reusable 4 5 7 9
    Cardstock fan; source-card sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9
    Thin paper, A4/letter 1/team for four 2 x 4 cm tabs and design sketch 4 5 7 9
    Ruler; blunt scissors; marker 1 each/team, reusable 4 5 7 9
    Tape 0.25 m/team/unit 1 m 1.25 m 1.75 m 2.25 m
    Timer 1/teacher; class runs synchronized trials 1 1 1 1
    Guarded tabletop fan, optional 1/class, adult-controlled 1 1 1 1

    No heat lamps, water turbines near electricity, unprotected wiring, or bare LEDs. Optional solar electricity demonstration requires a separate adult-reviewed manufacturer kit and specified supply/load; it is not part of this timed lesson or required purchases.

    VOCABULARY AND SOURCE CARDS¶

    Energy: capacity to cause change/do work; units include joules and kilowatt-hours. Power: rate of energy transfer; watts. Renewable: replenished on human-use timescales. Rotor: rotating blade assembly. Performance: measured result of a test. Tradeoff: gain in one criterion with a cost in another.

    Source Model fact card Tradeoff to consider
    Solar Photovoltaic panels transform light into electricity; output depends on conditions. Darkness/clouds, land/materials, storage or other supply
    Wind Moving air turns a rotor; a generator can transform motion into electricity. Variable wind, siting/habitat, maintenance
    Hydro Moving water drives turbines and generators. Ecosystems, available flow, effects of dams
    Fossil fuels Chemical energy is transferred through combustion. Finite fuels, emissions, transport
    Nuclear Nuclear reactions release energy; uranium fuel is generally classified nonrenewable. Waste, construction, fuel and safety systems

    These basic descriptions are models, not site-specific feasibility evidence. Renewable does not mean impact-free. Nuclear fuel did not form by the same process as fossil fuels.

    TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Our fan input ultimately uses muscular energy (or purchased electricity for the optional fan), not a demonstrated renewable electricity source. Counting turns per ten seconds compares rotor response under specified conditions. It does not measure joules, watts, voltage, or efficiency; efficiency would require comparable energy input/output measurements.

    Common misconception: fastest rotor is always the best generator. Useful output, loads, durability, and conditions also matter.

    If asked, "Did we make free electricity?" Answer: No. We observed wind-to-motion transfer in a model; no generator or energy meter is used.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    Meeting 1 - sources and test planning¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Read stewardship/community brief; ask who an energy decision affects.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Sort the five source cards; distinguish energy from power and renewable from impact-free.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams make a comparison chart; each student chooses two sources and a different tradeoff for each.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Demonstrate count of full rotor turns in 10 seconds. Plan same rotor, fan distance, operator/pace, interval, and room location.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Each writes change variable (tabs), measured response (turns/10 s), and two controls; practice counting.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: one energy/power distinction and one source tradeoff.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Store kits.

    Meeting 2 - compare and redesign¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Review controls and honest unsuccessful tests.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Measure 30 cm fan distance and run one unrecorded practice to coordinate counters.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Run three baseline trials, 10 seconds each; record every count. Fanner remains the same for comparison; swap roles only after that comparison block.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Attach four equal 2 x 4 cm paper tabs with matched tape pieces, clear of axle. Run three modified trials under same conditions; adult checks secure tabs.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Each graphs or compares baseline/modified counts; retain zero turns. Identify airflow inconsistency as a limitation.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual conclusion cites two counts and one uncertainty; no "percent efficiency" claims.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Remove tabs and inventory kits.

    Meeting 3 - communicate a design recommendation¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Revisit community brief; rotor evidence alone cannot choose a town's energy supply.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Explain a two-criterion decision table: reliability and effects on people/resources; list information still needed.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Teams sketch a revised rotor or a source combination; clearly separate tested result from proposed untested features.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Neighboring-team exchanges: explain data, ask one tradeoff question, revise recommendation. Nine teams use paired exchanges, not long public talks.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Each student annotates recommendation with evidence, limitation, and one fairness/stewardship concern.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: why rotor turns are not electrical efficiency and one needed real-world measurement.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Clean up, retain evidence.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS¶

    What stayed the same? Where did the model's input energy originate? Why can a zero count be valuable? What could winter change about a solar proposal? Whose needs would a cheap-but-unreliable choice ignore?

    WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    Each student names two controls, records six counts, compares using actual numbers, and explains one uncertainty and stewardship tradeoff. Grade 5 compares ranges/largest counts. Grade 6 calculates means and explains why a three-trial difference does not establish general superiority.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG¶

    Rotor sticks: stop, adult checks axle; do not force/bend sharp fasteners. Too fast to count: lower airflow or move hand fan farther and repeat both conditions. No rotor: use fictional counts baseline 8/9/7; tabs 6/8/7, labeled simulated; objective shifts to data interpretation, not building/testing a physical rotor. No electric fan: primary hand-fan route remains complete.

    SAFETY¶

    No exposed pins, projectiles, heat lamps, fire, mains wiring experiments, batteries, or water/electrical combinations. Adult operates optional guarded fan. Keep paper/tape out of guards, secure rotor/tabs, and stop when a part loosens. Student models are not installable generators.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6¶

    Grade 5: large marked blade, partner counter, table with trial numbers. Grade 5 challenge: compare count ranges. Grade 6: mean worked example and tradeoff matrix; challenge explain a better airflow control and why voltage alone would still not measure efficiency. Provide seated fans and alternative roles.

    INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    All primary testing is indoors, independent of sun, snow, or temperature. Outdoor weather is discussed as a design constraint, not required exposure.

    CLEANUP¶

    Stop optional fan, count pinwheels, remove loose tabs, recycle scraps, store fan away from paper and retain individual tables.

    FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Explored: energy sources and wind-model performance. Did: tested a rotor before/after and compared evidence. Learned: performance and efficiency are different. Catholic connection: wise care for resources and neighbors. Ask: "What tradeoff would your community need to investigate?" No routine homework or home electrical construction.

    Weeks 8-10: Biomimicry Design¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Teacher reference
    Grade / unit / title Grades 5-6 / Design B / Biomimicry Design
    Time Three 45-minute meetings; 135 total
    Domains C, S, E, A; measurement supports the investigation
    Big idea A natural form can inspire a design, but performance must be tested in its new context.
    Student objective I can observe a form, sketch a purposeful model, compare two designs, and revise using evidence.
    Why Designers combine observation, art, science, and tests rather than copying an attractive shape blindly.
    Catholic connection Wonder and stewardship, without claiming nature is perfect or proving God through a prototype; verified sources. Unsupported attributed saint quotation removed.
    Local standards / evidence CST-S3: individual form/function and model-limit explanation; CST-E2: before/after tested redesign; CST-A1: observational sketch; CST-A2: purposeful pattern/form choice and critique; CST-C3: material tradeoff. Five local codes only.
    Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None; optional approved printed photographs add context, not required internet research.
    Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; observe, draw, fold, count loads. No prior rotation, ratios, or biological research assumed.
    Prep / cleanup First kit 20 minutes; repeat 10 minutes; cleanup 4 minutes/meeting included.

    BEFORE CLASS¶

    1. Make ⅘/7/9 teams of at most three. On board draw a broad flat leaf with veins and a cylindrical stem with outer boundary; identify drawings as illustrative, not measured plant specimens.
    2. Provide an optional approved leaf/stem photo if available; otherwise use the illustrative drawings and state that students are interpreting a supplied model rather than observing a real specimen.
    3. Prepare two strips of equal paper 8 x 20 cm/team and two stable supports 10 cm apart, inside a catching tray. Adult prepares ten sealed 10 g load packets/class for serial tests.
    4. Brief: "Design a small paper bridge for a fictional garden model. Span 10 cm, use one strip, hold a centrally placed paper platform, and minimize new material." No claim of real habitat intervention.

    MATERIALS¶

    Supply Per student / team / class / teacher 10 15 20 25
    Pencil; journal, reusable 1 each/student 10 15 20 25
    Sketch/exit sheets 2/student/unit 20 30 40 50
    Paper strips 8 x 20 cm 2/team/unit, initial plus revision 8 10 14 18
    Matching low supports 2/team 8 10 14 18
    Catching tray; ruler; marker; blunt scissors 1 each/team 4 5 7 9
    Paper central platform, 3 x 3 cm 1/team 4 5 7 9
    Tape 0.25 m/team/unit 1 m 1.25 m 1.75 m 2.25 m
    Sealed 10 g packets 10/class, adult supervised serial tests 10 10 10 10
    Timer; board form drawings 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

    VOCABULARY¶

    Biomimicry: design inspired by living systems. Form: shape/arrangement. Function: what a part does. Model: simplified representation. Criterion: test for success. Revision: evidence-based change. Tradeoff: improvement with a cost elsewhere.

    TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Different plant forms perform different functions; no adaptation is a perfect universal design. Our folded/cylindrical paper shapes are analogies, not accurate biological structures. Geometry affects a paper strip's resistance to bending. Fair comparisons keep paper size/material, span, load placement, and loading sequence constant.

    Common misconception: looking like a leaf makes a bridge stronger. Similar appearance is not performance evidence.

    If asked, "Did plants invent bridges?" Answer: No. Designers interpret living forms to generate ideas, then test a new construction with different materials and purposes.

    Retain the original unit's optional research topics: burr-inspired hook-and-loop fasteners, kingfisher-inspired train forms, gecko-inspired adhesion, lotus-inspired surfaces, and animal thermal/water management. Their specific inventor stories, commercial claims, and quotations are VERIFICATION REQUIRED from reliable sources before extension use; no invented source cards or mandatory research homework.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    Meeting 1 - observe and design¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Introduce wonder, stewardship, and the fictional garden-model brief.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Model close observation: boundary, repeated veins/ridges, proportion; distinguish observation from claimed function.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Each student sketches the supplied form with three feature labels and one unanswered question; note drawing/model versus real specimen.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Teams propose two paper forms: flat, pleated/ridged, or rolled tube. Select one using span/material criteria; sketch before building.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Construct first paper bridge; each student explains the feature being translated and where analogy breaks.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit: form/function inference and one model limitation.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Store dry models and clean up.

    Meeting 2 - test and redesign¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Review fair comparison and safety cap.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Adult demonstrates central platform and 10 g increments, maximum 100 g, stopping at instability.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Serial adult tests for all teams; waiting teams trace force paths and predict outcomes. Record last safe load and any instability without deliberate destruction.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Use second equal strip to change form/fold only; sketch before/after. Hold span, paper, platform, and loading sequence constant.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Adult retests nine teams at most, about 40 seconds/team; no speeches during load tests.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Each student cites original/revised loads and states whether evidence supports improvement or is inconclusive.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): Return weights/supports and clean up.

    Meeting 3 - purposeful visual communication¶

    1. 0-5 (5 min): Distinguish a functional form from decoration and unsupported "best design" claims.
    2. 5-12 (7 min): Demonstrate a visual panel: observed form -> translated feature -> tested result -> limitation.
    3. 12-22 (10 min): Each student prepares a labeled panel with deliberate layout, not artistic-talent scoring.
    4. 22-32 (10 min): Neighboring teams interpret panels without coaching; record which labels/sequence were clear.
    5. 32-38 (6 min): Each student revises one visual choice or justifies a tested clear choice; add resource tradeoff.
    6. 38-41 (3 min): Individual exit explains design, evidence, limitation, and material stewardship.
    7. 41-45 (4 min): File panels, recycle scraps, tidy.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS¶

    What did you observe versus infer? What property did the model actually test? How did the same paper behave in another form? Which visual label helped your reader? What tradeoff came with an extra fold?

    WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    Each student labels three observed/model features, states an analogy limitation, compares two safe demonstrated loads, and revises a purposeful visual panel using reader feedback. Grade 5 uses count/mass comparisons. Grade 6 defends control variables and why a 100 g capped result cannot establish ultimate breaking strength or general biological superiority.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG¶

    Paper immediately bends: record zero safe added load and revise form. Both reach cap: neither is proven stronger; report equal demonstrated capacity under this test. No packets: use identical lightweight paper squares and report counts, not invented grams. No photos: label interpretation of teacher model, not specimen observation.

    SAFETY¶

    Adult alone loads; low supports, tray, 100 g cap, no body-weight tests, sharp fasteners, field collection, live animal handling, food specimens, or outdoor exposure. Student garden bridges are tabletop models, not real infrastructure or habitat installations.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE - GRADES 5 AND 6¶

    Grade 5: sketch frame and precreased paper, oral explanation. Challenge: compare flat/ridged forms. Grade 6: same core with control checklist; challenge propose a durability criterion not tested here. Scribe, large symbols, and alternate builder/observer roles preserve assessment.

    INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    Supplied forms and paper tests run indoors in any season. No field walk or device required.

    CLEANUP¶

    Adult counts ten packets, collect supports/trays/scissors, flatten recyclable drafts, retain before/after sketches and visual revisions.

    FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Explored: nature-inspired forms and tested design. Did: sketched, compared paper bridges, and revised visual explanations. Learned: resemblance is not proof of performance. Catholic connection: wonder and stewardship. Ask: "What did your model test, and what could it not prove?" No routine homework; optional conversation only.

    Week 11: Thanksgiving Data¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Reference
    Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / B / Data
    Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes
    Objective / why / big idea I can graph five fictional counts totaling 20 and interpret a comparison without measuring anyone's faith. Graphs describe defined categories, not human worth.
    Domains / Catholic connection M, T, C; gratitude may be private/voluntary; dignity means no spiritual ranking.
    Local standards CST-M2: graph/comparison; CST-T3: private-data boundary; CST-C2: opt-out. Official benchmarks VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Requirement None; graph paper primary; optional approved spreadsheet only if already working.
    Difficulty / entry Introductory; teach axes/scale; percentages scaffolded for Grade 6.
    Prep / cleanup Light: first 10 min, repeat 5 min; cleanup 4 min. Kit: Category Data.

    BEFORE CLASS / MATERIALS¶

    Review contact/accommodations. Seat tool teams ⅘/7/9. Copy invented dataset: nature 6, helpful actions 5, learning 4, creative play 3, quiet time 2. Exactly one category per fictional response; these are not school/class beliefs. Do not execute any personal gratitude/faith survey. Draw blank axes 0-6, one square = one response, horizontal categories; pilot five bars.

    Item Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Graph paper; paper exit; pencil 1 each/student 10 15 20 25
    Ruler; marker; dataset sheet 1 each/team 4 5 7 9
    Board; clock; roster 1 each/teacher 1 1 1 1

    Paper consumable; tools reusable, no account/device required.

    VOCABULARY / TEACHER BACKGROUND¶

    Category: group defined for counting. Frequency: count. Axis: graph reference line. Provenance: where data came from. Common misconception: graph counts generosity/grace. If asked, "May I share my thanks?" Privately/voluntarily, but not this dataset. Key: 6+5+4+3+2 = 20; nature minus quiet = 4; nature 6/20 = 30%, then 25/20/15/10%, sum 100%. No pie chart required; five bars enable comparison.

    EXACT LESSON SEQUENCE¶

    1. 0-4 (4 min): Ask "What can these fictional counts tell us?" Brief thanksgiving reflection without disclosure.
    2. 4-11 (7 min): Model axes/one-unit scale, total and honest "fictional" title.
    3. 11-25 (14 min): Each makes all five bars, labels axes/count units and total; partners check heights without doing work for them.
    4. 25-35 (10 min): Compare greatest/least/difference; diagnose deliberately missing category in teacher graph and fix. Grade 6 uses percentage scaffold.
    5. 35-41 (6 min): Individual graph, total 20, difference 4, private-data exclusion and respectful opt-out explanation.
    6. 41-45 (4 min): Cap/count tools, save graphs, reuse paper backs and tidy.

    QUESTIONS TO ASK STUDENTS / WHAT SUCCESS LOOKS LIKE¶

    "Where did data come from? Are categories overlapping? Can a bar show grace?" Each has five correct bars/labels/total, numerical comparison and privacy/ choice reason. 1 unsupported; 2 prompted; 3 independent; 4 explains another representation limit; NE if missing, not handwriting/art grade.

    IF THINGS GO WRONG / SAFETY¶

    Total wrong -> sum original counts; retain corrected work. Graph scale changed midway -> redraw consistent zero-based scale. No graph paper -> ruled axes. No personal survey, private names/prayers, health promise, public uploading or spiritual ranking. Stop/report accidental disclosure.

    SUPPORT / CHALLENGE / INDOOR FALLBACK¶

    Grade 5/support: labeled axes, one-square units, oral/scribed interpretation. Grade 6/challenge: verify percentages total 100 and explain sampling limits. Indoor paper path is complete without devices.

    CLEANUP / FAMILY NEWSLETTER¶

    Keep individual graphs, note needed reteaching; count tools. Explored: category data. Did: graphed an invented dataset. Learned: honest interpretation/privacy. Catholic connection: voluntary gratitude and dignity. Ask: "What can your graph not tell us?" No routine homework or home spiritual tracker.

    Week 12: Gifts of Service¶

    LESSON AT A GLANCE¶

    Field Reference
    Grade / schedule / rotation / unit 5-6 / Weekly / B / Service
    Time 1 meeting of 45 minutes
    Objective / why / big idea I can define a user criterion and design/test a clear choice-based activity card. Gifts should meet stated needs, not presumed disability or poverty.
