    Wonder Engineers¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Bi-Weekly A / Structures
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, E, M / A first engineering question names a need and a test.
    Student objective / why "I can build a low structure that stands and explain a changed support." New pupils can enter either rotation with concrete design routines.
    Catholic connection Share blocks fairly, save reusable materials and explain how careful work helps the group. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C3: stewardship and responsible work; CST-E1: needs, criteria and constraints; CST-E2: build, test and redesign; CST-M1: count, compare and measure. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Inspect planks, mark a 30 cm ceiling and choose a 10-second standing test. Draw ask/plan/try/change icons; do not prepare a tallest-tower contest.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: plan or prediction / actual result / reason or revision. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Wooden building planks / kit / items 72 90 126 162
    Metric ruler / kit / items 4 5 7 9

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Engineer = designs solutions; criterion = must do; base = bottom support.

    A low structure can solve a stability problem. Failure identifies a weak part, not a weak child.

    Common misconception: An engineer must make the tallest structure.

    If asked: "What if it falls?" Record that useful result and change a support.

    SAFETY¶

    Tabletop under 30 cm, hands clear during the standing test, no heavy loads or furniture climbing. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: First useful structure - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: State the need: a structure that stands 10 seconds in its tabletop space.
    2. 3-7: Model a broad base, measure from table level and show a plan -> test -> change record.
    3. 7-20: Teams use 18 planks to build/test, record height and change one support. Every child adds/directs a part and counts or measures.
    4. 20-26: Each child explains the need, first/revised result and a reusable-material care action.
    5. 26-30: Dismantle top-down and count all 18 planks; retain individual records. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which support did you change after the test?
    • How did we care for shared materials?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show a standing test, count/compare height and point to a changed support.

    Grade 2: Name the criterion and limit, compare measured results and explain a test-based change.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Prebuilt base example and large picture steps; accept equal-unit height counting. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Maintain height while using fewer planks and test the tradeoff. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No planks: use equal clean blocks and pretest a feasible low height. Immediate falls: widen base rather than add unsafe weight.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We began engineering with a clear standing test and careful shared-material work. Ask: "Which support did you change after the test?" Optional: notice a stable base in a pictured object. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Sources and claim boundaries¶

    These are local program competencies, not official Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmark numbers. See local standards and the source register. Catholic care, dignity and honest-inquiry applications follow that register; no unsupported scientist/saint biography, Scripture quotation or devotional history is required to execute this lesson. No external historical or official numeric claim is made.

    Gods Patterns¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Bi-Weekly A / Patterns
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, A, M / A repeating unit can organize a purposeful visual or rhythmic message.
    Student objective / why "I can make, extend and repair a pattern and explain its purpose." Pattern rules support mathematics and genuine artistic choices.
    Catholic connection Respect different creative choices and return shared pattern materials; a pattern is not scientific proof of a belief. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C3: stewardship and responsible work; CST-A2: purposeful form and pattern; CST-M2: represent and interpret data/patterns. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Moderate, 20-30 minutes first reusable set; light 5-10 minutes thereafter; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Count 30 existing large pattern shapes or batch-precut colored paper shapes per kit, enough for up to three 9-shape patterns. Draw AB and ABB examples plus one intentional error. Use paper crayons for a silent rhythm route.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: unit / next two elements / corrected pattern. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Pattern shape / kit / large reusable shapes 120 150 210 270

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Unit = repeated part; predict = say what comes next; rhythm = timed pattern.

    A repeated-looking natural feature is not always a strict mathematical repeat. Assess a constructed rule, not a claim that everything in nature repeats perfectly.

    Common misconception: Any decorative arrangement is a repeating pattern.

    If asked: "Must every leaf match exactly?" No; nature has variation. Our constructed pattern has a stated rule.

    SAFETY¶

    Large cards only; no beads, food props or loud compulsory clapping. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Pattern communication - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Show a patterned border intended to welcome a viewer; ask which part repeats.
    2. 3-7: Model AB twice, then an incorrect next card; explain how the unit predicts the correction.
    3. 7-20: Each child makes AB twice (Grade 1) or ABB/AAB three times (Grade 2), chooses a color/shape purpose and trades a next-two prediction. Partners insert one error; each author repairs it.
    4. 20-26: Each child identifies the unit, next two elements and purposeful visual choice; return reusable cards thoughtfully.
    5. 26-30: Count 30 cards per kit and save each child's drawn pattern before dismantling. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which part of your pattern repeats?
    • Why did you choose those shapes or colors?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Identify AB, extend by two elements and explain one purposeful choice.

    Grade 2: Identify ABB/AAB, repair an error and explain the prediction using the unit.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Use two high-contrast or tactile shapes with teacher oral rhythm; avoid color-only distinctions. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Show the same rule using a silent four-beat finger/tap representation. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Cards missing: draw shapes on allocated paper. Sound sensitivity: use a silent pointing pattern with the same rule; no music performance claim on that route.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We created purposeful patterns, predicted their continuation and repaired an error. Ask: "Which part of your pattern repeats?" Optional: tell or point to a two-part pattern indoors. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Sources and claim boundaries¶

    These are local program competencies, not official Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmark numbers. See local standards and the source register. Catholic care, dignity and honest-inquiry applications follow that register; no unsupported scientist/saint biography, Scripture quotation or devotional history is required to execute this lesson. No external historical or official numeric claim is made.

    Session 03: Bridge Building¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Structures / Bridge Building
    Time / domains One native 30-minute meeting, session 3 of 17 / C, E, M
    Big idea Shape can change how a bridge supports a load; fair tests compare evidence.
    Student objective "I can test two paper shapes and explain one improvement."
    Why Bridges serve people; engineers test safe models before trusting designs.
    Catholic connection Include neighbors and build relationships; this is a teacher metaphor, not Scripture or an attributed papal quotation. Service and dignity: CCC 2407.
    Standards Local CST-C2: explain who crossing helps; CST-E1: span/load criteria; CST-E2: two tests/redesign; CST-M1: count load; CST-M2: record/compare results. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path: physical paper tests answer the question.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Low; 10-15 minutes; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class / supplies¶

    1. On each table place two identical-height books 10 cm apart, measured between inside edges. Test ordinary A4/letter paper across gap; do not promise a flat sheet must fail. Make pairs, with one trio at odd enrollment: 5/7/10/12 active teams for 10/15/20/25 pupils. The table budgets ⅝/10/13 kits, retaining one reserve at 15/25.
    2. Cut/choose identical paper sheets; prepare equal broad wooden blocks as loads, maximum five, one at a time. Do not use pennies or heavy weights.
    3. Draw two-result chart (flat/folded). Demonstrate accordion folds; Grade 1 can use a teacher-started fold.
    4. Per student: half-sheet, crayon, individual evidence check.
    5. Per pair: two support books, two paper sheets, five identical broad blocks; ruler shared.
    6. Class: timer, class comparison board; optional bridge pictures.
    7. Teacher-only: scissors if paper needs cutting, model-preflight materials.
    Students Pairs / bridge kits Test sheets Broad blocks
    10 5 10 25
    15 8 16 40
    20 10 20 50
    25 13 26 65

    At 25 partners test simultaneously on low tables while teacher checks individuals; no 13-group sequential whole-class loading queue. In a trio, rotate builder, loader and observer so every child predicts, handles a safe test step and explains the result; the extra kit is not a lone child's pair.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Span = gap crossed; support = holds bridge at ends; load = what bridge holds; criterion = success requirement; redesign = change after testing. Beam bridges carry loads across supports. Folding can stiffen paper, but paper type, span and placement affect results. Model behavior is not proof a real bridge is safe. Misconception: the strongest student's bridge matters most. Same conditions and explaining evidence matter. If asked "Is a bridge a Bible verse?" No. Our relationship metaphor is a teacher illustration; the removed "bridges, not walls" quotation was not Scripture. Optional service reference: Galatians 5:13 in school-approved Bible, wording VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Show a bridge purpose; ask who needs safe access and how a design includes them. Optional original prayer asks for kind cooperation.
    2. 4-8: Demonstrate fixed 10 cm span and loading one equal block at center for five seconds, stopping at five or failure. Clear hands before loading.
    3. 8-14: Partners test flat paper; each predicts and counts/points to result. Record actual supported load before failure, not total dropped blocks.
    4. 14-21: Fold second sheet, keep supports/load alike, test again; swap loader/observer roles. If needed redesign one fold and retest within block.
    5. 21-26: Each child draws/shows a changed feature and compares two results; Grade 2 names what stayed the same. Partner explains who a real bridge serves.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / success¶

    What stayed the same? Which shape held more, or were they equal? What would you change next? Who benefits from crossing safely? - Grade 1: count/point to two loads, show one change and orally explain a user need; drawing replaces writing. - Grade 2: record two counts, identify same span/load, explain improvement from evidence, not appearance. - Record not yet / prompted / independent per child for comparison, change and criteria. Failed models can still demonstrate learning.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    Both hold five: record ceiling "at least five"; narrow paper equally or widen span slightly for a second comparison, labeling changed conditions. Neither holds one: reduce span equally. Missing books: identical boxes. All work indoors with no devices; no extended curing/glue time.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    Models on tables only, no student weight, floor crossings, climbing, heavy loads or loose coins. Broad loads maximum five; hands out during collapse. Never apply model capacity to a real bridge. Support: prestarted folds, four picture steps, adult scribing and oral count. Challenge: Grade 2 compare two fold patterns under identical criteria, not an unlimited load contest.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Count loads/books, flatten/recycle usable paper, return ruler, retain comparison sketch. We tested two paper bridge shapes and compared honest load counts. Catholic connection: designs that help neighbors cross safely. Ask: "What changed, and how did you know it helped?" Optional: notice a bridge in a picture or fold scrap paper with an adult; no supplies purchase or routine homework. CCC 2407. John Nepomucene patronage/history: VERIFICATION REQUIRED, optional and not needed for lesson; no attributed quote is used.

    Session 04: Robot Friends¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Coding / Robot Friends
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting, session 4 of 17 / C, T
    Big idea Remote control and a stored program are different ways to give input.
    Student objective "I can predict and run two stored actions, then fix one instruction."
    Why A useful program runs in order and is checked against its purpose.
    Catholic connection Share tools fairly and choose a helpful purpose; teacher application of CCC 2407. Human dignity is not machine obedience.
    Standards Local CST-C2: fair partner turn/helpful purpose; CST-T1: run/stop and input/output; CST-T2: order two actions/debug. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Required primary path: Dash plus compatible tablet and Blockly to run stored instructions. Go driving alone does not meet programming objective.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes initial setup plus charging; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class¶

    1. Confirm actual loan, compatibility/permissions and model charging instructions. Open Blockly, not just Go.
    2. Test drive forward 20 cm at low speed -> change light color using installed block names; write tested settings on board. Show Run and Stop.
    3. Mark a dry 1 m floor bay for each active kit, clear of exits; have a forward/light picture card and table token.
    4. Assign teams of 2-3; rotate programmer, observer and checker after every run. No prior Year A/B coding assumed.

    Supplies¶

    • Per student: half-sheet, crayon.
    • Per team: one charged Dash/tablet kit, two cards, token.
    • Whole class: floor tape, timer, board; reusable trays.
    • Teacher-only: chargers, installed help, roster.
    Students Teams / kits for simultaneous practice Papers
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    With three kits at 25, use three 4-minute waves (three teams/wave) at a teacher-supervised station; other teams predict with tokens. With one kit, not all children can receive adequate independent practice in 30 minutes: record missing device opportunities and repeat later. Do not count watching as operating/programming.

    Vocabulary / teacher background¶

    Program = stored instructions; input = what we send; output = movement/light; sequence = order; debug = correct a mismatch. Blockly is a stored block-based programming tool. Go joystick input steers in real time; it can illustrate input/output but cannot certify stored-code learning. Misconception: pressing a drive button proves programming. Require a connected stored sequence. If asked about Carlo Acutis: saint title/biography is optional; current official source is VERIFICATION REQUIRED before teaching details. A helpful technology choice can be assessed without a biography.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: State objective, bay/stop rules, fair turns and helpful-purpose question. Optional original prayer asks for wise use.
    2. 4-7: Every child predicts two picture actions; partner moves a tabletop token and points to light picture.
    3. 7-11: Teacher contrasts manual Go steering with Blockly two-block stored run; shows how to stop. Do not say driving was programming.
    4. 11-23: Each child predicts/runs the tested sequence, swaps a color or movement amount and reruns. Observer says what changed; rotate after each run. Teacher records individual run/stop, sequence and one change.
    5. 23-26: Each child points/draws two actions and explains why the second run differed; state one fair turn/helpful purpose.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / success¶

    Can it run without steering? Which instruction changed output? Did your partner get an actual turn? Grade 1: orally/visually order two actions, run/stop under supervision and point to one changed output. Grade 2: assemble two or three actions, predict, change one block and explain before/after. Both name a responsible use. Score not observed / prompted / independent per child. Unplugged evidence never earns physical-robot operation credit.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    After two minutes checking charge/selected robot, use cards and token. Child orders two actions, partner follows, child fixes reversed order. Assess CST-T2 conceptual sequence/debug only; no real robot programming or operation mastery. Poor travel: shorten/lower speed on same dry surface. All work indoors.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    No racing, chasing, running on tables or touching a moving robot; stop outside bay. Teacher-only charging; keep cables out of routes. Consent before physical assistance. Support: picture blocks, narrate each action, adult scribing and two-action starter. Challenge: Grade 2 add a short wait/light action; postpone maze/loops to a later measured opportunity.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Stop programs, power down, count kits/cards, clear tape and store labeled trays; teacher charges. We distinguished steering from stored code, predicted a sequence and changed one instruction. Our Catholic connection was responsible sharing. Ask: "What ran without steering?" Optional: two spoken instructions for a paper token; no device/purchase or routine homework. Blockly official app; CCC 2407. Colossians 3:23 is an optional school-approved Bible reference, no unverified quote.

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting.     Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Living = has life processes; once-living = came from a living thing; never-living = not formerly alive.

    A fallen leaf came from a living plant; a stone is not a dead animal. Movement alone is not a reliable life test.

    Common misconception: All nonmoving things are nonliving, or a fallen leaf was never alive.

    If asked: "Is a dormant tree dead?" Not necessarily; one still moment does not establish whether it is alive.

    SAFETY¶

    No tasting, wild collection, unknown plants or Sun-focusing magnifiers; use the screened indoor set. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Notice and sort - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Show the three examples and discuss observing without disturbing nature.
    2. 3-7: Model two picture details and a category reason based on origin/life processes, not movement.
    3. 7-20: Each child observes/draws two details, counts visible leaves/features in the selected picture and sorts all three examples. Partner asks for a reason rather than supplies it.
    4. 20-26: Each child points to two details, compares two visible feature counts and explains one category/protective action.
    5. 26-30: Return pictures/stone, save individual drawings and clear tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Was this example once living or never living?
    • Which details did you actually see?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Represent two details, distinguish leaf from stone and count visible features once.

    Grade 2: Explain all three categories and a count comparison without claiming a picture proves current growth.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Large category icons and tactile stone; teacher describes pictures for access. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain why a toy that moves is still never-living. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Plant image unclear: use a simpler drawn model with an explicit label; observation is of the representation. Outdoor cancellation: the whole primary task already works indoors.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We noticed nature details, compared visible counts and sorted examples with reasons. Ask: "Was this example once living or never living?" Optional: describe a nature picture without collecting specimens. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Sequence = ordered commands; output = character movement; debug = fix mismatch.

    The stage uses digital steps, not classroom centimeters. Reset character start before comparing motion counts.

    Common misconception: Dragging a sprite manually is executed programming.

    If asked: "Are two digital steps two centimeters?" No; different unit systems must not be equated.

    SAFETY¶

    Dry tablets, mute sound, no names/photos/accounts, purchases or uploads. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: First executed code - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Predict how an on-screen character will move from its starting point.
    2. 3-7: Model Green Flag -> Right 2 -> End, Run/Stop, reset and change 2 to 1.
    3. 7-20: Each team member gets a four-minute tablet turn: connect the three blocks, predict, Run/Stop, reset and change one motion count. Others trace/count block cards.
    4. 20-26: Each child shows a changed block and actual output, compares counts and explains careful tablet sharing/return; teacher checks during turns.
    5. 26-30: Return to Home, lock tablets, count cards and clear dry tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which block changed the output?
    • What unit are you counting?

    Grade 1: Individually connect/run the sequence and identify the changed motion count.

    Grade 2: Predict the changed endpoint, explain the rerun/reset and distinguish digital steps from cm.

At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. The card route does not establish digital-tool operation.

Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Add one opposite-direction motion and predict the net path before running. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    Catholic Inventors¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Student objective / why "I can count observations and communicate a clear inquiry panel." A brief source-checked historical context leads to hands-on evidence, not biography memorization.
    Catholic connection Mendel's pea investigations at an Augustinian abbey give a historical faith-community context; our task reports its own limited data honestly. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Investigate = check a question; data = records; category = group with a rule.

    The museum documents Mendel's Augustinian membership/abbot role and pea experiments. It does not establish his private motives or imply that our classroom repeats his research method. Our six invented model cards teach visible grouping/counting; they cannot demonstrate inheritance laws.

    Original teacher read-aloud, not a quotation by Mendel:

    "Mendel belonged to a Catholic religious community. He also studied pea plants. His museum preserves evidence of that scientific work. A person can have a religious vocation and also investigate nature."

    Reused from the original Mendel heritage card, with its institutional museum source. Ask which records would help compare plants honestly, then use the children's own labeled model graph. Biography recall alone does not earn inquiry or mathematics credit.

    Common misconception: Six classroom drawings prove Mendel's discoveries or prove religion.

    If asked: "Are these Mendel's real plants?" No; they are our labeled practice models.

    SAFETY¶

    No seeds/plants tasted, live collection, web accounts or independent online research. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Faith-community inquiry - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Read the short heritage text above. Ask "What records would help someone compare plants honestly?" Distinguish its historical facts from today's observations of DRAWN MODEL cards.
    2. 3-7: Model sorting one card by a visible shape and making one mark per card, not by a desired result.
    3. 7-20: Each child takes a turn sorting/counting the six cards, creates a two-category object/picture graph and draws an inquiry panel. Partner asks a clarity question; author revises.
    4. 20-26: Each child interprets the 3/3 counts, reports the visible grouping rule and explains that the class graph is its own model evidence, not Mendel's records or proof of inheritance. Connect honest labels to inquiry rather than quiz biography names.
    5. 26-30: Count six cards per kit and save individual graphs/panels. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What can our six model cards actually show?
    • How did you decide the grouping rule?
    • Which statement came from the museum source, and what did our cards actually show?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Sort by visible feature, count both groups and explain the panel.

    Grade 2: Interpret the equal counts, revise a clear data message and distinguish source-checked history from model data.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Two tactile/high-contrast shape icons and oral captions. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Propose another grouping rule and explain why its count does not change historical conclusions. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    Weather Watchers¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Bi-Weekly A / Weather
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, S, M / Repeated weather records describe actual conditions, not guaranteed forecasts.
    Student objective / why "I can record three same-window observations and interpret their counts." Indoor repeated Earth-system evidence works in Minnesota winter without outdoor instruments.
    Catholic connection Tell the truth about weather evidence and its limits while appreciating creation; a forecast is not a statement of faith. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C1: honest evidence and faith/reason; CST-S1: observations, questions and evidence; CST-S3: physical, life or Earth systems/models; CST-M2: represent and interpret data/patterns. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Choose an accessible same-window view and draw sky/precipitation icons. Fold the allocated work page into a three-time recording tool with columns for start, minute 7 and minute 20. Use the three blank cards to store actual class observations; no predetermined sunny/rainy results. If the view is inaccessible, teacher describes the actual view and labels teacher-observed records.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: actual time / sky and precipitation evidence / count comparison. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Index cards / kit / blank timed weather records 12 15 21 27

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Weather = conditions at a time/place; precipitation = rain/snow falling; observation = noticed condition; forecast = prediction.

    Three short observations can show change or no change; they do not measure temperature/wind or predict tomorrow. Precipitation returns water to Earth's surface, but this window record does not show every part of the water cycle.

    Common misconception: Cloud means rain is certain, or three equal observations are a failed investigation.

    If asked: "Will it snow tomorrow?" These short observations alone cannot tell us; a forecast needs more information.

    SAFETY¶

    Stay indoors and away from open windows/glass handling. No snow/ice exposure, roof access or unapproved weather instruments. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Repeated window weather and data - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Observe/describe actual sky/precipitation or visibility limits; make the first dated class record.
    2. 3-7: Model the folded three-time recording tool and a one-mark-per-time display; do not fill future columns yet.
    3. 7-20: At minute 7 make a second observation from the same view. Each child records both times and begins a precipitation/not-seen display using actual results; a partner checks the time labels. Keep unknown visibility separate, not counted as no precipitation.
    4. 20-26: At minute 20 make the third observation. Each child completes the chart, compares change/no change and precipitation/not-seen counts and states why these short records do not prove tomorrow's weather.
    5. 26-30: Keep dated class weather cards and individual recording tools; clear tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Did the same-window observations show change or no change?
    • What do these counts tell us and not tell us?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Represent three supported time records and count observed categories accurately.

    Grade 2: Interpret actual three-time category counts, identify the same-place condition and distinguish observation from forecast or unknown visibility.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Sky/rain icons, oral descriptions and high-contrast records. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Suggest two dated future observations to compare without adding counted teaching meetings. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No accessible window: teacher describes actual visible conditions at the three times and labels teacher-observed data. If no real view is available, draw three clearly labeled example records for chart practice and mark live weather evidence unassessed. No weather change: record honestly; do not force a trend.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We made three same-window weather records, interpreted actual counts and distinguished observation from forecast. Ask: "Did the same-window observations show change or no change?" Optional: describe weather from a safe indoor view; no required log. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Sprout = early emerging plant; pod = holds developing seeds; cycle = continuing stages.

    The represented bean stages continue through new seeds. A dormant seed may be alive; stages do not mean death and resurrection.

    Common misconception: A model proves the days needed for growth or plants eat soil.

    If asked: "Is soil plant food?" Plants make sugars using light and take water/minerals from their environment; the model does not test all needs.

    SAFETY¶

    No live seed tasting, chemicals, sharp tools or compulsory planting/home care. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Continuing plant model - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Read six stage names and explain the MODEL label.
    2. 3-7: Model arrows from seed through plant/pod to new seeds, not adult back into its own seed.
    3. 7-20: Each child orders/draws the six stages with teacher-read names, traces relationships and records a six-feature coverage checklist. Partner removes/swaps one stage; child repairs it.
    4. 20-26: Each child explains a transition, interprets coverage count and names something the model omits, such as actual timing.
    5. 26-30: Return six reference cards and save individual stage diagrams. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How do new seeds continue the cycle?
    • What does your model not measure?

    Grade 1: Order at least seed/sprout/plant/new seeds with the six-card support and identify one connection.

    Grade 2: Explain all six represented stages, repair an order error and interpret coverage without claiming real growth timing.

At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support / nonreader access: Large picture cards, four key stages first, then teacher-supported six-stage sequence. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain why a mature plant does not become its own original seed again. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Vibration = back-and-forth motion; pitch = high/low sound; volume = loud/soft; rhythm = timed phrase.

    A shorter freely vibrating part generally has higher pitch. Change length while using similarly gentle plucks; this is a guided comparison, not precise acoustic measurement.

    Common misconception: Louder means higher pitch, or a pupa/balloon instrument is needed for music.

    If asked: "Why can I feel sound?" Sound involves vibration; our strip lets us see/feel a vibration safely without putting anything in mouths.

    SAFETY¶

    No latex balloons, loose rubber bands, mouth-blown instruments or ruler snapping. Keep book/strip flat and stable; pluck minimally with fingers away from edges. Quiet volume, no compulsory loud sound; stop if strip cracks or securing fails. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Two-pitch instrument and rhythm - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Introduce quiet high/low/rest choices and ask what will vibrate.
    2. 3-7: Model two gentle plucks at each marked length; predict and record high/low, holding material and gentle technique consistent.
    3. 7-20: Each child directs/tries both lengths and records two outcomes. Teams adjust securing if the strip slips and retest. Each child composes four high/low/rest cards and performs or directs two repetitions at quiet volume.
    4. 20-26: Each child distinguishes pitch from volume, explains a securing/test revision and identifies the repeated four-beat musical phrase; peer suggests one purposeful rhythm change.
    5. 26-30: Stop sound, remove tape, return intact ruler/book and count eight beat cards. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which free length made the higher pitch?
    • How did your four-beat phrase express your idea?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Compare high/low outcomes and compose/repeat a four-beat phrase.

    Grade 2: Name the changed length and kept-same material, distinguish pitch/volume and explain an instrument/rhythm revision.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. A silent card phrase is rhythm evidence, not observed sound or physical instrument mastery.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Teacher/adult stabilizes the book while child directs length; silent beat cards support sensory access, with sound comparison recorded separately if unobserved. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Change one rhythm position and explain the musical effect without increasing loudness. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No distinguishable pitch: adult rechecks projecting lengths/security before class; record unclear results rather than louder plucks. No safe flexible ruler: quiet body percussion/card composition assesses rhythm only; strip-sound/engineering evidence remains unassessed.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We compared safe vibrating lengths and composed quiet four-beat music with accessible participation. Ask: "Which free length made the higher pitch?" Optional: tap or point a quiet four-beat phrase. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, T, M / A later robot mission rechecks individual code and uses a conditional plan honestly.
    Student objective / why "I can run and debug a stored Dash route and explain a conditional choice." One earlier robot contact does not establish expertise.
    Catholic connection Return scarce tools carefully and explain why sharing them serves classmates; no machine is credited with making a moral choice. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C3: stewardship and responsible work; CST-T1: tool use, input/output and troubleshooting; CST-T2: algorithms and debugging; CST-M1: count, compare and measure. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Check three charged kits and stored Blockly execution. Mark three 1 m dry clear lanes with a start and 10 cm-wide goal zone at a short pretested distance. Draw a blue/red mission card rule: if blue choose two short forward blocks; otherwise one. This is a human-selected condition, not a robot color sensor.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: input card / predicted route / measured result and correction. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Mission = criterion; debug = repair mismatch; condition = choice based on input.

    A condition can select a program; without an actual sensor/conditional block, do not call the robot autonomous. Measured endpoints depend on floor/start/heading.

    Common misconception: Watching a team run proves every member wrote code.

    If asked: "Did Dash see the blue card?" No; you read the input and choose stored instructions.

    SAFETY¶

    Three dry low-speed lanes in one sightline, no riders, collisions, attachments or crossing walking routes; adult charges devices. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Recheck, debug, choose - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Recheck Run/Stop and name the goal-zone criterion; teach the blue/red card rule.
    2. 3-7: Model Start -> short Drive -> Stop, predict, run, reset; change one drive parameter if endpoint misses.
    3. 7-20: Use two four-minute waves for 10/15 pupils or three for 20/25, three teams per wave. Each member gets about 40 seconds to choose/edit, predict, Run/Stop and identify output; waiting teams trace both card inputs.
    4. 20-26: Each child records measured endpoint/goal result and explains a code change plus the human-selected conditional choice; teacher checks individual actions during waves.
    5. 26-30: Stop/park robots, retain local projects, count cards and remove lane tape. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which change helped reach the goal zone?
    • Who read the card condition: you or the robot?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Individually Run/Stop a stored route and point to a changed block.

    Grade 2: Explain a reset/measured endpoint correction and trace both blue/red inputs without claiming robot sensing.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Neither token success nor human card selection proves autonomous hardware sensing.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Connected starter script, big input cards and oral directions. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain which extra hardware/software evidence would be needed for autonomous sensing. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Only one/two/no working kits: run feasible individual turns and trace cards for the rest; record missing hardware evidence. Connection failure: adult rechecks pairing/app; no manual steering substituted.

    Indoor: The indoor marked-lane route is primary; token/card work is available when safe floor space is absent.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We rechecked stored robot code, measured a mission result and traced a human-selected condition honestly. Ask: "Which change helped reach the goal zone?" Optional: choose between two paper-token routes using a color/shape card. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Community = people working together; organizer = helps find items; equal groups = same count in each.

    The task models useful organization at school, not a general device for disability. Six cards can be split into two equal groups of three.

    Common misconception: Service requires litter picking, food delivery or family purchases.

    If asked: "Can we build a bird feeder?" Not in this package; the requested classroom organizer has a bounded safe test.

    SAFETY¶

    No litter handling, food, outdoor feeders, sharp recyclables or outside deliveries. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Helper organizer - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Read the actual helper request and material limit.
    2. 3-7: Model folding two spaces and checking three cards in each plus retrieval without moving the holder.
    3. 7-20: Teams build, distribute six cards into two groups, test retrieval and revise one support/visibility feature. Each child conducts/directs one check and draws the allocation.
    4. 20-26: Each child names the user need, shows the two groups and explains a test-based improvement; giving the model is optional.
    5. 26-30: Return all six cards and save reusable organizer materials. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How do the two spaces help the classroom helper?
    • How did you split six cards?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show two groups of three and identify a useful feature/test.

    Grade 2: Explain 3 + 3 = 6 with a model, a material constraint and a revision linked to retrieval evidence.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Precreased broad spaces and picture-group icons; child directs placement. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Compare a four/two grouping with the requested equal grouping and explain why one does not meet the request. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Cards spill: widen/lower compartments and retest. Helper absent: teacher states the actual school sorting need; no community visit is required.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    We designed a useful classroom organizer and explained a six-card allocation. Ask: "How do the two spaces help the classroom helper?" Optional: notice how familiar objects are organized. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Grades 1-2 Year B

    🌟 Grades 1-2 Year B Bi-Weekly C-STREAM¶

    17 Sessions | 30 Minutes Each | Every Other Week

    This folder contains the condensed Grades 1-2 Year B C-STREAM curriculum for schools with bi-weekly STREAM classes. Year B features different projects, saints, and contexts than Year A while building the same foundational skills.

    Audit and entry conditions¶

    See the Grades 1-2 review and downloadable audit. This track has 17 actual meetings/17 files = 510 minutes; weekly has 32 meetings/960 minutes. Fewer contacts mean fewer independent device turns and science observations, not equivalent mastery.

    Year A is not a prerequisite. Teach safe handling, observation and picture sequences before challenges. Grade 1 can point, draw or respond orally without reading; Grade 2 should justify a feature/measurement and revise using evidence. Session 14 rechecks Session 03 stored-code start/stop rather than declaring students experts.

    All 17 files are complete documented packages: Meet Sphero and Garden Engineers are preserved references; the remaining 15 plans are rebuilt. Mathematics progresses through same-start measurement, repeated counts, two-part/equal-group operations and interpreted data, with distinct Grade 1/Grade 2 checks in the actual steps. Maria Agnesi's brief context is source-checked; unsupported quotations/history are omitted. School stock/policy and classroom pilots remain conditional, not documentation gaps or observed outcomes.

    For trio-based lessons, 10/15/20/25 pupils use ⅘/7/9 groups: two trios and two pairs; five trios; six trios and one pair; seven trios and two pairs. Optional reference routines support kit checks and individual evidence but do not replace the lesson's complete sequence, supplies or safety. Pair-based lessons keep their own allocation/reserve plan. Fewer devices use the lesson's stated waves/shared tests, not groups of four or credit for watching.

Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Design = purposeful choice; user = person; feature = part; measure = compare with units.

    A ruler's input is placement/readout, not an electronic action. A bookmark solves finding a page; a tool's presence alone is not mastery.

    Common misconception: Only computers count as technology.

    If asked: "Can a simple strip be a useful tool?" Yes, if it meets the user's page-finding need.

    SAFETY¶

    Teacher precuts strips; no rulers swung or snapped, no page tearing. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Investigate everyday design - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Show a book reader's page-finding problem and invite two design ideas.
    2. 3-7: Model a page strip's function and ruler zero/endpoints, separating length from "best."
    3. 7-20: Each child takes a strip, tests it in the book, measures/compares its length and draws user/job/feature. Partners suggest a helpful access choice; teacher checks tool handling individually.
    4. 20-26: Each child names user need and function, shows a correct measurement start and explains one inclusive use choice.
    5. 26-30: Return book/ruler/strips, keep evidence drawings and clear tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Whose problem does this tool solve?
    • Where did you start the measurement?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Name a tool's job and compare lengths from aligned starts.

    Grade 2: Record a length with units and explain a user/access feature rather than call longest best.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Provide job icons and child-directed partner measuring; use equal drawn units if needed. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain a feature that may help one use but hinder another. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No ruler: teacher prepares equal 1 cm marks on allocated paper before class, labeled units. No book: use a folded allocated paper booklet for function testing.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We investigated everyday tools, measured a feature and considered their users. Ask: "Whose problem does this tool solve?" Optional: describe the job of a familiar tool without using sharp equipment. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Tower Power¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Bi-Weekly B / Structures
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, E, M / A same-height tower test supports a useful stability comparison.
    Student objective / why "I can measure a low tower, revise its base and compare results." This applies the Session 1 endpoint measurement to a tested structure.
    Catholic connection Reuse counted blocks and explain why careful resource use matters. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C3: stewardship and responsible work; CST-E2: build, test and redesign; CST-M1: count, compare and measure; CST-M2: represent and interpret data/patterns. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Inspect planks; set target approximately 15 cm and absolute ceiling 30 cm. Draw before/after height and stand/fall boxes; pretest broad/narrow bases.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: height and units / stand result / revised base. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Wooden building planks / kit / items 72 90 126 162
    Metric ruler / kit / items 4 5 7 9

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Base = bottom support; stable = stays upright; height = table-to-top length.

    To compare bases fairly, keep the intended height approximately the same. A tie is a valid result.

    Common misconception: The tallest tower is always the strongest.

    If asked: "Should we add heavy weights?" No; this is a 10-second standing comparison, not a load test.

    SAFETY¶

    Low tabletop structures, hands clear, no climbing, pushing or heavy top loads. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Measured stable tower - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: State target, standing criterion and 18-plank limit.
    2. 3-7: Model ruler endpoints, a 10-second test and two-row result chart.
    3. 7-20: Teams build/test, record actual height/result, change a base feature and retest at similar height. Every child builds/directs and measures/counts one result.
    4. 20-26: Each child interprets before/after records, explains a changed/kept-same feature and a reusable-material action.
    5. 26-30: Dismantle from the top, count 18 planks and retain results. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Did the same-height comparison support your change?
    • What happened in each standing test?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Measure from the table and show a tested base change.

    Grade 2: Record units/two results, interpret the chart and explain why matching height matters.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Prebuilt base, picture chart and equal-unit counting. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Repeat a trial and discuss variation instead of increasing unsafe height. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Both designs pass: record a tie and compare used planks. No planks: use equal clean blocks with a pretested lower target, explicitly labeled.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We measured and compared tower stability using a before/after chart. Ask: "Did the same-height comparison support your change?" Optional: point out the base of an indoor structure. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.
