    Session 03: Meet Sphero¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Coding / Meet Sphero
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting, session 3 of 17 / C, T
    Big idea Code is stored input; rolling and light are observable output.
    Student objective "I can run two stored instructions, predict output, and change one block."
    Why Responsible programmers test short understandable sequences before complex paths.
    Catholic connection Fair turns and careful shared resources; teacher application of CCC 2407/2415.
    Standards Local CST-C3: equipment care; CST-T1: input/output and start/stop; CST-T2: sequence and one debug. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology Required primary path: compatible charged Sphero/tablet with Sphero Edu for physical stored-code execution. Token fallback assesses algorithms, not robot mastery.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20-30 minutes first model/app preflight plus charging; 4 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class / supplies¶

    1. Confirm real inventory/loan and school permissions. Check the exact model supports chosen blocks; do not assume Mini/BOLT features identical.
    2. In Blocks test light-color -> roll at heading 0 for 0.5-1 second at low speed -> stop; write model-specific working settings on board. Aim heading 0 away from children.
    3. Mark dry 1 m floor bays; prepare light/roll/stop picture cards, tabletop tokens and safe stop signal.
    4. Per student: half-sheet, crayon, individual roster check.
    5. Per team of 2-3: one robot/tablet kit and picture cards/token.
    6. Class: floor tape, timer, board, storage trays.
    7. Teacher-only: chargers, installed help and model screening. No attached pens.
    Students Teams / simultaneous kits Papers
    10 4 10
    15 5 15
    20 7 20
    25 9 25

    If only three kits exist, at 25 supervise one station with three 4-minute waves of three teams; off-device teams predict cards. With one kit, record unobserved individual runs and repeat assessment later. Do not infer mastery from watching another child's robot.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Sequence = instructions in order; program = stored instructions; input/output = code/result; aim = set direction reference; debug = fix a mismatch. Manual Drive mode is remote control. A connected stored sequence that executes hands-off is programming. Floor, charge and aim influence travel. Misconception: every rolling robot run matches an exact path. Observe before promising accuracy. If asked "Are we experts now?" We are beginning programmers; evidence shows specific skills, not expertise.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Show robot, purpose and care/turn rule. Optional original prayer asks for wise tool use.
    2. 4-7: Children predict color then forward movement using cards/token, orally or by pointing.
    3. 7-11: Teacher contrasts Drive with a stored Blocks sequence; demonstrate aim, Run and Stop.
    4. 11-23: Each child predicts and executes starter, changes a color or roll duration and reruns. Roles rotate after each run; teacher records each child's observed actions.
    5. 23-26: Individual exit: point to two ordered actions, name an output and one change; identify safe equipment care.
    6. 26-30: Cleanup.

    Questions / measurable evidence¶

    What is stored before Run? Why aim again? What changed after your edit? How did you protect shared equipment? Grade 1: order two action cards, personally Run/Stop under supervision and point to changed output. Grade 2: assemble at least two stored actions, predict, change a block and explain mismatch or change. Record not observed / prompted / independent for each criterion; care assessed through an action, not a saint fact.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    Connection failure: check selected robot/charge once, switch after two minutes. Token alternative: arrange two cards, have partner follow, fix one intentionally wrong card. Record algorithm/debug evidence only; no real robot operation/programming mastery. Mis-aim: stop/re-aim/shorten movement. All work indoors, no winter/outdoor condition.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    Low-speed marked bays; stop if out of area; no chasing/racing or holding running robots. Teacher handles chargers and small removable model components. Dry floor only, no art paint/markers attached to ball. Support: picture starter, narration, large cards, adult scribing and accessible tabletop token; Grade 1 needs no independent reading. Challenge: Grade 2 adds light/wait action or compares two durations, not expert mazes.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Stop/power down according to model guide, count kits, return trays, remove lesson tape; teacher handles charging. We contrasted driving with stored programs and tested one changed instruction. Catholic connection: stewardship and fair access. Ask: "What changed in your program?" Optional: give two directions to a paper token; no robot/tablet/purchase or routine homework. Sphero official education site, installed help requires preflight; CCC 2407/2415. Acutis biography/title: VERIFICATION REQUIRED before optional use, not needed for this lesson.

    Animal Adaptations¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Bi-Weekly B / Adaptations
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / CORE
    Domains / big idea C, S, A, M / A visibility model can explore camouflage without inventing animal facts.
    Student objective / why "I can compare two background tests and represent an animal feature with a model limit." Year B uses counted life-science model evidence, not "design" as proof of biology.
    Catholic connection Respect creation by reporting the model honestly and leaving wildlife undisturbed; a model result is not proof of a belief. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C1: honest evidence and faith/reason; CST-S2: safe investigations and variables; CST-S3: physical, life or Earth systems/models; CST-A1: observational representation; CST-M2: represent and interpret data/patterns. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Moderate, 15-25 minutes first batch-cut set; light 5-10 minutes thereafter; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Prepare equal-size silhouettes and high-contrast/matching backgrounds. Set the same viewing distance and five-second looking time. Read: "Some animals' colors/patterns can make them less visible in a habitat; this classroom model tests visibility, not survival or how traits arose." No camel-hump or species-history anecdotes are needed.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: background / number noticed out of three / model limitation. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Material / allocation / unit 10 pupils 15 pupils 20 pupils 25 pupils
    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50
    Crayons / student / items 10 15 20 25
    Team sorting tray / kit / items 4 5 7 9
    Simple timer / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Whiteboard marker / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher roster / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Teacher scissors / class / items 1 1 1 1
    Cardstock / kit / 20 cm squares: light and dark 8 10 14 18
    Teacher-cut animal silhouette / kit / 3 light and 3 dark, 5 cm minimum 24 30 42 54

    Teacher-only: roster/timer, advance screening and precutting; classroom handwashing/normal cleaning supplies. No optional item is necessary for the stated outcome.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Feature = characteristic; camouflage = reduced visibility against surroundings; model = representation.

    Shape, background, lighting and observer affect detection. Actual adaptations develop across populations; children drawing a trait do not engineer a living species.

    Common misconception: An animal chooses a new inherited feature instantly, or camel humps store water.

    If asked: "Can our test prove an animal survives?" No; it compares noticing silhouettes, not feeding, predators or survival.

    SAFETY¶

    Large dry silhouettes; no live animals, food, small beads or outdoor capture. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Counted visibility model - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Discuss a visible feature and a labeled model, distinguishing a prediction from a result.
    2. 3-7: Model placing three same-color silhouettes on each background, giving five seconds and recording number noticed out of three.
    3. 7-20: Rotate arranger/observer/recorder; each child tries both backgrounds at the same distance/time. Record actual counts, then draw an animal representation with a purposeful blending feature and label it MODEL.
    4. 20-26: Each child compares the two count records, represents an observed model feature and explains a limit; no guaranteed camouflage result is assigned.
    5. 26-30: Count six silhouettes and two background squares; save individual count/model pages. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How did the two visibility counts compare?
    • What can this model not tell us about a living animal?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Count noticed silhouettes in two trials and show a model feature.

    Grade 2: Interpret the two records, name a kept-same viewing condition and distinguish model visibility from survival or inherited change.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Large high-contrast/tactile outlines; an adult describes actual visible features. Sensory access route may model positions without claiming visual detection evidence. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Predict the reversed color/background test and explain why a fair comparison keeps silhouette size fixed. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Counts tie: report honestly, discuss contrast/observer limits, not alter the recorded result. No colored stock: crayon-shaded allocated paper works; label the actual setup.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We counted visibility in a camouflage model and explained its limits for living animals. Ask: "How did the two visibility counts compare?" Optional: notice blending/contrast in a picture, without animal handling. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    These are local program competencies, not official Minnesota/Archdiocesan benchmark numbers. See local standards and the source register.     Session 05: Garden Engineers¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 1-2 / Growth and design / Garden Engineers
    Time / domains One 30-minute meeting, session 5 of 17 / C, S, E, A
    Big idea A garden needs light, safe space and responsible care; design has constraints.
    Student objective "I can plant a seed and show where our pots and care path fit safely."
    Why Designers consider living needs and people who care for plants. Growth will not happen during today's meeting.
    Catholic connection Stewardship of plants/resources, CCC 2415; service through a shared accessible garden.
    Standards Local CST-C3: care plan/resource use; CST-S3: seed/seedling needs; CST-E1: light/access constraints; CST-E2: test/revise layout; CST-A1: garden plan. Official benchmarks: VERIFICATION REQUIRED.
    Technology None primary path: physical pot-layout model and planting suffice.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Moderate; 20 minutes initial setup plus 2-3 minute adult school-day care checks; 5 minutes cleanup included.

    Before class¶

    1. Verify one untreated seed variety's packet, allergy/school potting-mix guidance and suitable bright indoor space. No outdoor planting or grow light required.
    2. Teacher makes drainage holes in plastic pots and places them in leakproof trays. Premeasure about 200 mL mix/team.
    3. Draw a 30 x 40 cm tray model with light-side mark and a 10 cm-wide care access strip at its front. Use three paper pot circles/team; do not block an exit or window route.
    4. Name an adult to check moisture on school days, weekends/break plan and watering when needed. No daily automatic watering or required home care.
    5. Prepare a prestarted seedling/photo for showing future growth. Explicitly identify it as earlier/teacher evidence.

    Supplies / scaling¶

    • Per student: half-sheet garden sketch, crayon.
    • Per team of 2-3: one pot, two seeds, 200 mL commercial potting mix, tray space, three paper pot circles and 30 x 40 cm paper mat.
    • Class: water jug, scoop, spill cloth, seedling/photo, whiteboard care log, handwashing.
    • Teacher-only: hole tool, seed packet, water distribution, care responsibility.
    Students Teams / pots Seeds plus 4 backups Mix Student sheets
    10 4 12 0.8 L 10
    15 5 14 1.0 L 15
    20 7 18 1.4 L 20
    25 9 22 1.8 L 25

    At 25 trays stay on tables; one teacher distributes water and collects pots. A small school garden can use team pots; no need for 25 individual live plants.

    Vocabulary / background¶

    Seed = young plant with stored food; seedling = growing young plant; constraint = limit; access = reaching safely; care plan = who checks needs and when. Seeds may germinate without light depending on variety; green seedlings need light to make food. Soil provides support and nutrients, not the plant's food itself; suitable soilless growth is possible. No causal experiment or same-day growth is claimed. Misconception: a plant needs exactly the same water daily. Check moisture/packet guidance. If asked "Will mine sprout by next class?" Maybe; variety, conditions and viability matter. Record what actually happens.

    Exact numbered sequence (30 minutes)¶

    1. 0-4: Show seed versus earlier seedling and explain today's design/planting objective. Optional original prayer asks for responsible care.
    2. 4-8: Model pot circles on tray mat: three fit without overlap, face light-side, keep care strip clear. Deliberately block strip then revise.
    3. 8-14: Teams arrange three circles, partner checks constraints, revise one feature. Each child sketches/points to light and access path.
    4. 14-21: Demonstrate packet-based planting depth; teams fill pot, plant two seeds, lightly water and label date/team. Each child participates safely.
    5. 21-25: Individual exit: show two seedling needs and one layout/care choice. Identify adult moisture checker and record a prediction as a prediction.
    6. 25-30: Cleanup/handwashing.

    Questions / success and later observation¶

    Where does light reach? Can the caretaker reach without knocking pots? How do we know when water is needed? Which result is still a prediction? Grade 1: oral/drawn two needs, point to clear access path and one care action. Grade 2: explain both layout constraints and one revision after checking; distinguish germination from later seedling growth. Record not yet / prompted / independent for needs, criteria, revision and care. One planted seed does not prove growth or experimental mastery. Before Session 06, the named adult adds one dated drawing/photo or height observation during normal plant care (about 2-3 minutes, not an extra C-STREAM meeting). Session 06 may spend its opening minute comparing it; if unavailable, use labeled teacher data and do not certify firsthand observation.

    If things go wrong / indoor fallback¶

    No safe growing space or allergy clearance: use empty pots/paper circles and teacher seedling pictures. Assess layout/needs, not live planting/care mastery. No germination: retain honest record and use the labeled prestarted example. Mold: adult removes sealed pot and cleans tray per policy. All work indoors even in Minnesota winter.

    SAFETY / support / challenge¶

    No seed/mix tasting, pesticides, student puncturing, glass pots, spraying faces or standing water near electronics. Wash hands, keep moisture in trays; teacher handles water/spills. Support: prefilled pot, large paper circles, visual step-by-step model, adult scribing and oral responses. Challenge: Grade 2 compare two layouts/tradeoffs while keeping both constraints.

    Cleanup / family / sources¶

    Return scoop, wipe trays/tables, move labeled pots to safe indoor location, wash hands and save sketches; adult owns care. Taking plants home is optional with an equally valid school-care option. Family snippet: We designed a light-accessible garden layout and planted seeds, but did not expect instant growth. Catholic connection: stewardship. Ask: "How can someone reach your pots safely?" Optional: notice a plant or garden picture; no seed purchase or home watering requirement. No routine homework. CCC 2415. Genesis 2:15 is an optional school-approved Bible reference; no unverified quotation. Fiacre patronage/biography and seed-specific sprouting dates are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before optional use.

    Gratitude Gifts¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher plan
    Grade / track / unit Grades 1-2 / Bi-Weekly B / Service
    Native time / scope 1 meeting(s), 30 minutes each including cleanup / RECOMMENDED
    Domains / big idea C, A, M / Recipient-focused art and fair quantities make a thoughtful gift.
    Student objective / why "I can communicate thanks and explain how I allocated six visual spaces." Purpose and number reasoning replace a generic craft.
    Catholic connection Respect the recipient's preferences; gifts of attention do not depend on purchases. This is a classroom application, not a historical quotation or official academic standard.
    Local standards CST-C2: dignity, service and inclusion; CST-A3: artistic communication, critique and revision; CST-M3: quantities, operations and reasoning. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Ask a classroom helper for a clear thank-you picture. Draw a six-space card guide; each child chooses how many spaces show the message and how many form a meaningful border, total six.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: message spaces / border spaces / total and revision. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Recipient = viewer; allocate = assign amounts; revision = purposeful change.

    Visual spaces can support within-6 joining reasoning; the quantities do not measure generosity.

    Common misconception: More decoration or a larger gift means more love.

    If asked: "Must I give this away?" No; explaining to the classroom audience completes the task.

    SAFETY¶

    Dry crayons/card, teacher precuts, no food/donation collections or identifying messages. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Thanks with six spaces - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Read recipient request and six-space limit.
    2. 3-7: Model two message spaces plus four border spaces; show the six-space count and readable symbol.
    3. 7-20: Each child chooses a split totaling six, creates a purposeful card and asks a partner what it communicates. Revise an unclear feature and recount the two parts.
    4. 20-26: Each child explains audience/purpose, the two-part total and a revision from feedback, not artistic ranking.
    5. 26-30: Save cards/evidence, return unused cardstock and clear tables. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How do your two parts make six spaces?
    • What makes the message clear to its recipient?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Show a two-part total of six with drawn spaces and tell the message.

    Grade 2: Explain the number relationship, offer another valid split and show an audience-based visual revision.

At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits.     Support / nonreader access: Pre-drawn six-box guide and two simple symbol choices; oral explanation accepted. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain why changing the split need not change the total. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    Writing barrier: use symbols and dictation. No helper: teacher is audience for the stated request. Do not turn the card into an untested engineering claim.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Undo changes the stored image; erased paper does not use that software control. Count represented message features, not artistic merit.

    1. 0-3: Set a welcoming classroom message and privacy choice.

    4. 20-26: Each child explains a tool input/output, artistic revision and feature-count comparison, plus one safe-sharing choice. Teacher checks digital actions during turns.
    5. 26-30: Save locally using aliases, lock tablets and collect private evidence. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Plain paper / student / sheets per meeting 20 30 40 50

    Classroom board / class / items 1 1 1 1

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Attract = pull toward; magnetic = attracted in this test; prediction = expected result.

    Magnets attract some materials, not all metals. Our actual object results determine counts; a steel label does not guarantee the particular spoon's response.

    Common misconception: All metal attracts a magnet or an unseen force proves a theological claim.

    If asked: "Is the force invisible like God?" This is a measurable physical interaction; that analogy is not scientific proof of belief.

    SAFETY¶

    No loose high-powered magnets, tiny detachable magnets, iron filings or exposed clips. Count magnets before/after and keep away from mouths; suspected ingestion requires immediate medical response. Stop if a casing cracks; never open sample boxes. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Predict and sort six tests - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Review safe magnet handling and distinguish a physical observation from a belief comparison.
    2. 3-7: Model approaching one screened object gently and recording pull/no pull, not making an expected answer.
    3. 7-20: Each child tests/directs all six objects in turn, predicts and records actual attraction. Teams sort into two groups; each child makes a six-result chart and compares predicted/actual attracted counts.
    4. 20-26: Each child interprets group counts (sum six), gives a mismatch explanation and identifies magnet input/action/output. Teacher checks actual handling/results during practice.
    5. 26-30: Teacher counts and stores encased magnets/boxes; return six test objects, smooth foil and retain charts. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How did your prediction count compare with the actual count?
    • Did all metal objects attract?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Test or direct a test, sort actual outcomes and count groups totaling six.

    Grade 2: Compare predicted/actual counts, explain a mismatch and use sum/difference reasoning without assuming every metal attracts.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Large object icons and partner magnet handling under child direction; oral data accepted. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain why one sample does not establish a universal rule about all materials. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    No safe encased magnet: use teacher-supplied clearly labeled demonstration data for chart reasoning; physical tool operation is unassessed. Spoon not attracted: keep the actual result, do not silently replace it with a "correct" one.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We safely tested attraction, counted actual groups and revised predictions using evidence. Ask: "How did your prediction count compare with the actual count?" Optional: discuss the class chart; no home magnet experiment required. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    If asked: "When will ours hatch?" There is no classroom live animal in this plan; the cards are models, not dated observations.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Beat = steady time pulse; phrase = musical/gesture idea; rest = silence; pattern = organized repeat.

    A child-created rhythmic phrase is a musical composition. An Easter hope connection is expressive, not biological evidence; no copyrighted song/quotation is used.

    Common misconception: Louder music expresses more joy or everyone must sing/clap.

    If asked: "May my phrase be silent?" Yes, a directed gesture phrase gives pattern/communication evidence; sound performance is recorded separately.

    SAFETY¶

    Quiet volume, no shared mouth instruments, balloons, striking peers or compulsory sound/movement. All actions are seated or child-directed. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Compose hopeful rhythm - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Discuss a welcoming/hopeful idea and accessible tap/gesture/rest choices.
    2. 3-7: Model a steady four-beat phrase, repeat it twice and change one beat to express a calmer or livelier idea.
    3. 7-20: Each child lays four icon cards, composes a phrase, performs/directs two repeats and receives one specific audience comment. Revise one beat and record the four-position pattern.
    4. 20-26: Each child identifies the repeat unit, counts beats/rests and explains how the purposeful revision communicates hope while respecting listeners.
    5. 26-30: Count four cards per child, stop performance and save phrase drawings. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • Which four-beat unit repeats in your phrase?
    • Why did you change that beat?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Compose/repeat four positions and identify a purposeful beat/rest choice.

    Grade 2: Represent the repeated unit, predict its next four positions and explain a musical/gesture revision for audience meaning.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Silence or card direction is not claimed as physical sound production; mathematical pattern and artistic intent remain assessable.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Two initial action icons plus rest; adult keeps pulse, child points/directs or uses a seated gesture. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Compare two phrases with the same beat count but different rest positions. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Noise grows: pause, use silent gesture/card performance and record sound evidence accurately. Motor access: child directs a partner, preserving composition ownership.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Heading = travel direction; parameter = adjustable value; debug = test a correction.

    Travel is actual measured output, not commanded duration alone. Reset start/heading and change only one parameter before comparison.

    Common misconception: A good group endpoint proves all members programmed, or paper/hardware paths are equivalent.

    If asked: "Did it go farther because gravity grew stronger?" No; we compare a changed code setting on the same floor.

    SAFETY¶

    Low speed in dry lanes, no riding, added markers, collisions or crossing exits; adult handles chargers. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Measured mission recheck - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Recheck Run/Stop and show the goal criterion; recall safe resource sharing.
    2. 3-7: Model stored Start -> low-speed Roll -> Stop, predict endpoint, measure, reset/aim and change duration only.
    3. 7-20: Two four-minute waves for 10/15 pupils or three for 20/25, three teams per wave. Each child gets about 40 seconds to change/predict/Run/Stop/identify a result; waiting teams trace cards and draw two endpoint bars. Teacher checks individual actions during waves.
    4. 20-26: Each child compares an actual first/revised endpoint record, explains the changed parameter and kept-same conditions, and returns shared equipment carefully.
    5. 26-30: Stop/park robots, retain local projects, count cards and remove lane tape. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • How did the two measured endpoints compare?
    • What did you keep the same when debugging?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Individually Run/Stop a stored program and identify a changed block/result.

    Grade 2: Represent two measured endpoints with the same units, explain the one-parameter correction and a kept-same condition.

Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. No paper execution, group success or unsupported loop trace is called physical robot mastery.

Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Trace a supported finite Repeat 2 and compare expected/actual output, recording loop execution only after a device turn. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    Local standards CST-C2: dignity, service and inclusion; CST-S2: safe investigations and variables; CST-T1: tool use, input/output and troubleshooting; CST-M1: count, compare and measure; CST-M3: quantities, operations and reasoning. Only the evidence below supports these local claims.
    Technology requirement None. No digital device or home access needed.
    Difficulty / prep / cleanup Guided; Light, 10-15 minutes; final 4 minutes of every meeting.

    Before class¶

    1. Assign teams of at most three: 4 / 5 / 7 / 9 kits for 10 / 15 / 20 / 25 pupils. Keep work at tables; distribute materials, not roaming station rotations.
    2. Set one cardboard ramp using a 5 cm support and a second sloped length using both cardboard pieces overlapping. Mark the same top height, measure path lengths before class and keep difference within 20 cm. Pretest a wide stick lever over the other low support, lifting a broad block only 1 cm within the tray.
    3. Put two plain-paper sheets per child per meeting and crayons at tables. Draw this record on the board: ramp path lengths / difference / lever input-output. Children copy boxes/icons, not paragraphs. Teacher dates and saves each child's record between meetings.
    4. Read the SAFETY section, pretest the actual task with one issued kit and put a roster beside the timer. Demonstrate orally with objects; read every direction aloud. No independent reading, Year A completion or family donation is a prerequisite.

    Exact supplies and class-size allocation¶

    Quantities below are the whole package allocation, not an assumed school holding. Kit items are reused across meetings unless the preparation says otherwise. Plain paper includes one work/model page and one individual evidence page per meeting. Supplies are counted before issue and after return; the teacher demonstrates with an issued kit, not an unlisted extra.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Ramp = sloped path; lever = rigid tool turning on support; path = traveled length; tradeoff = gain/cost.

    A longer, gentler ramp can reduce required effort but adds distance. We measure path lengths here, not force/energy. The lever lifts slowly; it is not a catapult.

    Common misconception: Machines create energy or always make every part of work easier.

    If asked: "Can we flick the lever?" No; gently press to lift the block about 1 cm, then lower it.

    SAFETY¶

    No launches, marbles, heavy loads, high ramps or snapping rulers. Wide stick lever is contained in tray; fingers clear of support. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Ramps and gentle lift - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: State a helper need: moving/lifting a broad block safely on a tabletop.
    2. 3-7: Model measuring both ramp paths from common endpoints and gently operating the bounded lever.
    3. 7-20: Each child guides the block along both ramp paths, records lengths using the same units and tests/directs a gentle 1 cm lever lift. Partners check kept-same height and slow handling.
    4. 20-26: Each child compares the two lengths, shows their difference with drawn units and identifies ramp/lever jobs; no measured force claim is made.
    5. 26-30: Lower loads, return supports/stick/ruler, save comparison records and clear trays. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What is the distance tradeoff between your two ramps?
    • What did your gentle lever input do?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Compare path lengths and demonstrate/describe a safe lever lift.

    Grade 2: Calculate/explain the path-length difference within 20 using units and distinguish measured distance from unmeasured effort.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. Use the grade-level criterion, not handwriting, reading speed or religious worth.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Equal-unit strips and adult-stabilized lever, child directs the input/output. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain why a longer path alone does not prove the exact force needed. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    Ramps sag: overlap/stiffen cardboard before issue and remark actual lengths. No safe lever support/stick: compare ramps only and record lever operation unassessed; never improvise a launcher.

    Indoor: The complete primary lesson is indoors at tables; Minnesota weather, internet access and daylight are not prerequisites.

    Family copy - optional, no routine homework¶

    We compared ramp distances and explored a gentle lever as useful classroom tools. Ask: "What is the distance tradeoff between your two ramps?" Optional: identify a pictured ramp or lever; no construction or lifting task required. No purchase, donation, device, home teaching or required take-home project.

    Vocabulary and teacher background¶

    Reuse = use again; recycle = process accepted material; waste = unusable remainder; data = counts.

    Accepted recycling varies locally; a symbol does not guarantee school acceptance. A twelve-card model shows counts, not measured annual waste reduction.

    Common misconception: All materials with a recycling symbol go in every recycling bin.

    If asked: "May we pick up outdoor litter?" Not in this class; we use clean model cards and ordinary classroom reuse.

    SAFETY¶

    No litter, broken items, dirty containers, unknown waste, chemicals or outdoor collection. Keep aisles/exits clear. Stop for damaged materials; do not improvise a hazardous replacement. No student handles loose batteries or teacher cutting tools.

    Meeting 1: Count and choose stewardship - 30 minutes¶

    1. 0-3: Explain actual versus example local rules and a feasible classroom paper-care need.
    2. 3-7: Model one-card/one-category sorting and three count columns.
    3. 7-20: Each child sorts/directs all twelve cards, checks the 4/4/4 allocation and represents it. Teams propose reusing four scrap-paper cards instead of treating them as trash; represent example trash count 8 -> 4 without claiming real measured savings.
    4. 20-26: Each child explains the category rule, total twelve and modeled reduction of four; state a concrete classroom reuse action and its criterion/limit.
    5. 26-30: Count twelve cards, store reusable paper and clean the normal classroom area only. Collect each child's dated evidence, count kit items, return tools and clear tables. Cleanup is part of the period, not time added afterward.

    Questions to ask¶

    • What rule supports your sorting choice?
    • What does the modeled waste reduction show and not show?

    Individual evidence and success¶

    Grade 1: Sort with the supplied rules, count three groups and show a reuse action.

    Grade 2: Explain 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 and modeled 8 - 4 = 4, distinguish example data from actual waste and propose a feasible need/limit.

    Teacher visits three table teams during each of the first three four-minute blocks of practice (7-19), listening to or observing each member briefly; use the remaining practice minute and 20-26 for unfinished checks and comparison. At 25, this is nine table visits, not 25 presentations. Where a meeting specifies waves, use its supervised wave/check schedule instead of simultaneous table visits. Children keep separate records and partners may not answer for each other. Score each stated criterion not yet / prompted / independent; record absent/unobserved evidence as such. A group product, attendance, attractive art or a certificate is not individual mastery. No real annual waste reduction or official local acceptance is invented from the model.

    Support and challenge¶

    Support / nonreader access: Large category icons, teacher-read local rule and picture quantities. Adult scribing, pointing, tactile/large pieces and a seated partner-directed action can show understanding; do not score motor speed. Record who actually operated hardware/software: a partner's operation does not establish the child's independent operation.

    Challenge: Explain how a changed local acceptance rule would change counts without changing the total items. Do not add an unprepared activity or extend the native period.

    If things go wrong / indoor alternative¶

    School recycling rule unavailable: use labeled examples for math/model evidence and keep real disposal unchanged. No printing: teacher-drawn cards on allocated paper suffice.

    Grades 3-4 Year A

    Grades 3-4 Year A: Bi-Weekly C-STREAM 🔬¶

    Overview¶

    Grade Band: 3-4 | Duration: 40 minutes per session | Sessions: 17 over the school year | Rotation Year: A

    This bi-weekly schedule provides a condensed C-STREAM experience for schools with alternating week schedules. Each 40-minute session delivers high-impact learning with Catholic integration.

    Audit status and prerequisites¶

    These are 17 represented meetings / 680 minutes in 17 files, not half the weekly sequence compressed without loss. See the Grades 3-4 review and 71-lesson audit. All packages have complete quantities, native timelines and individual checks. Fourteen were completed in the all-60 follow-up; Dash, the updated Light & Circuits and Plants references remain unchanged. Document completion is not classroom certification.

    Either rotation may be a pupil's first year. Teach Grade 3 supported counts/measurement and Grade 4 repeat-test/limitation reasoning in either. Scratch Intro is the prerequisite for animation; verify that learning rather than assume attendance. Plants has a within-meeting evidence path; living growth still takes days and an assigned adult caretaker.

    CSCOE loan stock/dates, models, batteries, software and privacy permissions are VERIFICATION REQUIRED, not guaranteed. Paper route fallbacks evidence CT, not Dash operation. Circuits require approved low-voltage kits for real electrical outcomes; paper models do not light. No loose coin-cell cards are sent home. Weather and plant work have indoor/no-homework paths.

    New packages supply needed source facts or omit unneeded biographies/quotes. Gratitude/Easter slides and Scratch animation include concrete executable workflows; paper fallbacks explicitly shift objectives. LittleBits needs its own matching approved modules, not guessed Snap wiring. Home activities and donations remain optional.

    Optional preparation aid: Grades 1-6 reference routines. The complete lesson-specific supplies, individual checks and 40-minute sequence still govern. Dash retains its pair/trio budget; Light & Circuits retains the eight reported Snap kits and its actual station/wave plan. Waiting work is reasoning/design evidence, not a physical turn; groups never increase to four.

    Session 1: Engineering Design¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Grades 3-4; Bi-Weekly A; Foundations; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: define a display need, build/test a standing tower and retest a base change with measured evidence. Why: engineering is solving a problem, not winning tallest. Catholic/CST-C2 fair access/user need; CST-E1 criterion/ limits; CST-E2 retest; CST-M1 cm measurement. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; novice. Prep 10; cleanup 5 included.

    Before class and exact supplies¶

    Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9). Each: four build paper sheets, ruler, 40 cm tape. Each pupil: evidence paper/pencil. Teacher board/timer; demo from issued sheet. Mark 20 cm square bases. Brief: visitor needs a visible desk marker >=15 cm, standing ten seconds, 40 cm height cap. Tools reusable, paper/tape consumable.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Rulers (1/team) 4 5 7 9
    Build sheets (4/team) 16 20 28 36
    Tape (40 cm/team, cm total) 160 200 280 360
    Evidence paper; pencils (1/pupil each) 10 15 20 25

    Vocabulary/background/SAFETY¶

    Criterion = performance; constraint = limit; prototype = trial; redesign = evidence-based change. ASK/IMAGINE/PLAN/CREATE/TEST/IMPROVE may repeat. Misconception: tallest is the only success. If asked "What if it falls?" Record failed standing trial, change base, retest; no judgment of child. Desk paper only, no loads/climbing or snapping rulers. Stop/report damaged tools. Indoor primary, no unsourced saint analogy needed.

    Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: "Who needs to see the marker?" Optional original service prayer.
    2. 4-9: Model roll/fold, zero-based height and hands-off ten seconds.
    3. 9-21: Each sketches, team selects/builds, rotate builder/tester/recorder.
    4. 21-30: Measure/standing test; change base with same stock, retest.
    5. 30-35: Each records two heights/pass results, criterion/limit, kept-same condition and fair-turn action. "Which failure informed your change?"
    6. 35-40: Count rulers, flatten reusable paper, save dated evidence/clear.

    Success/access/troubleshooting¶

    Meets: user/criteria, two actual tests, justified change and individual fair turn. Grade 3/support: starter roll, scribing; same criterion. Grade 4/challenge: repeat standing trial and explain variation, no added weights. Collapse: widen/shorten, record result. No tape: folding-only limit for all, explicitly changed constraint. Early finish: new viewer, same height cap.

    Family: We tested and retested a display tower. Ask, "What did your first test teach you?" Optional: notice a structure in a picture, no home building.

    Session 2: Dash & Code¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit / title Grades 3-4 / Computing / Dash & Code
    Time One 40-minute meeting, including cleanup
    Domains Catholic inclusion, technology/computing, measurement
    Big idea Precise sequences need testing; real movement can differ from a paper model.
    Student objective "I can predict an L-shaped route, test it, and explain a correction."
    Why Programming is giving testable instructions, not remote-control play.
    Catholic connection St. Carlo Acutis inspires responsible use of skills in service; partners share meaningful turns. Canonization verified in the Vatican homily, September 7, 2025. No invented quotation.
    Local standards Local, not official: CST-C2 (inclusive roles); CST-T1 (input/output and troubleshooting); CST-T2 (sequence/debug); CST-M1 (distance comparison).
    Technology Required primary: 2 Dash robots and 2 compatible tablets with Blockly, not assumed Wonder/Blockly interchangeability. Robots enable executable movement testing. Paper fallback evidences CT only, not robot operation or sensors.
    Difficulty / prerequisites Moderate; arrows, left/right and whole-number centimeters. No previous Dash use assumed; Session 1 design practice helpful.
    Prep / cleanup 20 minutes with already charged/paired equipment; first installation/charging additional advance work. 5 minutes in class.

    Before class¶

    1. Check loan availability; do not assume CSCOE stock. Confirm tablet/model compatibility with Wonder Workshop Blockly. Exact installed block labels are VERIFICATION REQUIRED; test the sequence before pupils arrive.
    2. Charge in advance, label two pairs, connect Blockly to Dash. Test drive forward 20 cm; turn right 90 degrees; drive forward 20 cm, at the app's low-speed setting, then stop. This is an L, not a square. No sensor blocks required.
    3. Mark two 1 m square floor areas away from doors/stairs, each with start/direction and a soft cardboard boundary. Do not make pupils walk through a maze.
    4. Pair pupils, final trio if odd. Assign teams to seven one-minute testing rounds at most (two teams per round); all other work occurs at desks.
    5. Board: predicted path | actual endpoint | one correction. Draw a 4 by 4 grid for paper work. No printer required.

    Exact supplies¶

    Tables budget ceil(students / 2) kits. A final trio gives 5/7/10/12 active teams at 10/15/20/25 pupils; unused eighth/thirteenth paper kit is spare. Seven testing rounds cover up to thirteen teams, more than the twelve needed with a trio.

    • Per student: pencil and 1 evidence half-sheet.
    • Per team: 2 paper sheets (grid/record), ruler, paper token, 6 command cards hand-drawn on the sheets.
    • Class: 2 robots, 2 tablets, 2 chargers, 2 soft boundary sets, timer, 4 m floor-safe tape.
    • Teacher: kit instructions, stop control, charge access. No child plug handling.
    Students Teams / rulers / tokens Team paper Cards Evidence slips / pencils Robots / tablets / chargers
    10 5 each 10 sheets 30 10 each 2 each
    15 8 each 16 sheets 48 15 each 2 each
    20 10 each 20 sheets 60 20 each 2 each
    25 13 each 26 sheets 78 25 each 2 each

    Devices/rulers/cards/tokens reusable. Paper/tape consumable. One robot permits a teacher demo and limited operation checks; record missing pupil operation, not universal mastery.

    Vocabulary and background¶

    Algorithm: ordered instructions. Input: instruction/start action. Output: movement or light/sound. Debug: compare prediction to actual and correct. Relative turn: right/left from the robot's current facing direction.

    Dash does not read the floor tape in this route; tape marks our reference. Blockly programs are distinct from steering it by remote control. Two forward movements separated by one right turn form an L. A whole square needs four sides and turns.

    Misconception: "It knows where we want it to go." It follows the code using its hardware. If asked: "Why missed the target?" Answer: "Check the start/facing direction, units and turn. Change one setting, then run the same test."

    SAFETY¶

    Low-speed motion only, no races or intentional collisions. Teacher starts/stops demonstration; only scheduled teams enter a testing area. Hands off moving robots; retrieve after stop. Dry floor, no stairs/doorways; sound low. Teacher handles batteries/chargers. Stop if an area is no longer clear.

    Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Purpose. Original prayer: "God, help us use tools responsibly and include each classmate." Ask: "Is steering by hand the same as running saved instructions?"
    2. 4-9: Demonstration. Identify robot, Blockly blocks, start and stop. Run the pretested L. Ask: "Which instruction changed its direction?"
    3. 9-14: Paper rehearsal. On a grid, one forward command means one square. Trace forward; right turn; forward; swap executor/reader. Draw expected endpoint. Explain that the grid is a model, not a physical centimeter measurement.
    4. 14-27: Build/run slots. Teams plan code on paper, then use a one-minute robot slot. First child enters forward; second adds right turn/forward; run and measure endpoint difference from the taped target. A trio's third child starts/stops and explains output. Teacher logs observed operations. Waiting teams find a deliberately wrong left-turn card in a paper route.
    5. 27-32: One correction. Teacher chooses a route that missed, checks start and facing, then adjusts one distance/turn. Predict and retest. "What changed? Which part did we keep the same?"
    6. 32-35: Individual evidence. Every child draws the L and identifies the turn, a debug change and its reason. Actual operators additionally identify start/stop and one measured result. Mark paper only when appropriate.
    7. 35-40: Cleanup/exit. Stop programs, teacher powers off/stores robots/tablets, pupils gather cards/tokens/rulers and restore lanes. Collect slips. Ask: "What does our paper test fail to test?"

    Low-tech substitute path / indoor alternative¶

    Use the same time windows; replace steps 2/⅘ with teacher/partner token execution on grids. Give a wrong-turn route, identify the first mismatch, replace one instruction and retest. Record computational-thinking sequence/debug evidence. Do not claim CST-T1 Bluetooth/device operation, robotics or sensor mastery. All pathways are indoors; Minnesota winter has no effect.

    Success, troubleshooting, support and challenge¶

    Success: child traces a sequence, identifies the wrong turn and explains a testable correction. Device success is separately observed editing/running/stopping, not merely watching a partner. Score 1 guess; 2 trace with help; 3 independent trace/debug reason; 4 explains model-versus-device limitations using a measured result.

    • Pairing fails after 2 minutes: announce paper path and notify regular teacher of missing operation evidence.
    • Wrong turn: check relative left/right and robot starting direction; no floor-line sensing assumed.
    • Support / Grade 3: three cards, oral prompts, turn one's own paper token, ruler assistance; no angle calculations required.
    • Challenge / Grade 4: repeat test and compare whole-number endpoint errors, explaining why traction/units may matter.
    • 25 pupils: thirteen teams, two areas, seven one-minute rounds within the thirteen-minute window; no five-mission race.

    Family snippet¶

    We planned and debugged an L-shaped sequence. Paper tracing demonstrates computational thinking; robot use adds measured input/output evidence. Our Catholic connection was sharing skills and safe tools fairly. Ask: "Which command changed direction?" Optional at home: trace three arrow directions with a token; the original scratch.mit.edu resource is optional, not required. No devices or homework.

    Session 3: Bridge Engineering¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Grades 3-4; Bi-Weekly A; Structures; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: build an 8 cm span, compare two capped loads and justify an overlap change. Why: access structures need fair tests, not unlimited loading. Catholic/CST-C2 access/user; CST-E1 criteria/limits; CST-E2 actual retest; CST-M1 span/count comparison. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; developing. Prep 15 with stock, loans extra; cleanup 5.

    Before class and exact supplies¶

    Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9). Each kit: 20 inspected KEVA planks, two flat closed books, ten identical plastic counters, tray, ruler. Each pupil paper/pencil. Teacher board/timer/demo from kit; pretest stable low supports with 8 cm gap. Books don't move during tests; save record, dismantle. Rectangular blocks may replace KEVA for all; label substitution, do not mix material claims.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Trays; rulers (1/team each) 4 5 7 9
    Planks (20/team) 80 100 140 180
    Books (2/team) 8 10 14 18
    Counters (10/team) 40 50 70 90
    Paper; pencils (1/pupil each) 10 15 20 25

    Vocabulary/background/SAFETY¶

    Span = gap; deck = crossing surface; overlap = shared contact; load = objects. Loose unjoined planks aren't rigid triangular trusses; demonstrate stable overlap rather than promise all triangles strong. Misconception: ten held proves maximum ten. If asked "More weights?" No; record "at least ten." Bridge is a model, never for people/pets. Low trays only, no heavy loads/throwing/hands underneath. Stop/reset sliding books and report damaged planks. Indoor primary.

    Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: "Who benefits from safe access?" Optional service prayer; criteria.
    2. 4-9: Demo center loading, one counter/three-second hold; last successful count (fails at 7 -> record 6).
    3. 9-21: Each sketches; build version 1, check 8 cm gap, rotate roles.
    4. 21-30: Test/cap at ten, record; change overlap only, same gap/stock/counters, retest. All nine desks test simultaneously.
    5. 30-35: Each child records both counts, whole-number difference, one control/ change reason and access need.
    6. 35-40: Remove loads, count 20 planks/ten counters, return books/tools.

    Success/access/troubleshooting¶

    Meets: measured span, two actual counts, criterion/control and evidence-based revision. Grade 3/support: overlap starter/tally/dictation. Grade 4/challenge: repeat at cap, explain lower bound. Collapse: record zero, improve support contact. All hold ten: compare design limits, not unsupported strength ranking. Missing supports: neighboring shared tray, alternate within test block; record missing physical turns. Early finish: new equal test, no longer unsafe span.

    Family: We tested plank bridges fairly. Ask, "What does 'at least ten' mean?" Optional: discuss who a bridge serves.

    Session 4: Animal Habitats¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Grades 3-4; Bi-Weekly A; Life science; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: model food/water/shelter/space needs, support one organism-specific relationship and label unknown details honestly. Why: habitat care requires evidence, not pretending animals are perfectly suited to any environment. Catholic/CST-C3 responsible habitat-care choice; CST-S3 needs/model limit; CST-A1 explanatory labeled model. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology None; introductory. Prep 10; cleanup 5 included.

    Before class and exact supplies¶

    Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9): cardstock base, two markers, source card. Per pupil paper/pencil. Teacher board/timer; copy card from retrieved Monarch Joint Venture life cycle: monarch larvae eat milkweed; adults and larvae are different life stages. Card gives one food relationship, not all habitat facts. Water, shelter and space placements in model are proposed needs diagrams, not approved live-animal housing. Teacher demo from issued paper; no specimens/natural-material collecting.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Bases; source cards (1/team each) 4 5 7 9
    Markers (2/team) 8 10 14 18
    Paper; pencils (1/pupil each) 10 15 20 25

    Vocabulary/background/SAFETY¶

    Habitat = place providing conditions/resources; need = requirement; adaptation = inherited feature useful in conditions; model = representation. Misconception: every animal can live in any box with food. If asked "Can we put a caterpillar here?" No; this drawing is not a checked care plan. Species requirements need further evidence/adult ecological approval. No animals, unknown plants, mold, sun-focused lenses or classroom releases. Paper indoors, stop/report damaged materials. Winter fallback is the primary.

    Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: "What would responsible habitat care require?" Optional care prayer.
    2. 4-10: Read source card; model supported food claim versus proposed needs.
    3. 10-22: Each sketches; team builds folded-paper habitat explanation on base, labels four needs and larva/milkweed link.
    4. 22-30: Peer checks all needs/labels, questions unsupported claims; revise one misleading feature, mark unknown species detail as unknown.
    5. 30-35: Each child names four needs, explains sourced link and model limit, draws one labeled relationship and care choice.
    6. 35-40: Cap/count tools/cards, save dated models/evidence, clear.

    Success/access/troubleshooting¶

    Meets: four needs, supported relationship, readable model and honest limit. Grade 3/support: four pictured boxes/read-aloud/scribing. Grade 4/challenge: compare larval/adult questions needing further sources, no guessed diets. No cards: copy supplied facts/citation to board. Overclaim: replace "perfectly designed home" with proposed model and evidence needed. Early finish: identify safe future observation, not collect wild creatures.

    Family: We modeled habitat needs responsibly. Ask, "Which relationship had a source?" Optional: notice an animal picture, no collection.

    Session 5: Scratch Intro¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Grades 3-4; Bi-Weekly A; Computing; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: edit/run a finite loop, predict four movements and explain a correction. Why: execution makes repeated instructions observable. Catholic/CST-C2 accessible turns/respectful message; CST-T1 actual edit/run/stop; CST-T2 loop/debug; CST-M3 four repeats/whole-number turn total. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Required; novice. Prep 20 after Scratch 3 works, installation extra; cleanup 5.

    Before class and exact supplies¶

    Guest/offline Scratch; build starter, run twice, Stop, local .sb3 save/reopen. Leave sample/save location. Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9): computer/four counters. Per pupil paper/pencil; teacher board/timer, demo uses kit. No accounts/projector purchase. Failed preflight -> paper trace and missing operation report.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Computers (1/team) 4 5 7 9
    Counters (4/team) 16 20 28 36
    Paper; pencils (1/pupil each) 10 15 20 25

    Starter, vocabulary and background¶

    On one sprite:

    when green flag clicked
go to x: (0) y: (0)
point in direction (90)
repeat (4)
  move (20) steps
  turn clockwise (90) degrees
  wait (1) seconds
end
say [Welcome!] for (2) seconds

    Stage = display; sprite = character; loop = repeated enclosed blocks; event = trigger. Misconception: a block below the loop repeats. If asked "Why not forever?" Finite repeat permits an exact prediction and clear end. Scratch steps are screen coordinates, not physical centimeters.

    SAFETY/privacy¶

    Dry seated devices/counters; no public accounts/media, passwords or downloaded assets. Counters off bodies/away from mouthing pupils. Stop/report damaged gear. God-as-programmer is not a literal scientific model. Indoor primary.

    Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: "Which action happens four times?" Optional inclusive-work prayer.
    2. 4-10: Tour stage/sprite/Code; model starter and Stop.
    3. 10-21: Every child edits/runs in a three-minute turn; peers trace with four counters and record four moves/turns.
    4. 21-29: Change repeat to 3, predict/run, then restore 4 and retest; locate misplaced block or document correct operation.
    5. 29-35: Each explains inside/outside loop and actual result; roster logs individual edit/run/stop. Four 90-degree turns total 360, no ratios.
    6. 35-40: Stop/save/reopen, count counters, return devices, file dated trace.

    Success/access/troubleshooting¶

    Meets: four-repeat prediction, correction/retest and observed operation/ fair turn. Grade 3/support: copied stack/token trace/scribing. Grade 4/challenge: compare ¾ repeats and total turns. Sprite drifts: reset position/direction, check block enclosure, rerun. Half stations: two waves of three-minute turns within work blocks; fewer means reschedule operation. No device: same times token/block cards, CT/counting only, Scratch operation not observed. Early finish: new message, not unbounded program.

    Family: We executed and checked a finite dance loop. Ask, "What repeated?" Optional: trace four turns verbally; no home device.

    Session 6: Gratitude Tech¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Grades 3-4; Bi-Weekly A; Gratitude communication; one 40-minute meeting. Objective: create/run two digital slides naming a helpful action and revise their readability for a peer. Why: presentation software supports editable visual communication, not merely screen consumption. Catholic/CST-C2 respectful thanks; CST-T1 actual edit/present/save; CST-T3 private sharing decision; CST-A3 critique/revision. Official alignment VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Technology Required; novice. Prep 20 after approved presentation software works; installation extra; cleanup 5. No podcast/QR/photo workflow or compulsory personal disclosure.

    Before class and exact supplies¶

    Use approved offline LibreOffice Impress: blank presentation, Slide > New Slide, Insert > Text Box, Slide Show > Start from First Slide, Escape, File > Save As local .odp; test/reopen two-slide sample. Leave sample/save location. If this app unavailable, teacher pretests equivalent school software and leaves exact commands; otherwise paper pathway. Teams <=3 (⅘/7/9) computer/team; paper/pencil per child. Board/timer, demo on issued device. Software is access resource, not physical supply or price.

    Allocation 10 15 20 25
    Computers (1/team) 4 5 7 9
    Paper; pencils (1/pupil each) 10 15 20 25

    Vocabulary/background/SAFETY¶

    Slide = display page; audience = reader; contrast = visible difference; consent = permission. Slide 1 "Thank you, classroom helpers"; slide 2 "You prepare our shared tools." Original fictional/classroom message, no quoted biography. Misconception: digitally made means publicly shared. If asked "Can we send it?" Adult checks recipient consent/school approval first; this lesson assesses local display, not delivery. Dry devices, no names/photos/voices/passwords/cloud upload; stop/report damage. Indoor primary.

    Meeting 1: exactly 40 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: "What helpful action can thanks name?" Optional gratitude prayer.
    2. 4-10: Demo blank/two slides/text boxes/present/Escape and privacy rule.
    3. 10-21: Every pupil edits/presents for three minutes, peers plan/read; each records one actual command/action.
    4. 21-29: Reader states helpful action/message at normal viewing distance; record feedback, revise font/wording, present again.
    5. 29-35: Each child explains before/after choice and private delivery plan; roster marks actual edit/present/save separately.
    6. 35-40: Save/reopen locally, exit, return device, collect dated evidence.

    Success/access/troubleshooting¶

    Meets: specific respectful message, observed digital actions, reader-backed revision and safe sharing choice. Grade 3/support: copied sample/motor assistance/ dictation. Grade 4/challenge: contrast/space tradeoff. Wrong text box: select slide/box then edit; no audio workaround. No app/device: two paper slides and same reader test, communication/privacy only, digital operation not observed. Half devices allow two waves of turns within work windows; below that reschedule. Early finish: new reader, not more untested formats.

    Family: We made private thank-you slides and revised for a reader. Ask, "What made the message clearer?" Optional thanks, no home app.

    Session 7: Light & Circuits¶

    Lesson at a glance¶

    Field Teacher information
    Grade / unit Grades 3-4 / Circuits / Light & Circuits
    Time One 40-minute meeting, including 5-minute cleanup
    Domains Catholic audience care, science systems, technology tools, artistic communication
    Big idea / objective "I can trace and test an open/closed light circuit, then communicate what the light means."
    Why Safe testing helps us understand everyday tools.
    Catholic connection Advent light symbolizes hope in Christ (John 8:12); electricity does not prove Christ's divinity. Use the school's approved Scripture translation and design a respectful message without judging the reader's circumstances.
    Local standards Local, not official: CST-C2 (respectful message), CST-S3 (circuit model), CST-T1 (test/repair), CST-A3 (message feedback/revision).
    Technology None: no computing device or software. Approved electrical hardware is required for actual operation; paper is a model, not circuit mastery.
    Prerequisites No prior circuit lesson or Year B assumed
    Prep / cleanup First kit inspection 30 minutes; repeat prep 15 minutes; missing instructions/approval extra. Cleanup 5 minutes included.

    Before class¶

    Complete the OLP Snap Circuits guide preflight for the eight individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits (OHM-135). Use the actual model's documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project. Leave the approved diagram and counted station list ready for a substitute. Do not assume holder protection, a two-AA allocation or LED current limiting.

    Exact supplies¶

    • Per pupil: pencil, evidence half-sheet, art/message half-sheet.
    • Per team: diagram sheet, shared marker, dry work area.
    • Per hardware station: approved Snap kit with only project parts, grid and tray. Battery type/count and checked reserves follow the guide.
    • Teacher/class: approved instructions, setup card, board, timer, roster, dry storage and adult-controlled cells; demo uses a station kit.
    Pupils Teams / diagram sheets Kits / trays Waves Student half-sheets / pencils
    10 4 4 1 20 / 10
    15 5 5 1 30 / 15
    20 7 7 1 40 / 20
    25 9 5 2 50 / 25

    Reuse the same hardware for Year B Christmas Circuits; no second kit purchase.

    Vocabulary, background and safety¶

    Circuit: complete conducting path, including return. Open: interrupted. Closed: complete. Switch: opens/closes the path. Current: charge flow. The battery supplies energy; light symbolism is not an electrical explanation of faith or human dignity. A lamp project does not establish LED polarity mastery.

    Misconception: touching any two conductors makes a safe circuit. If asked: "Why is it off?" Trace the approved path while power is isolated; ask the adult to check contacts/cells. Never short the supply.

    SAFETY: follow the guide's manufacturer/school gate, adult source isolation before snap changes and adult inspection before power is restored. No pupil battery access, coin cells, mains/USB power, extra loads, fan blades, live shorts, bare LED substitutions or take-home circuits. Warm/smelly/leaking/damaged: stop/report, adult isolates and marks OUT OF SERVICE.

    Numbered sequence: exactly 40 minutes¶

    1. 0-4: Purpose/symbol. Prayer: "Jesus, help us share hope and care for one another." Explain symbol versus physical explanation and the real-turn rule.
    2. 4-8: Model safely. Teacher traces the approved full path, demonstrates OFF/ON and models source isolation/inspection.
    3. 8-10: Predict individually. Each child traces battery -> switch -> light -> return and predicts both states.
    4. 10-22: Wave A. Follow the guide's isolated team build, adult checks, each child's two OFF/ON cycles and one teacher-managed open-path repair/retest. Waiting teams draw diagrams and draft an Advent message with a named reader.
    5. 22-23: Reset. Adult isolates power and transfers/resets station kits.
    6. 23-35: Wave B / communicate. Remaining teams get the identical hardware routine; finished teams peer-check and revise one message detail, record repair evidence and answer individual path/state questions. At smaller enrollment all teams use this window for retests/feedback. Ask: "Where is the gap? What showed the repair worked? What does your message mean?"
    7. 35-40: Cleanup. Isolate/count/return parts and cells, store dry kits and collect sheets. Record any missing physical turns explicitly.

    Success, support, troubleshooting and indoor fallback¶

    Each child traces a full path, predicts and operates both states twice, explains a repair using observed evidence and revises a respectful message. Record physical contribution/test observed / prompted / not yet separately from reasoning/art. Score 1 decoration only; 2 prompted path; 3 independent path/state/repair and message evidence; 4 explains a model limitation or two possible open-path faults without unsafe live testing.

    • Grade 3/support: traced diagram, large words/symbols, oral responses, motor help for snaps; still collect each child's prediction and switch turn.
    • Grade 4/challenge: compare two drawn faults; no extra branches or loads.
    • 25 pupils: nine pairs/trios, five stations, two 12-minute waves. Each child must have an observed turn; defer unfinished evidence rather than rush inspection. No four-person hardware groups.
    • No working kit: isolate/report, use a checked reserve or the guide's verified protected-AA route. Never connect Snap parts to that supply.
    • Paper route: use identical times with drawn paths and an on/off token. Record circuit reasoning/art only; electrical operation not observed. A demonstration alone does not prove each child's assembly/testing.

    Family snippet¶

    We traced, predicted and tested a switched light, then revised a hopeful Advent message. Physical light is a symbol of Christ, not a theological experiment. Describe the actual hardware or paper route. Ask: "Where is the gap when the light is off?" Only paper goes home; no electrical homework or purchases.
