    Teacher Resources

    C-STREAM quick start guide¶

    October 2026. C = Catholic identity; S = science; T = technology; R = religion/faith integration; E = engineering; A = arts including music; M = mathematics. Catholic purpose shapes choices, not only opening prayer. Art involves observation, composition, form, pattern or communication, not just decoration/digital tools.

    Before the first meeting¶

    1. Confirm weekly/bi-weekly schedule and A/B rotation with the school. Use the lesson index; do not assume the same Week 1 filename or commercial-kit schedule for every band.
    2. Read the actual lesson objective, background, vocabulary, safety, individual check and timed sequence. Use the common lesson format.
    3. Confirm supplies and location with inventory checklist. Default 10/15/20/25 pupils = ⅘/7/9 teams <=3. School provides required supplies.
    4. Perform the teacher pretest and count trays. Have the substitute fallback ready.
    5. Prepare family copy. No routine homework.
    Grade Native period Protect inside this time
    K 25 minutes Oral modeling, each child's action/evidence, 3-minute cleanup
    1-2 30 minutes Hands-on turns/test/redesign, individual check, 3-minute cleanup
    3-4 40 minutes Evidence-based testing/redesign, individual check, 3-minute cleanup
    5-6 45 minutes Reasoning/tradeoffs, individual check, 4-minute cleanup

    Your first two weeks¶

    Start with a completed band lesson, not a generic untimed welcome sequence. Model "notice -> try -> tell"; nonreader card. State "Today I can..." and give every child a turn to show the objective. Next meeting, use observation/design/measurement appropriate to prerequisites. Failure in engineering is information, not failure of a student.

    If a source question arises, say "We need to check that" and record VERIFICATION REQUIRED. The Catholic heritage guide is background for source checking, not a mandatory biography every lesson. No internet image search, unlicensed image or unverified quotation is needed.

    If conditions change¶

    • Time short: stop new construction; keep individual evidence and cleanup.
    • Kit absent: use the named safe fallback, recording any objective change.
    • Devices absent: unplugged concepts still work; real programming/robot execution evidence must be deferred, not claimed from drawings.
    • Unsafe materials/weather: stop and use a seated indoor task; notify the responsible school adult if safety needs escalation.

    Next links: materials plan, technology plan, assessment, FAQ, differentiation, templates.

    Materials inventory checklist¶

    The authoritative October 2026 planning records are Materials Plan and Materials Inventory CSV. They include normalized names/aliases, unit estimates, 10/15/20/25 stock, annual replacement, storage/safety/batteries, exact kits and \(250/\)500/\(1,000/\)2,500 bills of materials. This checklist does not maintain a contradictory price or loan-stock table.

    Reported school holdings¶

    Reported OLP holdings records 8 individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits, item OHM-135, reported on 2026-10-04. This is a school-reported total, not a completed physical inspection. Keep actual holdings separate from the CSV's 10/15/20/25-pupil planning quantities; check contents, condition, location, manufacturer age guidance and battery/power safety before classroom use. For the four selected Grades 3-6 lessons, use the Snap Circuits classroom guide: label SC01-SC08, record the matching manual/project and fitted cell count, and release only checked kits. At 25 pupils use nine teams at five stations in two waves, not nine simultaneous kits or groups larger than three.

    Beginning-of-year stock check¶

    • Confirm planned schedule/rotation and actual cohorts/enrollment.
    • Count physical stock by normalized ID; record condition/location/date/checker. NOT VERIFIED in the CSV is not zero and is not confirmed ownership.
    • Check school basics assumed by budgets: 25 pencils, 25 blunt scissors, crayons/markers, board, 18 stable supports, teacher timer, cleaning/handwashing.
    • Inspect every reusable kit; complete counted labels and an actual shelf map.
    • Verify supplier packs, current prices, shipping/tax assumptions and yearly consumables. Estimates dated October 2026 are NOT vendor quotations.
    • Verify electrical current protection/ratings, secure battery covers, ingredients, age suitability and accessible response tools before purchasing.
    • Choose only confirmed optional devices/loans. No app license or school account is assumed. Technology Plan.
    • Schedule one-time kit/card preparation and teacher prep tests before substitutes arrive; note shortages explicitly.

    Before each unit / after each lesson¶

    Use Materials List Template. Separate per-student, team, class, teacher-only and optional materials. Nine complete kits accommodate 25 at teams <=3; if switching to pairs, recalculate for 13 pairs. The selected Snap lessons instead use their explicit two-wave allocation. Count fitted/spare batteries separately. Issue exact amounts, record actual use, count returns, dry wet supplies, disconnect/off electrical parts and remove cells for long storage. Mark damaged kits OUT OF SERVICE and notify the responsible adult.

    Safety and optional donations¶

    No button cells, latex balloons or projectile activities in the core; no neodymium magnets in K. Do not use unverified electrical parts, loose high-strength magnets, unknown chemicals, sharp metal/glass or food-soiled recyclables. Donations of screened clean dry cardboard are welcome but the school provides paper/cardstock alternatives. Never require families to bring materials or buy equipment.

    Optional request copy: "If convenient, you may donate clean, dry flat cardboard after checking with the teacher. Please send no glass, metal, batteries, magnets, chemical containers or food-soiled items. Donations are optional: every child will have school-provided materials."

    Loan and audit evidence limits¶

    CSCOE planning requires confirmation; there is no guaranteed free loan, fixed stock count or two-week entitlement. Four band audits are available; their as-read counts and specific stock questions are summarized in Materials Plan. Current inventory use counts are explicitly estimated core uses; coverage of all 251 legacy lesson documents has not been established.

    OLP Snap Circuits classroom guide¶

    Reported stock: 8 individual Snap Circuits STEM Classroom Activity Kits, item OHM-135, reported 2026-10-04. This means eight student activity kits, not eight six-kit classroom packs. See the holdings record. Physical inspection and classroom approval are still required.

    Before teaching: release the hardware pathway¶

    Allow 30 minutes for first inspection/pretesting, plus time to obtain any missing instructions or parts; allow 15 minutes for repeat preparation. Leave a prepared kit, approved diagram, component list and this guide for a substitute. A substitute must not invent a circuit or approve unfamiliar parts.

    1. Label the individual kits SC01-SC08. Record the actual manufacturer model, instruction/workbook edition, contents, condition, location and checker. OHM-135 is the supplier item number, not a verified manufacturer model.
    2. Read the matching in-box manufacturer instructions. Select one documented battery/slide-switch/lamp project with a complete return path. Record its project/page number and component IDs on the teacher's setup card. Use the same project in every station; do not mix modules from different systems.
    3. Verify manufacturer age guidance for the actual pupils, battery access, holder protection and the school's electrical-safety requirements. The supplied holder is not assumed equivalent to a screw-secured, current-protected AA holder. If it does not meet school requirements, use the protected-AA alternative or paper route, not improvised covers or protection.
    4. Adult installs only the battery type/count specified for that project. Record b = fitted cells per station and the chemistry/voltage. Count fitted cells as stations * b; reserve complete kits need their own checked cells. Keep replacement cells separately in adult-controlled storage. Do not assume the kit uses the earlier lessons' two-AA allocation.
    5. Pretest the documented switch-OFF/light-off and switch-ON/light-on states twice. An LED project is allowed only if the matching instructions document polarity and required current limiting; never substitute a bare LED for a lamp.
    6. Teach power isolation, not just switch OFF: before changing snap connections, the adult disconnects the battery holder from the build as directed by the manufacturer. Pupils do not handle cells or holder contacts. Adult checks the complete approved layout before reconnecting power.
    7. Issue only the approved project's parts, grid, component list and diagram. Leave motors/fan blades, sound modules, extra loads and unused holders stored. No free wiring, shorts, series/parallel extensions or assumed sensors.

    Stop conditions: missing matching instructions, unsuitable age rating, unapproved holder/protection, missing parts, failed pretest, warmth, smell, damage or leakage. Mark the kit OUT OF SERVICE, tell the responsible adult and use a named alternative. A lit lamp alone does not certify safe wiring.

    The supplier description lists switches, lamps, LEDs and battery holders and recommends upper elementary. It describes a six-kit classroom pack, not OLP's eight individual kits. It does not verify OLP's exact model, battery allocation or school approval. This guide provides original teaching routines, not a replacement for that model's manufacturer instructions or a claim of official standards alignment.

    Station capacity: no group larger than three¶

    Use balanced pairs/trios, not a singleton. Each kit is one hardware station. The teacher demonstration uses a station kit before pupil work, not a ninth kit.

    Pupils Teams (size distribution) Hardware stations Hardware waves Unissued kits available as reserves
    10 4 (two trios, two pairs) 4 1 4
    15 5 (five trios) 5 1 3
    20 7 (six trios, one pair) 7 1 1
    25 9 (seven trios, two pairs) 5 2 3

    These numbers assume all eight kits pass preflight. Reserves are not automatically complete or powered. Recalculate when a kit is out of service; do not increase team size or mark a paper turn as electrical operation. One wave cannot serve more than 24 pupils with eight kits.

    The 25-pupil rotation¶

    Assign teams 1-5 to wave A (15 pupils) and teams 6-9 to wave B (10 pupils). Provide nine team work areas but only five dry hardware stations. Waiting teams work on their own prediction, diagram and audience/design task. The timed lessons include one minute for transfer/reset; supplies move, not live circuits. Adult isolates power and checks stations before the second wave.

    Each hardware wave gives a team 12 minutes in Grades 3-4 or 14 minutes in Grades 5-6: follow the approved build, adult inspection, individual switch tests, and one teacher-managed open-path repair/retest. Every child contributes a designated snap connection to the isolated team build and then operates the switch for two OFF/ON cycles. Rotate connector/tester/recorder; a role label alone is not evidence. The teacher checks each team before energizing and again after a repair. Never create a live short as the fault.

    At smaller enrollments, all teams use wave A; wave B is extra retesting, feedback and individual checking time, not an additional meeting. If inspections or motor/access needs take longer, record unfinished physical evidence and schedule a supervised completion turn. Do not rush a safety check or report that every child operated a kit unless observed.

    Individual evidence sheet: draw or copy onto paper¶

    No printer, account, app or additional workbook purchase is required. Each pupil records:

    Check Pupil response / teacher observation
    Full path Label battery, switch, light and conducting return path
    Prediction OFF -> expected output; ON -> expected output
    Test OFF/ON observations for cycle 1 and cycle 2
    Open-path repair Gap, one approved correction and observed retest result
    Design/message Intended user/reader; one choice and specific feedback
    Evidence level Physical contribution and switch test observed / prompted / not yet; paper reasoning recorded separately

    Teacher key for the approved simple switched light: OFF opens the path and the light is off; ON closes the path and the light is on. If observation differs, report the actual result. Disconnect power; adult checks the diagram, contacts and cells. Do not substitute parts or bypass protection.

    Protected-AA alternative: separate equipment, not a Snap conversion¶

    Keep the original protected circuit option if already verified and available. Do not attach Snap parts to its supply or LittleBits modules.

    • Grades 3-4: screw-secured covered 2-AA holder with documented protection, matching cells, switch, enclosed current-limited 3 V LED module and three insulated leads. Pretest holder + -> switch -> module +; module - -> holder -.
    • Grades 5-6: enclosed, current/short-circuit-protected switched 2-AA holder, push switch, adult-prepared sleeved red LED/220-ohm ¼-watt series-resistor assembly and three insulated leads. Pretest the complete series return path. Supply OFF before reconnection; adult checks before ON.

    Use the same station/wave counts above. Add one complete spare: ⅚/8/6 kits at 10/15/20/25 pupils, 10/12/16/12 fitted AA cells, and 15/18/24/18 leads. This is a selected-path allocation, not a change to the shared purchasing BOM. For Grades 5-6 retain the original four-state evidence: supply OFF with button released/pressed -> off/off; supply ON with button released/pressed -> off/on. Snap's slide switch instead uses two OFF/ON states repeated twice; do not claim push/release behavior or four independently controlled states from that route.

    Safety and return¶

    Adult supervision, dry seated stations, counted small parts and teacher-managed power throughout. No button/coin cells, household/mains/USB power, soldering, cutting wires, exposed fan blades, battery-terminal shorts or take-home circuits. Never mix cell types/old and new cells or recharge disposable cells. Use manufacturer-directed isolation and adult handling of damaged/hot cells.

    Reserve the lesson's final cleanup block: isolate power, count issued parts and cells against each station list, return parts to SC01-SC08, flag discrepancies, and store in a dry adult-controlled location away from water. Adult removes cells for long storage as directed. Only diagrams and paper art go home. Kindergarten remains adult-demonstration only after preflight; no new student circuit-building objective is introduced.

    CSCOE library planning guide¶

    Preserve the useful browse/reserve/check/return workflow. Library entry point. VERIFICATION REQUIRED for current availability, eligibility, fees, loan periods, transport, account process, kit contents and support. Earlier counts such as "98 items," "53 EiE kits" or two seven-robot sets are not verified October 2026 holdings and must not be used as procurement guarantees. This resource is not an official inventory or Archdiocesan policy.

    Before selecting a loan-dependent unit¶

    1. Define the objective and select the technology label.
    2. Check current listings and contact the lender; record confirmed dates and complete usable quantities. Check early, but no universal two-week lead time or free entitlement is promised.
    3. Confirm all included guides, power supplies, chargers, hosts, consumables, software, licenses and age ratings. A commercial kit is not automatically complete for this class or a 25-minute period.
    4. Plan native meetings: K 25, 1-2 30, 3-4 40, 5-6 45 minutes, including hands-on turns, individual evidence and cleanup.
    5. Have a named school-funded low-tech alternative. If the objective requires program/robot execution, explicitly defer that evidence if the loan fails.

    Loan planning record¶

    Lesson/unit Objective Item and confirmed usable count Dates/fees/transport Host/app/power/age checks Tested by/date Fallback/objective change
    [ ] [ ] [VERIFICATION REQUIRED until lender confirms] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]

    At 25, nine teams <=3 need nine complete team kits, or documented rotations with individual turns and enough meetings. Watching one borrowed robot is not equivalent to each child's programming evidence.

    When items arrive / return¶

    • Count parts against the lender's actual packing list; report shortages/damage.
    • Read the supplied instructions and test the complete activity before class.
    • Verify electrical protection and battery restrictions; no button cells, latex balloons or projectile accessories in the core; no neodymium magnets in K.
    • Store in labeled counted containers; teacher manages batteries/charging.
    • On return, count/dry/clean according to confirmed lender directions, note damage/missing parts and meet the agreed return date. Do not invent sanitation chemicals or attempt unsupported repairs.

    Optional legacy candidates, not a required shopping list¶

    Dash, Sphero, Bee-Bot/Ozobot/EV3-type robotics, Engineering is Elementary, modular electronics and USB input kits appear in legacy planning. Availability, product support, proprietary power/hosts, apps and licenses need verification. Do not assume every EiE unit contains nine 45-minute lessons; inspect the actual guide and split learning appropriately. VR is not a core need and requires additional school/manufacturer age/accessibility review.

    Seasonal themes remain useful: fall structures, winter indoor light/systems, spring environmental observations. Confirm schedule/rotation against actual lessons rather than booking by old week numbers. The materials core operates without these loans.

    Catholic scientific heritage¶

    Use these original, short source cards where they deepen a lesson. Catholic identity also appears in truthful evidence, dignity, stewardship and service; a biography or prayer is not compulsory in every investigation.

    The sources below were directly inspected on October 4, 2026. They verify the stated facts, not an invented quotation, personal motivation or sole-discovery claim. The cards are paraphrases, not reproductions of biography text.

    Four usable source cards¶

    Gregor Johann Mendel: observation and inquiry¶

    Verified facts: Masaryk University's Mendel Museum describes Mendel as a member and abbot of the Augustinian order, identifies his pea experiments and displays original objects and his work on plant hybrids.

    Read aloud: "Mendel belonged to a Catholic religious community. He also studied pea plants. His museum preserves evidence of that scientific work. A person can have a religious vocation and also investigate nature."

    Student action: compare two clearly labeled plant observations or a teacher-provided model dataset. Explain which detail is observed and which is a question or prediction. Do not run a one-period inheritance claim from two seedlings or infer a person's genes from classroom traits.

    Question: "What records would help someone compare plants honestly?"

    Source: Masaryk University Mendel Museum. Institutional museum history grounded in the collection; not a medical or complete genetics standard. Source facts do not prove every historical experiment used the classroom's method.

    Georges Lemaitre: religious and scientific roles¶

    Verified facts: The Pontifical Academy of Sciences identifies Lemaitre as a monsignor, lists cosmology as his field, records a university professorship in mechanics/mathematical methodology and gives his life dates as 1894-1966.

    Read aloud: "Lemaitre was a Catholic priest and a university scholar whose field included studying the universe. We can learn about a person's scientific and religious roles without pretending that a classroom model proves a belief."

    Student action: distinguish a sky/model observation, a scientific explanation and a taught faith reflection. Label what a model can and cannot show. Do not claim that a drawing or an expansion demonstration proves creation.

    Question: "What kind of evidence would a scientific explanation need?"

    Source: Pontifical Academy of Sciences record. Primary institutional membership record. Its directly inspected fields are the basis for this card; no unsupported priority dispute, personal quotation or account of a papal conversation is asserted.

    Saint Albert the Great: noticing and classifying¶

    Verified facts: Benedict XVI's 2010 audience describes Albert as a Dominican, teacher of Thomas Aquinas and scholar of natural disciplines. It explicitly distinguishes his observation/description/classification methods from scientific methods developed in later centuries.

    Read aloud: "Albert was a Dominican who studied many subjects, including living things and the natural world. He described and grouped what he studied. Science methods have developed since his time; we should not call a medieval practice the same as every modern experiment."

    Student action: group safe objects/pictures by a visible rule, explain the rule and correct an item that does not fit. Older pupils distinguish that classification from a controlled causal investigation.

    Question: "What did you observe that supports your grouping?"

    Source: Benedict XVI, March 24, 2010. Official Church teaching/historical presentation, not a numbered science benchmark. No unattributed Albert quotation is supplied.

    Maria Gaetana Agnesi: mathematics, clarity and service¶

    Verified facts: The University of St Andrews' MacTutor biography describes Agnesi's mathematical teaching text and later charitable work, including care for infirm women. It discusses Catholic doctrine and corrects simplistic claims about whether she actually taught at Bologna.

    Read aloud: "Agnesi wrote a mathematics book intended to make ideas easier to learn. Later she devoted herself to caring for people in need. Clear explanations and service are valuable uses of knowledge."

    Student action: explain an already-taught mathematical idea using a diagram, objects or a worked example; ask a partner what is unclear and revise the explanation. Assess correctness and clarity, not beautiful handwriting.

    Question: "What change made your explanation easier for someone to use?"

    Source: University of St Andrews MacTutor biography. Scholarly institutional secondary history, with identified references. It is not presented as a primary personal testimony or an official Church standard. No "first woman professor" claim or fabricated faith quotation is used.

    Grade-appropriate use¶

    Grade Teacher approach Individual evidence
    K-1 Read one short card; model one observation/group/explanation action. Point, draw, sort or tell one source fact and distinguish it from the classroom action.
    2-3 Compare a source fact with the investigation's own evidence. Give a reason supported by the card/record; identify a question still unanswered.
    4-6 Identify institution, source type and scope; separate historical claims from scientific explanation. Explain one verified fact, source limitation and evidence-supported scientific/mathematical decision.

    One or two minutes of heritage may replace part of a hook, not add a second unclocked lesson. Biography recall alone does not evidence a science/math/ computing competency. No independent web account, routine homework or home research is required.

    Source-check questions¶

    1. Who published the source, and what specific fact does it establish?
    2. Is the claim history, Church teaching, scientific evidence or our own classroom interpretation?
    3. Does it report a contribution, or are we wrongly claiming sole invention?
    4. Is a quotation actually documented? If not, omit it rather than changing it into an attributed paraphrase.
    5. What does the source not establish?

    The earlier unsourced Pasteur/Copernicus/Pascal quotations, Jesuit instrument/ crater totals, first/sole-discovery claims and date-sensitive sainthood titles are not retained as classroom facts. They may be researched later with exact sources; no compulsory research task depends on them.

    Copy-ready family statement¶

    We used a documented historical example to connect faith, inquiry and service, then practiced an actual observation or explanation. Ask your child, "Which fact came from the source, and what did you find out yourself?" Optional conversation only; historical biography is not a substitute for the child's own learning evidence.

    See verified Church teaching and local standards. These cards make no NCEA, state, diocesan or accreditation approval claim.

    ✨ Wonder and Curiosity Guide¶

    This resource provides strategies for cultivating the sense of wonder that is foundational to Catholic STEM education.

    October 2026 teaching/source note: Preserve the observation/questioning practices; numerical claims, quotations and historical/theological attributions below are VERIFICATION REQUIRED before classroom copying. An observation does not experimentally prove a theological conclusion. Invite gratitude without grading spontaneous awe or interior belief. Use concrete stewardship/dignity decisions, not a literal comparison of God to an engineer/scientist/artist. Magnet demonstrations require age-appropriate large encapsulated ferrite equipment; no neodymium magnets in K. See safety and kits.

    "Approaching education from the perspective of wonder, exploration, and faith will ignite the love of learning."

    📋 Overview¶

    Wonder is the starting point of both scientific inquiry and faith. When we marvel at God's creation, we are drawn to understand it more deeply through science and to worship the Creator who made it.

    The Wonder Cycle: 

         +----------------------+
     |                      |
     v                      |
  WONDER          GRATITUDE/WORSHIP
     |                      ^
     v                      |
 CURIOSITY         UNDERSTANDING
     |                      ^
     v                      |
  INQUIRY ---------------►-+

    🌟 What is Wonder in Catholic Education?¶

    Wonder vs. Simple Curiosity¶

    Simple Curiosity Catholic Wonder
    "How does that work?" "How amazing that God designed this!"
    Satisfied by an answer Deepened by understanding
    Leads to knowledge Leads to knowledge AND worship
    Self-focused learning Learning as response to God

    Wonder as Gateway to Faith and Science¶

    Wonder serves as a "privileged gateway into the divine order of things." When students wonder at creation:

    • They are drawn to study it (science)

    • They are drawn to praise the Creator (faith)

    • They see that faith and science lead to the same truth

    🎯 Strategies for Cultivating Wonder¶

    1. Wonder Questions¶

    Start lessons with questions that evoke awe:

    For Young Children (K-2)¶

    • "Have you ever watched a butterfly and wondered how it knows how to fly?"

    • "Isn't it amazing that tiny seeds grow into huge trees?"

    • "Why do you think God made so many different kinds of animals?"

    • "Have you ever wondered why the sky changes colors?"

    For Grades 3-5¶

    • "How is it possible that your heart beats 100,000 times every day without you thinking about it?"

    • "What do you wonder about when you look at the stars?"

    • "Did you know there are more stars in the universe than grains of sand on Earth?"

    • "How do birds know where to fly when they migrate thousands of miles?"

    For Grades 6-8¶

    • "Scientists estimate there are 37 trillion cells in your body, all working together. How is that possible?"

    • "The same mathematical patterns appear in shells, flowers, and galaxies. Why do you think that is?"

    • "What would it be like to be the first person to discover something no one knew before?"

    • "How can studying atoms help us understand the universe?"

    2. Wonder Moments¶

    Build "wonder pauses" into your lessons:

    Before Instruction: "Before I tell you how this works, take a moment to wonder about it. What do you notice? What surprises you?"

    During Activities: "Stop and look at what you created. Isn't it amazing that you figured that out?"

    After Learning: "Now that you understand this better, does it make you wonder about anything else?"

    Connecting to Faith: "When I learned this, I was amazed at how God designed creation. What amazes you?"

    3. The "Wow" Collection¶

    Create a classroom practice of collecting "wows":

    Daily Wow Board: Students can add observations that made them say "wow" throughout the week.

    Wonder Journal: Students keep a journal where they record things that amaze them about creation.

    Wow Sharing: Begin or end class with students sharing something that made them wonder.

    4. Mystery Before Explanation¶

    Present phenomena before explaining them:

    Traditional Approach: "Today we're going to learn about magnets. Magnets have two poles..."

    Wonder Approach: Show two magnets attracting and repelling "Watch this... Why do you think that happens? What do you wonder about this?" Let students observe and question before explaining

    5. Connecting Wonder to the Creator¶

    Explicitly connect wonder to faith:

    Example Script: "Scientists have discovered that butterfly wings have tiny scales that create their beautiful colors. When I learned this, I was amazed at how detailed God's creation is—even in things we can barely see! What does this tell us about God?"

    Reflection Questions:

    • "What does this tell us about the Creator?"

    • "Why do you think God made the world with so much detail and beauty?"

    • "How does understanding this make you feel about God?"

    • "What might you say to God about what you learned today?"

    📚 Wonder Practices by Lesson Phase¶

    Opening Wonder (5 minutes)¶

    Purpose: Spark curiosity and connect to faith

    Activities:

    • Wonder question

    • Mystery object/phenomenon

    • "What do you notice? What do you wonder?"

    • Brief moment of awe at creation

    Prayer Connection: "Lord, open our eyes to the wonders of Your creation today."

    Sustained Wonder (During Instruction)¶

    Purpose: Maintain engagement and curiosity

    Techniques:

    • Pause for "wow moments" when content is particularly amazing

    • Ask "Isn't that amazing?" and mean it

    • Share your own wonder: "When I first learned this, I couldn't believe..."

    • Point out complexity and beauty: "Think about how intricate this is..."

    Reflective Wonder (Closing)¶

    Purpose: Deepen learning and connect to faith

    Activities:

    • "What was the most amazing thing you learned today?"

    • "What new questions do you have now?"

    • "How does what you learned today make you think about God?"

    • "What do you want to explore more?"

    Prayer Connection: "Thank You, Lord, for the wonder of [specific content]. Help us to keep wondering and learning about Your creation."

    🎨 Creating a "Place of Wonder and Awe"¶

    Transform your STEM space into a wonder-inducing environment:

    Physical Environment¶

    • Display "wonder questions" on walls

    • Include images of amazing natural phenomena

    • Create a "wonder corner" with intriguing objects

    • Use natural light when possible

    • Include plants or natural elements

    • Display student "wow" discoveries

    Learning Environment¶

    • Welcome questions without judgment

    • Model curiosity yourself

    • Celebrate "I wonder..." statements

    • Allow time for observation

    • Connect discoveries to the Creator

    • Create space for quiet wonder

    Spiritual Environment¶

    • Include religious imagery connecting faith and creation

    • Display quotes from Catholic scientists

    • Post relevant Scripture verses

    • Pray with wonder and gratitude

    • Reference patron saints of science

    📋 Wonder Question Bank¶

    Life Sciences¶

    • "Did you know that you started as a single cell smaller than a dot?"

    • "How do plants 'know' to grow toward light?"

    • "Why do you think there are so many different species of beetles?"

    • "How does your body know how to heal a cut?"

    Earth Sciences¶

    • "What do you think the Earth looked like a million years ago?"

    • "How did mountains form?"

    • "Why does the moon change shape?"

    • "What's at the center of the Earth?"

    Physical Sciences¶

    • "Why does ice float when most things sink?"

    • "How can sound travel through walls?"

    • "What makes fire?"

    • "Why is the sky blue?"

    Technology/Engineering¶

    • "How did people solve this problem before technology?"

    • "What if you could invent anything—what would help people most?"

    • "How do computers 'think'?"

    • "What makes a bridge strong?"

    Space¶

    • "How far away is the nearest star?"

    • "What do you think is beyond the edge of the universe?"

    • "How many galaxies do you think exist?"

    • "What would it be like to stand on Mars?"

    🙏 Wonder and Worship Connection¶

    From Wonder to Praise¶

    Help students see the natural connection between wonder and worship:

    Wonder Statement → Worship Response

    Wonder Worship
    "The human body is so complex!" "Thank You, God, for making us so wonderfully."
    "The universe is so vast!" "How great is our God who made all this!"
    "This pattern is so beautiful!" "Lord, You are an amazing artist."
    "How can this work so perfectly?" "Your wisdom, God, is beyond understanding."

    Scripture Connections for Wonder¶

    Psalm 19:1 - "The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of his hands."

    Psalm 139:14 - "I praise you because I am fearfully and wonderfully made; your works are wonderful, I know that full well."

    Job 12:7-10 - "But ask the animals, and they will teach you, or the birds in the sky, and they will tell you; or speak to the earth, and it will teach you, or let the fish in the sea inform you. Which of all these does not know that the hand of the Lord has done this?"

    Sirach 42:15-17 - "Now I will recall God's works; what I have seen, I will describe... The clear vault of the sky shines forth like heaven itself, a vision of glory."

    📝 Teacher Self-Evaluation for C-STEM Excellence¶

    This local self-evaluation tool helps teachers reflect on Catholic identity, hands-on learning, inclusion and instructional planning. It does not establish NCEA/Cognia certification, accreditation or compliance with official standards.

    October 2026 status: Treat the following as legacy/local reflection prompts, not a verified official NCEA, Minnesota or Archdiocesan instrument. Attribution, quoted wording and the numbered characteristics/factors are VERIFICATION REQUIRED against a primary source before claiming official alignment. Teacher reflection is separate from student achievement. Use objective-linked evidence and Local Standards, including authentic arts/music (A) and mathematics (M). Do not grade students for apparent joy, participation, interior faith or family practice.

    📋 Overview¶

    Purpose: Self-assessment tool for teachers to evaluate and improve their C-STEM instruction

    Frequency: Complete at the beginning and end of each semester, or after each unit

    Scoring: Honestly rate your current practice to identify areas for growth

    🎯 Part 1: Ten Local Reflection Themes¶

    Legacy attribution to NCEA and the italicized wording below: VERIFICATION REQUIRED. These prompts are not an official certification checklist.

    Rate your alignment with each characteristic:

    • 4 = Consistently exemplify this characteristic

    • 3 = Usually demonstrate this characteristic

    • 2 = Sometimes demonstrate this characteristic

    • 1 = Rarely or never demonstrate this characteristic

    Characteristic 1: Catholic Identity Integration¶

    "Integrate Catholic identity into every aspect of the curriculum"

    Indicator Self-Rating (1-4)
    Faith is woven throughout lessons, not just in opening/closing prayer
    Students see faith and science as complementary
    Catholic teaching is meaningfully connected to STEM content
    Scripture is used appropriately in STEM lessons
    Catholic scientists/heritage are highlighted
    Average Score: /4

    Reflection: How well do I integrate Catholic identity into my STEM teaching?

    Action Step for Improvement:

    Characteristic 2: Culture of Innovation with Ethics¶

    "Promote a culture of innovation with commitment to ethical behavior"

    Indicator Self-Rating (1-4)
    Students are encouraged to innovate and create
    Ethical implications of technology are discussed
    Students consider impact of innovations on others
    Catholic Social Teaching informs technology discussions
    Responsible technology use is modeled and taught
    Average Score: /4

    🌈 C-STREAM Differentiation Guide¶

    Location: Our Lady of the Prairie Catholic School · Belle Plaine, MN · Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis

    Practical strategies for meeting the needs of all learners in your C-STREAM classroom.

    October 2026 operating rule: Preserve the stated concept objective while changing access: read aloud, demonstrate one step, gesture, scribe, use larger tools, bilingual response, quiet/seated route or extra wait time. A digital design is not proof of physical testing/program execution. Use the nonreader card and objective-linked assessment. Access supports do not cap achievement; participation/handwriting are not mastery proxies. Use the actual school accommodation plan, not assumptions from a diagnostic label. A = arts including music; M = mathematics.

    🎯 Universal Design Principles¶

    Before modifying for individuals, build accessibility into every lesson:

    Principle How to Apply
    Multiple means of representation Show AND tell. Use visuals, verbal, hands-on
    Multiple means of expression Let students show learning in different ways
    Multiple means of engagement Offer choice when possible

    👤 Students with Learning Differences¶

    Attention Challenges (ADHD)¶

    Strategy Example
    Chunk activities Break 30-min lesson into 3 segments with movement
    Provide fidgets Offer something to hold during listening
    Use timers Visual countdown for transitions
    Movement breaks "Stand up and stretch" between activities
    Clear workspace Only current materials on desk
    Proximity Seat near you during instructions
    Written + verbal Post steps AND say them aloud

    What works especially well in C-STREAM:

    • Hands-on building naturally engages kinesthetic learners

    • Short segments (explore → build → test → share)

    • Movement built into engineering activities

    Reading/Writing Challenges (Dyslexia, Dysgraphia)¶

    Strategy Example
    Reduce writing load Use drawings, verbal responses, check boxes
    Provide templates Pre-printed worksheets with sentence starters
    Use visuals Picture instructions, not just text
    Allow dictation Student speaks, partner or teacher writes
    Larger print Enlarge worksheets to 125%
    Color coding Highlight key words or steps
    Audio options Read instructions aloud, use text-to-speech

    Worksheet Modifications:

    • Use Engineering Design Process worksheet with drawing boxes

    • Accept labeled diagrams instead of paragraphs

    • Offer verbal project reflections

    Processing Differences (Autism Spectrum)¶

    Strategy Example
    Consistent routine Same structure each C-STREAM session
    Visual schedule Post lesson flow on board
    Prepare for transitions "In 2 minutes we will clean up"
    Reduce sensory input Quiet corner option, headphones available
    Clear expectations Specific, concrete instructions
    Social stories "During C-STREAM, we share materials with friends"
    Warn about changes Preview if doing something different

    Sample Visual Schedule: 

    1. Prayer (2 min)
2. Wonder Question (3 min)
3. Learn Together (8 min)
4. Build/Create (12 min)
5. Share (3 min)
6. Closing Prayer (2 min)

    Motor Skill Challenges¶

    Strategy Example
    Larger materials Use bigger blocks, thicker markers
    Adaptive tools Scissors with spring return, pencil grips
    Partner assistance "You design, partner builds"
    Modified expectations Quality over quantity
    Alternative methods Stamp instead of write, voice instead of type
    Stable surfaces Tape paper down, use non-slip mats

    Building Modifications:

    • Pre-cut materials for students who struggle with scissors

    • Offer larger KEVA planks or DUPLO instead of small pieces

    • Allow digital design (drawing app) instead of physical building

    🚀 Advanced Learners¶

    Extension Strategies¶

    Strategy Example
    Deeper questions "What would happen if...?"
    Additional constraints "Now build it using only 10 pieces"
    Leadership roles Materials manager, group facilitator
    Peer teaching Help struggling classmates
    Research extensions Investigate related Catholic scientist
    Complex challenges Add variables to engineering problem
    Documentation Create how-to guide for others

    Sample Extensions by Activity Type¶

    Activity Extension
    Bridge building Repeat a fair test or justify a constraint; use ratios only after prerequisites are taught
    Coding Add sound effects, create multi-level game
    Robotics Add sensors, create obstacle course
    Science investigation Design additional tests, graph data
    Engineering challenge Present to another class, create tutorial

    Enrichment Questions¶

    • "How could you make this help someone in our community?"

    • "What would a professional engineer do differently?"

    • "Can you teach this to a younger student?"

    • "What other problems could you solve with this method?"

    🌍 English Language Learners (ELL)¶

    Visual Supports¶

    Strategy Example
    Picture vocabulary Show images alongside new words
    Labeled diagrams Parts of robot, design process steps
    Video demonstrations Model before expecting output
    Gestures Use consistent hand signals
    Real objects Hold up actual materials when naming

    Language Supports¶

    Strategy Example
    Sentence frames "I noticed _____" "My design _____"
    Key vocabulary preview 3-5 words before lesson
    Partner translation Pair with bilingual buddy
    Simplified instructions Shorter sentences, one step at a time
    Repeat and rephrase Say key ideas multiple ways
    Wait time Allow extra processing time

    For Engineering:

    For Faith Connection:

    • "We can help others by _____."

    Student progress tracker¶

    Retain the useful fall/winter/spring growth conversation, but track taught objectives rather than enthusiasm or generic participation. October 2026. Use assessment, rubrics and Local Standards.

    Lesson evidence roster¶

    Student Date/grade/unit/lesson Objective/local code Exact action/words or artifact Mode/access support ½/¾ or NE Feedback/next check
    [One row per child; extend to actual enrollment, including 25] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]

    Levels: 1 Beginning, 2 Developing, 3 Meets Expectation, 4 Extends Learning. Use the lesson's specific descriptors. NE means no adequate evidence yet (absence, unavailable equipment, missed check); it is not a zero. Ordinary read-aloud, gesture, bilingual response, scribe and motor assistance do not lower achievement. Record conceptual hints separately.

    Termly growth summary¶

    Student/objective/local code Fall evidence/date/level Winter evidence/date/level Spring evidence/date/level Next teaching
    [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ] [ ]

    Examples of appropriate evidence by grade, not new official benchmarks:

    Grade Possible individual evidence when corresponding objective taught
    K Points/sorts by an observed feature; shows a two-action sequence; tells one detail
    1 Names the problem/user; compares two results; explains one design choice
    2 Records an equal-condition comparison; explains a changed sequence
    3 Shows common test conditions and links one redesign to the result
    4 Measures in the specified unit and uses results to justify an improvement
    5 Compares two designs using taught criteria/constraints
    6 Defends a choice with evidence, cost/tradeoff and a taught ethical consideration

    This is not an independent progression specification: use the shared grade progression and local definitions for expected outcomes. Real program/robot execution is only recorded when actually demonstrated on a working device. Never fill those cells from an unplugged activity.

    Workload and privacy¶

    During hands-on time sweep the roster; pair a simultaneous point/show/draw exit response with short targeted conversations. At 25, record unobserved children NE and collect later rather than assuming all groups mastered the concept. Review at project completion and termly; do not require daily long checklists. At expected-mastery checkpoints, retain two dated observations on separate occasions as required by Local Standards, including an individual demonstration and changed context/follow-up explanation. Both must meet the target; one lesson rating is not end-of-grade mastery. Store named records under the school's actual privacy practice. Do not publish names, scores or photographs in newsletters without verified permission.

    Behavior/engagement notes may inform support but remain separate from subject mastery. Report "measured the span accurately; next compare repeated trials," not "participates well, therefore proficient."

    C-STREAM substitute teacher guide¶

    C = Catholic identity, R = religion/faith integration, A = arts including music, M = mathematics. Thank you for leading hands-on learning. October 2026. Use the actual scheduled lesson, not a generic assurance that every old lesson is ready. Readiness review.

    Twenty minutes before class¶

    Minutes Do this
    0-4 Read objective, background/vocabulary and native timed steps; identify each child's evidence prompt
    4-8 Find the kit at the location supplied by school; count student/team/class/teacher items for enrollment
    8-12 Read SAFETY; check accommodations, materials condition and actual school emergency/office contact
    12-16 Perform the exact lesson model/pretest, then place counted trays and assign roles
    16-20 Draw/read aloud short steps; rehearse individual check, cleanup and the named fallback

    School must fill lesson/date [ ], kit/actual location [ ], office/contact [ ], accommodations [ ], emergency instructions [ ] before handoff. Do not assume "STREAM closet," iPads, apps, loan kits or a quick-reference card exists.

    Grade 3 example: rebuilt Week 10 Bridge Engineering. Use its precise quantities/span/load/check and 40-minute period. If its kit or prep test fails, use the fallback below and record the changed objective. This guide does not certify all legacy lessons.

    SAFETY: stop rather than improvise¶

    No button cells, latex balloons, projectile activities or neodymium magnets in K. No unknown chemicals, food experiments, glass, hot surfaces, unsafe cold exposure or electrical repair. Teacher controls batteries/clip leads/small loads. Do not use unfamiliar electric/magnetic equipment without a verified pretest. Stop, isolate unsafe materials, move to a seated safe task and notify the responsible school adult. Injury, suspected ingestion of a battery/magnet or other urgent danger requires the school's emergency escalation immediately. Do not send pupils hunting for missing dangerous parts.

    Fallback A: paper structure comparison¶

    Objective: Compare flat and folded paper under the same span and load. Big idea: Shape can affect a structure; a fair comparison keeps test conditions the same. Catholic connection: Reliable design serves people; shared resources are used responsibly. No "God is an engineer" comparison. Technology Requirement: None. Difficulty: introductory comparison. Prep: 10 minutes if counted stock/supports exist; cleanup included below. Vocabulary: span = gap between supports; load = what a structure supports; compare = notice how results are alike/different.

    Background/misconception: Folded and flat paper may respond differently. The result can be the same under a small load; report that honestly. A collapse is information, not failure of the student. If asked why a fold matters, show the changed shape; do not promise that every fold always improves it.

    Scope/material Rate 10 pupils 15 20 25
    Student response paper (or oral response) 1/child 10 15 20 25
    Team paper 2/team 8 10 14 18
    Team index-card test loads 10/team 40 50 70 90
    Team ruler 1/team 4 5 7 9
    Stable support books/blocks 2/team 8 10 14 18
    Teacher 2 demonstration sheets, 10 cards, timer, evidence roster One class set in addition to team issue quantities

    Pencils/crayons are school basics. Total paper at 25 = 25 + 18 + 2 = 45 sheets; total cards = 90 + 10 = 100. No scissors, coins, tape, devices or donations. Books/supports must be confirmed; without them use fallback B, not an unsafe stack.

    Before class: Set stable supports 10 cm apart on each desk; lay one sheet flat across. Fold the second lengthwise into an accordion with adult modeling. Try adding cards one by one at the center in both tests; reset with the same gap and count. Test before class; reduce the gap if neither supports even one card and record that shared change. No escalating to heavy falling weights. K adult places loads; child still predicts/points/compares.

    Exact native timing (choose the grade column)¶

    Step K 25 1-2 30 3-4 40 5-6 45 What to do/say
    Hook/purpose 0-3 0-3 0-4 0-4 "What might a fold change?" Explain objective and stewardship
    Model/vocabulary/safety 3-7 3-8 4-10 4-11 Align supports, show flat/folded examples, demonstrate one load placement
    Build/test first comparison 7-14 8-18 10-24 11-27 Students take turns placing paper/cards; count or point to result
    Improve/retest 14-19 18-23 24-32 27-36 Change one paper shape; keep gap/load placement. "What stayed the same?"
    Individual check 19-22 23-27 32-37 36-41 "Show the result. What stayed the same in the test?"
    Cleanup/close 22-25 27-30 37-40 41-45 Count cards/rulers/supports, retain dry paper, clear desks, brief thanks

    Meets: Each child identifies the observed comparison (including equal results) and shows one common condition. For K, adult reads/models and accepts pointing/gesture. Use Show, Try, Tell. Support: Pre-fold paper, steady supports, scribe or allow a large gesture. Challenge: Repeat the comparison and explain whether it supports the first result; older pupils can compare equal-material versions without untaught ratios. At 25: Nine seated teams, rotating turns; check children during tests plus simultaneous show/draw exit. Mark unobserved evidence NE and leave a follow-up. Troubleshoot: Sliding supports -> stabilize or stop that test; equal results -> record them, not "wrong"; time short -> stop new construction, keep check/cleanup. Family copy: "We compared paper structures using the same gap and loads. Ask: 'What stayed the same, and what changed?' Optional: discuss a folded object already nearby. No home project needed."

    Fallback B: no devices, no consumable supplies, or unsafe weather¶

    Objective: Make and distinguish a direct observation from a guess. Materials: A familiar safe classroom object/view already present; no handling of hazardous objects. Technology: None. Prep: 2 minutes. Vocabulary/background: Observe = notice directly; guess/inference = an idea that needs more evidence. "Looks wooden" does not prove material composition.

    Follow the same native timing columns above: 1. Hook: "What can we actually notice about this desk/door/window view?" 2. Model one observation and one inference; safety: seated, no climbing/touching. 3. Each child notices/points/tells one feature; partners compare. 4. Identify which claim can be checked by looking; refine it. 5. Each child shows one observable feature (older pupils distinguish a guess). 6. Restore room, finish the evidence notes and close.

    Meets: Child points/names an observable feature; for a stated older-grade inference objective also explains why a guess needs evidence. Read aloud, model, allow gesture/gaze/home-language response. Challenge: propose a safe way to check a guess. Record objective change; no claim of engineering/programming mastery. Cleanup: no materials to collect; reset seating and leave evidence/NE. Family: "We practiced observing carefully. Ask: 'What did you notice directly?'" At -10 F remain indoors; if there is no safe view, use an ordinary indoor object.

    Device/supply contingency and return note¶

    Paper algorithms preserve sequence/debugging concepts, not real programming or robot-operation mastery. Defer those objectives if devices fail; do not invent accounts or app permissions. Technology Plan.

    Leave lesson/steps completed, actual individual evidence or NE, objectives changed/deferred, restock counts, broken parts OUT OF SERVICE, safety/source questions and the next check. Named evidence stays under school privacy practice. See handoff template and Local Standards; official alignment and unverified Church/supplier claims are VERIFICATION REQUIRED.

    Kindergarten reference routines¶

    Read this page with the selected lesson. It supplies reusable routines, not permission to omit that lesson's exact materials, test or safety instructions. Every minimum pathway works indoors, without independent reading or a device.

    Twenty-minute substitute gate¶

    1. 0-4 minutes: read the objective, background, test and individual check.
    2. 4-8: locate actual supplies; count the selected enrollment column.
    3. 8-12: inspect materials and confirm accommodations, school contact and any adult-only preparation. A supply estimate is not an owned kit.
    4. 12-16: perform the lesson's demonstration/pretest and distribute kits.
    5. 16-20: draw directions and rehearse the check and cleanup.

    If a safety condition or exact material is missing, use only the lesson's named alternative. Record the different/deferred objective; do not improvise unknown substances, electrical connections, outdoor exposure or a human trial.

    Common teacher kit: one classroom timer/clock, paper roster and school pencil or school-approved equivalent writing tool, for any enrollment. No pupil device is implied. The audit indexes this common kit separately from student supplies. Adult cutting, secured AA cells and Winter Science tongs are indexed where the selected lesson needs them. Prepared-resource prices do not include these tools or imply verified school stock.

    Teams and quantities¶

    Pupils Active pair/trio teams Kit budget Additional reserve
    10 5 pairs 5 0
    15 6 pairs + 1 trio 8 1
    20 10 pairs 10 0
    25 11 pairs + 1 trio 13 1

    Lesson tables use the kit budget, not a lone child working in a "pair." Unless a lesson explicitly adds teacher supplies, demonstrate with one budgeted kit and return it before practice. Never count a reserve twice.

    With fewer kits, use groups no larger than three: ⅘/7/9 groups respectively (2 trios + 2 pairs; 5 trios; 6 trios + 1 pair; 7 trios + 2 pairs). Recalculate the per-kit issue quantities. Preserve the test and every child's turn; do not change a learning target merely to fit a materials shortage. If individual turns cannot fit, record missing evidence and schedule follow-up.

    Nonreader directions and access¶

    Demonstrate one action, say it, let children show it, then add the next action. Use large drawings of an eye, hands, two arrows and a return box. No printout or icon-reading skill is assumed. A child can point, describe, dictate, build or direct an adult to act. Ask permission before physical assistance.

    Swap chooser/builder, tester and reporter roles during work. A third child gets a full choice and test turn, not permanent observation duty. Provide a seated route, large parts and a quieter/visual alternative as needed.

    Individual evidence without a serial exit line¶

    Prepare a roster with the lesson's two or three observable checks. Begin checking during 8-17 minutes, then finish during 17-21 while partners work. Thirteen combined minutes provide an average of about 31 seconds per child at 25 enrollment; actual processing needs may require later follow-up. Record not yet / prompted / independent separately for each check. Do not convert an unobserved response into a pass.

    Show what was tested, distinguish prediction from result, and ask one real question. Group products, compliance, handwriting and artistic polish are not mastery. A failed prototype can still produce excellent evidence. The local progression's mastery checkpoints need two dated individual observations; one lesson or a certificate cannot establish grade readiness.

    Common safety and cleanup¶

    Use teacher-inspected large paper pieces and sound blocks, seated desk tests, no student weight on models and no food/unknown nature materials. Do not taste, sniff closely, collect nests or view the Sun. No small magnets, button cells, lasers, flames, latex balloons, projectiles or mouth-contact instruments. Adults control scissors, batteries and wet setup. Keep paths/exits clear. Follow actual school allergy, hygiene, emergency and accommodation procedures.

    At 21-25 minutes, stop the test; count reusable pieces into their labeled kit; cap school-approved glue; retain dated evidence; flatten dry scrap for reuse/recycling; clear tables. Store models by kit number rather than publishing student names. Wet lessons use their own hygiene/cleanup plan.

    Catholic connection and source use¶

    Teach honest evidence, care of creation, dignity, inclusion and service. Prayer is optional according to the school's practice and is not a mastery check. Classroom applications are local, not official religious standards. Use the verified Church teaching register: CCC 159 (faith/reason), 1702/1704 (dignity/reason), 2415-2418 (creation care), 2427-2428 (work), 2468-2469 (truth). Do not attribute original classroom language to a saint or Scripture. An approved religion reading is an optional addition, not a scientific explanation.

    Continuity and family communication¶

    Keep one dated sheet per child when a lesson specifies it. Use an envelope by class/meeting; no expensive journal is required. Multi-meeting models stay at school. If prior work is unavailable, use the lesson's fresh-evidence route, never invent a past result.

    Newsletter statements describe what was actually taught and observed. Family questions are optional and ungraded. No home device, purchase, donation, collection, adult teaching or homework supplies an essential assessment.

    Grades 1-6 reference routines¶

    Use this guide with the actual lesson. It does not replace that lesson's supplies, timed sequence, safety rules, objective or individual check.

    Native periods and release gate¶

    Grades 1-2 use 30 minutes, Grades 3-4 40, Grades 5-6 45. Distribution, testing, individual evidence and cleanup fit inside the chosen period. First-time kits, cards, account approval, charging/freezing and longitudinal care are advance work, not hidden substitute tasks.

    Before handoff, read the lesson, locate/count the kit, check safety/access, pretest the actual pathway and rehearse the evidence/cleanup prompts. Record the real school contact and storage location. A complete document does not approve unfamiliar equipment or supply missing materials.

    Balanced groups and meaningful turns¶

    Pupils Groups <=3 Size distribution
    10 4 Two trios and two pairs
    15 5 Five trios
    20 7 Six trios and one pair
    25 9 Seven trios and two pairs

    Pair-based lessons use their own allocation, often 5/7/10/12 active teams and ⅝/10/13 budgeted kits including odd-enrollment reserve. Do not issue a generic nine-kit set to every pair lesson or leave a lone child as a "pair."

    Rotate planner/builder/tester/reporter so each pupil makes a decision, contributes and explains evidence. Observing another child execute software or operate hardware does not establish the observer's operation mastery. Waiting work is meaningful prediction/recording/design, not passive watching.

    Individual assessment¶

    Begin roster checks while pupils investigate/build, then finish within the lesson's evidence block. Record not yet / prompted / independent for each objective separately, with the actual response/result. Unobserved is not a pass. At 25 enrollment, avoid serial class presentations or a single exit queue; use paired exchanges and a teacher sweep.

    An oral, drawn, pointed, dictated or assistive response can preserve a target. Grade 1 directions are modeled/read aloud; handwriting and artistic polish are not graded unless explicitly the objective. Older-grade challenge adds evidence, precision, variables, limitations or tradeoffs, not simply more work. The local progression's mastery checkpoints need two dated individual observations.

    Truthful pathways¶

    • Actual tests compare the stated same conditions and keep failed results.
    • Prepared numerical examples and fictional scenarios are labeled model/ supplied data, not pupil-collected observations.
    • A model has limits; tabletop structures, assistive-device models and water demonstrations are not safe real-person devices or potable-water tests.
    • Paper algorithms can support computational reasoning. Actual software execution, robot/sensor operation and electrical assembly require actual approved equipment and individual turns.
    • Preserve relevant source facts without inventing a biography, quotation, scientific priority or official benchmark.

    Common teacher kit and cleanup¶

    Teacher timer/clock, paper roster and pencil/approved marker are common tools. Check the actual selected lesson's measuring, cutting, electrical or wet-work tools; they are not implied by a generic pupil kit. Stop and isolate unsafe equipment, apply the school's emergency/hygiene plan, count issue/return quantities, save dated evidence and clear exits/surfaces. Do not use surface-cleanup cloths as shared hand towels.

    Family and school follow-up¶

    Copy the lesson's actual concept/action/evidence/Catholic connection and a child-answerable question. Home activities are optional; devices, transport, donations, purchases or parent teaching never supply essential assessed evidence. The school release checklist records the remaining physical/policy/pilot checks without inventing approval.

    C-STREAM FAQ and troubleshooting¶

    October 2026. Start with Quick Start and a completed lesson template. Generalist teachers can teach a clear lesson; not every legacy file is ready. Confirm rotation/calendar and the actual lesson rather than promising no repetition or universal substitute-readiness.

    Time and classroom management¶

    Running long? Stop new construction, retain the individual check and cleanup, store dry labeled work and continue next meeting. Do not delete evidence collection to add an extra activity or prayer.

    Finished early? Ask for a repeated fair test, alternative constraint or explanation of evidence. Faster pupils are not automatically unpaid helpers.

    Students excited/arguing? Give instructions before materials, use a stop signal, assign builder/tester/reporter and rotate actual turns. Ask each to show an idea and test alternatives under the same conditions. Refer persistent behavior/safety concerns through actual school procedures.

    A child needs more time? Model one step, reduce choices, pre-cut/larger materials, allow gesture/voice/scribe/quiet or seated response. Keep the concept criterion unless documenting an explicit objective change.

    Missing supplies or technology¶

    Problem Safe response Learning limit
    Building blocks absent Paper/cardstock/sticks with a stated new constraint Compare evidence; do not silently claim identical load capacity
    Robot/app/host unavailable Desk-grid arrow cards and pointer Sequence/debugging concepts only; execution/robot mastery deferred
    Internet absent Teacher-vetted read-aloud source or confirmed offline tool Actual online/source-navigation objective may change
    Some devices work Document turn/reset time, smaller test rotations or more meetings Each child needs individual real-device evidence if that is O1
    Electrical gear damaged Switch off/disconnect; OUT OF SERVICE; safe paper-path model Paper path is not practical circuit-building mastery
    No safe materials or weather Seated observation fallback Record actual observation objective, not unperformed investigation

    Do not open personal accounts, install unapproved apps, bypass safeguards or improvise power supplies. Technology Plan. Borrowing lead times/fees/stock are VERIFICATION REQUIRED, not guaranteed two-week free access. Library planning.

    Assessment¶

    How do I grade? Use the objective -> prompt -> success condition -> individual evidence chain. Project rubric. Participation, effort, handwriting, neatness and confidence are not mastery. An artistic criterion is used only for an explicit arts objective.

    What if the model fails? A child can still explain valid evidence and redesign. A successful team model does not prove each member understands. NE means not yet evidenced; unobserved/absent/device-blocked is not a zero.

    How much paperwork? Short roster evidence during work plus one exit check; review termly with Progress Tracker. Named records/photos follow verified school privacy/consent practice; do not assume a digital account or public portfolio.

    Faith, arts and grade differences¶

    Faith connection feels forced? Use a concrete Catholic decision about dignity, truth, stewardship or service. R identifies the explicit reflection. Prayer supports but does not substitute for this purpose. Verify Church quotations, biographies and standards; never make an experiment theological proof.

    Hard science/faith question? Acknowledge uncertainty, distinguish observation from belief/interpretation and consult the verified source record or appropriate school faith educator. Avoid a simplistic "science only how, faith only why" rule or "God is an engineer" analogy.

    What does A mean? Arts including music: observational drawing, composition, visual communication, form, rhythmic phrases and performance, not just digital art/decoration. M means mathematics.

    K cannot read? Use Show, Try, Tell. An attempt is welcome but does not automatically demonstrate the concept. Assess pointing/sorting/building/telling with the same explicit success condition.

    Mixed grades / older students need challenge? Same materials can support different evidence expectations; use the shared progression and actual prerequisites. Add repeat trials, constraints, measurement or tradeoffs, not untaught ratio work or leadership as a substitute for subject learning.

    Safety and families¶

    No button cells, latex balloons or projectiles in the core; no neodymium magnets in K. Stop unsafe activities, isolate hazards and contact the school's responsible adult. Possible battery/magnet ingestion needs urgent emergency escalation. Use indoor alternatives in unsafe Minnesota conditions.

    No routine homework, required donations or home purchase/device. Explain concept + action + evidence + Catholic choice using family communication.

    Parent Resources

    Parent communication guide¶

    Use one family communication system and newsletter template; K-6 unit examples and specific oral questions are supplied there. Retain plain language, welcoming invitations, positive evidence notes and family feedback. No routine homework or donation prerequisite. October 2026.

    Introduction letter (copy and personalize)¶

    Dear Families,

    In C-STREAM, children learn through observing, building, measuring, testing, improving, composing and explaining. C means Catholic identity; R is religion/faith integration; A includes arts and music; M means mathematics. Our Catholic purpose includes dignity, stewardship, truthful reasoning and using gifts to serve others. Faith reflection does not replace scientific evidence. Art includes genuine choices about pattern, form, sound and communication, not just decorating a product.

    We use hands-on materials first and devices when they add meaningful learning. Every child has school-provided supplies and classroom work time. There is no routine C-STREAM homework, purchase, device or donation requirement. Newsletters include a specific question you can ask and an optional no-purchase activity. Your child may show learning by speaking, pointing, drawing, modeling or recording, with needed access support.

"What questions remain?" Event planning: STREAM Night.

    Source questions about Church teaching, scientists, official standards or diocesan policy are VERIFICATION REQUIRED. Local codes link to Local Standards; they are not official accreditation.

    C is Catholic identity; R is religion/faith integration; A is arts including music; M is mathematics. No comparisons that make God an engineer/scientist or turn a physical result into theological proof. No compulsory scientist spotlight. Church quotations/biographies require verification before copying.

    No routine homework. School supplies all required learning materials; donations and optional activities never affect participation or grades. No identifiable student names/images/scores without the verified school consent/privacy process.

    🙋 C-STREAM Volunteer Guide¶

    Location: Our Lady of the Prairie Catholic School · Belle Plaine, MN · Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis

    Thank you for volunteering in our C-STREAM classroom! This guide will help you support hands-on, faith-integrated STEM learning.

    October 2026 safety/access note: The teacher retains responsibility. Confirm school screening, safeguarding, supervision, emergency and privacy requirements before volunteering; any claimed Archdiocesan requirement needs source verification. Share only accommodation information necessary for your assigned role. No button cells, latex balloons or projectile activities; no neodymium magnets in K. Do not repair electrical gear or handle batteries without the teacher's assigned procedure. Stop hazards and notify the teacher; suspected battery/magnet ingestion requires immediate emergency escalation. Use materials kit counts and the substitute safety guide.

    🎯 Your Role as a Volunteer¶

    You ARE here to:¶

    ✅ Support students as they work
    ✅ Encourage when things don't work the first time
    ✅ Ask questions that help students think
    ✅ Assist with materials and supplies
    ✅ Celebrate effort and creativity
    ✅ Model curiosity and wonder

    You are NOT expected to:¶

    ❌ Know all the answers (it's okay to say "Let's find out together!")
    ❌ Do the work for students
    ❌ Teach the lesson (the teacher leads instruction)
    ❌ Grade or evaluate student work
    ❌ Discipline students (refer behavior issues to the teacher)

    📅 Before You Arrive¶

    What to Know¶

    • Arrival time: _____________

    • End time: _____________

    • Where to meet: _____________

    • What to wear: Comfortable clothes that can get messy

    • What to bring: Just yourself! (We provide materials)

    Check with the Teacher¶

    • What is today's activity?

    • What grade level?

    • Which access/safety instructions are necessary for my assigned role?

    • Where should I be stationed?

    School Requirements¶

    • Signed volunteer form on file

    • Required screening/safeguarding confirmed with school (exact Archdiocesan policy: VERIFICATION REQUIRED)

    • Sign in at the office

    ⏱️ Typical C-STREAM Session¶

    Time What's Happening Your Role
    Opening (2-3 min) Prayer, wonder question Participate, model reverence
    Introduction (5-10 min) Teacher explains activity Listen, prepare materials
    Hands-On Time (15-25 min) Students build/create/explore Circulate, assist, encourage
    Sharing (3-5 min) Students share work Listen, celebrate
    Closing (2 min) Cleanup, closing prayer Help with cleanup

    💬 How to Talk to Students¶

    Instead of... Try...¶

    Instead of... Try...
    "That's wrong" "Tell me about your design"
    "Do it this way" "What happens if you try...?"
    "That won't work" "Interesting! What do you think will happen?"
    "Let me fix it" "What could you change?"
    "Good job!" "I noticed you tried 3 different ways—that's perseverance!"

    Great Questions to Ask¶

    To spark thinking:

    • "What are you trying to make?"

    • "What's your plan?"

    • "What do you think will happen?"

    When they're stuck:

    • "What have you tried so far?"

    • "What could you try next?"

    • "Who could you ask for ideas?"

    After testing:

    • "What happened?"

    • "What worked well?"

    • "What would you change?"

    Faith connections:

    • "What does this teach you about God's creation?"

    • "How could this help someone?"

    • "What are you grateful for in this project?"

    🔧 Common Volunteer Tasks¶

    Before Class¶

    • Set out materials at stations

    • Count supplies (enough for each group)

    • Test technology if applicable (iPads charged, apps open)

    • Prepare any teacher-requested materials

    During Class¶

    • Circulate among groups

    • Distribute additional supplies as needed

    • Help with technology issues (basic troubleshooting)

    • Encourage struggling students

    • Redirect off-task behavior gently ("What's your next step?")

    • Take photos if requested (check photo policy first!)

    After Class¶

    • Help students clean up their areas

    • Sort and organize materials

    • Count/inventory supplies

    • Wipe down tables if needed

    • Debrief with teacher (What went well? Any concerns?)

    🛠️ Working with Different Ages¶

    Kindergarten (25-minute sessions)¶

    • Need lots of support — Stay close, help with fine motor tasks

    • Short attention spans — Keep them focused on one step at a time

    • Encourage exploration — Mistakes inform learning; observe the specific concept and safety rules

    • Celebrate everything — "Look what you made!"

    Grades 1-2 (30-minute sessions)¶

    • Building independence — Let them try before helping

    • Reading support — They may need instructions read aloud

    • Partner work — Help them collaborate nicely

    • Encourage iteration — "What if you tried it again?"

    Grades 3-4 (40-minute sessions)¶

    • More independent — Step back, observe, intervene less

    • Group dynamics — Help ensure everyone participates

    • Deeper questions — Push their thinking with "why" and "how"

    • Documentation — May need help recording their process

    Grades 5-6 (45-minute sessions)¶

    • Very independent — Your role is mostly material support

    • Complex projects — Ask about their design thinking

    • Leadership opportunities — Can they help others?

    • Critical thinking — Challenge them to go deeper

    🚨 What to Do When...¶

    A student is frustrated¶

    1. Acknowledge feelings: "This is tricky, isn't it?"
    2. Normalize struggle: "Real engineers face problems too!"
    3. Focus on process: "What have you tried?"
    4. Suggest a break: "Take a breath, then look again"
    5. Celebrate effort: "I see you're not giving up!"

    A project "fails"¶

    1. Reframe it: "That's data! Now you know what doesn't work."
    2. Connect to learning: "What did you learn from this?"
    3. Encourage iteration: "How could you change it?"
    4. Share stories: "Even famous inventors failed many times!"

    Students are arguing¶

    1. Stay neutral: "What's the disagreement about?"
    2. Facilitate: "Can you each share your idea?"
    3. Problem-solve: "Is there a way to try both?"
    4. Involve teacher if needed

    You don't know the answer¶

    1. Be honest: "Great question! I'm not sure."
    2. Model learning: "Let's think about this together."
    3. Ask the student: "What do YOU think?"
    4. Check with teacher if needed

    A student is off-task¶

    1. Redirect gently: "What step are you on?"
    2. Give a job: "Can you be the materials manager?"
    3. Move closer: Sometimes proximity is enough
    4. Involve teacher for persistent issues

    Technology doesn't work¶

    1. Basic troubleshooting: Restart app, check connections
    2. Use the teacher's named backup; paper algorithms do not demonstrate real programming/robot execution
    3. Pair students: Share working devices
    4. Stay calm: Tech problems happen to everyone

    ✝️ Faith Integration Tips¶

    C-STREAM isn't just STEM—it's Catholic STEM! Help students make faith connections:

    Simple Connections¶

    • "Isn't it amazing that God created all of this?"

    • "How does this show God's love for us?"

    • "Engineers help people—just like we're called to do!"

    • "What can this teach us about being patient like God is with us?"

    When Students Struggle¶

    • "God doesn't give up on us, and we don't give up on our projects!"

    • "Making mistakes is part of how God helps us learn."

    • "Let's ask God to help us figure this out."

    During Teamwork¶

    • "How are we showing kindness to our teammates?"

    • "Jesus worked with a team too—his disciples!"

    • "Using our talents together is how we serve God."

    Print and keep with you! ✂️¶

    C-STREAM VOLUNTEER QUICK GUIDE

    DO:

    • Ask questions, don't give answers

    • Encourage every attempt

    • Let them struggle a little (productive struggle!)

    • Celebrate effort, not just success

    • Connect to faith when natural

    SAY:

    • "Tell me about your design"

    • "What could you try next?"

    • "That's great problem-solving!"

    • "How does this help us appreciate God's creation?"

    WHEN STUCK:

    • "What have you tried?"

    • "What's one thing you could change?"

    • "Can you ask a classmate?"

    REMEMBER:

    • It's okay not to know the answer

    • "Failure" is learning

    • Process matters more than product

    • You're modeling curiosity!

    ❓ Frequently Asked Questions¶

    Q: What if I'm not good at science/technology?
    A: That's okay! You're here to support and encourage, not teach. Your enthusiasm matters more than expertise.

    Q: Can I help my own child's class?
    A: Usually yes! Check with the teacher about classroom policies.

    Q: What if a student says something about faith I don't know how to answer?
    A: It's fine to say, "That's a great question! Let's ask [teacher] or you could ask your parents."

    Q: Should I post photos on social media?
    A: Please don't post photos of students without explicit school permission. Many families have privacy concerns.

    Q: How often should I volunteer?
    A: Whatever works for you! Weekly, monthly, or special events—all help is appreciated.

    Q: What if I can't make my scheduled time?
    A: Let the teacher know as soon as possible so they can adjust plans.
